\n \n

\n\n`--cmd 'render {\"view\": \"{3D}\", \"path\": \"house-3d.png\"}'` adds the 3D view (`azimuth` and `elevation` turn it);\n`render {\"view\": \"Section 1\"}` draws the sample's section, `South` (or `North`, `East`, `West`) one of its elevations, and\n`render {\"view\": \"A102\"}` one of its sheets. `--save sheets.pdf` prints every sheet, a page each.\n\nA script is one command per line, `id {json params}`, with lengths in millimetres:\n\n```text\nwall {\"points\": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000],[0,6000]], \"closed\": true, \"type\": \"Exterior - 300mm\"}\ndoor {\"at\": [2000, 0]}\nwindow {\"at\": [8000, 3000]}\nroom {\"point\": [4000, 3000], \"name\": \"Living\"}\nfloor {}\nroof {}\n```\n\nA script stops at its first failing line and names it. Through MCP, `script {\"text\": …, \"atomic\": true}` runs it all or nothing:\na line that fails takes back the lines before it, and one that goes through is a single undo step.\n\n```sh\nbimcraft-cli run --script house.txt --save house.ifc\nbimcraft-cli convert building.ifc building.bimcraft # an IFC file from Revit or any BIM tool, as a project\nbimcraft-cli info house.bimcraft # levels, counts, types and warnings\nbimcraft-cli info building.rvt # a Revit file: release, last save, levels, elements by category\nbimcraft-cli convert building.rvt building.ifc # a Revit project, imported, then written as IFC4\nbimcraft-cli convert house.bimcraft plan.svg\nbimcraft-cli commands # every command and its parameters\n```\n\n## The desktop app\n\n`bimcraft [FILE] [--sample]` opens a `.bimcraft` project, imports an `.ifc` file, or starts on the sample house. The layout\nis Revit's, so it should feel familiar: the Quick Access Toolbar; the ribbon's File, Architecture, Annotate, View and Modify\ntabs, with a green contextual tab (Modify | Place Wall, Modify | Walls) for the tool or the selection; the Options Bar;\nProperties over the Project Browser; views in tabs with a navigation bar; and the tool's prompt in the status bar. The\nicons and colours are BIMCraft's own: BIMCraft starts in your system's theme. View > Dark Mode opens a menu for Light, Dark,\nDark UI, Light Canvas, or As the System; File > Settings offers the same choices. The choice is saved between sessions.\n\nAutosave runs in the background every two minutes while the model has unsaved changes (File > Settings > Files changes\nthe interval or disables it). A saved project's recovery copy is `.autosave.bimcraft` beside the project;\nan untitled project's copy is under the system temporary folder's `bimcraft-autosave` directory. Opening a project with a\ncopy offers **Recover**, **Discard**, or **Postpone**. Recover opens unsaved work, Discard removes the copy, and Postpone\nprotects it for later through File > Recover Autosave. Orphaned untitled copies are offered at startup. Successful Save\nor an explicit Don't Save removes the current recovery copy, except a postponed copy. See [autosave design](docs/autosave.md).\n\n| To | Do |\n|---|---|\n| Draw walls | Wall (WA), click points: each click builds a wall from the point before, one undo step each; Enter or Esc ends the chain, and a click back on its start closes it. Ends snap to wall ends and location lines; Shift keeps a segment square. The Draw panel draws a Line, or a Start-End-Radius Arc: its start, its end, then a point it passes through. The Options Bar sets the height (up to a level, or unconnected), the Location Line (the line of the wall you click along) and Chain. A wall's exterior is to your left as you go, so draw clockwise for walls that face out |\n| Flip, attach walls | Select walls, and Modify \\| Walls has Flip (or Space) to turn their exterior side round about their location line, Attach Top/Base to pick a roof or a floor for their tops (or, as the Options Bar says, their bases) to follow, and Detach Top/Base. Properties shows their Location Line (pick another and the wall stays where it is) and whether they're attached |\n| Place doors, windows | Door (DR) or Window (WN), click a wall; the Type Selector at the top of Properties picks the type. Before the click the door or window is sketched in the wall under the cursor, with how far it stands from each end of the wall |\n| Place rooms | Room (RM), click inside walls; the outline and area show before you click, and the tag's area follows the walls |\n| Place columns | Column (CL), click where it stands; it snaps to wall ends and centre lines. The Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected), the Type Selector rectangular or round |\n| Plumbing tab | Plumbing > Pipe (PI), Plumbing Fixture (PX), Pipe Fitting (PF), Pipe Accessory (PA). A pipe takes two clicks or a chain of them, as a beam does; the Options Bar sets its justification (the middle by default) and its height over the level, and Properties its two heights, so a drain falls and a riser rises. A fixture, a fitting or a valve is a family's type where you click, the Type Selector listing only the families of its kind, Space turning it. Edit Type of a pipe sets its diameter, whether it is round and its material |\n| Electrical tab | Electrical > Electrical Equipment (EE), Device (DV), Lighting Fixture (LF), and Conduit & Wire > Conduit (CN), Cable Tray (CT), Wire (EW). A run takes two clicks or a chain, as a pipe does, its Options Bar the justification (the middle) and the height; a board, a device or a luminaire is a family's type where you click, the Type Selector listing only the families of its kind (an outlet and a switch under Device), Space turning it. Edit Type of a tray sets its width and depth, of a conduit or a wire its diameter |\n| Lightning Protection tab | Lightning Protection > Air Terminal (AT), Down Conductor (DC), Earthing Electrode (EG), Inspection Box (IB), Earthing Conductor (GC): free letters, since Revit has none. Runs and fixtures as the other tabs'; the vocabulary is the standard's (captor, condutor de descida, haste de aterramento, caixa de inspeção, condutor de aterramento) |\n| Data tab | Data > Data Outlet (DT), Voice Outlet (VO), Rack (RK), Patch Panel (PN), and Cabling > Cable Tray (CT, the Electrical tab's), Cabling (CB). Free letters where Revit has none; the Type Selector lists only the families of the tool's kind |\n| Structure tab | Structure > Column (CL on this tab; Revit's own), Beam (BM), Floor: Structural (SB), and Foundation > Isolated Footing (FI), Wall Footing (FW; Revit's FT is Filters here), and Reinforcement > Reinforce (RF, ours: it arms the element selected; RB is the Massing tab's Roof by Face). A beam or a wall footing takes two clicks, or a chain of them (Options Bar > Chain), each step a beam; the Options Bar sets a beam's justification (top, centre or bottom) and its height over the level, a footing's thickness and where its top is, a structural column's height. The tool sketches what the click would make and the beam's length; a beam seen under, over or through the plan is picked by its centre line; Properties shows its Start and End Level Offset, Z Justification and System, and Edit Type its section. A structural floor is the Floor tool with its `structural` flag |\n| Add stairs, ramps | Stair: click where it starts (the middle of its first riser), then where its run ends. Past the end of a run of all its risers, it climbs to the level above in one run; short of it, a landing follows, and the next click says which way the next run goes from it: on, left, right, or back beside the last. Risers are at most 180 mm; the Options Bar sets its width and Railings, Properties its riser, tread and top. Ramp: the same clicks, its runs as long as the Options Bar's slope makes them, as high as its Height says |\n| Add railings | Railing: click a stair or a ramp for a railing down each side, or click a path's points and press Enter for one along it on the plan's level; the Type Selector picks its type, Type Properties its height and baluster spacing |\n| Roof the building | Roof, in a plan: click inside the walls, and a roof goes on the level above, over their outline and past their faces, whatever its shape, and open over a courtyard: a loop of walls standing free inside the others, with no room in it; its hips and valleys show before you click. The Options Bar sets the slope (0° for a flat roof), the overhang, and gable ends for a rectangle. Select a roof, and Modify \\| Roofs has Gable Edge: click an edge of its footprint (a courtyard's too) to stand it upright, a gable end, and again to slope it. Roof by Extrusion: click a line's start and end, then how far across the roof is swept; its profile rises from the line at the Options Bar's slope to a ridge over its middle, or with Shed along its whole length |\n| Dormers | Architecture > Opening > Dormer: click a roof's slope where the dormer's front wall goes; the Options Bar sets its width, its height over the roof at the front, its roof's slope and whether its front has a window. Its walls stand on the roof, its own gable roof runs back into the host, and the host opens under it |\n| Floors, slopes | Floor: click inside the walls, and a slab goes under their outline, open over a courtyard (a loop of walls standing free inside the others, with no room in it), its top at the level; Properties sets its Height Offset From Level. Selected, Shape Editing > Slope Arrow: click its tail, then its head, and the floor rises toward the head at the Options Bar's slope; Properties changes the slope |\n| Ceilings | Ceiling: click inside a room, and a ceiling fills it out to its walls' faces, open round any walls standing free inside it, at the Options Bar's height (2600 mm); the outline shows before you click, and the Type Selector picks a plain one or tiles. The Project Browser's Ceiling Plans open each level's reflected ceiling plan |\n| Shafts | Architecture > Opening > Shaft: click two opposite corners; the Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected). It cuts the floors, ceilings and roofs on its way |\n| Masses | Massing > Conceptual Mass > Mass (MS): click the footprint's corners; the Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected); Enter, or the first corner again, finishes. Before you do, the outline it would make shows, with its area. With a mass selected, Model by Face makes Mass Floors (MF: a floor at each level it crosses), Wall by Face (WB: a wall on each edge), Floor by Face (FB) and Roof by Face (RB) on its top face, and Update to Face (UF) makes what they made follow the mass again; Show Mass (MH) hides and shows masses in the view on screen. Properties shows its constraints, its Top Outline (corners as `x, y; x, y`, blank for none: typed, the mass is lofted), area, volume and gross floor area. View > Schedules lists Mass and Mass Floor schedules |\n| Add levels, grids | Level (LL) takes an elevation in the Options Bar; Grid (GR) takes two clicks |\n| Select | Click; Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's underneath (the wall under a door). Drag across empty floor for a box: left to right takes what's wholly inside, right to left what it crosses too; in a section or an elevation, any drag draws one. The selection stays as you open other views, the 3D view and schedules among them |\n| Edit, delete | Properties edits the parameters of everything selected, in one step, grouped as Revit groups them; the Type Selector changes the type; Delete removes the selection |\n| Move, copy | Drag a selected element, or Move (MV) and Copy (CO): click a base point, then where it goes. Walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, so room areas follow; doors and windows slide along their walls. Constrain keeps the move square; Multiple goes on copying |\n| Rotate, mirror | Rotate (RO) turns the selection about its middle: click the angle's start, then its end, or type an angle in the Options Bar; Place Centre moves the centre. Mirror Pick Axis (MM) mirrors across a wall or grid you pick, Mirror Draw Axis (DM) across a line you click; Copy is on, as in Revit |\n| Align, trim, split, offset | Align (AL): hover to highlight an edge or centre line, pick the reference, then the target edge. The tool stays on until Esc |\n| Design options | Manage > Design Options (DO): New Set (with a name typed) makes a set with one option; pick an option and Add Option, Rename Option, Make Primary or Delete Option, or Edit Option, which makes it the active one. The status bar's Active design option (once there are sets) is what new elements are made in, Main Model for none, and the view on screen shows it too; it turns red in a view that shows another option of its set, and picking it again shows it there |\n| Lengths | While a tool waits for its next point, type a length and press Enter: it goes that far toward the cursor. A selected wall shows its length as a temporary dimension, and a selected door or window two, to its middle from the faces of the walls meeting its wall either side of it (or its wall's ends); a selected column, structural column, footing or component shows how far it stands from the nearest wall centre line or grid east, north, west and south, and the Column and Component tools sketch the same before the click; click a number to type a new one (the wall's end moves, the opening slides along its wall, the column or component moves) |\n| Snaps and the ruler | While a tool picks points, what a click would land on is marked: a square for an end, a triangle for a middle, a cross for a crossing, a circle for a centre, a right angle for a perpendicular, a diamond for the nearest point of a wall, a dot on an angle guide, each named beside it. Past the last point a dashed guide runs at the angle the direction sticks to (from east, and from the line before), and the new line wears a ruler: its length and angle read beside it, and at a corner the angle between the two walls, shown as an arc, so a 60° corner is easy to hit. Shift keeps a step square. Manage > Snaps turns each snap off, and sets the angle steps or turns them off; typed over the plan, SE, SM, SI, SC, SP or SN snap to endpoints, midpoints, intersections, centres, perpendiculars or the nearest point alone for the next point, SO to nothing, and SS puts the snaps back (the status bar says which is waiting; a click, Esc, another tool or another view ends it) |\n| Measure | Annotate > Measure (ME): click two points; a ruler with its graduations lies between them, reading its length, its angle and its parts along x and y. Esc takes the ruler away, then the tool |\n| Turn a wall's points | Select one wall: a grip stands at each end. Drag one to move that end: its angle and length follow the cursor, with the snaps and angle guides from the other end, and the walls joined there follow; Ctrl keeps the wall's length, so it turns about its other end. Beside each end is the wall's angle: click it and type a new one, and the wall turns about that end (a wall joined at its other end stays joined, the corner sliding along the wall it meets) |\n| Edit types | Edit Type opens Type Properties, one dialog for every kind of type, as Revit's: the family and the type at the top with Duplicate and Rename, the type's parameters in a table under group bars that fold (Construction, Dimensions, Materials and Finishes, Graphics, Text…), and OK, Cancel and Apply. Change the type everywhere it's used, Duplicate it into a new one, or Rename it (what's of it follows). A wall type's layers, from the exterior in, or a floor's, roof's or ceiling's, from the top down: each one's function, material and thickness; Insert Layer, and Out and In (Up and Down) and Delete on each |\n| Place components | Component (CM): pick a family's type in the Type Selector, or in the Project Browser's Families, then click where it goes; Space turns it a quarter turn first. Selected, its own parameters are in Properties, its type's in Type Properties (Edit Type), with Duplicate. Load Family, on Modify \\| Place Component, loads a family saved as .json. A door's or a window's family is picked in the Type Selector of the Door or Window tool, or of a selected door or window, as `Family: Type` beside the project's own types, which a new door takes from the project's single door or fixed window; its Edit Type is the family type's |\n| Family Editor | Manage > New Family (a category's template) and Edit Family (the family of what's selected, or of the component being placed): the family's name and category; Parameters (name, kind, instance, value, formula); Types (a name and the type parameters' values, a blank one the family's own; add, duplicate, delete); Forms (a profile's corners, a circle, a revolve's axis and degrees, a void, its plane, from and to, material and the parameter or formula it's visible by; moved up and down, deleted; Add Box, Cylinder, Revolve, Void); Symbols for a door or window. A preview of the type picked, turned by dragging. Apply makes the project's family what's typed, one undo step; OK also closes; Save Family writes a `.json` file; Load Family reads one; Add to Favorites keeps it in your Favorites |\n| Favorites | Manage > Favorites: the materials and families you keep for every project, listed with a swatch; Add to Project (under another name when the project has that one) and Remove. A material comes in with the picture its texture is made of, a family with the materials it's made of |\n| Paint | Modify > Paint (PT), in the 3D view: pick the material in the Options Bar, then click a face; Remove Paint takes it off the face clicked |\n| Materials | Manage > Materials: the project's library. Pick a material, or New for another, and set its name, colour, cut pattern and surface pattern; Delete takes one out that no layer uses. A layer picks its material from the library. Texture picks a pattern drawn in code, or Picture… a PNG or JPEG file from your disk, for the 3D view; its tile's width and height, angle and offset follow; Save to Favorites keeps the material, and Favorites… opens them |\n| Project parameters | Manage > Project Parameters: New makes one; name it, choose its type of parameter (text, number, length or yes/no) and the categories it's for. Select an element and its values are under Project Parameters in Properties; empty a field to take a value away |\n| Schedules | View > Schedules > Schedule/Quantities: pick a category and name it. In Properties, a schedule's Fields, Filter and Sorting/Grouping each open Schedule Properties: add its category's fields, take them away and order them, give one a heading or Calculate totals, add a Calculated Value (`Area * 120`); filter its rows; sort them, and untick Itemize every instance for a row per group. The Room, Door, Window, Wall, Floor and Level Schedules open from the browser, and become the project's once changed. A schedule highlights the rows of what's selected; click a row to select what it lists (Ctrl adds, Shift takes away) |\n| Views | The Project Browser opens floor plans, ceiling plans, elevations, sections, the 3D view and schedules in tabs; View > Close Inactive closes the others. Its tabs keep it to Views, Schedules, Sheets or Families (Legends are still to come), and its search narrows it as you type, marking what matched: each word must match an entry or a group it's in (`ceiling 2`), `*` stands for any run of characters and `?` for any one. View > Duplicate View (DP) makes a plan view of the plan on screen, plain, with detailing or as a dependent; so does a right click on a plan in the Project Browser, where a plan view also has Delete, and a plan view's name, view range and crop are in Properties as a level's are. The Project Browser's Families lists each system category's types (walls, floors, doors…) and the project's component families; a right click on a type or a family has Delete, which the project refuses while something uses it. Manage > Link Model (LK) links another project, and the Project Browser lists the linked models. Manage > Purge Unused (PU) lists what nothing uses, by kind (types and families checked, as Revit's), and takes it out in one undo step. A right click in any view opens a menu of what it and the selection can do: Cancel, Edit Type, Select All Instances, Delete, Hide Element, Hide Category, Override Graphics, Zoom to Fit, Zoom In, Zoom Out, and in 3D Home View |\n| Lay out sheets | View > Sheet makes one (A101, A102…); on it, Place View puts a view that's on no sheet yet: a plan, a section or an elevation at its own scale (1 : 100 with none), the 3D view as it's turned on screen, or a schedule. Drag a view or a note to move it, set its scale in Properties, double-click it to open it. File > Export > Sheets as PDF prints them all |\n| Cut a section, add an elevation | View > Section (CR): click its start and end; it looks to the left of the line, so drawn west to east it looks north. View > Elevation: click beside the building, and it looks at that side. Open them from the browser, or double-click their marks in a plan; in them, click to select what they cut or see |\n| Look in 3D | The cube on the Quick Access Toolbar (or View > 3D View, or {3D} in the browser) opens the 3D view. Shift and the middle button orbit, as in Revit; the middle button pans, the wheel zooms; Home in the navigation bar goes back to the south-east view. Click to select, or drag a box, as in plan |\n| Move around | The wheel zooms at the cursor, the middle button pans, the navigation bar or ZF (ZE, ZA) zooms to fit; TL toggles Thin Lines |\n| Shortcuts | Type a tool's two letters over a view, as in Revit (WA, DR, CR…). CS (Create Similar) starts the tool of the one element selected, with its type picked; SA selects every element of the selected ones' types that the view shows; PP shows or hides Properties; UN opens Project Units; VV (VG) opens Visibility/Graphics, FT Filters and VT View Templates; EH, VH and EU hide an element, a category, or list what's hidden (with Reveal Hidden Elements on, picking a hidden element brings an Unhide Element button, EU too, and VU or Unhide Category its category back); HH, HC, HI, IC, HR and RH hide, isolate, reset and reveal for now; WF, HL and SD set the 3D view's visual style, and GD opens its Graphic Display Options; PH opens Phasing, DO Design Options and DW picks the Demolish tool. KS lists them all, adds your own, changes one, loads a file of them (JSON, Revit's `` lines or `KEY - Name` lines) and restores the defaults; yours are kept in `settings.json`, so they are there the next time BIMCraft starts |\n| Change theme | View > Dark Mode: choose light, dark, system, or a dark UI with a light canvas; sheets stay white paper |\n| Arrange the palettes | Drag Properties or the Project Browser by its title: strips along the edges of the view show where it lands, docked down the left or right side or along the bottom (one over another there, or side by side along the bottom), onto another palette's title as a tab of it, or anywhere else to float in a window of its own, which its title moves. Its Dock menu (beside its close button) does the same by name; closed, View > User Interface or PP brings it back where it was |\n| Float a view | Drag a view's tab off the tab bar, or right-click it and Float: it opens in a window of its own, the active view, and the tools work in it. The views behind stay drawn; a click on one makes it the active view. Drag the window's title back onto the tab bar, or press its Dock button, to make it a tab again. The last tab can't float |\n| More room | Double-click a ribbon tab (or press the arrow at the right of the tabs) and the ribbon folds to its tabs; a click on a tab then shows its tools over the view until one is picked. Double-click again to open it |\n| Settings | File > Settings (Ctrl+, or the cog on the Quick Access Toolbar): the theme, language, ribbon and palettes under User Interface, with Plans' two working aids, the origin marker (a small mark at the project's 0, 0 with the directions of x and y) and the view's name in a plan's bottom left corner, both on at first and drawn on the screen only, never in a PNG, a sheet or a printout; background autosave and its interval under Files; whether to look for updates. Performance holds Draw the 3D view on the graphics card (off until you turn it on); the rest of Performance, and Graphics, show settings still to come, greyed out. They're kept in `settings.json` beside the favorites, with where the palettes are |\n| Units | Manage > Project Units (UN): millimetres, centimetres, metres, inches, feet, or feet and inches. Dimensions, spot elevations, room areas, schedules, Properties and the Options Bar follow; fields read what's typed in those units, or in the unit typed with it, and so do lengths typed while drawing |\n| Language | View > User Interface > Language: English, Português (Brasil), Español, Čeština, Français, Deutsch, Nederlands or Italiano (and Tiếng Việt, 简体中文 or 繁體中文); the window starts in the system's language (on Windows and macOS, its display language). Manage > Project Language: English, Português (Brasil), Español, Svenska, Čeština, Français, Deutsch, Nederlands or Italiano for what the project's drawings print, and how new levels, views, sheets and rooms are named. A new project takes the window's language when it is also a project language |\n| Select by ID, IDs of Selection | Manage > Inquiry, as Revit's, and more. Select by ID takes as many IDs, GUIDs or IFC GlobalIds as you paste (from a schedule, a clash report, an IFC viewer), says as you type what it finds and what nothing has, adds to the selection or replaces it, and opens the plan they are in, zoomed to them. IDs of Selection lists each selected element's category, name, ID, GUID and IFC GlobalId, each selectable, and copies one row, a column (IDs, GUIDs, GlobalIds) or all of it, tab-separated for a spreadsheet |\n| Undo, redo | Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y, or the Quick Access Toolbar. The arrow beside Undo (and Redo) lists the steps, the latest first, named for what each made or took away (Create Walls, Delete Door) or else its command (Move); hovering one marks it and those above it, and a click undoes (or redoes) them all, up to the last 200 |\n| Start page | Started with no file, the window opens on a start page: New Project and Open, the last ten files as tiles with a picture of each project's 3D view (drawn on a thread of its own; right-click to take one off the list), and along the bottom the source code's page, the version and whether an update is out (with Update now or Download). The quick access bar's Home or Ctrl+D (as in Revit) brings it back over the open project, and Back (top left), Back to the project, Home or Ctrl+D again go back to it as it was |\n| Files | Ctrl+N, Ctrl+O, Ctrl+S; Open takes IFC files too, and a note says what came in and what was left out; the File tab saves, and exports IFC, the sheets as PDF, and the view on screen as PNG (or a plan as SVG) |\n| Updates | File > Check for Updates Now looks by hand, and File > Check for updates at startup (on) says whether BIMCraft looks when it starts. A banner under the Options Bar offers a newer version: Update now (for the Windows installer's copy, an AppImage or the macOS app: it downloads and checks the update, then Restart and install asks to save, closes BIMCraft, replaces it and opens the same project again), or Download (every other copy: it opens the release's page), Later (it asks again next time), and Skip this version (not until a newer one) |\n", "numLines": 120, "startLine": 300, "totalLines": 804}}

That builds the sample house and saves the project, an IFC4 file and the Level 1 plan:

`--cmd 'render {"view": "{3D}", "path": "house-3d.png"}'` adds the 3D view (`azimuth` and `elevation` turn it); `render {"view": "Section 1"}` draws the sample's section, `South` (or `North`, `East`, `West`) one of its elevations, and `render {"view": "A102"}` one of its sheets. `--save sheets.pdf` prints every sheet, a page each. A script is one command per line, `id {json params}`, with lengths in millimetres: ```text wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000],[0,6000]], "closed": true, "type": "Exterior - 300mm"} door {"at": [2000, 0]} window {"at": [8000, 3000]} room {"point": [4000, 3000], "name": "Living"} floor {} roof {} ``` A script stops at its first failing line and names it. Through MCP, `script {"text": …, "atomic": true}` runs it all or nothing: a line that fails takes back the lines before it, and one that goes through is a single undo step. ```sh bimcraft-cli run --script house.txt --save house.ifc bimcraft-cli convert building.ifc building.bimcraft # an IFC file from Revit or any BIM tool, as a project bimcraft-cli info house.bimcraft # levels, counts, types and warnings bimcraft-cli info building.rvt # a Revit file: release, last save, levels, elements by category bimcraft-cli convert building.rvt building.ifc # a Revit project, imported, then written as IFC4 bimcraft-cli convert house.bimcraft plan.svg bimcraft-cli commands # every command and its parameters ``` ## The desktop app `bimcraft [FILE] [--sample]` opens a `.bimcraft` project, imports an `.ifc` file, or starts on the sample house. The layout is Revit's, so it should feel familiar: the Quick Access Toolbar; the ribbon's File, Architecture, Annotate, View and Modify tabs, with a green contextual tab (Modify | Place Wall, Modify | Walls) for the tool or the selection; the Options Bar; Properties over the Project Browser; views in tabs with a navigation bar; and the tool's prompt in the status bar. The icons and colours are BIMCraft's own: BIMCraft starts in your system's theme. View > Dark Mode opens a menu for Light, Dark, Dark UI, Light Canvas, or As the System; File > Settings offers the same choices. The choice is saved between sessions. Autosave runs in the background every two minutes while the model has unsaved changes (File > Settings > Files changes the interval or disables it). A saved project's recovery copy is `.autosave.bimcraft` beside the project; an untitled project's copy is under the system temporary folder's `bimcraft-autosave` directory. Opening a project with a copy offers **Recover**, **Discard**, or **Postpone**. Recover opens unsaved work, Discard removes the copy, and Postpone protects it for later through File > Recover Autosave. Orphaned untitled copies are offered at startup. Successful Save or an explicit Don't Save removes the current recovery copy, except a postponed copy. See [autosave design](docs/autosave.md). | To | Do | |---|---| | Draw walls | Wall (WA), click points: each click builds a wall from the point before, one undo step each; Enter or Esc ends the chain, and a click back on its start closes it. Ends snap to wall ends and location lines; Shift keeps a segment square. The Draw panel draws a Line, or a Start-End-Radius Arc: its start, its end, then a point it passes through. The Options Bar sets the height (up to a level, or unconnected), the Location Line (the line of the wall you click along) and Chain. A wall's exterior is to your left as you go, so draw clockwise for walls that face out | | Flip, attach walls | Select walls, and Modify \| Walls has Flip (or Space) to turn their exterior side round about their location line, Attach Top/Base to pick a roof or a floor for their tops (or, as the Options Bar says, their bases) to follow, and Detach Top/Base. Properties shows their Location Line (pick another and the wall stays where it is) and whether they're attached | | Place doors, windows | Door (DR) or Window (WN), click a wall; the Type Selector at the top of Properties picks the type. Before the click the door or window is sketched in the wall under the cursor, with how far it stands from each end of the wall | | Place rooms | Room (RM), click inside walls; the outline and area show before you click, and the tag's area follows the walls | | Place columns | Column (CL), click where it stands; it snaps to wall ends and centre lines. The Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected), the Type Selector rectangular or round | | Plumbing tab | Plumbing > Pipe (PI), Plumbing Fixture (PX), Pipe Fitting (PF), Pipe Accessory (PA). A pipe takes two clicks or a chain of them, as a beam does; the Options Bar sets its justification (the middle by default) and its height over the level, and Properties its two heights, so a drain falls and a riser rises. A fixture, a fitting or a valve is a family's type where you click, the Type Selector listing only the families of its kind, Space turning it. Edit Type of a pipe sets its diameter, whether it is round and its material | | Electrical tab | Electrical > Electrical Equipment (EE), Device (DV), Lighting Fixture (LF), and Conduit & Wire > Conduit (CN), Cable Tray (CT), Wire (EW). A run takes two clicks or a chain, as a pipe does, its Options Bar the justification (the middle) and the height; a board, a device or a luminaire is a family's type where you click, the Type Selector listing only the families of its kind (an outlet and a switch under Device), Space turning it. Edit Type of a tray sets its width and depth, of a conduit or a wire its diameter | | Lightning Protection tab | Lightning Protection > Air Terminal (AT), Down Conductor (DC), Earthing Electrode (EG), Inspection Box (IB), Earthing Conductor (GC): free letters, since Revit has none. Runs and fixtures as the other tabs'; the vocabulary is the standard's (captor, condutor de descida, haste de aterramento, caixa de inspeção, condutor de aterramento) | | Data tab | Data > Data Outlet (DT), Voice Outlet (VO), Rack (RK), Patch Panel (PN), and Cabling > Cable Tray (CT, the Electrical tab's), Cabling (CB). Free letters where Revit has none; the Type Selector lists only the families of the tool's kind | | Structure tab | Structure > Column (CL on this tab; Revit's own), Beam (BM), Floor: Structural (SB), and Foundation > Isolated Footing (FI), Wall Footing (FW; Revit's FT is Filters here), and Reinforcement > Reinforce (RF, ours: it arms the element selected; RB is the Massing tab's Roof by Face). A beam or a wall footing takes two clicks, or a chain of them (Options Bar > Chain), each step a beam; the Options Bar sets a beam's justification (top, centre or bottom) and its height over the level, a footing's thickness and where its top is, a structural column's height. The tool sketches what the click would make and the beam's length; a beam seen under, over or through the plan is picked by its centre line; Properties shows its Start and End Level Offset, Z Justification and System, and Edit Type its section. A structural floor is the Floor tool with its `structural` flag | | Add stairs, ramps | Stair: click where it starts (the middle of its first riser), then where its run ends. Past the end of a run of all its risers, it climbs to the level above in one run; short of it, a landing follows, and the next click says which way the next run goes from it: on, left, right, or back beside the last. Risers are at most 180 mm; the Options Bar sets its width and Railings, Properties its riser, tread and top. Ramp: the same clicks, its runs as long as the Options Bar's slope makes them, as high as its Height says | | Add railings | Railing: click a stair or a ramp for a railing down each side, or click a path's points and press Enter for one along it on the plan's level; the Type Selector picks its type, Type Properties its height and baluster spacing | | Roof the building | Roof, in a plan: click inside the walls, and a roof goes on the level above, over their outline and past their faces, whatever its shape, and open over a courtyard: a loop of walls standing free inside the others, with no room in it; its hips and valleys show before you click. The Options Bar sets the slope (0° for a flat roof), the overhang, and gable ends for a rectangle. Select a roof, and Modify \| Roofs has Gable Edge: click an edge of its footprint (a courtyard's too) to stand it upright, a gable end, and again to slope it. Roof by Extrusion: click a line's start and end, then how far across the roof is swept; its profile rises from the line at the Options Bar's slope to a ridge over its middle, or with Shed along its whole length | | Dormers | Architecture > Opening > Dormer: click a roof's slope where the dormer's front wall goes; the Options Bar sets its width, its height over the roof at the front, its roof's slope and whether its front has a window. Its walls stand on the roof, its own gable roof runs back into the host, and the host opens under it | | Floors, slopes | Floor: click inside the walls, and a slab goes under their outline, open over a courtyard (a loop of walls standing free inside the others, with no room in it), its top at the level; Properties sets its Height Offset From Level. Selected, Shape Editing > Slope Arrow: click its tail, then its head, and the floor rises toward the head at the Options Bar's slope; Properties changes the slope | | Ceilings | Ceiling: click inside a room, and a ceiling fills it out to its walls' faces, open round any walls standing free inside it, at the Options Bar's height (2600 mm); the outline shows before you click, and the Type Selector picks a plain one or tiles. The Project Browser's Ceiling Plans open each level's reflected ceiling plan | | Shafts | Architecture > Opening > Shaft: click two opposite corners; the Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected). It cuts the floors, ceilings and roofs on its way | | Masses | Massing > Conceptual Mass > Mass (MS): click the footprint's corners; the Options Bar sets how high it goes (up to a level, or unconnected); Enter, or the first corner again, finishes. Before you do, the outline it would make shows, with its area. With a mass selected, Model by Face makes Mass Floors (MF: a floor at each level it crosses), Wall by Face (WB: a wall on each edge), Floor by Face (FB) and Roof by Face (RB) on its top face, and Update to Face (UF) makes what they made follow the mass again; Show Mass (MH) hides and shows masses in the view on screen. Properties shows its constraints, its Top Outline (corners as `x, y; x, y`, blank for none: typed, the mass is lofted), area, volume and gross floor area. View > Schedules lists Mass and Mass Floor schedules | | Add levels, grids | Level (LL) takes an elevation in the Options Bar; Grid (GR) takes two clicks | | Select | Click; Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's underneath (the wall under a door). Drag across empty floor for a box: left to right takes what's wholly inside, right to left what it crosses too; in a section or an elevation, any drag draws one. The selection stays as you open other views, the 3D view and schedules among them | | Edit, delete | Properties edits the parameters of everything selected, in one step, grouped as Revit groups them; the Type Selector changes the type; Delete removes the selection | | Move, copy | Drag a selected element, or Move (MV) and Copy (CO): click a base point, then where it goes. Walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, so room areas follow; doors and windows slide along their walls. Constrain keeps the move square; Multiple goes on copying | | Rotate, mirror | Rotate (RO) turns the selection about its middle: click the angle's start, then its end, or type an angle in the Options Bar; Place Centre moves the centre. Mirror Pick Axis (MM) mirrors across a wall or grid you pick, Mirror Draw Axis (DM) across a line you click; Copy is on, as in Revit | | Align, trim, split, offset | Align (AL): hover to highlight an edge or centre line, pick the reference, then the target edge. It turns and moves walls, columns, components, slabs, roofs, structural/MEP runs and detail geometry onto the reference in one undo step; hosted doors and windows slide along their wall. While sketching, align sketch lines to model edges or other sketch lines; joined endpoints follow, with sketch undo until Finish. Trim/Extend to Corner (TR): pick two walls on the parts to keep. Split Element (SL): click a wall where to cut it. Offset (OF): point to a wall, and a copy goes to the cursor's side at the Options Bar's distance | | Dimension, tag | Annotate > Aligned (DI): pick parallel references, each the line nearest the cursor (a wall's face, centre line or end, a door's or window's centre or jamb, a grid), or endpoints (a wall's end or corner, a line's or a grid's end), which a square marks, then click away from them where the dimension line goes; more picks make a chain. Linear: pick endpoints, then click where it goes, horizontal or vertical as the cursor lies; the Options Bar's Place (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them) lays either tool's dimension. Angular: pick two lines that meet, then click where the arc goes; the angle on that side. Radial and Diameter: pick a round column, a curved wall, a circle or an arc, then click where it goes. Arc Length: pick a curved wall or an arc, then, to measure part of it, two ends on it, then click where the dimension's arc goes. Edit Type on a dimension opens Dimension Type Properties; a double click on one of its numbers opens Dimension Text, that segment's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, or text in its place. Selected, a dimension shows a padlock under each segment and EQ past its end: a click locks a segment at its length, or keeps the segments equal, and what it measures to then moves with what moves, as in Revit. Annotate > Tag by Category (TG): click any element with a place in a plan (a door or window, a wall, a column, a component, a floor, ceiling or roof, a room, a beam or pipe, a stair) to tag it with its type, a door's or window's with its mark, a room's with its name, or with any other field its schedule has (Height, Area, a project parameter) typed in Label in the Options Bar, with a leader when it says so; Tag All tags the doors and windows of the view not tagged yet. Drag a dimension or a tag to move it | | Spot elevations, text | Annotate > Spot Elevation (EL): click a floor, a roof, a stair or a wall in plan, and it reads the height of its top there, following it; in a section, click a point to mark its height. Annotate > Text (TX): type the note in the Options Bar (`\n` breaks a line), then click its top left corner, in a plan, a section or on a sheet; Properties sets its size and angle | | Crop, view range | View > Crop View crops a plan or a section to what it shows; drag the grips at its edges' middles to move them (a section's sides move its line). Off shows it all again: a section or an elevation, all there is along its line, past its ends. Properties of a plan holds its View Range: Top (clear it for the level above), Cut Plane, Bottom and View Depth, in mm above the level | | Filled regions | Annotate > Filled Region (FR) and Masking Region start a boundary sketch. Edit Type opens Type Properties for a selected region or the current sketch: duplicate and rename types; choose foreground and background patterns and colors separately; set masking; check the combined preview. A pattern's … button opens the patterns, to create and edit them. Apply/OK save the draft as one undo step; Cancel drops unapplied work. A type change updates every region using it; the palette's Type Selector controls the instance's type. Non-masking fills keep cut foreground patterns and projected model lines visible; masking fills cover the model. 306 307 `--cmd 'render {"view": "{3D}", "path": "house-3d.png"}'` adds the 3D view (`azimuth` and `elevation` turn it); 308 `render {"view": "Section 1"}` draws the sample's section, `South` (or `North`, `East`, `West`) one of its elevations, and 309 `render {"view": "A102"}` one of its sheets. `--save sheets.pdf` prints every sheet, a page each. 310 311 A script is one command per line, `id {json params}`, with lengths in millimetres: 312 313 ```text 314 wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000],[0,6000]], "closed": true, "type": "Exterior - 300mm"} 315 door {"at": [2000, 0]} 316 window {"at": [8000, 3000]} 317 room {"point": [4000, 3000], "name": "Living"} 318 floor {} 319 roof {} 320 ``` 321 322 A script stops at its first failing line and names it. Through MCP, `script {"text": …, "atomic": true}` runs it all or nothing: 323 a line that fails takes back the lines before it, and one that goes through is a single undo step. 324 325 ```sh 326 bimcraft-cli run --script house.txt --save house.ifc 327 bimcraft-cli convert building.ifc building.bimcraft # an IFC file from Revit or any BIM tool, as a project 328 bimcraft-cli info house.bimcraft # levels, counts, types and warnings 329 bimcraft-cli info building.rvt # a Revit file: release, last save, levels, elements by category 330 bimcraft-cli convert building.rvt building.ifc # a Revit project, imported, then written as IFC4 331 bimcraft-cli convert house.bimcraft plan.svg 332 bimcraft-cli commands # every command and its parameters 333 ``` 334 335 ## The desktop app 336 337 `bimcraft [FILE] [--sample]` opens a `.bimcraft` project, imports an `.ifc` file, or starts on the sample house. Opening a project with a 347 copy offers **Recover**, **Discard**, or **Postpone**. Recover opens unsaved work, Discard removes the copy, and Postpone 348 protects it for later through File > Recover Autosave. Orphaned untitled copies are offered at startup. With a mass selected, Model by Face makes Mass Floors (MF: a floor at each level it crosses), Wall by Face (WB: a wall on each edge), Floor by Face (FB) and Roof by Face (RB) on its top face, and Update to Face (UF) makes what they made follow the mass again; Show Mass (MH) hides and shows masses in the view on screen. Properties shows its constraints, its Top Outline (corners as `x, y; x, y`, blank for none: typed, the mass is lofted), area, volume and gross floor area. View > Schedules lists Mass and Mass Floor schedules | 371 | Add levels, grids | Level (LL) takes an elevation in the Options Bar; Grid (GR) takes two clicks | 372 | Select | Click; Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's underneath (the wall under a door). Drag across empty floor for a box: left to right takes what's wholly inside, right to left what it crosses too; in a section or an elevation, any drag draws one. The selection stays as you open other views, the 3D view and schedules among them | 373 | Edit, delete | Properties edits the parameters of everything selected, in one step, grouped as Revit groups them; the Type Selector changes the type; Delete removes the selection | 374 | Move, copy | Drag a selected element, or Move (MV) and Copy (CO): click a base point, then where it goes. Walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, so room areas follow; doors and windows slide along their walls. Constrain keeps the move square; Multiple goes on copying | 375 | Rotate, mirror | Rotate (RO) turns the selection about its middle: click the angle's start, then its end, or type an angle in the Options Bar; Place Centre moves the centre. Mirror Pick Axis (MM) mirrors across a wall or grid you pick, Mirror Draw Axis (DM) across a line you click; Copy is on, as in Revit | 376 | Align, trim, split, offset | Align (AL): hover to highlight an edge or centre line, pick the reference, then the target edge. It turns and moves walls, columns, components, slabs, roofs, structural/MEP runs and detail geometry onto the reference in one undo step; hosted doors and windows slide along their wall. While sketching, align sketch lines to model edges or other sketch lines; joined endpoints follow, with sketch undo until Finish. Trim/Extend to Corner (TR): pick two walls on the parts to keep. Split Element (SL): click a wall where to cut it. Offset (OF): point to a wall, and a copy goes to the cursor's side at the Options Bar's distance | 377 | Dimension, tag | Annotate > Aligned (DI): pick parallel references, each the line nearest the cursor (a wall's face, centre line or end, a door's or window's centre or jamb, a grid), or endpoints (a wall's end or corner, a line's or a grid's end), which a square marks, then click away from them where the dimension line goes; more picks make a chain. Drag a view or a note to move it, set its scale in Properties, double-click it to open it. File > Export > Sheets as PDF prints them all | 403 | Cut a section, add an elevation | View > Section (CR): click its start and end; it looks to the left of the line, so drawn west to east it looks north. View > Elevation: click beside the building, and it looks at that side. Open them from the browser, or double-click their marks in a plan; in them, click to select what they cut or see | 404 | Look in 3D | The cube on the Quick Access Toolbar (or View > 3D View, or {3D} in the browser) opens the 3D view. The last tab can't float | 410 | More room | Double-click a ribbon tab (or press the arrow at the right of the tabs) and the ribbon folds to its tabs; a click on a tab then shows its tools over the view until one is picked. Double-click again to open it | 411 | Settings | File > Settings (Ctrl+, or the cog on the Quick Access Toolbar): the theme, language, ribbon and palettes under User Interface, with Plans' two working aids, the origin marker (a small mark at the project's 0, 0 with the directions of x and y) and the view's name in a plan's bottom left corner, both on at first and drawn on the screen only, never in a PNG, a sheet or a printout; background autosave and its interval under Files; whether to look for updates. 419	
420	Each of these runs a command, so what you do in the window is checked, undone and saved exactly as from the CLI or an agent.
421	
422	## Drive it from agents, MCP and the CLI
423	
424	`bimcraft-cli mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio, on a model of its own.
425	Add it to Claude Code:
426	
427	```sh
428	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp
429	```
430	
431	or to any MCP client's configuration:
432	
433	```json
434	{ "mcpServers": { "bimcraft": { "command": "/path/to/bimcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
435	```
436	
437	| Tool | What it does |
438	|---|---|
439	| `execute {command, params}` | Any command with JSON parameters |
440	| `script {text, atomic?}` | Several commands, one per line; `atomic`: all or nothing, one undo step |
441	| `list_commands {filter?}` | The catalog, with parameters and shortcuts |
442	| `inspect_model` | Levels, counts, types, warnings and undo history |
443	| `query_elements {category?, level?}` | Elements with derived values: wall length and height, room area, door position |
444	| `schedule {name?, category?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?}` | A schedule's columns, rows and totals; a new one, or one changed, as the command makes it |
445	| `render {view?, ceiling?, width?, height?, azimuth?, elevation?}` | A level's floor plan (or reflected ceiling plan), a section or elevation by name, a sheet by number, or with `view: "{3D}"` the 3D view, as a PNG the agent can look at |
446	| `new_model`, `open`, `save` | Projects; `open` imports `.ifc` files, `save` to `.ifc`, `.svg` or `.png` exports |
447	
448	A command that fails comes back as a tool error saying what to fix (`door: no wall at [4000, 3000] on Level 1`), and it
449	changes nothing.
450	
451	### On the project you have open
452	
453	Start the window with `--control PORT` (`0` for any free port) and an agent can work on the project in front of you instead of
454	a copy of its own: what it makes appears in the window, as an undo step you can take back, and is saved with Ctrl+S.
455	
456	```sh
457	bimcraft --control 0                       # the window says the port; bridge.json beside the favorites holds it and a token
458	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp --connect
459	```
460	
461	`mcp --connect` takes the port from that file (or `--connect PORT` names it, which must be the window's). The port is on this
462	machine's own address only, a connection that does not say the token in its first line is dropped, and only the user can read
463	the file. The tools are the same, except `new_model` and `open`, which would replace your project: start or open another in
464	the window. The window answers between its frames, so a long command holds the window as it would from a button.
465	
466	File > Settings > Agents opens the same port without `--control` (and again at each start), on a port you choose or any free one,
467	and closes it. With **Allow agents to edit this project** off, an agent only reads your project: it inspects it, reads its schedules,
468	renders its views and exports it to new files (the sheets to PDF among them), and every change it asks for comes back as an error
469	that says so. The view control bar shows the port: off, listening on its number, or how many agents are connected, and read-only.
470	An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
471	for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.
472	
473	## Commands
474	
475	| Command | Shortcut | Parameters |
476	|---|---|---|

Each of these runs a command, so what you do in the window is checked, undone and saved exactly as from the CLI or an agent.

## Drive it from agents, MCP and the CLI

`bimcraft-cli mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio, on a model of its own.
Add it to Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp
```

or to any MCP client's configuration:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "bimcraft": { "command": "/path/to/bimcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `execute {command, params}` | Any command with JSON parameters |
| `script {text, atomic?}` | Several commands, one per line; `atomic`: all or nothing, one undo step |
| `list_commands {filter?}` | The catalog, with parameters and shortcuts |
| `inspect_model` | Levels, counts, types, warnings and undo history |
| `query_elements {category?, level?}` | Elements with derived values: wall length and height, room area, door position |
| `schedule {name?, category?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?}` | A schedule's columns, rows and totals; a new one, or one changed, as the command makes it |
| `render {view?, ceiling?, width?, height?, azimuth?, elevation?}` | A level's floor plan (or reflected ceiling plan), a section or elevation by name, a sheet by number, or with `view: "{3D}"` the 3D view, as a PNG the agent can look at |
| `new_model`, `open`, `save` | Projects; `open` imports `.ifc` files, `save` to `.ifc`, `.svg` or `.png` exports |

A command that fails comes back as a tool error saying what to fix (`door: no wall at [4000, 3000] on Level 1`), and it
changes nothing.

### On the project you have open

Start the window with `--control PORT` (`0` for any free port) and an agent can work on the project in front of you instead of
a copy of its own: what it makes appears in the window, as an undo step you can take back, and is saved with Ctrl+S.

```sh
bimcraft --control 0                       # the window says the port; bridge.json beside the favorites holds it and a token
claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp --connect
```

`mcp --connect` takes the port from that file (or `--connect PORT` names it, which must be the window's). The port is on this
machine's own address only, a connection that does not say the token in its first line is dropped, and only the user can read
the file. The tools are the same, except `new_model` and `open`, which would replace your project: start or open another in
the window. The window answers between its frames, so a long command holds the window as it would from a button.

File > Settings > Agents opens the same port without `--control` (and again at each start), on a port you choose or any free one,
and closes it. With **Allow agents to edit this project** off, an agent only reads your project: it inspects it, reads its schedules,
renders its views and exports it to new files (the sheets to PDF among them), and every change it asks for comes back as an error
that says so. The view control bar shows the port: off, listening on its number, or how many agents are connected, and read-only.
An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.

420	Each of these runs a command, so what you do in the window is checked, undone and saved exactly as from the CLI or an agent.
421	
422	## Drive it from agents, MCP and the CLI
423	
424	`bimcraft-cli mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio, on a model of its own.
425	Add it to Claude Code:
426	
427	```sh
428	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp
429	```
430	
431	or to any MCP client's configuration:
432	
433	```json
434	{ "mcpServers": { "bimcraft": { "command": "/path/to/bimcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
435	```
436	
437	| Tool | What it does |
438	|---|---|
439	| `execute {command, params}` | Any command with JSON parameters |
440	| `script {text, atomic?}` | Several commands, one per line; `atomic`: all or nothing, one undo step |
441	| `list_commands {filter?}` | The catalog, with parameters and shortcuts |
442	| `inspect_model` | Levels, counts, types, warnings and undo history |
443	| `query_elements {category?, level?}` | Elements with derived values: wall length and height, room area, door position |
444	| `schedule {name?, category?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?}` | A schedule's columns, rows and totals; a new one, or one changed, as the command makes it |
445	| `render {view?, ceiling?, width?, height?, azimuth?, elevation?}` | A level's floor plan (or reflected ceiling plan), a section or elevation by name, a sheet by number, or with `view: "{3D}"` the 3D view, as a PNG the agent can look at |
446	| `new_model`, `open`, `save` | Projects; `open` imports `.ifc` files, `save` to `.ifc`, `.svg` or `.png` exports |
447	
448	A command that fails comes back as a tool error saying what to fix (`door: no wall at [4000, 3000] on Level 1`), and it
449	changes nothing.
450	
451	### On the project you have open
452	
453	Start the window with `--control PORT` (`0` for any free port) and an agent can work on the project in front of you instead of
454	a copy of its own: what it makes appears in the window, as an undo step you can take back, and is saved with Ctrl+S.
455	
456	```sh
457	bimcraft --control 0                       # the window says the port; bridge.json beside the favorites holds it and a token
458	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp --connect
459	```
460	
461	`mcp --connect` takes the port from that file (or `--connect PORT` names it, which must be the window's). The port is on this
462	machine's own address only, a connection that does not say the token in its first line is dropped, and only the user can read
463	the file. The tools are the same, except `new_model` and `open`, which would replace your project: start or open another in
464	the window. The window answers between its frames, so a long command holds the window as it would from a button.
465	
466	File > Settings > Agents opens the same port without `--control` (and again at each start), on a port you choose or any free one,
467	and closes it. With **Allow agents to edit this project** off, an agent only reads your project: it inspects it, reads its schedules,
468	renders its views and exports it to new files (the sheets to PDF among them), and every change it asks for comes back as an error
469	that says so. The view control bar shows the port: off, listening on its number, or how many agents are connected, and read-only.
470	An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
471	for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.

602	## Roadmap
603	
604	Done: views and notes (view ranges, crop regions, text notes, spot elevations, angular and radial dimensions and dimensions to
605	wall ends and openings, schedules and the 3D view on sheets), project units (metric, or feet and inches), Portuguese and
606	Spanish, for the desktop and for projects, real walls (compound types with layers, joins at any angle, curved walls,
607	walls attached to roofs and floors, other location lines), sloped floors with openings, ceilings with openings and reflected ceiling plans, and shaft
608	openings, stairs of several runs with landings, ramps and railings, and roofs over any footprint (hips and valleys, gable
609	ends, courtyards), extrusion roofs and dormers, materials, with floors, roofs and ceilings built of layers as walls
610	are, families, BIMCraft's own parametric components (never Autodesk's `.rfa`), and project parameters and schedules with
611	chosen fields, filters, sorting and formulas, and visibility and graphics (overrides, view filters, view templates, phases and design options, which go out to IFC and come back), and families done: revolves and voids, doors and windows as families, the Family Editor, textures by material or from pictures you add, Paint, and favorites kept for every project, and updates (a check at startup, and the Windows installer's copy, an AppImage and the macOS app upgrading themselves).
612	Next, in order: locked and equal dimensions, arrays and groups; fill patterns of your own; DXF and DWG export, more of
613	IFC, and gbXML; the rest of structure (beams, columns, footings and structural floors are in), then MEP (its four tabs are designed in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md)); site and massing; several people editing one model; and signed installers (macOS
614	signing and notarization are wired up, waiting on a Developer ID). Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public specification, so BIMCraft reads it only through a reader of its own under the fence in
615	[docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md): it lists what a file holds (`bimcraft-cli info`) and imports its levels, walls, floors, doors
616	and windows, columns, rooms and roofs into a project, from the command line and from the desktop's File > Open, listing what was left out and why.

620	### Windows
621	
622	| Build | Download |
623	|---|---|
624	| x64 (64-bit Intel/AMD), installer | `bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64.msi` |
625	| x64, no installer: unzip and run | `bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64-portable.zip` |
626	
627	The installer is a short setup wizard. It puts BIMCraft and `bimcraft-cli` for every user in `Program Files\BIMCraft`, or in
628	the folder you pick on its folder page (Change, on any drive), adds BIMCraft to the Start menu, asks whether to put it on the
629	desktop too, opens `.bimcraft` projects in it, and offers it under Open with for `.ifc` files. It needs no Visual C++
630	runtime, and a newer version upgrades an older one, keeping the folder and the desktop shortcut as they were. For a silent
631	install with a desktop shortcut, in a folder of your own: `msiexec /i bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64.msi /qn DESKTOPSHORTCUT=1
632	INSTALLFOLDER="D:\Apps\BIMCraft"`. It isn't code-signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen asks before it runs: More info, then Run anyway.
633	
634	The portable zip is for a PC where you can't install software: unzip it anywhere (a USB stick will do) and run `bimcraft.exe`.
635	It holds `bimcraft.exe`, `bimcraft-cli.exe`, the licences and this readme, needs no rights and no Visual C++ runtime, and leaves
636	nothing behind but its settings (the favorites, the recent files and `bimcraft.log`) in `%APPDATA%\BIMCraft`. It isn't code-signed
637	either. BIMCraft only replaces the installer's copy in Program Files by itself, so a portable copy is told of a newer version

## Roadmap

Done: views and notes (view ranges, crop regions, text notes, spot elevations, angular and radial dimensions and dimensions to
wall ends and openings, schedules and the 3D view on sheets), project units (metric, or feet and inches), Portuguese and
Spanish, for the desktop and for projects, real walls (compound types with layers, joins at any angle, curved walls,
walls attached to roofs and floors, other location lines), sloped floors with openings, ceilings with openings and reflected ceiling plans, and shaft
openings, stairs of several runs with landings, ramps and railings, and roofs over any footprint (hips and valleys, gable
ends, courtyards), extrusion roofs and dormers, materials, with floors, roofs and ceilings built of layers as walls
are, families, BIMCraft's own parametric components (never Autodesk's `.rfa`), and project parameters and schedules with
chosen fields, filters, sorting and formulas, and visibility and graphics (overrides, view filters, view templates, phases and design options, which go out to IFC and come back), and families done: revolves and voids, doors and windows as families, the Family Editor, textures by material or from pictures you add, Paint, and favorites kept for every project, and updates (a check at startup, and the Windows installer's copy, an AppImage and the macOS app upgrading themselves).
Next, in order: locked and equal dimensions, arrays and groups; fill patterns of your own; DXF and DWG export, more of
IFC, and gbXML; the rest of structure (beams, columns, footings and structural floors are in), then MEP (its four tabs are designed in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md)); site and massing; several people editing one model; and signed installers (macOS
signing and notarization are wired up, waiting on a Developer ID). Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public specification, so BIMCraft reads it only through a reader of its own under the fence in
[docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md): it lists what a file holds (`bimcraft-cli info`) and imports its levels, walls, floors, doors
and windows, columns, rooms and roofs into a project, from the command line and from the desktop's File > Open, listing what was left out and why.

## Downloads

### Windows

| Build | Download |
|---|---|
| x64 (64-bit Intel/AMD), installer | `bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64.msi` |
| x64, no installer: unzip and run | `bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64-portable.zip` |

The installer is a short setup wizard. It puts BIMCraft and `bimcraft-cli` for every user in `Program Files\BIMCraft`, or in
the folder you pick on its folder page (Change, on any drive), adds BIMCraft to the Start menu, asks whether to put it on the
desktop too, opens `.bimcraft` projects in it, and offers it under Open with for `.ifc` files. It needs no Visual C++
runtime, and a newer version upgrades an older one, keeping the folder and the desktop shortcut as they were. For a silent
install with a desktop shortcut, in a folder of your own: `msiexec /i bimcraft-<ver>-windows-x64.msi /qn DESKTOPSHORTCUT=1
INSTALLFOLDER="D:\Apps\BIMCraft"`. It isn't code-signed yet, so Windows SmartScreen asks before it runs: More info, then Run anyway.

The portable zip is for a PC where you can't install software: unzip it anywhere (a USB stick will do) and run `bimcraft.exe`.
It holds `bimcraft.exe`, `bimcraft-cli.exe`, the licences and this readme, needs no rights and no Visual C++ runtime, and leaves
nothing behind but its settings (the favorites, the recent files and `bimcraft.log`) in `%APPDATA%\BIMCraft`. It isn't code-signed
either. BIMCraft only replaces the installer's copy in Program Files by itself, so a portable copy is told of a newer version

Between releases, the Release workflow (Actions > Release > Run workflow) builds them all 685 for any commit, as that run's artifacts. The scripts behind them are in `packaging/` (`linux/package.sh`, 686 `linux/flatpak-bundle.sh`, `linux/arch-package.sh`, `macos/package.sh`, each with its `--help`), and run on your own 687 machine too. 688 689 ### Updates 690 691 The desktop app looks for a newer release when it starts: one HTTPS request to `api.github.com` for this repository's latest 692 release, made on a thread of its own with a 15 second timeout, so the window never waits for it. Being offline, being rate 693 limited, or getting a reply that isn't a release is ignored without a word. It sends nothing of yours beyond what any HTTPS 694 request carries: your address, and a `User-Agent` naming BIMCraft's version (it follows `HTTPS_PROXY` and `ALL_PROXY` like 695 other tools do). A release counts when it's published (not a draft, not a pre-release) and its tag, `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, is 696 a later version than the one running, as semver orders them. A banner then offers it: Update now, Later (it asks again next 697 time), or Skip this version (it stays quiet until a newer one comes). File > Check for Updates Now looks by hand, and says 698 when there's nothing newer or the check failed. 699 700 The check is switched off in File > Check for updates at startup; that choice is kept in `update.json` beside your 701 favorites, in your own configuration folder (`%APPDATA%\BIMCraft`, `~/Library/Application Support/BIMCraft`, or 702 `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bimcraft`, else `~/.config/bimcraft`; `BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES` moves both), not in a project. Setting the environment variable `BIMCRAFT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` (to anything but empty) 703 keeps the app from making any request, and hides the menu items. `bimcraft-cli` and the MCP server never check for anything. 704 705 **Windows.** Update now works for the copy the installer put in `Program Files\BIMCraft`; a copy in a folder you picked is 706 told of the new version with a Download button, and the new installer offers that folder again. It downloads 707 `bimcraft--windows-x64.msi` from the release into a new folder in your temp folder and checks it. Restart and install 708 then asks to save any unsaved changes, closes BIMCraft, and hands over to a copy of itself that waits for BIMCraft to be 709 gone, checks the file once more, runs Windows' own `msiexec` on it while holding the file open, so that nothing can change it 710 (`/passive`: a progress bar, and Windows asks permission, because the installer is for every user) and starts BIMCraft again 711 with the project that was open. If you cancel the permission prompt the old version starts again, and the offer comes back at 712 the next start unless you skipped it. The installer's log is `install.log` in that folder, which BIMCraft removes at a start 713 a day or more later. 714 715 **Linux.** Update now works for an AppImage whose folder you can write to, on x86_64 or aarch64 (if you start it through a 716 link, the file the link points to is the one replaced). It downloads `bimcraft--linux-.AppImage` into a new folder 717 in your temp folder and checks it. Restart and install then asks to save, checks the file once more, and copies it next to your 718 AppImage under a hidden name, on the same disk, so that the last step can't be left half done. It runs that copy with 719 `--version`, as you would run it and, if that fails (no FUSE, say), once more asking it to unpack itself first, which needs 720 none, giving each try at most a minute; the copy must print `bimcraft ` for the release's version. Only then is it 721 renamed over your AppImage, and the new one starts (unpacking itself, if it had to for the check) with the project that was 722 open as BIMCraft closes. The file keeps its name, so a shortcut to it keeps working, even when the name holds the old version. 723 If the new build doesn't run, or says another version, your AppImage is as it was, the hidden copy is deleted and a note says 724 why. A package from your distribution (`.deb`, `.rpm`, Arch) is files that belong to root and to your package manager, so it is 725 told of the newer release and not replaced; so are the tarball, a build from source, and an AppImage in a folder you can't 726 write to. A Flatpak has no network and never checks. None of this has run against a real AppImage: it is tested with scripts 727 that stand in for one, which is what the checks on the new file and the swap need, but not the AppImage runtime itself. 728 729 **macOS.** Update now works for BIMCraft.app when its folder is one you can write to (Applications, for an administrator, or 730 `~/Applications`). It downloads `bimcraft--macos-universal.dmg` into a new folder in your temp folder and checks it. 731 Restart and install then asks to save, checks the file once more, mounts the disk image read-only and out of Finder's sight, 732 copies BIMCraft.app out of it with `ditto` to a hidden app beside yours, lets the image go, and runs `codesign --verify 733 --strict --deep` on the copy, as the release script does. It runs the copy once with `--version`, which must print `bimcraft 734 `, and swaps it in by two renames: the old app is put back if the second fails, and deleted once the new one is in. 735 The new app starts with the project that was open as BIMCraft closes. If a step before the swap fails, your app is as it was, and 736 a note says why; if the new app is in but won't start, the note says that, and BIMCraft stays open. **This has not run on a Mac.** The steps are tested only against shell scripts that stand in for `hdiutil`, `ditto`, 737 `codesign` and `open`, so three things stay open until someone tries it. Whether macOS asks permission, or refuses, when an 738 app signed ad hoc replaces its own bundle (macOS 13 and later guard apps against changes by others; if it refuses, the update 739 fails with that error and the old app stays). Whether Gatekeeper asks again about the new app: it is signed ad hoc like the 740 old one, and the copy BIMCraft makes carries no mark from a download. And whether `open` hands the project to the new app: Finder 741 hands projects over another way, which the app also reads, and if `open` doesn't do it the new version starts with a blank 742 project, while the project is still in the file you saved. An app run from the disk image itself, or from the folder it was 743 downloaded to, can't be replaced (macOS runs a downloaded app from a read-only copy until it is moved): it is told of the newer 744 version and sent to the page, so move BIMCraft to Applications first. 745 746 **Everything else.** A build from source, a copy kept anywhere else, and a Windows copy running as an administrator are told 747 of a newer release, and the banner's Download button opens its page. Replacing a program that came from `cargo` or a package 748 manager is not the updater's to do, and the copy that runs the Windows installer would have an administrator's rights, in a 749 folder other programs can write to. Run BIMCraft as yourself. 750 751 **What the check protects against.** The update is fetched only from this repository's release on github.com and GitHub's 752 release CDN, over HTTPS: the address is built from the release's tag, never taken from the reply, redirects are followed one 753 by one and only into this repository's releases on github.com or to the CDN, and an asset is taken only if it's named exactly 754 for that version and kind of install. The reply is read up to 1 MiB, and the download is held to the size GitHub lists for the 755 file (at most 128 MiB) and must match it to the byte. Its SHA-256 must equal the digest GitHub's API gives for that asset, when 756 it arrives and again just before it is installed; and where the release lists a `SHA256SUMS` file, the sum in it must be the 757 same one. The two come from different places (the release workflow writes the file, GitHub works out the digest when an asset is 758 uploaded), so a file replaced afterwards without the other being updated is refused. Nothing runs that failed a check, and the 759 file is deleted. A damaged or truncated download, a cache or a mirror serving something else, and a server that sends more than 760 it should are all stopped by this. On Linux and macOS the new build must also run and say its version before it takes the old 761 one's place, which shows that it loads here, though not that its window opens. 762 763 **What it doesn't.** None of the three files is signed by a developer identity that BIMCraft checks: the Windows installer isn't 764 code-signed (so Windows can't say who made it), the macOS app is signed ad hoc (which says that it is intact, not who made it), 765 and the AppImage isn't signed. The digest says only that the file is the one GitHub lists: someone who could publish a release 766 in this repository (a stolen token or account), or GitHub itself, would publish a digest that matches their file. On Linux and 767 macOS the new build is run once, as you, with `--version` before it replaces the old one; that is no more trust than starting it 768 after, and the digest check comes first, but it is a program from the internet that runs because you clicked. A program already 769 running as you could swap the file in your temp folder after the first check, and the second check, made just before the install, 770 catches that. On Linux and macOS nothing holds the file between that check and its use, which is a matter of moments, and a 771 program that could win that race could replace your AppImage or your app directly. On Windows the copy that runs the installer 772 holds the file open so that nothing can write to it until Windows Installer is done. If Windows Installer won't open a file held 773 that way, the copy lets go, checks it once more and runs it unheld, and then a swap is possible for as long as you take over the 774 permission prompt, which looks the same either way, since it can't say whose file it is. The updater doesn't mark the file as 775 downloaded from the internet, so SmartScreen doesn't ask as it does for one saved by a browser; the permission prompt still 776 comes from Windows. The certificates it trusts are Mozilla's, built in, so a network that inspects HTTPS with a certificate of 777 its own makes the check fail, quietly, and a corporate root isn't consulted. Signed installers are on the roadmap. 778 779 ## License and credits 780 781 BIMCraft is dual-licensed under [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) or [Apache-2.0](LICENSE-APACHE), at your option. 782 Copyright (c) 2026 IPedrax and the BIMCraft contributors. 783 784 The one exception is the Revit file reader, [`crates/rvt`](crates/rvt), which holds code ported from 785 [rvt-rs](https://github.com/DrunkOnJava/rvt-rs) (Copyright 2026 Griffin Long) and is Apache-2.0 only: see its 786 [LICENSE](crates/rvt/LICENSE) and [NOTICE](crates/rvt/NOTICE).
