# Importing and linking CAD drawings

On the roadmap under 0.9 Interoperability, as Revit's Import CAD and Link CAD: a consultant's or a surveyor's DXF drawing
brought into a project and drawn under the model in the plans of a level, to trace walls over and to check against. A project
holds each drawing once, an import element places it, plans draw and snap to it, and the desktop brings one in (Insert > Import
CAD, Link CAD). A DWG comes in as the DXF it becomes (below); DXF export, exploding an import into detail lines (which waits on detail lines, issue #58), and
images and PDFs as underlays are still to come.

## The reader

`dxf.rs` reads ASCII DXF of any version from Autodesk's public DXF reference: pairs of a group code and a value, read in
sections. From the header it takes `$INSUNITS` (the drawing's unit, `Dxf::unit` and `Dxf::scale`, mm to each of its units),
`$ACADVER` and `$LTSCALE`; from the tables its layers (colour, off when the colour is negative, frozen by flag, linetype, line
weight) and its linetypes' dash patterns; from the blocks section the blocks; and from the entities section what model space
draws (an entity with code 67 set is paper space's, and left out). Entities come in as a short list of `Shape`s, in the
drawing's own units: LINE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (bulges become arcs; a 3D mesh or polyface is left out), CIRCLE, ARC,
ELLIPSE (as a polyline), SPLINE (its fit points, else its control points), POINT, TEXT and MTEXT (its formatting codes taken
out, aligned as the file says), SOLID and TRACE, and HATCH (its boundary loops, solid or patterned; a patterned one is drawn as a
pale fill of its colour, since its pattern isn't kept). An INSERT places its block's entities, scaled, turned and arrayed, up to
`MAX_DEPTH` blocks deep; an entity on layer 0 of a block takes the insert's layer, and one by block its colour. DIMENSION draws
its anonymous block. What the reader doesn't know (3DFACE, a viewport, an image, a proxy) is counted by kind in
`Dxf::left_out`, and the command lists it. The text itself is read as UTF-8 where it is, and else by the code page the header names in
`$DWGCODEPAGE`: the East Asian pages and the Windows ones decode through `encoding_rs`, and a page without a decoder here (the DOS
ones) reads as Latin-1, as it always has.

A file is hostile: `MAX_BYTES` caps its size, `MAX_PAIRS` its pairs, `MAX_SHAPES` the shapes, `MAX_WORK` the points the blocks
may multiply into, and every coordinate is a finite number within `MAX_FILE_COORD` (one past that is left out as "past what a
drawing holds"). A file that ends after a group code, a value that isn't a number, a binary DXF and a DWG each say why.

## DWG

The core reads no DWG of its own. `crates/dwg` (`bimcraft-dwg`) is a bridge: the acadrust crate (pure Rust, MPL-2.0, used
unmodified as a separate library; its DWG code is ported from ACadSharp, MIT, after the Open Design Alliance's published DWG
specification; NOTICE carries both) reads the file in failsafe mode, and its DXF writer writes what it read as ASCII DXF, which
`dxf.rs` reads as any other. `Limits` holds a DWG to 64 MB before the decoder runs and its DXF to `dxf::MAX_BYTES` while it is
written; a read that left object records out says how many, of which kinds, in `import_cad`'s `notes` (the desktop puts them on
the status bar). The project holds the DXF, so a project file opens where no DWG reader is.

A session reads a DWG through the `DwgReader` it is given (`Session::dwg`; `read_dxf_file` in `commands.rs` is the one place
`import_cad`, `reload_cad` and opening a project read a drawing), and one without says to save it as DXF. The desktop and the
command line (so MCP too) hand theirs `bimcraft_dwg::reader()` behind their default `dwg` feature: it starts the program
itself as a child (`--dwg-to-dxf <path>`, answered by `child_main` before anything else runs) and reads the DXF from its
output. The decoder allocates what a file declares and can't be interrupted, so a hostile file could abort the process; in
the child it takes only the child, which is also stopped after `CHILD_TIME` or past the limits, and the reply says the file
couldn't be read. Tests make their DWG files from DXF text with the same library (`dwg_from_dxf`, the `testing` feature),
since Autodesk's are never committed; `BIMCRAFT_DWG_SAMPLES` names a folder of real ones for
`real_drawings_where_a_folder_of_them_is_named`, and `apps/bimcraft-cli/tests/dwg.rs` drives the child.

## The project

A project holds each drawing once, by name, as a `Cad` in `Model::cads` (a library entry of kind `Cad`, so it has an id and a
GUID; `cad.rs`): the bytes of its file, kept as they were and read again when the project opens (a file holds them deflated and in
base64, `CadFile`), the file's name, and, for a linked drawing, its path. `MAX_CADS` drawings and `MAX_HELD` bytes among them
are the most a project holds, and `cad::deserialize_cads` holds a file to them while it is read. `Cad::bulk` is the box round
what the drawing draws with what lies far from the rest left out (more than `FAR` times the spread of the middle of it from the
middle; a stray point at a survey's origin), which centring, zooming and the extents use; `far` counts what it left out.

A `CadImport` element places a drawing: on a `level`, in each of its plans or, with `view`, in that plan only (Revit's Current
view only), its `origin` (in the drawing's units) on `at` (mm), at a `scale` (mm to each of its units) and turned by `angle`
about `at`. It holds the layers it hides everywhere (`hidden`, by name) and how it colours (`colors`: preserve, invert, as on a
dark screen, or black). `cad_place` and `cad_unplace` take a point of the drawing to the model and back. `Model::check` holds it
to a drawing the project has, a level, a view of that level, a scale within `CAD_SCALE`, the names of layers it has, and its
bulk within `MAX_COORD` once placed (a survey's coordinates far off say to place it nearer the origin, with `position`: center).
The engine removes a drawing nothing places after each command, and forgets the layers views hide of it; undo brings both back.

## Commands

- `import_cad` reads a file (`path`) or places one the project holds again (`cad`). Its units are auto (the file's, else mm),
  a unit given, or a `scale`; `position` puts its middle (center, the default) or its origin on `at`; `layers` shows those its
  file has on (visible), all, or a list; `link` remembers the file. It returns what came in: the unit, the counts, the extents,
  the entities far off and what was left out.
- `cad_layers` lists an import's layers with their colours and linetypes and which are shown, and hides or shows them
  everywhere or, with `view`, in that view (its Visibility/Graphics, which `graphics` also sets with `layers`).
- `reload_cad` reads a linked drawing's file again; opening a project does so for each (`cads_not_reloaded` names those whose
  file is gone, which keep what they had).
- `cad_query` names the entity nearest a point: its layer, kind, colour and linetype (Revit's Query).
- `move`, `rotate`, `copy` and `delete` take an import as any element; `mirror` is refused, since a drawing's text would read
  backwards; `modify` changes its level, `at`, `angle`, `scale` and `colors`.

## Drawing and snapping

`render::cad_imports` draws a plan's imports under all the rest but its scans, as Revit draws an import in the background: each
entity of a layer the import and the view show, in its colour (the view's ink when it has none or the import draws in black),
its pen (`Cad::pen`, the entity's or its layer's line weight) and its dashes (`Cad::dash`, its linetype by `$LTSCALE`, scaled to
the view, left solid when a dash would be under a pixel). Text is lettered with `font.rs` at its height, turned and aligned; a
solid hatch is filled. What lies outside the view is passed over, so a large site plan zoomed in draws only what's on screen. An
import is one element: picked by any of its lines, selected whole. Sections, elevations and the 3D view leave imports out, as
Revit's do for a drawing placed in a plan; IFC export leaves them out too. The category is `cadimport`, Revit's Imported
Categories: Visibility/Graphics hides it or halftones it in a view like any other.

`snap.rs` gathers a plan's imports' endpoints, midpoints and centres, and their segments for crossings and nearest points, so a
wall drawn from corner to corner of a drawing lies on its lines; a layer hidden isn't snapped to.

## The desktop

Insert > Link CAD (in the Link panel) and Import CAD (a panel of its own) ask for a file, then a box (`crates/ui-egui/src/cad.rs`)
for its name, colours, layers (visible or all), units (auto-detect, or one), positioning (center to center, or origin to origin)
and whether it's for the current view only; it runs `import_cad` on the plan on screen's level, selects what came in, and keeps
the box open with the reason when a file can't come in. The Properties palette shows an import's drawing, file, unit, counts,
level, position, angle and scale, and a drop-down for its colours. Visibility/Graphics has an Imported Categories tab: the
category's row, and under each drawing of the project a check box for each of its layers, cleared for those the view hides. A right click on linked drawings selected offers Reload CAD, which runs `reload_cad` for each.

# Point clouds

On the roadmap under 0.9 Interoperability. A project holds scans and places them, the 3D view, plans and sections draw them,
plans snap to them, and the desktop brings them in (Insert > Point Cloud). IFC leaves them out, as Revit's export does: IFC4 has
no point cloud, and `ifc_leaves_scans_out_as_revit_does` keeps the file what it was without them.

Point clouds (`cloud.rs`) come from public specifications: PTS and XYZ text, PLY (text or either byte order) and ASPRS LAS 1.0
to 1.4 uncompressed, and ASTM E57 (`Format::from_extension` says why LAZ and ReCap's RCP/RCS don't). `cloud::read` parses a file twice,
once to measure it (`Stats`: the count, the bounds, the ranges of intensity and colour) and once to keep it: every `stride`th
point so `Options::cap` is never passed, then one in each cube of `spacing`, the same every time. A `Scan` keeps its points as
`f32` about `origin`, the middle of its bounds, so a survey's coordinates far off keep their millimetres within `MAX_SPAN`;
colour comes in eight bits whether the file has eight, sixteen or nought to one, and intensity alone is grey.

E57 (ASTM E2807, `cloud/e57.rs`) is read from the standard with no library: the 48-byte header, pages of 1024 bytes whose last
four are a CRC-32C (`Paged` reads the 1020 logical bytes of each; the checksums aren't checked, so a page that lies reads as
points that lie, never a crash), and the XML section, read by a small parser of its own (elements, attributes, text, CDATA;
capped in depth and size). Every `data3D` scan comes in, placed by its `pose` (a quaternion and a translation), as one `Scan`
whose `read` is the sum of their `recordCount`s. Each scan's points are a CompressedVector: a section header, then data packets
whose bytestreams, one for each field of the `prototype`, are bit-packed and run on from packet to packet; `Pack` decodes
Float (single or double), Integer and ScaledInteger, and only bit-packing, the one codec E57 writes, is read. Cartesian or
spherical coordinates both come in, a point marked invalid doesn't, and colour is scaled from `colorLimits` (or its field's
range) to eight bits. `images2D` is passed over. A file is held to `Caps` before anything is unpacked: up to 4096 scans, 100 million
points in all of them, 32 fields to a point, no two scans on one section, a section with room for the bits its count asks for (a
field of no bits is legal, so eight points can share a byte), and no stream more than 4 MiB ahead of the others. The tests write E57 files of their own (`e57` in the module's tests), with
values that cross packets and pages; the reference survey's 177 MB file reads its 6.6 million points in under two seconds.

A project holds each scan once, by name, as a `Cloud` in `Model::clouds` (a library entry of kind `Cloud`, so it has an id and a
GUID): its points and colours shared behind an `Arc`, the file it came from, and where its middle was there. A project file holds
it as `CloudFile`, the points as little-endian `f32` and the colours as bytes, each deflated and in base64, packed once and kept

A project holds up to `MAX_CLOUDS` scans and `MAX_CLOUD_POINTS` points among them (`Model::check`), so the `point_cloud` command
thins a new one to what the others leave. A project file is held to the same while it is read, not after: `Model::clouds` reads
through `cloud::deserialize_scans`, which refuses the entry past the count, and the scan that takes the points past the budget,
before unpacking the next (unpacking is where the memory goes, and the file is read twice, by the lenient walk and the strict read).

A survey's stations come in as one scan, as ReCap gathers a project's scans and Revit links the project: `path` may be a list of
up to `MAX_STATIONS` files. Each is read with an even share of what the project leaves, and `cloud::merge` puts them about the
middle of them all, keeps one point in each cube of `spacing` across them (so where stations overlap they aren't kept twice), and

no point cloud, and `ifc_leaves_scans_out_as_revit_does` keeps the file what it was without them.

Point clouds (`cloud.rs`) come from public specifications: PTS and XYZ text, PLY (text or either byte order) and ASPRS LAS 1.0
to 1.4 uncompressed, and ASTM E57 (`Format::from_extension` says why LAZ and ReCap's RCP/RCS don't). `cloud::read` parses a file twice,
once to measure it (`Stats`: the count, the bounds, the ranges of intensity and colour) and once to keep it: every `stride`th
point so `Options::cap` is never passed, then one in each cube of `spacing`, the same every time. A `Scan` keeps its points as
`f32` about `origin`, the middle of its bounds, so a survey's coordinates far off keep their millimetres within `MAX_SPAN`;
colour comes in eight bits whether the file has eight, sixteen or nought to one, and intensity alone is grey.

four are a CRC-32C (`Paged` reads the 1020 logical bytes of each; the checksums aren't checked, so a page that lies reads as
points that lie, never a crash), and the XML section, read by a small parser of its own (elements, attributes, text, CDATA;
capped in depth and size). Every `data3D` scan comes in, placed by its `pose` (a quaternion and a translation), as one `Scan`
whose `read` is the sum of their `recordCount`s. Each scan's points are a CompressedVector: a section header, then data packets
whose bytestreams, one for each field of the `prototype`, are bit-packed and run on from packet to packet; `Pack` decodes
Float (single or double), Integer and ScaledInteger, and only bit-packing, the one codec E57 writes, is read. Cartesian or
spherical coordinates both come in, a point marked invalid doesn't, and colour is scaled from `colorLimits` (or its field's
range) to eight bits. `images2D` is passed over. A file is held to `Caps` before anything is unpacked: up to 4096 scans, 100 million
points in all of them, 32 fields to a point, no two scans on one section, a section with room for the bits its count asks for (a
field of no bits is legal, so eight points can share a byte), and no stream more than 4 MiB ahead of the others. The tests write E57 files of their own (`e57` in the module's tests), with
values that cross packets and pages; the reference survey's 177 MB file reads its 6.6 million points in under two seconds.

A project holds each scan once, by name, as a `Cloud` in `Model::clouds` (a library entry of kind `Cloud`, so it has an id and a
GUID): its points and colours shared behind an `Arc`, the file it came from, and where its middle was there. A project file holds
it as `CloudFile`, the points as little-endian `f32` and the colours as bytes, each deflated and in base64, packed once and kept

through `cloud::deserialize_scans`, which refuses the entry past the count, and the scan that takes the points past the budget,

it, and greyed out when a view template controls the categories. It sets the category's override and no other: `Look::of` applies the

thins a new one to what the others leave. A project file is held to the same while it is read, not after: `Model::clouds` reads
through `cloud::deserialize_scans`, which refuses the entry past the count, and the scan that takes the points past the budget,
before unpacking the next (unpacking is where the memory goes, and the file is read twice, by the lenient walk and the strict read).

A survey's stations come in as one scan, as ReCap gathers a project's scans and Revit links the project: `path` may be a list of
up to `MAX_STATIONS` files. Each is read with an even share of what the project leaves, and `cloud::merge` puts them about the
middle of them all, keeps one point in each cube of `spacing` across them (so where stations overlap they aren't kept twice), and
greys a file with no colours among ones with. The `Cloud` keeps a `Station` for each file, its name and its share of the points
in order, so a view may one day show or hide a station; it is known by the first file's name, and the element's JSON lists the
stations. A list of one is that file alone.

A `PointCloud` element places a scan, as a component places a family: its `cloud` (a library name, a GUID in a file), its `level`,
its middle at `at` and `offset` over the level, turned `angle` degrees about it; `Model::cloud_place` is that transform and
`Model::cloud_box` the box round what it places. It holds no `params`, so phases, design options and paint don't reach it. It moves,
turns and copies as any element; it doesn't mirror, since a scan is what was measured. The `point_cloud` command brings a file in
(`path`) or places a held scan again (`cloud`); by default its middle goes on `at` and its foot on the level (Revit's Auto - Center
to Center), and with `origin: file` where the file's coordinates put it (Origin to Origin) when that is within `MAX_COORD`. A scan
that nothing places any more goes after the command that left it so (`Model::unplaced_clouds`, in `Session::execute`), and undo
brings it back with its element. Insert from File brings the scan with the element. IFC export leaves scans out.

The 3D view (`view3d.rs`) keeps each placed scan as a `Scan`: its points and colours shared with the model's, and where they
go. After the opaque surfaces are rasterised, `Scene::dots` draws each point as a square [`DOT`] pixels wide into the same
depth buffer, so what is nearer hides a scan and a scan hides what is behind it, and what the view sees through is drawn over
it. A point's pixel holds its scan's slot after the triangles', so it picks, box-selects and tints as its element; it has no
face to paint and draws no edge. Points are not lit: they keep the scan's colours, grey (`cloud::GREY`) for a scan with none,
or the colour the view's projection fill gives. A picture draws at most `DRAWN` points, an even share of each scan's past
that, as Revit's density does. The view fits round its scans, and a level's plane reaches past them (`Model::model_extent`).
A 3D view's section box keeps a scan's points inside it and no others, so its floors and ceilings can be cut away to show the walls to
model against ([views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)); in a plan the view range does it, or the box itself when the plan follows it. Views hide and override point clouds by element or by the category `pointcloud` (`graphics::SCANS`, apart from `MODEL`:
Revit has a tab of its own for them in Visibility/Graphics, and Object Styles no row). The graphics card doesn't draw them
yet: `gpu::Mesh::new` refuses a view that shows one, and the processor draws it. The wireframe style leaves them out.

A section's or an elevation's picture is the same rasteriser with a `Clip`, and `Scene::dots` keeps a point as `raster` keeps a
pixel: between the line and the far clip, inside the crop. A plan draws what its view range sees, from the cut plane down to
the view depth (`render::scans`, under everything else), from above: each point a dot `DOT` pixels wide in its colour or the
view's, the highest at each pixel on top, `DRAWN` among the scans as in 3D. Each scan is one `Prim::Image` owned by its
element, no bigger than its dots and clear between them; a picture picks where it isn't clear (`drawn_near` in `Drawing::pick_all`),
so a click between a scan's points finds what is there, and a sheet's opaque pictures pick as they did. A PDF masks a picture
that isn't all there with its alpha (`/SMask`), and an SVG holds it as a PNG. A reflected ceiling plan leaves scans out. The
desktop's plan canvas loads a drawing's pictures as textures once for as long as it is shown (`PlanCache::pictures`) and, on a
dark canvas, dims them so the lightened ink over them still reads. A scan the view fills with one colour (its projection's fill,
`Look::filled`) is ink itself: its picture is marked `ink` and the dark canvas leaves it undimmed.

A scan's own colours are mid-tones that read poorly over paper or the dark canvas, so the view control bar (`footer.rs`) has
High Contrast Point Clouds wherever the project or a model it links holds a scan (the bar asks the model the views draw whether it holds
one, which is cheap because a command drops a scan nothing places): it fills the view's `pointcloud` category with `HIGH_CONTRAST`, a
crimson that reads on both and apart from the model's black lines (or the colour the user picks in Settings > Graphics, kept
as `high_contrast` in `settings.json` and read back only when it is `[r, g, b]`), through the `graphics` command (merged into the category's
override, so its halftone or lines stay), and again takes the fill away. It is lit whenever the category has a fill, whoever set
it, and greyed out when a view template controls the categories. It sets the category's override and no other: `Look::of` applies the
category's, then each view filter's, then the element's own, the last prevailing, so a scan given a colour of its own in
Visibility/Graphics (or picked out by a filter that fills) keeps it whatever the button does. The button is lit for the category
and can't tell, since what the scans come to is the whole `Look` for every frame of the bar; its tooltip says so instead.

A plan snaps to a scan where its cut plane cuts it, to trace what was measured: of the points within `snap::CUT_BAND` of the cut,
the nearest to the cursor seen from above (`Kind::Point`, "Point Cloud", switched by `Snaps::cloud` in Manage > Snaps). It comes
after what the model has to snap to (ends, middles, centres, crossings), so a wall's end beats a point nearer the cursor, and
before the perpendicular, the angle guides and a wall's centre line. `snap::cloud_point` turns the cursor into each shown scan's
own terms and asks `Cloud::nearest`, which looks only in the squares of the scan's `Grid` (its points by `CELL` mm squares from
above, made the first time something snaps to it and shared by its clones) that the reach touches, so a snap on millions of points
costs microseconds.

In the desktop (`clouds.rs`), Insert > Point Cloud, in the Insert tab's Link panel beside Link Model as in Revit, asks for one
file or several (`BimApp::ask_files`: a dialog's answer is a list of paths now) and opens `CloudBox`: its name (the first file's),
the units of its coordinates, a spacing, and Revit's positioning, Auto - Center to Center or Auto - Origin to Origin. OK runs
`point_cloud` on the level of the plan on screen and selects what it placed; a refusal stays in the box with its reason
(`point_cloud_paths` opens the box, what a test hands the files to). The Properties palette shows a point cloud's level and offset
(edited), its scan, file and points, its origin and angle; Visibility/Graphics lists `pointcloud` after the model's categories.
# Importing and linking CAD drawings

On the roadmap under 0.9 Interoperability, as Revit's Import CAD and Link CAD: a consultant's or a surveyor's DXF drawing
brought into a project and drawn under the model in the plans of a level, to trace walls over and to check against. A project
holds each drawing once, an import element places it, plans draw and snap to it, and the desktop brings one in (Insert > Import
CAD, Link CAD). A DWG comes in as the DXF it becomes (below); DXF export, exploding an import into detail lines (which waits on detail lines, issue #58), and
images and PDFs as underlays are still to come.

## The reader

`dxf.rs` reads ASCII DXF of any version from Autodesk's public DXF reference: pairs of a group code and a value, read in
sections. From the header it takes `$INSUNITS` (the drawing's unit, `Dxf::unit` and `Dxf::scale`, mm to each of its units),
`$ACADVER` and `$LTSCALE`; from the tables its layers (colour, off when the colour is negative, frozen by flag, linetype, line
weight) and its linetypes' dash patterns; from the blocks section the blocks; and from the entities section what model space
draws (an entity with code 67 set is paper space's, and left out). Entities come in as a short list of `Shape`s, in the
drawing's own units: LINE, LWPOLYLINE and POLYLINE (bulges become arcs; a 3D mesh or polyface is left out), CIRCLE, ARC,
ELLIPSE (as a polyline), SPLINE (its fit points, else its control points), POINT, TEXT and MTEXT (its formatting codes taken
out, aligned as the file says), SOLID and TRACE, and HATCH (its boundary loops, solid or patterned; a patterned one is drawn as a
pale fill of its colour, since its pattern isn't kept). An INSERT places its block's entities, scaled, turned and arrayed, up to
`MAX_DEPTH` blocks deep; an entity on layer 0 of a block takes the insert's layer, and one by block its colour. DIMENSION draws
its anonymous block. What the reader doesn't know (3DFACE, a viewport, an image, a proxy) is counted by kind in
`Dxf::left_out`, and the command lists it. The text itself is read as UTF-8 where it is, and else by the code page the header names in
`$DWGCODEPAGE`: the East Asian pages and the Windows ones decode through `encoding_rs`, and a page without a decoder here (the DOS
ones) reads as Latin-1, as it always has.

A file is hostile: `MAX_BYTES` caps its size, `MAX_PAIRS` its pairs, `MAX_SHAPES` the shapes, `MAX_WORK` the points the blocks
may multiply into, and every coordinate is a finite number within `MAX_FILE_COORD` (one past that is left out as "past what a
drawing holds"). A file that ends after a group code, a value that isn't a number, a binary DXF and a DWG each say why.

## DWG

The core reads no DWG of its own. `crates/dwg` (`bimcraft-dwg`) is a bridge: the acadrust crate (pure Rust, MPL-2.0, used
unmodified as a separate library; its DWG code is ported from ACadSharp, MIT, after the Open Design Alliance's published DWG
specification; NOTICE carries both) reads the file in failsafe mode, and its DXF writer writes what it read as ASCII DXF, which
`dxf.rs` reads as any other. `Limits` holds a DWG to 64 MB before the decoder runs and its DXF to `dxf::MAX_BYTES` while it is
written; a read that left object records out says how many, of which kinds, in `import_cad`'s `notes` (the desktop puts them on
the status bar). The project holds the DXF, so a project file opens where no DWG reader is.

A session reads a DWG through the `DwgReader` it is given (`Session::dwg`; `read_dxf_file` in `commands.rs` is the one place
`import_cad`, `reload_cad` and opening a project read a drawing), and one without says to save it as DXF. The desktop and the
command line (so MCP too) hand theirs `bimcraft_dwg::reader()` behind their default `dwg` feature: it starts the program
itself as a child (`--dwg-to-dxf <path>`, answered by `child_main` before anything else runs) and reads the DXF from its
output. The decoder allocates what a file declares and can't be interrupted, so a hostile file could abort the process; in
the child it takes only the child, which is also stopped after `CHILD_TIME` or past the limits, and the reply says the file
couldn't be read. Tests make their DWG files from DXF text with the same library (`dwg_from_dxf`, the `testing` feature),
since Autodesk's are never committed; `BIMCRAFT_DWG_SAMPLES` names a folder of real ones for
`real_drawings_where_a_folder_of_them_is_named`, and `apps/bimcraft-cli/tests/dwg.rs` drives the child.

## The project

A project holds each drawing once, by name, as a `Cad` in `Model::cads` (a library entry of kind `Cad`, so it has an id and a
GUID; `cad.rs`): the bytes of its file, kept as they were and read again when the project opens (a file holds them deflated and in
base64, `CadFile`), the file's name, and, for a linked drawing, its path. `MAX_CADS` drawings and `MAX_HELD` bytes among them
are the most a project holds, and `cad::deserialize_cads` holds a file to them while it is read. `Cad::bulk` is the box round
what the drawing draws with what lies far from the rest left out (more than `FAR` times the spread of the middle of it from the
middle; a stray point at a survey's origin), which centring, zooming and the extents use; `far` counts what it left out.

A `CadImport` element places a drawing: on a `level`, in each of its plans or, with `view`, in that plan only (Revit's Current
view only), its `origin` (in the drawing's units) on `at` (mm), at a `scale` (mm to each of its units) and turned by `angle`
about `at`. It holds the layers it hides everywhere (`hidden`, by name) and how it colours (`colors`: preserve, invert, as on a
dark screen, or black). `cad_place` and `cad_unplace` take a point of the drawing to the model and back. `Model::check` holds it
to a drawing the project has, a level, a view of that level, a scale within `CAD_SCALE`, the names of layers it has, and its
bulk within `MAX_COORD` once placed (a survey's coordinates far off say to place it nearer the origin, with `position`: center).
The engine removes a drawing nothing places after each command, and forgets the layers views hide of it; undo brings both back.

## Commands

- `import_cad` reads a file (`path`) or places one the project holds again (`cad`). Its units are auto (the file's, else mm),
  a unit given, or a `scale`; `position` puts its middle (center, the default) or its origin on `at`; `layers` shows those its
  file has on (visible), all, or a list; `link` remembers the file. It returns what came in: the unit, the counts, the extents,
  the entities far off and what was left out.
- `cad_layers` lists an import's layers with their colours and linetypes and which are shown, and hides or shows them
  everywhere or, with `view`, in that view (its Visibility/Graphics, which `graphics` also sets with `layers`).
- `reload_cad` reads a linked drawing's file again; opening a project does so for each (`cads_not_reloaded` names those whose
  file is gone, which keep what they had).
- `cad_query` names the entity nearest a point: its layer, kind, colour and linetype (Revit's Query).
- `move`, `rotate`, `copy` and `delete` take an import as any element; `mirror` is refused, since a drawing's text would read
  backwards; `modify` changes its level, `at`, `angle`, `scale` and `colors`.

## Drawing and snapping

`render::cad_imports` draws a plan's imports under all the rest but its scans, as Revit draws an import in the background: each
entity of a layer the import and the view show, in its colour (the view's ink when it has none or the import draws in black),
its pen (`Cad::pen`, the entity's or its layer's line weight) and its dashes (`Cad::dash`, its linetype by `$LTSCALE`, scaled to
the view, left solid when a dash would be under a pixel). Text is lettered with `font.rs` at its height, turned and aligned; a
solid hatch is filled. What lies outside the view is passed over, so a large site plan zoomed in draws only what's on screen. An
import is one element: picked by any of its lines, selected whole. Sections, elevations and the 3D view leave imports out, as
Revit's do for a drawing placed in a plan; IFC export leaves them out too. The category is `cadimport`, Revit's Imported
Categories: Visibility/Graphics hides it or halftones it in a view like any other.

`snap.rs` gathers a plan's imports' endpoints, midpoints and centres, and their segments for crossings and nearest points, so a
wall drawn from corner to corner of a drawing lies on its lines; a layer hidden isn't snapped to.

## The desktop

Insert > Link CAD (in the Link panel) and Import CAD (a panel of its own) ask for a file, then a box (`crates/ui-egui/src/cad.rs`)
for its name, colours, layers (visible or all), units (auto-detect, or one), positioning (center to center, or origin to origin)
and whether it's for the current view only; it runs `import_cad` on the plan on screen's level, selects what came in, and keeps
the box open with the reason when a file can't come in. The Properties palette shows an import's drawing, file, unit, counts,
level, position, angle and scale, and a drop-down for its colours. Visibility/Graphics has an Imported Categories tab: the
category's row, and under each drawing of the project a check box for each of its layers, cleared for those the view hides. A right click on linked drawings selected offers Reload CAD, which runs `reload_cad` for each.

steps.message: Let me survey the `info` command on all the RVT assets to see the scale of that feature.

arguments.command: cd /tmp && for f in /workspace/assets/test_revit/*.rvt; do echo "=== $(basename $f)"; /workspace/executable info "$f" 2>&1 | head -30; echo "EXIT: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; done 2>&1 | head -400
arguments.description: Run info on RVT test assets

raw_arguments.command: cd /tmp && for f in /workspace/assets/test_revit/*.rvt; do echo "=== $(basename $f)"; /workspace/executable info "$f" 2>&1 | head -30; echo "EXIT: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; done 2>&1 | head -400
raw_arguments.description: Run info on RVT test assets

steps.message: Let me save all outputs to files for systematic reference.

arguments.command: mkdir -p /tmp/obs/revit_info && cd /tmp && for f in /workspace/assets/test_revit/* /workspace/assets/test_imports/*; do b=$(basename $f); d=$(basename $(dirname $f)); /workspace/executable info "$f" > /tmp/obs/revit_info/$d.$b.out 2> /tmp/obs/revit_info/$d.$b.err; echo $? > /tmp/obs/revit_info/$d.$b.code; done; cat /tmp/obs/revit_info/test_revit.atom_bad_deflate.rvt.out; cat /tmp/obs/revit_info/test_revit.atom_bad_deflate.rvt.err
arguments.description: Save info outputs for all RVT assets

raw_arguments.command: mkdir -p /tmp/obs/revit_info && cd /tmp && for f in /workspace/assets/test_revit/* /workspace/assets/test_imports/*; do b=$(basename $f); d=$(basename $(dirname $f)); /workspace/executable info "$f" > /tmp/obs/revit_info/$d.$b.out 2> /tmp/obs/revit_info/$d.$b.err; echo $? > /tmp/obs/revit_info/$d.$b.code; done; cat /tmp/obs/revit_info/test_revit.atom_bad_deflate.rvt.out; cat /tmp/obs/revit_info/test_revit.atom_bad_deflate.rvt.err
raw_arguments.description: Save info outputs for all RVT assets

arguments.command: cd /tmp/obs/revit_info && for f in *.code; do b=${f%.code}; c=$(cat $f); if [ "$c" != "0" ]; then echo "[$c] $b: $(cat $b.err | head -3)"; fi; done
arguments.description: Show failing info runs with errors

Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)\n## add_point [] | Add Point | None\n{id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height\n## add_split_line [] | Add Split Line | None\n{id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now\n## reset_shape [] | Reset Shape | None\n{id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again\n## falls [] | Falls | None\n{id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain\n## mass ['MS'] | Mass | None\n{boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`\n## mass_floors ['MF'] | Mass Floors | None\n{mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level\n## wall_by_face ['WB'] | Wall by Face | None\n{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on\n## floor_by_face ['FB'] | Floor by Face | None\n{mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on\n## roof_by_face ['RB'] | Roof by Face | None\n{mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on\n## update_by_face ['UF'] | Update to Face | None\n{mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`\n## show_mass ['MH'] | Show Mass | None\n{view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's\n## room ['RM'] | Room | Architecture > Room\n{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen\n## room_separator [] | Room Separator | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids\n## rebar [] | Rebar | None\n{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule\n## reinforce [] | Reinforce | None\n{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` \"NBR 6118\" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes\n## reinforcement_preset [] | Reinforcement Presets | None\n{name?, kind?: beam|column|footing|floor, params?, rename?, delete?: true} a named set of the parameters `reinforce` takes for one kind of host (`params`: its `cover`, `grade`, `grade_stirrup`, `clearance` and what its kind takes, and not `host`), kept in the project; `reinforce` with `preset` takes it and lets what is given with it replace its own. Without `name`, lists them. It is not checked against any host until it arms one\n## voltage [] | Voltage Definitions | None\n{name?, nominal?, min?, max?, rename?, delete?: true} a voltage of the project's electrical settings, in volts: `nominal`, and the band a device may read within, `min` to `max` (10 per cent either way unless given). Without `name`, lists them. A voltage a distribution system names cannot be deleted; renamed, the systems follow\n## distribution_system [] | Distribution Systems | None\n{name?, phases?: 1|2|3, wires?, l_l?, l_n?, l_g?, ground?, rename?, delete?: true} a distribution system of the project's electrical settings. `wires` counts the line conductors and the neutral, not the protective one (3 phases: 3 or 4). `l_l`, `l_n` and `l_g` name the voltages between two lines, a line and the neutral, and a line and earth (at least one; `l_l` from 2 phases; with 3 phases `l_l` is about 1.73 times `l_n`), each a `voltage` of the project; \"\" takes one away. `ground` is the earthing: TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT or IT. A voltage the project lacks is refused, and the refusal lists the ones it has. Without `name`, lists them\n## wire_type [] | Wire Types | None\n{name?, material?: copper|aluminium, temperature?, insulation?, note?, sizes?: [{section, ampacity, label?}], rename?, delete?: true} a wire type of the project's electrical settings: a conductor's `material`, working `temperature` (°C) and `insulation`, and its table, `sizes`: the `section` of each row in mm² (smallest first, never less than the row before) and the `ampacity` it carries in amperes, with a `label` for how its standard names it (12 AWG). Giving `sizes` replaces the table. `note` says where the ampacities come from. Without `name`, lists them\n## column ['CL'] | Column | Architecture > Column\n{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`\n## structural_column ['CL'] | Structural Column | None\n{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one\n## footing ['FI'] | Isolated Footing | None\n{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below\n## beam ['BM'] | Beam | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°\n## strip_footing ['FW'] | Wall Footing | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)\n## pipe ['PI'] | Pipe | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to (\"Água fria\", \"Esgoto\")\n## duct ['DU'] | Duct | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to (\"Supply air\", \"Exhaust\")\n## conduit ['CN'] | Conduit | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit\n## cable_tray ['CT'] | Cable Tray | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep\n## wire ['EW'] | Wire | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit\n## down_conductor ['DC'] | Down Conductor | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to\n## ground_conductor ['GC'] | Earthing Conductor | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)\n## cabling ['CB'] | Cabling | None\n{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to\n## stair [] | Stair | Architecture > Stair\n{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too\n", "numLines": 121, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 121}}
