Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)\n## section_box [] | Section Box | None\n{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again\n## perspective [] | Perspective | None\n{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands\n## graphic_display_options ['GD'] | Graphic Display Options | None\n{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), edges?: true | false, silhouette?: px, ambient_shadows?: true | false} how a 3D view draws its edges and shadows, as Revit's Graphic Display Options: `edges`, the lines where its surfaces meet in Shaded (on unless turned off; Hidden Line always draws them); `silhouette`, an outline that many pixels wide (a whole number, 0 to 10; 0, the default, for none) round what stands in front of what is further off or of nothing; `ambient_shadows`, soft shadows where faces meet inside a corner (off unless turned on). What is left out stays as it was; with none of them it only says what the view has\n## camera [] | Camera | None\n{eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number (\"Camera 1\", \"Camera 2\"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in\n## work_plane [] | Work Plane | None\n{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level\n## filter [] | View Filter | None\n{name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one\n## template [] | View Template | None\n{name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one\n## phase [] | Phasing | Manage > Phasing\n{name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides\n## phase_filter [] | Phase Filter | Manage > Phasing\n{name, new?, existing?, demolished?, temporary?, delete?} a phase filter: how a view shows each status of what's in its phase, each `by-category` (as its category and the view's overrides say), `overridden` (as the project's overrides for that status say) or `not-displayed`. A project has Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New; any may change. A new one starts by category throughout. One in use by a view or a template can't be deleted. Replies with the filter\n## option [] | Design Options | Manage > Design Options\n{set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)\n## measure ['ME'] | Measure | None\n{from: [x, y], to: [x, y]} what a ruler laid between two points reads (mm): its `length`, its parts `dx` and `dy`, and its `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing\n## circuit [] | Size a Circuit | None\n{load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it\n## conduit_fill [] | Conduit Fill | None\n{section, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, circuits?, reduced_neutral?, family?, size?} the fill of a conduit as NBR 5410 asks, for the conductors of a circuit (its phases, neutral and protective conductor, of `section` mm²) times `circuits` in the same conduit (1): their cross-sections by outside diameter over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. `family` (pvc-thread, pvc-solder, steel-heavy, steel-rir; pvc-thread) and `size` (its mark, e.g. 3/4\"; none: the smallest that fits). The dimensions are the makers' own from their catalogues, each family naming maker, document, page and address; the inside diameter is the outside less twice the wall. The data covers the flexible 750 V PVC cable of 0.5 to 240 mm² only: there is no `insulation` key, and a section above 240 mm² is `pending`, never guessed. `sections_mm2` lists the conductors of one circuit (`circuits` of them are in the conduit). Cable trays are not sized. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## drain_size [] | Size a Sanitary Drain | None\n{units?, fixtures?: {wc?, lav?, sink?, shower?, laundry?}, role?: branch|main|stack, slope?, floors?, min_dn?} the DN of a sanitary drain as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) it carries: `units`, or `fixtures` counted (Tabela 3: a water closet 6 UHC and DN 100, a lavatory 1 and 40, a sink 3 and 50, a shower 2 and 40, a laundry tub 3 and 40; the drain is never smaller than the fixtures' own). `role`: a `branch` (ramal de esgoto, Tabela 5, the default), a `main` (subcoletor or coletor predial, Tabela 7 by `slope`, a fraction, 0.01 by default; DN 100 at least) or a `stack` (tubo de queda, Tabela 6 by the building's `floors`, up to three or more). `min_dn` is the largest drain flowing into it. Replies with the `dn`, what it carries (`capacity`) and the `minimum_dn` the fixtures ask. A blank in the standard's table means not allowed: DN 100 and 150 carry nothing in a building drain at 0.5 %, and a branch or a building drain never borrows the other's table. For a `main` every fixture given counts, where item 5.1.4.2 counts only the largest fixture of each bathroom in a residential building: pass `units` already reduced to follow it. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## vent_size [] | Size a Sanitary Vent | None\n{units, wc?, stack_dn?, length?, trap_dn?} the DN of a sanitary vent as NBR 8160 asks, by the units (UHC) of what it vents: a branch vent (ramal de ventilação, Tabela 8; `wc` says a water closet is in the group), or, with `stack_dn` (the DN of the stack or drain served) and `length` (mm, from its foot to its open end), a vent stack or header (Tabela 2). `trap_dn` adds the longest run from a trap of that DN to its vent (Tabela 1). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## hydrant_size [] | Size Hydrants | None\n{column?: 1-5, area?, type?: 1|2|3|4-40|4-65|5, hydrants?, inside?, nominal?, material?: steel|steel-wet|copper|pvc|pex, length?, rise?} hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks. With `column` (of Tabela 3, by the occupation) and `area` (m², built) it replies the system type and the fire reserve (m³). With `type` (Tabela 2; 4 comes as 4-40 or 4-65 by its nozzle) it replies the design flow, that of the two most unfavourable jets (`hydrants`, 2 by default), and the head at the nozzle; with `inside` (mm) it also replies the speed (5 m/s at most), the Hazen-Williams head loss over `length` (m) of the `material` (Tabela 1: `steel` is black steel in a dry system, C 100, the lowest steel row and the default, `steel-wet` is galvanised or wet, C 120), the head needed at the start of the pipe with its `rise` (mm, up) and, with `nominal` (mm), whether the pipe is big enough (DN 65; DN 50 for types 1 and 2). `length` and `rise` are in millimetres. `need_mca` is the nozzle head + the head loss of the straight pipe + the rise: it leaves out the hose, the fittings and the pressure at the source (`need_covers` says so), and `ok` is only the nozzle head within 100 mca, the speed and the pipe's size (`ok_covers`), not a verdict on the design. A `type` that contradicts `column` and `area` is an error. Notes 1 and 2 of Tabela 3 (a system one type lower in some cases) are not applied. `region` is SP, the only one: this is the São Paulo rule, and no other state's. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## load_points [] | Residential Load Points | None\n{rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish. A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## water_size [] | Size Cold Water Pipes | None\n{fixtures?: {wc, lav, sink, shower, laundry: count}, flow?, method?: weights|sum, dn?, length?, fittings?: {elbow90, elbow45, tee_through, tee_side, gate, globe, check: count}, pressure?, rise?} a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/s), or the design flow of the `fixtures` by the `method` the project chooses: weights (the empirical method, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, never more than the fixtures' own flows; the default) or sum (every fixture at once). The fixture flows and weights are Tigre's (Manual Técnico, page 198), not the standard's; `wc` is the WC with a flush tank only (a flush-valve WC is not in the table here). Without `dn` it replies the smallest DN chosen by speed alone (3 m/s at most; the pressure is not used to choose it); with `dn`, whether that pipe keeps the speed. The head loss is Darcy-Weisbach (Colebrook, PVC at 20 °C) over `length` (mm) plus the equivalent length of the `fittings`; with `pressure` (kPa, dynamic, upstream) and `rise` (mm, up) it replies the pressure left at the end, 10 kPa at least at a point of use, and `ok` covers both; without `pressure` `ok` is the speed alone (`ok_covers` says which). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## storm_size [] | Size a Storm Drain | None\n{kind: downpipe|horizontal, area?, rainfall?, flow?, outlet?: edge|funnel, gutter?, length?, slope?, inside?} a storm drain as NBR 10844 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/min), or the rain on `area` (m², as the standard counts a roof) at `rainfall` (mm/h; 150 by default, which the standard allows for up to 100 m² only: above that `rainfall` is required): Q = I·A/60. A `downpipe` (condutor vertical) takes the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses by Q, the water depth in the gutter `gutter` (50 to 100 mm), its `length` (mm, 0.3 m or more) and the gutter's `outlet` (edge: sharp-edged, the default; funnel); 70 mm inside at least. A `horizontal` drain takes Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, PVC only, from the standard's Table 2) at its `slope` (a fraction, 0.005 at least): the inner diameter it needs, and with `inside` (mm) whether that pipe carries the flow. Off the abacuses (more than 150 mm inside) nothing is read. A key that does not apply to the `kind`, or `flow` together with `area`, is an error. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing\n## library [] | Library | None\n{kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too\n## select_by_id [] | Select by ID | Manage > Select by ID\n{text} the elements a list names, each by its id, its GUID (dashes and braces or not) or its IFC GlobalId, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or lines: `ids` found, each once in the order named, `missing` (what named none), and `plan` and `extent` ([[x, y], [x, y]] mm), the level's plan that shows them and where; it selects nothing itself, a front end does\n## ids_of [] | IDs of Selection | Manage > IDs of Selection\n{ids: [id or GUID, …]} what names each element: its `id`, its `guid`, its `ifc` GlobalId, its `category` and its `name` (or type, number, mark)\n## filter_selection [] | Filter | None\n{ids: [id or GUID, …], by?, keep?: [value, …]} Revit's Filter on a selection: `groups` [{value, count, ids}, …], the values `by` takes among the elements (by default `Category`, whose values are categories' keys: wall, door, detail_line…; else a parameter as `fields` lists them, values as schedules show them, `\"\"` for none), and `fields`, the parameters every one of them has, to filter by. With `keep`, `ids`: those holding one of its values, the selection to keep; it selects nothing itself, a front end does\n## elements [] | Elements | None\n{category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do\n", "numLines": 105, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 105}}

## line_pattern [] | Line Patterns | None
{name?, segments?: [{dash: mm} | {space: mm} | "dot" | {dot_length: mm} | {offset: {length, count, distance}} | {wave: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {zigzag: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {text: {length, size, text}}, …], rename?, delete?: true} a line pattern of the project's: 1–32 freely ordered graphic segments, each 0.05–100 mm long on paper, so it reads the same at any scale. Offsets have 2–9 lines spaced symmetrically; frequency is cycles per segment, 0.1–100; amplitude and spacing are mm. Text uses bundled IBM Plex Sans, size is maximum capital height (shrinks to fit length), 1–256 single-line characters, following the curve. All graphics preserve the centerline. A project starts with Dash, Long Dash, Dot, Dash Dot, Hidden and Centre; Solid is a line with none. `rename` renames it, the line styles using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no style uses it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern
## line_style [] | Line Styles | Manage > Line Styles
{name?, pen?, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], pattern?: name | "Solid", rename?, delete?: true} a line style of the project's, as Revit's: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) its lines draw in, their colour (black unless told) and their line pattern. A new one needs `pen`; one changed keeps what it isn't given. A project starts with Hairline, Thin Lines, Medium Lines, Wide Lines, Hidden Lines, Centre Lines and Overhead Lines. `rename` renames it, the lines drawn in it following; `delete` takes it away, while no line is drawn in it. Without `name`, it lists every style
## fill_pattern [] | Fill Patterns | Manage > Fill Patterns
{name?, target?: drafting|model, lines?: [{angle, spacing, origin?: [x, y], shift?, dashes?: [mm, -mm, …]}, …], drawn?: scale | null, rename?, delete?: true} a fill pattern of the project's, as Revit's (and a PAT file's): families of parallel lines, each at `angle` degrees through `origin`, its lines `spacing` apart and each `shift` along from the last, whole or dashed (`dashes`: a dash's length, a space's as a negative one, 0 a dot); no lines, it fills solid. A drafting pattern's lengths are mm on paper, the same at any scale; a model pattern's mm in the building. A project starts with Solid fill, Diagonal Up and Down, Crosshatch, Diagonal Crosshatch, Horizontal, Vertical, Sand, Brick 225 x 75 and Tile 300. `rename` renames it, the region types filling with it following; `delete` takes it away while no type uses it. `drawn` is the scale (1 : n, its n) of the view one made of lines (`make_fill_pattern`) was drawn in: such a one given a new `target` and no `lines` is rescaled, a drafting one being the drawing on paper at that scale; null forgets it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern
## make_fill_pattern [] | Make Fill Pattern | None
{ids, from: [x, y], to: [x, y], name, target?: model|drafting} a fill pattern made of the detail lines `ids` (all of one view), as pyRevit's Make Pattern makes one: the rectangle between corners `from` and `to` (in the view's terms) is the tile the pattern repeats, and what of the lines lies outside it is cut off. Each line becomes a family that runs on into the next tiles' copies of itself; one at a slope that never meets itself again is turned to the simplest slope within 0.25° that does (else the nearest, at most 48 tiles across or up). A model pattern (the default) is as drawn; a drafting one is the drawing on paper, at the view's scale. The tile is 0.05 to 100000 each way, and holds at most 256 lines. It returns the pattern's `name` and the `pattern`
## linework ['LW'] | Linework | None
{view?, id, at: [x, y], style? | invisible?: true, remove?: true} Revit's Linework: the edge of element `id` that a plan (`view`, a level's or a plan view; the lowest level's by default) draws nearest `at` (within 200 mm), drawn in that view only in line style `style`, or not at all with `invisible`; `remove` takes the Linework nearest `at` off that edge again (one edge, even where another lies within reach; where that edge has none, the nearest entry within reach on an edge the element no longer draws, one a call). A view holds at most 2000 edges. It returns the edge, `from` and `to`, or with `remove` how many were `removed`
## import_fill_patterns [] | Import Fill Patterns | None
{path | text, replace?: false} the fill patterns of a PAT file (AutoCAD's and Revit's), from the file at `path` or as `text`: each `*Name` and its families of lines, in mm unless the file says `;%UNITS=INCH`, drafting unless a pattern says `;%TYPE=MODEL`. A pattern the project already has is left as it is unless `replace`; one that can't be a pattern (no lines, an offset of 0, dashes that are all spaces, too many families) is left out. A file is read up to its first 2000 patterns. It returns those `imported`, those `left_out` (the first 100, each with why) and `left_out_count`, all of them
## export_fill_patterns [] | Export Fill Patterns | None
{path?, names?: [name, …]} the project's fill patterns (those `names` says, else all but the solid ones, which a PAT file can't hold) as a PAT file in mm, written to `path`, or returned as `text` without it
## filled_region_type [] | Filled Region Types | None
{name?, foreground?: pattern | null, foreground_color?, background?: pattern | null, background_color?, masking?, rename?, delete?: true} a filled region type of the project's: its foreground pattern over its background one, each in its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), over the paper when `masking` (it hides what's under it). A new one starts with none. A project starts with Solid Black, Diagonal Up, Crosshatch, Sand, Brick and Masking. `rename` renames it, its regions following; `delete` takes it away while no region is of it. 56	{view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)
57	## section_box [] | Section Box | None
58	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again
59	## perspective [] | Perspective | None
60	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands
61	## graphic_display_options ['GD'] | Graphic Display Options | None
62	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), edges?: true | false, silhouette?: px, ambient_shadows?: true | false} how a 3D view draws its edges and shadows, as Revit's Graphic Display Options: `edges`, the lines where its surfaces meet in Shaded (on unless turned off; Hidden Line always draws them); `silhouette`, an outline that many pixels wide (a whole number, 0 to 10; 0, the default, for none) round what stands in front of what is further off or of nothing; `ambient_shadows`, soft shadows where faces meet inside a corner (off unless turned on). What is left out stays as it was; with none of them it only says what the view has
63	## camera [] | Camera | None
64	{eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in
65	## work_plane [] | Work Plane | None
66	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level
67	## filter [] | View Filter | None
68	{name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. 69	## template [] | View Template | None

Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one
71	## phase [] | Phasing | Manage > Phasing
72	{name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides

74	{name, new?, existing?, demolished?, temporary?, delete?} a phase filter: how a view shows each status of what's in its phase, each `by-category` (as its category and the view's overrides say), `overridden` (as the project's overrides for that status say) or `not-displayed`. A project has Show All, Show Complete, Show New, Show Previous + Demolished and Show Previous + New; any may change. A new one starts by category throughout. One in use by a view or a template can't be deleted. Replies with the filter

steps.message: GUIDs are random per project. I'll extract the per-language default project templates (GUIDs replaced with placeholders) into a Rust data file.

arguments.command:
mkdir -p /tmp/tpl && cd /tmp/tpl && for l in en pt es sv cs fr nl de it; do /workspace/executable run --cmd "new {\"language\": \"$l\"}" --save $l.bimcraft > /dev/null; done; /workspace/executable run --save default.bimcraft >/dev/null; python3 /tmp/tools/norm.py default.bimcraft > d.norm; python3 /tmp/tools/norm.py en.bimcraft > e.norm; diff d.norm e.norm && echo "default==en"; cat > /tmp/tools/mktpl.py <<'EOF'
import json, re, sys
langs = ['en','pt','es','sv','cs','fr','nl','de','it']
out = ['//! The default contents of a new project in each language: what `new` makes, with',
       '//! `@G<n>` standing for a GUID made fresh for each project.',
       '']
for l in langs:
    s = open(f'/tmp/tpl/{l}.bimcraft').read()
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": 0', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m:
            m[g] = '@G%d' % len(m)
        return m[g]
    s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
    d = json.loads(s)
    mini = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(',',':'))
    assert '"#' not in mini
    out.append(f'pub const {l.upper()}: &str = r##"{mini}"##;')
open('/workspace/src/templates.rs','w').write('\n'.join(out)+'\n')
EOF
python3 /tmp/tools/mktpl.py; wc -c /workspace/src/templates.rs; head -c 300 /workspace/src/templates.rs

I reimplemented the Revit reader in `src/rvt/` (Rust standard library only). For every asset file, `info`, `run` and the saved project now match the original. Imports of damaged files still differ in a few cases.

**Branch and commit:** `worktree-agent-aa2f380508e653094`, latest commit `88dcc42`. Three earlier commits on this branch (`213bd85`, `add9c60`, `14a24c8`) are missing the Co-Authored-By line; the rest have it.

**Asset results (207 files in `test_revit` and `test_imports`):**

| Check | Matching |
|---|---|
| `info` (stdout, stderr, exit code) | 207 / 207 |
| `run <file>` reply line | 207 / 207 |
| `run <file> --save out.bimcraft` | 207 / 207 |
| `convert x.rvt out.bimcraft` | 207 / 207 |

- **One caveat on the saved projects:** a component's `params` are keyed by random parameter GUIDs, and the original writes them sorted by GUID. Their order therefore changes on every run, for the original as well as for mine. Numbering GUIDs in the order they appear cannot match those files. My check replaces those keys with their library names first. This affects the files that contain components (the generic, house and levels files and a few others).
- **IFC:** `convert x.rvt out.ifc` was skipped, as asked.

**Damaged files**
- **`info`:** I ran about 2,300 crafted CFB files through `info`. They covered every header field, FAT and MiniFAT entries, directory entries, truncation and random byte flips; all match. I also ran about 1,400 files with damaged gzip data, records, ElemTable, BasicFileInfo, PartAtom or ProjectInformation; all match.
  - Getting there meant emulating the newer cfb crate and adding my own miniz-style deflate decoder (`src/rvt/deflate.rs`).
  - It also changed how 2024 records are found (by marker, not by walking the chain), plus the ElemTable layout rules and the level-block checks.
- **Import:**
  - About 5 of 100 randomly damaged copies of `house2024.rvt` still import differently. Most involve sketch lines that have no data of their own and don't close the sketch; the original leaves them out.
  - The order chosen between two equally near room grid cells is untested.
  - The level tolerances for floors and roofs aren't fully pinned down.

**Edits outside `src/rvt`**
- `src/main.rs`: `run` and `convert` print Revit import errors without the `open: ` prefix, as the original does.
- `src/commands/basic.rs`: the script `open` command reads project JSON whatever the extension, as the original does; Revit paths given on the command line still go to the importer.
- I did not touch the shared `src/inflate.rs`.

**What the core will need to provide later**
- **Room enclosure:** the test of whether walls enclose a point. It traces faces of the wall centrelines, using the walls cut by a plane 1200 mm above the room's level. It currently lives in `src/rvt/plan.rs` and `src/rvt/rooms.rs`.
- **Model checks:** these drop elements with the rule's wording. They cover wall height, doors and windows overlapping in a wall, roof profile, sweep and boundary, and runs "too short". They are emulated in `src/rvt/drop.rs`. Column type width and depth must be above zero; that check is in `import::check_types`. The core's own validation should eventually take these over.
- **MCP `open` tool:** it should call `rvt::import` for Revit paths.

My scratch scripts are all outside the repository, in `/tmp/rvt-agent/`.

1	# The Revit file reader: where every part of it comes from
2	
3	BIMCraft reads Autodesk Revit files (`.rvt`, `.rfa`) with a reader of its own, `crates/rvt` (package `bimcraft-rvt`). Revit's
4	format has no public specification, so [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) and [ROADMAP.md](../ROADMAP.md) allow it only under the fence
5	below. This document is the record the fence asks for: every module and every format finding names its source here. A change
6	to the reader that adds a module or a finding adds its row in the same commit (`crates/rvt/src/tests.rs` fails when a source
7	file has no row).
8	
9	## The risk, stated plainly
10	
11	The project owner chose this on 2026-10-21 and accepted the risk below. None of it is a legal conclusion.
12	
13	- The agent that wrote this reader is not a lawyer. It did not verify rvt-rs's claim that its work is clean-room, and it makes
14	  no claim of its own about whether reading Revit's format is lawful in any country, or whether Autodesk's terms for Revit or
15	  for its sample files allow it. Those are the owner's to decide, with counsel if they want it.
16	- rvt-rs has one author. Its `CLEANROOM.md` describes a process (accepted and forbidden sources, a declaration on each pull
17	  request). Whether that process was followed was not audited here, and could not be from the outside.
18	- Some of rvt-rs's findings are second-hand: it credits Discussion #112 of its own repository (a user, STE1200), puzzbobb's
19	  measurements across 30 files, and `ahzs645/reviter`, whose "ODA loader analysis" is named as the independent source of the
20	  stored-page constants in `compression.rs`. What those people used to find them was not checked. Where this reader uses such a
21	  finding, the row says so and says how it was confirmed here (by the bytes of a sample file), which shows the finding is true
22	  and does not show where it came from. The stored-page constants are the exception: they were derived again from the bytes
23	  alone, by someone who had not seen them (see their section below).
24	- Autodesk's sample projects were downloaded from Autodesk's own public download host (see Sample files). Their terms of use
25	  were not checked.
26	
27	## The fence
28	
29	1. **A crate of its own.** `crates/rvt`, package `bimcraft-rvt`, `license = "Apache-2.0"` (not the repository's
30	   MIT OR Apache-2.0, because it holds Apache-2.0 code ported from rvt-rs). `bimcraft-core` never depends on it, and neither
31	   does `crates/update`, `crates/ui-egui` or the MCP server's core path. The command line (`apps/bimcraft-cli`) and the desktop
32	   (`apps/bimcraft`) take it through the Cargo feature `rvt`, which is on by default; a build without it is
33	   `--no-default-features`. A test reads the manifests (`crates/rvt/src/tests.rs`).
34	2. **Attribution, as Apache-2.0 asks.** `crates/rvt/LICENSE` is the licence text; `crates/rvt/NOTICE` carries rvt-rs's
35	   copyright line (Copyright 2026 Griffin Long) and says what was taken; every file with ported code opens with a header that
36	   names the rvt-rs source file and commit and says it was changed. A build that includes the crate is distributed under
37	   Apache-2.0: the README says so, every package (deb, rpm, Arch, AppImage, the AppStream metainfo, the Windows installer and the
38	   macOS bundle) names Apache-2.0, and each ships the root `NOTICE`, which starts with a copy of the crate's (a test keeps it
39	   so) and goes on to the interface fonts' notice.
40	3. **This document.** Every module and every format finding has a source from the accepted list below.
41	4. **Nothing inside an Autodesk file becomes BIMCraft content.** No family, template, icon or help text is bundled, extracted
42	   or shipped. The reader reads a file the user gives it. Test fixtures are synthetic files written by the tests; Autodesk's
43	   files are never committed.
44	5. **The policy documents say so.** CLAUDE.md's clean-room rule and principle 5 of the roadmap point here.
45	
46	### Accepted sources
47	
48	1. Public specifications: MS-CFB (the Compound File Binary format, which Revit files are), RFC 1951 and RFC 1952 (deflate and
49	   gzip), the PNG specification, and for the schema of the model, IFC4 (ISO 16739).
50	2. Byte observations of files we are entitled to open: files the user gives the program, and the sample files in the table
51	   below. An observation says the file and the offsets.
52	3. rvt-rs's code and documents, under its Apache-2.0 licence, at the commit named below.
53	4. Autodesk's publicly exported symbol names and its published API constants (the `BuiltInCategory` values such as
54	   `OST_Walls`). Names and numbers, not behaviour.
55	5. Autodesk's open-source IFC exporter, `revit-ifc`, to learn what Revit's own IFC export writes. Read, never copied: its code
56	   is LGPL and would bring that licence in. Part 1 uses none of it.
57	
58	### Forbidden sources
59	
60	- Autodesk SDK source, or disassembly or decompilation of Autodesk's binaries beyond their public export names.
61	- Open Design Alliance SDK source or internals.
62	- Leaked, breached or NDA material of any kind.
63	- Copying or translating `revit-ifc`'s code.
64	- Anyone who has signed an NDA covering Revit internals does not contribute findings that NDA covers.
65	
66	If a finding's source is not on the accepted list, it does not go in. If one turns out to have come from the forbidden list,
67	the code goes out, and a different person re-derives it.
68

77	| How it was used here | Read for the container, the streams, the schema and the partition records; code ported file by file as the module table says; and built from a scratch clone with its own target directory, to compare its output with this reader's on the same files. 122	| A `Global/*` stream is eight bytes and then one gzip member; `Formats/Latest` starts with its member at byte 0 | rvt-rs `compression.rs` (`inflate_at_auto`); observation | the four samples (the member is found in the first 256 bytes) |
123	| A partition is a 44-byte header and then gzip members of about 128 KiB of output each, with 40 bytes between one and the next: the previous member's CRC-32 and length, then 32 bytes of header the reader does not read; in 52 gaps of each sample there are 188 more bytes (a small structured item with UTF-16 text and length fields, 228 bytes between the members in all) | byte observation (rvt-rs finds members by scanning for the magic and does not describe the gap) | the four samples: the first member at byte 44, 40 bytes between members in 334 of 386, 362 of 414, 363 of 415 and 361 of 413 gaps and 228 in the 52 others, with the pages' runs taken out. 169	### The stored-page constants, and where they come from
170	
171	`gzip.rs` has two numbers and a list: a stored page is 65,249 bytes, of which the first 64,896 are data and the last 353 a run
172	that belongs to no gzip member, and the container pages the partitions, the schema and six `Global` streams. The list is
173	rvt-rs's. The two numbers (and so the 353) are derived from the bytes of the samples, by someone who had not seen them.
174	
175	**Why a second derivation.** rvt-rs's `compression.rs` credits the numbers to "ahzs645/reviter's ODA loader analysis and
176	Discussion #112". ODA internals are on the forbidden list and the claim cannot be audited, so the owner had the numbers derived
177	again. A separate agent session did it on 2026-10-21. It was told not to open `gzip.rs`, any other code that handles pages or trailers, the
178	earlier rows and text about them in this document, the part 1 hand-over note, rvt-rs's `compression.rs`, or anything of
179	reviter, ODA or Autodesk until its derivation was written down; it used its own Compound File reader (MS-CFB only), raw inflate
180	(RFC 1951) and the CRC-32 and length at the end of a gzip member (RFC 1952). It wrote its notes first (`derivation.md` and its
181	Python programs, kept with the session notes, not in this repository) and read `gzip.rs` and this document after. The earlier
182	scratch check, which searched a window "chosen around the known answer", is replaced by this.
183	
184	**What it did, on the four samples** (`rstbasicsampleproject.rvt`, 2023 to 2026; all Compound Files of version 4):
185	
186	1. Checked every gzip member as stored (header per RFC 1952, raw inflate, CRC-32 and length). The small streams verify. Every
187	   stream longer than 64,896 bytes does not: in the partition, 300 of 387 members verify in 2023 (324 of 415, 326 of 416 and
188	   322 of 414 in the others), and `Global/Latest`, `Formats/Latest`, `Global/ContentDocuments` and, from 2024,
189	   `Global/ElemTable` fail whole. A failing member can still end exactly at its own trailer with too much output (Huffman codes
190	   resynchronise), so only the CRC and the length count, never "inflate finished".
191	2. Searched for a run to remove, with no prior. In the first member of each sample's partition that zlib rejects, every cut of 1
192	   to 4,096 bytes was tried at every offset up to the byte zlib rejects (a cut at or after it leaves that byte as it was). One
193	   pair makes the member verify, in all four samples: 353 bytes at stream offset 130,145.
194	3. Cut every failing member by 353 bytes, trying every offset: 86 of 87, 91 of 91, 90 of 90 and 92 of 92 are repaired by one
195	   cut at one offset (one offset in each has an equal neighbour); the 87th, in 2023, holds two runs.
196	4. Fitted the spacing: every integer period from 2 to 65,249, the smallest distance between two cuts (two runs cannot be
197	   closer than the period), was tried against all the cuts. Three fit by congruence, 71, 919 and 65,249 (71 x 919 = 65,249); the
198	   first two would put a run through members that verify as stored. The first run ends at 1 x 65,249, so pages count from byte 0
199	   of the stream, the eight-byte prefix of a `Global/*` stream included.
200	5. Without the fitted model: the single-member streams have a unique cut at 64,896 in 2023 `Global/Latest` and 2024
201	   `Global/ElemTable`, and a unique second cut at 130,145 in 2023 `Formats/Latest` and `Global/ContentDocuments` once the first
202	   is removed.
203	6. Checked the result on everything: remove, from every stream, the bytes at offsets `o` with `o mod 65,249 >= 64,896`, and verify
204	   every gzip member. **1,664 of 1,664 verify** (36 streams, 388 runs: 93, 98, 98 and 99 per sample), and in the 1,632
205	   partition members the size in the 32-byte record in front of each (a `u32`, 16 bytes before the magic, equal to the member's
206	   length from its magic to the end of its trailer, plus 8) equals that length, with no exception. The 388 runs are all different, look random (about 7.4 bits a byte) and all begin with a
207	   `00` byte; nothing was read into them.
208	
209	| Sample | Partition | Bytes | Members | Verify as stored | Runs | Verify after removal |
210	|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
211	| 2023 | `Partitions/20` | 5,751,736 | 387 | 300 | 88 | 387 |
212	| 2024 | `Partitions/21` | 5,962,991 | 415 | 324 | 91 | 415 |
213	| 2025 | `Partitions/20` | 5,998,302 | 416 | 326 | 91 | 416 |
214	| 2026 | `Partitions/21` | 6,003,729 | 414 | 322 | 92 | 414 |
215	
216	Moving a number breaks it (members verifying out of 1,664): the layout above 1,664; a start a byte earlier or later 1,293 or
217	1,290, and 1,289 for the eight-byte prefix; 352 or 354 bytes of run 1,289; a page of 65,248 or 65,250 bytes 1,290 or 1,289; a
218	page of 65,536 bytes 1,064; no stripping 1,289 (the members that lie inside one page). `a_wrong_page_layout_breaks_the_real_files`
219	and the other page tests in `crates/rvt/src/tests/mod.rs` keep this: a change of one byte in either constant fails nine tests.
220	
221	**Compared with the ported values.** Equal: 65,249, 64,896, the 353 run, and stripping from byte 0 of the stored stream. The
222	list of paged streams is equal where the bytes can tell. Five of its entries are longer than a page in some sample and are
223	paged (`Partitions/NN`, `Formats/Latest`, `Global/ContentDocuments`, `Global/Latest`, and `Global/ElemTable` from 2024).
224	`Global/DocumentIncrementTable`, `Global/History` and `Global/PartitionTable` are under 18 KB in every sample, so stripping
225	removes nothing from them and the samples cannot confirm or refute their place in the list, nor the absence from it of
226	`Contents`, `BasicFileInfo`, `TransmissionData` and `ProjectInformation` (under 4.1 KB).
227	
228	**Not derived.**
229	
230	- What a run holds, or why it is there.
231	- What a stream that was cut off inside the last 352 bytes of a page looks like (no sample does; the largest remainder of a
232	  stream length modulo 65,249 below 64,896 is 64,737). `strip_pages` keeps a short last page whole, and a test pins that choice.
233	- Anything about 32-bit files (there is no such sample), releases before 2023 or after 2026, files that are not this one
234	  project saved four times, families, or Compound Files of another version than 4.
235	- Whether `BasicFileInfo`, `TransmissionData` and `ProjectInformation` are paged.
236	- The head of a partition, the 32-byte records, the 188-byte items and the bytes after a stream's last member. Only the size
237	  field of the record was used, as a cross-check.
238	
239	**What this shows about where the numbers come from, and what it does not.** They follow from the bytes of the samples and the
240	public formats, and the derivation was written down before the ported values were read; they equal rvt-rs's. The code's use of
241	them therefore rests on observation and not on rvt-rs's second-hand credit. Two limits, plainly. The same numbers are public in
242	rvt-rs, and the derivation did not see them first, which nobody can verify from the outside. And the agent that wrote this reader
243	and the one that derived the numbers are language models: whether either met these numbers in its training data cannot be
244	inspected from here, so no analysis of that can be made. The claim is only that the bytes force these numbers, not that nobody
245	involved could have known them.

324	
325	## What the reader does with what it cannot read
326	
327	Where the file says less than BIMCraft's element needs, the reader may take the nearest thing the file does say and put the element
328	in the project, and the report says what was not read of it. That is an approximation, not a finding about the format, none of
329	these fallbacks is checked against another reader, and none of them counts as read whole. What the project cannot hold at all is
330	left out and counted: `N kinds left out, why`, which the desktop adds up.
331	
332	Measured on the local copies of Autodesk's samples (the files are never committed; `BIMCRAFT_RVT_SAMPLES` names them):
333	
334	| Sample | Elements in | Left out |
335	|---|---|---|
336	| `racbasicsampleproject.rvt` (2023, 2024, 2025) | 118 | 6: 4 rooms the walls do not enclose, 2 skylights |
337	| `Snowdon Towers Sample Structural.rvt` (2024) | 178 | 0 |
338	| `Snowdon Towers Sample Architectural.rvt` (2024) | 1,791 | 84: 46 doors and windows that overlap a neighbour in their wall, 36 rooms the walls do not enclose, 2 levels inside other elements |
339	
340	Stand-ins, each told in the report with its ids:
341	
342	- A type with no compound structure (a curtain wall, a storefront, a tilted solar panel, a roof type of the 2026 sample) has no
343	  thickness: a wall takes the thickness its own box gives, and a floor, a ceiling or a roof the height of its box. The panels and
344	  mullions of a curtain wall, and the layers of such a type, are not read.
345	- A floor, a ceiling or a roof whose box is taller than its type is thick is sloped or stepped: it comes in level, as thick as its
346	  type, at the bottom of its box. The slope blocks of the edges (rvt-rs RE-56) are not read, and no sample's slopes were compared
347	  with another reader's. A wall is never attached to such a roof, because the stand-in is not the roof its top would follow.
348	- A sketch whose lines do not close joins its open ends by a straight line; one whose loops cross, or one of whose lines has no
349	  curve, comes in as the footprint of its box. Such a floor's area is not the floor's, and the tests do not compare it.
350	- A wall whose record holds no curve (a family instance of the wall category, a trellis member) comes in along the long side of
351	  its own box; one that names no type of the category comes in with a type of its own, as thick as its box says. A turned column
352	  whose family symbol's size is not known comes in as its box, turned.
353	- A roof of the class that is neither a roof by footprint nor one by extrusion (a roof by face, over a mass) comes in as the
354	  footprint of its own box.
355	- An opening whose box overruns its wall - Revit's frame runs a few millimetres past the wall's box, a door through a wall the file
356	  cuts short - comes in as far as the wall goes. A sill within 2 mm below the wall's base is taken as zero.
357	
358	Left out and counted: a window set in a roof or a floor (a skylight; BIMCraft's windows stand in walls), a room no walls enclose
359	(Revit's own not-enclosed room, or one bounded by room separation lines, which BIMCraft has none of: it comes in again when the
360	walls enclose its box), a level inside another element (a group's, a family's), and an opening the model's rules refuse where it
361	overlaps a neighbour in its wall. The last is the rule `Model::check` applies to every project: it counts two openings as
362	overlapping where they share a place along the wall, whatever their heights, so a window over a door is refused. Letting openings
363	overlap only where they also share a height would bring the 46 of the Snowdon sample in; that is a change of the model's rule,
364	for every project, and is made on its own.
365	
366	## Not verified

368	- Whether any of this is lawful, or allowed by Autodesk's terms (see the risk, above).
369	- Anything about releases other than the samples (2018, 2023 to 2026, and the two Snowdon Towers files of 2024), and nothing about
370	  files that are not Autodesk's own sample projects. Releases 2015 to 2017, 2019 to 2022 and 2027 are decoded by the same rules and
371	  tested only on synthetic files; the same goes for a linked model and a file that has passed through several saves. The three 2018
372	  samples (the two basic ones and the advanced architectural one, none workshared) come in through the readers made for 2023 and
373	  later, with their levels, walls, floors and columns (`autodesks_2018_samples_come_in_through_the_readers_made_for_2023`); they
374	  were not compared with rvt-rs. A workshared file is covered by no Autodesk sample. One workshared Revit 2018 file the project owner gave (a pipework and ductwork project: 9 levels, 68,811 element records) reads with the rows above: its levels, walls, floor, 4,407 of 4,410 pipes, 1,194 ducts and 31 cable trays come in as what they are, 8,847 fittings, fixtures, equipment and terminals as boxes, and 3,348 elements of categories the name table above has not as boxes of a family named by the category's id (nothing here says what they are, so they are not guessed at). What is left out is listed in the notes: 23,554 model lines, which have no reader, 11,664 companions of the pipes, fittings, ducts, duct fittings and flex ducts whose box is that element's (the last finding above), and 2,242 elements whose box has no volume. A pipe, duct or tray is not connected to its neighbours, and a fitting is a box, not an elbow or a tee.
375	- The element readers have not been compared with rvt-rs on anything but the basic samples; Snowdon Towers (1,062 walls) was
376	  imported, validated and looked at, and its numbers were not set against an export.
377	- A roof by extrusion with an arc (a barrel vault), one in a plane at an angle, or one that rises in steps: the one real roof is a gable, and
378	  nothing else of the kind was seen. A wall of a type with no layers: none of the 51 in the samples (the 9 of the architectural sample, the 42 of
379	  Snowdon Towers: storefront, glazing and solar-panel types and one type named `_Not Defined`) holds a width the reader can find (the data of the eight Snowdon types that have any is 350 to 402 bytes, and the only lengths in it are a
380	  curtain grid's spacings; the architectural sample's type has no data object at all), so none comes in as a single layer; each is left out and listed under its type's name. The categories `info` prints as bare ids: no table of Autodesk's
381	  `BuiltInCategory` values was found that could be checked against a file (the published reference lists the names without their numbers, and
382	  the files hold no `OST_` names), so none was added.
383	- What no sample sets: a roof slope (rvt-rs's RE-56 is not ported), a curved wall that hosts an opening (left out; one at an angle is solved from the box, checked on the Snowdon sample only), a

A file is read under limits (its size, its streams, what each inflates to) and a damaged or hostile one is an error that says what is wrong. Nothing is taken from inside the file (families, templates, icons) for BIMCraft's own content. Builds that include the reader are Apache-2.0 (see License); `--no-default-features` leaves it out |
  underneath.
- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around
  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
  every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone.
- **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with
  IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public
  specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md):
  `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import
  its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds
  by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read
  while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out.
- **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to
  check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI.
- **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on
  Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet.
- **Free.** MIT OR Apache-2.0, with no account and no subscription.
```

A script stops at its first failing line and names it. Through MCP, `script {"text": …, "atomic": true}` runs it all or nothing:
a line that fails takes back the lines before it, and one that goes through is a single undo step.

```sh
bimcraft-cli run --script house.txt --save house.ifc
bimcraft-cli convert building.ifc building.bimcraft   # an IFC file from Revit or any BIM tool, as a project
bimcraft-cli info house.bimcraft                      # levels, counts, types and warnings
bimcraft-cli info building.rvt                        # a Revit file: release, last save, levels, elements by category
bimcraft-cli convert building.rvt building.ifc        # a Revit project, imported, then written as IFC4
bimcraft-cli convert house.bimcraft plan.svg
bimcraft-cli commands                                 # every command and its parameters
```

## The desktop app
are, families, BIMCraft's own parametric components (never Autodesk's `.rfa`), and project parameters and schedules with
chosen fields, filters, sorting and formulas, and visibility and graphics (overrides, view filters, view templates, phases and design options, which go out to IFC and come back), and families done: revolves and voids, doors and windows as families, the Family Editor, textures by material or from pictures you add, Paint, and favorites kept for every project, and updates (a check at startup, and the Windows installer's copy, an AppImage and the macOS app upgrading themselves).
Next, in order: locked and equal dimensions, arrays and groups; fill patterns of your own; DXF and DWG export, more of
IFC, and gbXML; the rest of structure (beams, columns, footings and structural floors are in), then MEP (its four tabs are designed in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md)); site and massing; several people editing one model; and signed installers (macOS
signing and notarization are wired up, waiting on a Developer ID). Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public specification, so BIMCraft reads it only through a reader of its own under the fence in
[docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md): it lists what a file holds (`bimcraft-cli info`) and imports its levels, walls, floors, doors
and windows, columns, rooms and roofs into a project, from the command line and from the desktop's File > Open, listing what was left out and why.

import struct, sys, zlib
class CFB:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.d = data
        h = data[:512]
        self.sig = h[:8]
        self.minor, self.major, self.bom, self.ssh, self.mssh = struct.unpack_from('<HHHHH', h, 24)
        self.ss = 1 << self.ssh
        self.mss = 1 << self.mssh
        (self.ndir, self.nfat, self.dirstart, self.txn, self.cutoff, self.minifatstart, self.nminifat, self.difatstart, self.ndifat) = struct.unpack_from('<IIIIIIIII', h, 40)
        self.difat = list(struct.unpack_from('<109I', h, 76))
        # follow difat chain
        s = self.difatstart
        n = 0
        while s < 0xFFFFFFFA and n < self.ndifat:
            sec = self.sector(s)
            vals = struct.unpack_from('<%dI' % (self.ss//4), sec)
            self.difat += list(vals[:-1])
            s = vals[-1]; n += 1
        fatsecs = [x for x in self.difat if x < 0xFFFFFFFA][:self.nfat]
        self.fat = []
        for fs in fatsecs:
            self.fat += list(struct.unpack_from('<%dI' % (self.ss//4), self.sector(fs)))
        self.dirdata = self.chain(self.dirstart)
        self.entries = []
        for i in range(len(self.dirdata)//128):
            e = self.dirdata[i*128:(i+1)*128]
            nl = struct.unpack_from('<H', e, 64)[0]
            name = e[:max(0,nl-2)].decode('utf-16le', 'replace')
            typ, color = e[66], e[67]
            left, right, child = struct.unpack_from('<III', e, 68)
            start, size = struct.unpack_from('<IQ', e, 116)
            self.entries.append(dict(i=i, name=name, type=typ, color=color, left=left, right=right, child=child, start=start, size=size, clsid=e[80:96].hex()))
        root = self.entries[0]
        self.ministream = self.chain(root['start'])[:root['size']] if root['start'] < 0xFFFFFFFA else b''
        self.minifat = []
        if self.minifatstart < 0xFFFFFFFA:
            mf = self.chain(self.minifatstart)
            self.minifat = list(struct.unpack_from('<%dI' % (len(mf)//4), mf))
    def sector(self, s):
        off = (s+1)*self.ss
        return self.d[off:off+self.ss]
    def chain(self, s, limit=10**7):
        out = []
        seen = 0
        while s < 0xFFFFFFFA and seen < limit:
            out.append(self.sector(s))
            s = self.fat[s] if s < len(self.fat) else 0xFFFFFFFE
            seen += 1
        return b''.join(out)
    def minichain(self, s):
        out = []
        while s < 0xFFFFFFFA:
            off = s*self.mss
            out.append(self.ministream[off:off+self.mss])
            s = self.minifat[s] if s < len(self.minifat) else 0xFFFFFFFE
        return b''.join(out)
    def read(self, e):
        if e['size'] < self.cutoff and e['type'] == 2:
            return self.minichain(e['start'])[:e['size']]
        return self.chain(e['start'])[:e['size']]
    def walk(self, idx=None, path='', out=None):
        if out is None:
            out = []
            root = self.entries[0]
            self.walk(root['child'], '', out)
            return out
        if idx >= 0xFFFFFFFA or idx >= len(self.entries): return out
        e = self.entries[idx]
        self.walk(e['left'], path, out)
        p = path + e['name']
        out.append((p, e))
        if e['type'] == 1:
            self.walk(e['child'], p + '/', out)
        self.walk(e['right'], path, out)
        return out
if __name__ == '__main__':
    d = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
    c = CFB(d)
    print('ver', c.major, c.minor, 'ss', c.ss, 'mss', c.mss, 'ndir', c.ndir, 'nfat', c.nfat, 'dirstart', c.dirstart, 'cutoff', c.cutoff, 'minifat', c.minifatstart, c.nminifat, 'difat', c.difatstart, c.ndifat)
    for p, e in c.walk():
        print(p, e['type'], e['size'], e['start'])

import sys, zlib, struct
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/rvt-agent')
from cfb import CFB

def hexdump(b, base=0, maxlen=4096):
    out = []
    for i in range(0, min(len(b), maxlen), 16):
        chunk = b[i:i+16]
        hx = ' '.join('%02x' % x for x in chunk)
        asc = ''.join(chr(x) if 32 <= x < 127 else '.' for x in chunk)
        out.append('%06x  %-48s  %s' % (base + i, hx, asc))
    return '\n'.join(out)

def gunzip_members(b, start=0):
    """find gzip members from start; return list of (offset, data, consumed)"""
    res = []
    i = start
    while True:
        j = b.find(b'\x1f\x8b\x08', i)
        if j < 0: break
        # parse header
        flg = b[j+3]
        p = j + 10
        if flg & 4:
            xl = struct.unpack_from('<H', b, p)[0]; p += 2 + xl
        if flg & 8:
            p = b.index(b'\0', p) + 1
        if flg & 16:
            p = b.index(b'\0', p) + 1
        if flg & 2: p += 2
        d = zlib.decompressobj(-15)
        try:
            out = d.decompress(b[p:])
            consumed = len(b[p:]) - len(d.unused_data)
            res.append((j, out, p + consumed))
            i = p + consumed
        except Exception as e:
            res.append((j, ('ERR %s' % e).encode(), p))
            i = j + 3
    return res

if __name__ == '__main__':
    d = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
    c = CFB(d)
    which = sys.argv[2:] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else None
    for p, e in c.walk():
        if e['type'] != 2: continue
        if which and p not in which: continue
        data = c.read(e)
        print('=====', p, len(data))
        print(hexdump(data))
        if p != 'BasicFileInfo':
            for (off, out, end) in gunzip_members(data):
                print('  -- gzip member at', off, 'ends', end, 'out', len(out))
                print(hexdump(out))

files = sorted(glob.glob('/workspace/assets/test_revit/*')) + sorted(glob.glob('/workspace/assets/test_imports/*'))
for f in files:
    tag = os.path.basename(os.path.dirname(f)) + '.' + os.path.basename(f)
    try:
        c = CFB(open(f, 'rb').read())
    except Exception:
        continue
    b = c.stream('BasicFileInfo')
    if b is None: continue
    # head
    head = []
    try:
        p = 0
        v0 = struct.unpack_from('<I', b, 0)[0]
        p = 4 + 10
        for k in range(3):
            n = struct.unpack_from('<I', b, p)[0]; p += 4
            head.append(b[p:p+2*n].decode('utf-16le', 'replace')); p += 2*n
    except Exception as e:
        head.append('ERR %s' % e)
    i = b.find('Worksharing'.encode('utf-16le'))
    lines = b[i:].decode('utf-16le', 'replace') if i >= 0 else ''
    if i >= 0 and i % 2 == 1:

    info = open('/tmp/obs/revit_info/' + tag + '.out').read()
    rv = json.loads(info)['revit'] if info.strip() else None
    print(tag, 'v0=%d' % v0, 'head=%r' % head, 'ws_at=%d' % i, 'len=%d' % len(b))
    if rv: print('    info build=%r release=%r' % (rv['build'], rv['release']))
    else: print('    ERR', open('/tmp/obs/revit_info/' + tag + '.err').read().strip())
