# Levels, walls, roofs, floors, ceilings, shafts, stairs

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the
boundary it has when frozen, both ways it can be measured (`Room::kept`, given after the command that froze it by
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it
and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time
of many rooms; moved, rotated or mirrored, its boundary goes with it, and only a bounded room can be frozen. Walls and columns (and structural columns) bound
rooms while their Room Bounding is on (`Wall::room_bounding`, `Column::room_bounding`, on unless set; `Model::room_bounding`,
`bounding_columns`, `room_lines`): a column's outline either way rooms are measured, a free one an island. A wall with it off
still bounds floors and roofs picked by their walls. Walls and columns bound a level's rooms where its
Computation Height (`Level::computation_height`, 1200 mm unless set) cuts them; room separation lines bound them whatever
it is. Two rooms can't share a space (`Model::room_bound`, `Unbound`): the one placed first (the lower id) keeps it, the
other is unbounded, and `room` and `inspect` warn. A room can be placed where nothing encloses it: unbounded, it covers a
`UNBOUNDED_ROOM` square round its point (`Model::room_outline`), as Revit's. A plan labels it NOT ENCLOSED, or REDUNDANT where another
room has its space. Its reference, a cross from the point it was placed at out along the diagonals to its boundary
(`geom::ray_hit`), drawn as the room's own lines (a click on it picks the room), is the subcategory `roomreference` under
Rooms, off unless shown (`graphics {show: ["roomreference"]}`), beside `roomseparator`, the separation lines.
Subcategories are general (`graphics::SUBCATEGORIES`: a key, its category, a name, whether it is off unless shown):
a view holds them as categories, with `Override::shown` for the ones off unless shown, `Graphics::hides` answers for
them (a category hidden hides its subcategories), and Visibility/Graphics folds them under their category. In a 3D
view rooms are off until shown (`graphics::OFF_IN_3D`, `Graphics::shows_in_3d`; `graphics {view: "{3D}", show: [rooms]}`,
or ticked in its Visibility/Graphics), every new 3D view so; shown, each is drawn as below, fainter than a selected one,
and a selected room is seen whatever the view says: a see-through solid in the selection's colour from its bottom to its top
(`orbit::room_solid`, drawn over the picture, so it shows through walls). With `room_area {at: "finish"}` (`Model::room_area`, Revit's Area and
Volume Computations) room areas are measured at the walls' faces instead (`face_lines` and the separators), the floor inside them; the IFC space
takes that outline, and its `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities` give both whichever is set: `GrossFloorArea` and `GrossPerimeter` at
the centre lines, `NetFloorArea` and `NetPerimeter` at the faces, `Height` (the room's Unbounded Height) and `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`. Walls, slabs, doors and windows
carry theirs too (`ifc::wall_quantities`): a wall its `Length` on its axis, `Width`, `Height` and side and volume, gross and less the
doors and windows in it (each cut to its height; joins aside), or only `Length` and `Width` when attached, as its height then varies;
a level slab its `Width` (depth), `Perimeter` and area and volume less its openings, a sloped one only its `Width`; a door or window
its `Width`, `Height`, `Perimeter` and `Area`. An attached top or base follows the roof's or floor's plane
over each part of the wall (a roof's slopes each over its own part of the plan); a mirrored wall runs back the other way.
A wall's top is `Model::own_top`, and 3D, sections, plans, IFC and what a wall is attached to all read it there (`walls::heights`
takes it, or what the wall is attached to): its `top_level`'s elevation plus its `top_offset` (file format 15, Revit's Top Offset,
mm, negative below the level), or its base plus its `height` when it has no top level, which an offset does not touch.
`Model::check` refuses a wall whose top does not come out above its base, saying how tall it comes out and by how much to raise it.
The Properties palette shows Top Offset under Top Constraint for a wall that has one.
A roof by footprint is the straight skeleton of its outline and its `courtyards` (`skeleton::faces`: the outline
counter-clockwise, the courtyards clockwise, the roof to the left of every edge): each edge moves in at speed 1, a gable's at
0, and its slope rises from it, reaching the roof's base `overhang` in from its eaves; a courtyard's edges number on after
the outline's, and every ring keeps its numbers whichever way round it runs, so `gables` stay put through a mirror.
`Roof::slopes` (file format 15) gives each edge a slope of its own, in degrees, numbered as `gables` are: 0 is the roof's `slope`,
and an empty list, every edge. `Model::roof_faces` then moves an edge in at the run over the rise of its slope, scaled so the
shallowest moves at 1 (every edge at one slope still moves at exactly 1), so edges of different slopes reach the same height
together and the slopes meet along their hips; the eaves stay level, the roof's base `overhang` in from them lowered by the roof's
`slope`, whatever the edges' own. A gable stays upright whatever its slope, and a flat roof (`slope` 0) keeps its `slopes` as it keeps
its `gables`, unused. `Model::check` refuses a list of the wrong length, saying how many edges there are, and a slope outside 0
to 75°, saying which edge. A sketch line may carry a `slope` (`SketchLine::slope`; the Slope row of Properties, with one line of a
roof's sketch picked, sets it): the roof keeps it as the `slopes` of the edges along that line (`sketch::along`), never in its
`sketch`, which `sketch::check` refuses to hold one. `edit_boundary` keeps the slope of an edge that stays or that a new
line cuts in two (an edge lying along an old one), the lines' own `slope` (0 sets the roof's) winning over it, and without
`slope` on the lines it keeps what the edges had; `edit_boundary` without a sketch gives the lines with the slope their edges share.
Over the walls (`floor_outline`, which `roof_footprint` grows by the overhang), a loop of them standing free inside the outer
ones, joined to none of them and with no room in it, is a courtyard, open through the floor and the roof; one joined to them,
or with a room in it, is rooms, and both run over it.
`Model::roof_faces` are its slopes, each the loops round it in plan (a slope can close round a courtyard whose far side is a
gable) with the plane of its underside, trimmed where it `join`s another; `Model::roof_pieces` are those less their holes
and its `openings`, convex where cut. A floor's top is at its level plus `offset`,
or with a slope arrow, there at the arrow's tail and rising `slope` degrees toward its head (`Model::floor_top`); it's its
type's thickness across the slope, so plumb it's thicker. Its `openings` are holes inside it, apart, and `Model::floor_slabs`
what's left, convex where cut. A floor's `shape` (IDEAS MOD-16, [design](../shape-editing.md)) folds its top into planes:
points `z` mm above (negative, below) where the top would be without them, and split lines it folds along, each a part
with an id and a GUID (`ShapePoint`, `SplitLine`). `Model::shape_planes` triangulates its outline, openings, points and
lines (`triangulation::constrained`), lifts each corner by the point there (a corner with none stays at 0) and merges
neighbours in one plane; `Model::floor_faces` are those planes in convex pieces, or the unshaped top, and `floor_slabs`,
the 3D view, sections and the element's details take them. In IFC a shaped slab is one closed `IfcFacetedBrep`
(`Model::shape_solid`: its top's planes, the same planes under them, plumb sides round its outline and openings, each
corner written once), and a sloped or shaped slab gives `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`, its plan through its depth plumb;
every floor's details give `volume_m3`, what's left of it in plan (shafts too) through that depth. A shaped floor is its type's thickness plumb, so its planes meet
underneath too, and has no slope arrow (`Model::check`, `shape_ok`, refuses one, and points outside the outline or in an
opening, points within a millimetre of each other, a split line's end that is no point and no corner, and lines that
cross). A wall attached to one follows `Model::shape_triangles`, its top over the whole outline as if its openings were
closed, as a slope arrow's plane runs on over them. Plans draw each plane's edges as thin as the outline. `edit_shape`
gives the shape anew or says what it is, `add_point`, `add_split_line` and `reset_shape` change it a piece at a time (an
end of a line that is no point becomes one, at the height the top has there), `edit_boundary` keeps what stays inside the
new outline and its openings, cuts a split line where it leaves them, and gives each new end and each new corner a point at
the height the top had there, so a hole cut through a shaped top leaves it as it was round the hole; it names what it
`dropped`, `cut` and `added`. Moves and mirrors take the shape along, and snaps find its points. A flat roof by
footprint (`slope` 0, no extrusion, joining none) takes a shape too (`Roof::shape`, `Roof::unshapeable` says why another
can't): the commands, checks and both views' tools see its top as a floor's (`Model::shapeable`, `Model::roof_as_floor`:
its footprint, its courtyards and openings as openings, at its top), and `roof_faces` lays each plane's underside its
thickness below, plumb (`roof_rise`), so its slabs, IFC, sections and the walls attached under it follow its falls; plans
draw its creases thin. Under its type's variable layer a shaped roof's underside stays level at its base
(`Model::roof_under`, `roof_prisms`), as a floor's does: its layers in 3D and sections share `Variable::bounds` through
`Model::variable_under`, walls attached under it stop at that underside, IFC writes it as one closed faceted Brep
(`Model::roof_solid`), and `Model::check` refuses a point that leaves the layer thinner than nothing. `falls` (`falls.rs`) gives a floor or a flat roof its shape from its drains and the least fall:
catchments nearest each drain, ridges between them at the top's height, valleys from each drain to its catchment's corners,
each drain as deep as the fall takes its farthest corner; round an opening the valleys turn at its corners, which lie on
the drain's cone, and ridges drawn part the top first. A slab or flat roof whose top isn't one plane comes in from IFC
shaped (`import::shaped_top`), its variable layer marked by its `Description` or, under a level underside, guessed
(`import::guess_variable`); and a spot slope (`Spot::slope`) reads a floor's or roof's fall in a plan. A layer of a floor or roof type may be `variable` (one a type at most; never a wall's or a ceiling's): under a
shaped floor of that type, the underside stays level where the unshaped floor's was (`Model::floor_under`), the layers
above the variable one follow the top, those below it stay level, and the variable one takes up the difference
(`Variable::bounds`, which the 3D view's layers and sections share). Its pieces are then prisms from that level underside
(`Model::floor_prisms`), its volume is less where its top falls (`Model::floor_volume`, `model::volume` for IFC), a wall
attached under it stops at the level underside, and `Model::check` refuses a point that would leave the variable layer
thinner than nothing, saying by how much to raise it. Reinforcement arms a shaped floor only when a variable layer lies
over all its structure: the bars keep to the layers under it, as on a level floor that thick. Without one it refuses,
saying why. In the desktop, a floor selected shows Shape Editing in its contextual tab: Slope Arrow, Modify Sub Elements (a point, a corner or an edge's two ends,
`Floor::shape_pick`, to the Options Bar's Elevation), Add Point (a
click on the top, at the Options Bar's Elevation, above the unshaped top or, with Absolute, above the level; empty, the
top's height there), Add Split Line (two clicks, snapping to points, corners and edges) and Reset Shape, each a command.
While one is on, each point's height is labelled beside it (`Model::shape_labels`); under Modify Sub Elements a point's
grip drags it in plan at its height, its split lines with it (`Shape::moved`), in one `edit_shape`. In the 3D view the
same tools work on the floor's top: each point's and corner's grip drags its height up or down, and clicks land on the top
(`view3d::shape_handles`, `on_floor_top`, `shape_pick_3d`); both views run `shape.rs`. While a grip is held, either
view draws the creases its release will leave (`Model::shape_creases` of the floor with the shape it would have). Type Properties ticks a floor's or a roof's variable layer. A ceiling's `offset` is its underside; its `openings` are holes as a floor's
are, and `Model::ceiling_slabs` what's left. A shaft cuts each floor,
ceiling and roof its span reaches into over its outline, all the way through (`Model::less_shafts`). A stair or a ramp
is runs and landings laid out from its start (`stairs::stair`, `stairs::ramp`): a landing after `at` risers (a ramp's, `at`
mm up), as deep as the runs are wide, the next run turning by its `turn`; a railing on one follows its walk line moved out to
its side (`stairs::railing`), so it goes wherever its host goes. `modify` merges into fields that are objects (JSON Merge Patch), so `{"view_range": {"cut": 1500}}` keeps the rest; an element's own field can't be
called `category`, the tag every element carries.

Sketches (`sketch.rs`) are how an outline is drawn, the one solver everything with an outline and holes uses: floors,
ceilings, roofs by footprint, shafts and filled regions now, topography next. A sketch is `SketchLine`s, straight or
arcs (a point `through`), in any order, either way round; `sketch::solve` cuts arcs into chords no more than 5° round,
welds ends within `TOL`, then names every problem at once with the lines it's about, what to fix first first
(`Problem::rank`: a line too short or out of range; two lines crossing, or one ending part way along another; two along
each other; three or more at a point; an end no other meets; a loop with no area), and otherwise walks the loops and nests
them by how many others each is inside: even, an outline (counter-clockwise), odd, a hole (clockwise) of the innermost loop
round it, so an island in a hole is an outline again. `solve_one` wants one outline (a floor's, a roof's). The element
keeps the sketch it was drawn or last edited by (`sketch` on floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; empty when it was made
over the walls or read from a file): each line is a part with an id and a GUID of its own (`HasPart`, listed in
`parts_now` by the element's GUID), going with the element when it moves and new on a copy; part ids are not given
again once a line is gone, for as long as the project is open (the library remembers the lowest it has held; a file holds the
ids in use, so one a line had before it was deleted and the file saved may be given again after the file is reopened). Commands take `sketch` (lines `[[x,y],[x,y]]`, arcs `[[x,y],[x,y],[x,y]]`, or
`{start, end, through?, id?}`) in place of `boundary` and its holes; `edit_boundary` without one gives the lines to edit
(the kept sketch while it still draws the outline, `sketch::draws`, else the outline's edges as new lines) and with one
redraws it, a line sent back with its `id` keeping it (keeping a roof's gables on edges that stay); the `sketch` command
solves without making anything. Messages name a line by its id, or its place in the list while it has none. A boundary
given as points is cleaned (a repeated point dropped, and one within a millimetre of the last), and every outline a command
makes or changes, whichever command (`floor`, `modify`, `edit_boundary`, `move`…), is judged as the sketch of its edges
(`Model::check_edits`, asked by the engine after each command but Insert from File): a floor's, ceiling's or roof's boundary,
an opening or a courtyard, a shaft's boundary, that crosses itself or lies along itself, has an edge ending part way along
another, or a spike or keyhole slit, is refused, saying which edges and where, and what to do: redraw it with `edit_boundary`; give
`boundary` or `sketch` (with the walls that touch at a corner named only when it was taken from walls), or simple `openings` or
`courtyards` for one of those rings, for one a command was making;
redraw the mass whose outline it is, for one made by face or by `mass_floors` (a mass itself may still have a bow tie outline,
a spike or a corner touching an edge, so the message says the outline isn't simple, not that it crosses itself);
and, for a roof's opening, which `edit_boundary` does not edit, give `modify` a simple `openings`, and from `dormer` change the
dormer's width, height or position. That is a change from the base, which let
`modify` and the commands that weren't given points set such an outline. `Model::check` doesn't judge the whole project by
it: a file, an IFC import or a Revit import with a keyhole outline still opens, and what leaves its outline alone (`modify`
of its offset, `delete`, `edit_boundary` with a sketch that is simple) still works, and so does what moves, copies, turns or mirrors
it, which makes it no worse (a copy is judged against the elements the command was given, so a new floor drawn with a bow tie
the file also holds is refused); what changes its shape is asked to redraw it first. One line that crosses itself (a closed polyline round a bow tie, a spline with a loop) is found as two lines
crossing are, and a sketch is refused at once past 200,000 straight pieces (a circle is up to 8,193 of them), or when its
pieces lie so close together that telling which cross would take six million steps.

The desktop's sketch mode (`crates/ui-egui/src/sketch.rs`) holds the lines until Finish Edit Mode, which solves them
first and says what's wrong for whoever drew it (`sketch::friendly`: what to fix, kind by kind, where, in the project's
units, and the lines by id) with those lines in the error colour; solved, it runs the command. Draw has every shape of
the Draw panel (`draw.rs`; lines, rectangles, polygons, circles, the arcs, Fillet Arc on two sketch lines, splines, ellipses,
polylines, Pick Lines: see [views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)) and Pick Walls (a line along each wall's location
line, an arc along an arc wall); a sketch line is any curve, so a circle or an ellipse is a loop of its own. Modify picks
sketch lines (a click, a window box from the left, a crossing box from the right), a picked line's handles (its corners, a
spline's points, a circle's centre) are grips that take every one joined there with them, and Delete removes them; Ctrl+Z takes back a line; the plan's snaps take the
sketch's own ends, middles, crossings and curves as well as visible view-specific detail (`snap::in_sketch`). Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft each start a new one (Boundary
Line, Sketch Ceiling); Edit Boundary redraws one selected. The Mode panel (Finish, Cancel; Edit Boundary) stands at the
ribbon's right end.

What the line tools hold to, and don't (`curves.rs`, `draw.rs`, `sketch.rs`). A curve is drawn as chords none further than `FLAT`
(0.25 mm) from it: a polyline's arcs, a circle, a spline and a fitted spline (a span of a spline is cut by the greatest
second derivative on it, so a ten metre arch is hundreds of chords), up to `MAX_DRAWN` extra points in all; a polyline whose
arcs would take more is refused, and a circle past about 3.4 km of radius (`MAX_DRAWN` chords stray `FLAT` from it there) is drawn coarser than `FLAT` rather than in more, 0.37 mm off at 5 km and 2 mm off at 27 km.
An arc, a circle or an ellipse reaches no further than `MAX_COORD` from the origin, as a wall's arc must; a spline lies inside
its control points, and a fitted spline is held to its points only, a cubic through them straying a little past. A curve's
start and end are the points it was given. Offset moves a polyline's lines along themselves and its arcs about their own
centres and makes each corner where the moved sides cross; it gives nothing where a side would vanish or turn round, or a
corner is so sharp its mitre would be 50 offsets long, and it does not trim a fold it makes in a concave shape (Revit's
does); an ellipse or a spline offsets to a fitted spline within 0.05 mm. Fillet on walls keeps their doors and windows
where they stand and refuses to cut one off, but does not stretch a third wall that ended on the corner. A detail line with
no style gets Thin Lines by the project's name, else the English one, else the thin black solid style. Of the line tools,
Revit has default shortcuts for Trim/Extend to Corner (TR), Offset (OF), Fillet (FL), Split (SL) and Detail Line (DL), which
`corner`, `offset`, `fillet`, `split` and `detail_line` have; it has none for Trim/Extend to a boundary, vertices, Convert
Spline, Edit Boundary, line patterns and styles or fill patterns, which have none here. Explode Polyline is EX, ours (PX is
the desktop's Plumbing Fixture).

results.content:
# Masses

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

A mass (`Mass`, category `mass`) is a footprint (`Mass::footprint`: counter-clockwise whichever way `boundary` runs) extruded from
`base_offset` over `level` up to `top_level` or `height`, as a shaft is, with `params`. Given a `top` outline (as many points as
`boundary`, twin for twin, and running the same way round; `Mass::top_ring` has it counter-clockwise like the footprint) it is lofted
straight between the two (`Mass::lofted`: a `top` equal to the footprint is no loft, and the `mass` command drops it; its `lean`
parameter makes `top` by moving the footprint sideways, a sloped mass). `Model::mass_outline(ms, z)` is the cross section at a height,
the footprint, or each corner that far along its way to its twin (`massing::ring_at`), and everything that measures a mass asks it:
floors, the `massfloor` and `mass` schedules, gross floor area, the plan, snaps. The area is a quadratic of the height, so
`Model::mass_volume` is Simpson's rule on three cross sections, exact. `massing::loft_problem` (which `Model::check` and the IFC import
both ask) refuses a top outline that doesn't pair up, runs the other way round, or collapses the cross section at some sixteenth of
the way up. A plan dashes the outline at its cut height where the plane passes through it (`Model::mass_cut_by`); a section outlines
where its line cuts it and never fills it in poché (`section` leaves masses out of `cuts`; a straight one's stretches come from
`view3d::crossings`, a lofted one's lines from `massing::section_lines`, the cut of its skin of triangles, joined end to end); 3D draws
a straight one as a slab and a lofted one as `massing::tris`, a closed skin turned out (two triangles on a side whose twin
edges are parallel, which makes it flat; a side that twists is cut into `massing::STRIPS` strips up its height, so a twisted loft's volume
in 3D and IFC is a percent or two under the exact one, while the areas and volumes the model reports are exact),
see-through by `graphics::MASS_TRANSPARENCY` unless the view's graphics say otherwise (`Look::with` starts a mass's override there, so a
project with masses never takes its plain shortcut). Show Mass (`show_mass`, MH) is `graphics {hide|show: [mass]}` on one view.
`Model::mass_slices` is the levels it crosses, from its base up to, not including, its top, each with how far the mass goes up from
there: `mass_floors` and the rows of the `massfloor` schedule (`schedule::sources`; a `Row` carries the schedule's category, not its
element's) come from it.
What a mass makes remembers it, under reserved names in `params` as phases and paint are held (`massing.rs`; no project or family
parameter may take them, `Model::check` holds each to a real mass and a level or a face of the right kind, `delete` takes off the marks
naming a mass that goes, and a copy or a split piece loses its own). `mass_floors` leaves `Mass Floor`, `{mass, level}`, on its floors,
so a second run finds them by it, gives them the mass's outline at their level (and the type, if one is given), makes none again, lists
as `stale` the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses and deletes those only with `prune`. `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and
`roof_by_face` build their element by running `wall`, `floor` and `roof` with the face's parameters, so those commands' checks stay the
one place, and leave `Mass Face`, `{mass, face}`: an edge number (numbered from the first point, counter-clockwise) for a wall, `"top"`
for a floor or a roof. A wall stands plumb, so only on a face whose top edge is right over its bottom edge (`massing::plumb`); a floor
and a roof lie on the top outline. `update_by_face` (UF; Revit's Update to Face has no default shortcut) rebuilds the geometry of the
ones asked for, a mass's, or all of them (`massing::follow`: a wall's ends, level, offset and height or top level; a floor's or roof's
boundary, level and offset; the type, a roof's slope and the rest stay) and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. A mass
mirrored in place runs its outline round the other way, so `relocate` renumbers the faces its walls hold (`massing::mirrored`). Nothing
else ties them to the mass, and IFC carries no mark: what comes back from a file is ordinary. `commands::category` reads `mass` and
`masses` as `mass` (it trims every trailing `s`, which would make `ma`). IFC writes a mass as an `IFCBUILDINGELEMENTPROXY` of object type
`Mass`, its footprint swept up; a lofted one is a closed `IFCTRIANGULATEDFACESET` with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set (`ifc::LOFT`) whose
`Loft` says as JSON how the footprint and the top outline pair up, since a face set doesn't. Import reads those before the proxies that
become components of families, and takes a lofted one only when that set's outlines are the body's bottom and its top; a mass whose
outline changes from base to top with no such set is left out and listed. The desktop's Massing tab has the Mass tool (`Tool::Mass`:
corners clicked, Enter or the first corner again finishes, `finish_mass`), Show Mass (the button is pressed while the view shows
masses) and, for each selected mass, the Model by Face buttons, which run the face commands, and Update to Face; a mass's Properties
hold its levels and offsets and `Top Outline`, its corners as `x, y` parted by `;`, blank for none.

# Shape editing for floors and flat roofs: design

This is the plan for IDEAS **MOD-16**: points and split lines on the top of a floor or a flat roof, so one element can fall
to drains, carry cross-falls, ridges and valleys, and keep a flat structure under a screed that tapers. It is what a
terrace, a roof garden, a podium's paving, a shower floor or a car park deck needs, and what BIMCraft can't model today:
each floor is level or one sloped plane, and nothing else. The rules in [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) apply to all of it
(everything is a command, `Model::check` validates, the core has no UI, test first, clean room).

Status, on the branch `mod-16-shape-editing` (raised upstream as IPedrax/BIMCraft#183):

- **Phase 0**, the triangulation, is built (`crates/core/src/triangulation.rs`).
- **Phase 1**, shapes on floors, is built (`crates/core/src/shape_tests.rs`, and
  [levels, walls and roofs](areas/levels-walls-roofs.md) says how): the data and parts, the four commands, the checks,
  `floor_faces` and `shape_planes`, 3D, plans, sections, IFC (one closed faceted Brep per slab, `Model::shape_solid`,
  with `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`), `volume_m3` in a floor's details, attached walls, transforms, `edit_boundary`,
  snaps and file format 13 (12 when written; upstream took 12 meanwhile). IfcOpenShell validates it with `express_rules=True` (`ci/ifc-coverage.txt` has a shaped
  floor) and measures the slab's volume as BIMCraft gives it.
- **Phase 2**, the variable layer, is built: `Layer::variable`, one a floor or roof type; a shaped floor's level underside
  (`Model::floor_under`) and prisms (`floor_prisms`); its layers in the 3D view and sections (`Variable::bounds`); its
  volume (`floor_volume`, and IFC's from its closed solid); attached walls under it; `Model::check` refusing a point that
  leaves the variable layer thinner than nothing; and reinforcement keeping to the structure under it.
- **Phase 3**, the desktop, is built: Shape Editing's Modify Sub Elements (a point, a corner, or both ends of an edge
  picked, `Floor::shape_pick`, set to the Options Bar's Elevation in one `edit_shape`), Add Point (Elevation, and
  Absolute), Add Split Line and Reset Shape, and a Variable box for a floor's or a roof's layers in Type Properties

## What users expect

The workflow architects know from the established tools, in our own words:

- A floor (or a roof with no sloped edges) gets **points** on its top. Each point has a height relative to the top the
  element would have without them. The corners of the outline are points too, at 0 until raised or lowered.
- **Split lines** cross the top between two points. They are creases the surface must fold along, so the user decides
  where a ridge or a valley runs instead of leaving it to the triangulation.
- The surface between the points and lines is **flat triangles**. The tool picks the creases it needs and draws them
  apart from the user's own.
- A layer of the type can be **variable**. Then the bottom of the element stays flat and that layer takes up the
  difference: the screed tapers, the concrete under it doesn't. With no variable layer, the whole slab follows its top
  at its type's thickness.
- **Reset Shape** takes it all off again.

## The approach: a top made of planar pieces

One new query gives every consumer what it needs:

```rust
/// A floor's top as planar pieces in plan, each with its plane: one piece for a level or sloped floor,
/// the triangles of its shape (coplanar neighbours merged) for a shaped one.
pub fn floor_faces(&self, f: &Floor) -> Vec<(Vec<P2>, walls::Plane)>
```

`floor_top` stays for the unshaped case and as the reference the point heights are measured from. `floor_slabs` is
rebuilt on `floor_faces`. For a roof, `roof_faces` gains the same branch for a shaped flat roof, so `roof_pieces`,
`roof_slabs` and everything downstream work as they do for slopes.

### Data

```rust
/// Points and split lines on a floor's or a flat roof's top (IDEAS MOD-16).
pub struct Shape {
    pub points: Vec<ShapePoint>,
    pub lines: Vec<SplitLine>,
}

/// A point on the top, `z` mm above (negative: below) where the top would be without the shape.
pub struct ShapePoint { pub id: Id, pub guid: Guid, pub at: P2, pub z: f64 }

/// A crease the top folds along, between two of the shape's points or outline corners.
pub struct SplitLine { pub id: Id, pub guid: Guid, pub a: P2, pub b: P2 }
```

- `Floor` and `Roof` get `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Shape::is_empty")] pub shape: Shape`.
- `ShapePoint` and `SplitLine` are **parts** (`HasPart`, listed in `parts_now`, `sync_parts`, `forget_parts`), as sketch
  lines are, so a schedule, an agent or a later "edit this point" can name one by id.
- Heights are **relative** to the unshaped top, so changing the floor's `offset` moves the whole shape with it. Commands
  may take `absolute: true` and convert when they run.
- A corner of the outline (or of an opening) not listed among the points is at 0. A point may lie on an outline edge,
  where it adds a corner.
- Every end of a split line is one of the points or an outline corner. A command that adds a line with a loose end adds
  that end as a point, at the height the top has there at the time.
- `Layer` gets `#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Not::not")] pub variable: bool`.
- **File format 13** (upstream's 12 came first), with a no-op step in `Model::migrate`. An older build that read a shaped floor would drop the shape
  and draw it flat. That's a misreading, not a field it can do without, so the bump is needed (CLAUDE.md, "A file is read
  kindly").

### Geometry

1. **Triangulate in plan:** a constrained Delaunay triangulation of the outline and its openings. The constraints are the
   outline edges, the opening edges and the split lines; the points are the inner vertices. Delaunay makes the result
   deterministic: the same points always give the same creases. Ties between cocircular points are broken by the
   corners' order, x and then y.
2. **Lift:** each vertex's z is the unshaped top there plus its point's `z`.
3. **Merge:** neighbouring triangles whose planes agree (within 0.01 mm at the shared vertices) merge into one polygon.
   A floor with points all at 0 is still one piece, and plans and IFC don't fill with needless diagonals.
4. **Thickness is plumb** for a shaped element: the type's thickness measured vertically, not square to each facet.
   Facets of different pitch then meet without gaps or overlaps underneath. At drainage falls of 1–2 % the difference is
   under 0.03 %. Sloped floors without a shape keep today's rule.
5. **With a variable layer**, the bottom is flat: the unshaped top less the type's thickness. Layers above the variable
   one follow the top, layers below it follow the bottom, and the variable layer is whatever is left at each point. Each
   facet becomes a `Solid::Prism` between its top plane and the flat bottom, not a `Solid::Slab` with a uniform rise.
6. **Caps:** `MAX_SHAPE_POINTS` (2,000) and `MAX_SPLIT_LINES` (2,000); every `z` within `MAX_COORD`. A triangulation
   past the cap is refused with the count, never truncated.

**The triangulation (built, phase 0).** The codebase writes its own geometry (the straight skeleton, the sketch solver,
CSG), its lints forbid panics, and the 3D view and plans run outside `Session::execute`'s `catch_unwind`, so a panic in
a dependency there would take the window down. So it is written here rather than taken from a crate such as `spade`:
`triangulation::constrained(outline, holes, points, lines)`, about 500 lines and 350 of tests.

- **Corners:** those within `TOL` of each other become one, the first in order of x and then y. An edge is cut at any
  corner within `TOL` of it, so a point on the outline bends it there.
- **Exact:** whether a corner lies left of a line, or inside a circle, is worked out in whole numbers on a 0.01 mm grid
  (`i128`), so a nearly flat triangle can't come out the wrong way round. That bounds a region to `MAX_ACROSS`, 10 km,
  well inside the 19 km where the in-circle sum would no longer fit.
- **Steps:** a sweep west to east triangulates the corners' convex hull; Lawson's flips make it Delaunay; Sloan's flips
  bring in each missing edge of the outline, the holes and the lines; Lawson's flips again, never across those edges; and
  a walk in from the hull, changing between outside and inside at each outline or hole edge, keeps the region's
  triangles.
- **Same answer in any order:** the output's corners and triangles are in a fixed order, so the same input in any
  order, either way round, gives an equal `Triangulation`.
- **Refused, saying why:** more than `MAX_CORNERS` (20,000) corners; a point not finite or past `MAX_COORD`; a region
  more than 10 km across; an outline or a hole with no area; a hole outside the outline or over another; a point or a
  line outside the outline or in a hole; a line shorter than a millimetre; edges that cross. Past 20 million flips it
  gives up rather than hold a command.
- **Speed:** 2,000 points with two lines in an L with a hole: about 17 ms, in the test build (the core is optimised
  there too).
- **Tests:** in the module. A random sweep of 400 cases, at least 100 of which must come out, checks that every triangle
  turns counter-clockwise, that they cover the region, and that no edge crosses a line. Leaving out the last Lawson pass
  or Sloan's flips each fails tests.

## Commands

The ids follow the established tool names, as the codebase does elsewhere.

| Command | Params | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `edit_shape` | `{id, points?: [{at, z, id?}], lines?: [{a, b, id?}], absolute?}` | Replaces the shape all at once, as `edit_boundary` does a sketch: what is sent back with an `id` keeps it. Without `points` or `lines`, it replies with the shape as it is: the points, including the corners with their heights; the split lines; the generated creases; and the pieces with their planes. That reply is what agents need to reason about falls. |
| `add_point` | `{id, at, z?, absolute?}` | One point; `z` defaults to the top's height there now (0 relative). |
| `add_split_line` | `{id, a, b}` | One line; loose ends become points at the current height. |
| `reset_shape` | `{id}` | Removes the shape. |
| `type` (floor, roof) | layers take `variable: true` | At most one per type; not on walls or ceilings. |
| `modify` (floor) | unchanged | Rejects `slope` or `arrow` on a shaped floor, with the reason (see Validation). |
| `falls` (phase 5) | `{id, drains: [[x, y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x, y], [x, y]], …]}` | Better than the established tools: sets point heights so water runs to the drains at no less than `fall` %, adding split lines along the valleys. Agents and architects describe a terrace this way, not point by point. |

Every reply lists the pieces' count and the lowest and highest point of the top. `inspect` on a floor already reports
`top: [lo, hi]` (`commands.rs:2122`); it must take the shape's points into account, not only the outline's.

## Validation (`Model::check`)

New rules, each with an error that says what to fix:

- A point outside the outline, or inside an opening: "point 100231 at (12500, 3400) is outside floor 100190: move it inside, or delete it".
- A split line that crosses another, crosses an opening, or leaves the outline (reuse `sketch::solve`'s problem kinds and wording).
- A split line end that is neither a point nor an outline corner.
- Two points within 1 mm of each other.
- A shape on a sloped floor (with `arrow`), or on a roof that isn't by footprint with `slope` 0. In version 1 the two are
  exclusive: shape a level element, and give its slope through the points.
- More than one variable layer in a type.
- **A variable layer thinner than nothing** anywhere: "at point 100231 the screed would be −12 mm: raise the point by 12
  mm or thicken the variable layer".
- With no variable layer, nothing bounds the depth: the slab just follows the top.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

import json, re, sys
langs = ['en','pt','es','sv','cs','fr','nl','de','it']
out = ['//! The default contents of a new project in each language: what `new` makes, with',

for l in langs:

    m = {}
    def rep(mo):

        if g not in m:

    assert '"#' not in mini
    out.append(f'pub const {l.upper()}: &str = r##"{mini}"##;')

use std::process::exit;

pub const VERSION: &str = "0.10.0";

fn usage_exit(prefix: Option<String>) -> ! {
    if let Some(p) = prefix {
        eprint!("{}\n\n", p);
    }
    eprint!("{}", catalog::USAGE);
    exit(1);
}

enum Action {
    Open(String),
    Sample,
    Highrise,
    Cmd(String),
    Script(String),
    Save(String),
}

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
    if args.is_empty() {
        usage_exit(None);
    }
    match args[0].as_str() {
        "--version" | "-V" if args.len() == 1 => {
            println!("bimcraft-cli {}", VERSION);
        }
        "commands" if args.len() == 1 => {
            let v = json::parse(catalog::CATALOG).unwrap();
            println!("{}", v.to_pretty());

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/<area>-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999 via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session) ; `alloc_id()` for element ids (from `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case, from the catalog), snapshots the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (which calls every module's `check(pr)`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step labelled by the command's catalog label (`always_step` hooks force a step even when nothing changed).
- `src/commands/mod.rs` (dispatch: each module's `dispatch(s, cid, p)` is tried in turn), `src/commands/basic.rs` (new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid; `open_path`, `write_atomic`), `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers producing the original's texts: `` `x` in mm is required``, ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9), `src/model.rs` (levels by elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` with the original's errors, `find` by id/GUID, `normalize_guid`), `src/check.rs` (core rules: level/grid; your rules go in your module's `check`).
- Done by others (reuse, don't redo): `src/rvt/` (Revit import; `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a planar-faces tracer and `src/rvt/rooms.rs` a room-enclosure test), `src/cloud/` (point clouds), `src/deflate.rs` (zlib/deflate byte-identical to the original's flate2: `zlib_compress` fast, `zlib_compress_level`), `src/inflate.rs`, `src/util.rs` (base64, fnv1a64), `src/media/` (pictures, `material`, `favorite`, `library`, `paint`), `src/styles/` (line/fill patterns, line styles, region/text/dimension types, line weights, object styles, units, room_area, language, standard, phase, phase_filter, option, parameter, voltage, distribution_system, wire_type, reinforcement_preset; `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` give new/copied elements their phase/option params; `styles::phasing::check_view_graphics` for view graphics; `styles::parameters::key_of` for project parameter keys), `src/mcp/`.
- Being written in parallel by others (don't implement these; if you need one, write a minimal private stand-in inside your area and note it): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors, ceilings, shafts, roofs, dormers, rooms, room separators, stairs, ramps, railings, masses and by-face, sketch/edit_boundary/edit_shape/add_point/add_split_line/reset_shape/falls, flip, show_mass; `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`), STRUCTURE (column, structural_column, footing, beam, strip_footing, pipe, duct, conduit, cable_tray, wire, down_conductor, ground_conductor, cabling, rebar, reinforce, type, family, symbol_set, component, the sizing calculators; `src/structure/`), VIEWS (sections, elevations, sheets, place, crop, duplicate_view, scale, detail, visual_style, graphics, filter, template, section_box, perspective, graphic_display_options, camera, work_plane, text, dimension*, tag, spot, spot_slope, detail_line and its join/explode/vertex/convert_spline/offset/trim_extend, filled_region, groups, linework, make_fill_pattern; `src/views/`), EDIT (modify, move, copy, rotate, mirror, corner, split, fillet, align, match_properties, delete, insert, link, reload, purge, delete_type, rename_type, autosave, recover; `src/edit/`), READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, measure, select_by_id, ids_of, filter_selection, and the project-file loader `src/load.rs`; `src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`), IFC-EXPORT (`src/ifc/export*`), IFC-IMPORT (`src/ifc/import*`). Rendering (render, PNG/SVG/PDF/GLB), CAD/DXF, the sample house and the highrise come later.

## How to test
`MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels exactly. Useful trick: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`) and run both programs on that file — the loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params` text) and the README/docs (`/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md` especially); then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases, every error and the order of checks). Learn element formats from the original's saved files.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't; edits outside your area; what other areas must provide or call.

## YOUR AREA: VIEWS (`src/views/`)
Commands: `section`, `elevation` (incl. the four building elevations, `facing`, `at`), `sheet`, `place` (viewports, schedules on sheets, the 3D view coming to be), `crop`, `duplicate_view` (plan views, detailing, dependent), `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `graphics` (categories, elements, overrides, filters, phase/phase_filter via styles, options, layers, template, background_grid, reset; the reply listing the view's settings), `filter`, `template`, `section_box`, `perspective`, `graphic_display_options`, `camera`, `work_plane`, `text`, `dimension` (aligned/linear/angular/radial/diameter/arc_length; refs to walls' faces/centres/ends, doors'/windows' centres and jambs, grids, detail lines, points, `{endpoint}`), `dimension_3d`, `dimension_constraint`, `dimension_text`, `dimension_value`, `tag` (labels, leaders, tag-all), `spot`, `spot_slope`, `detail_line` (lines, polylines with arcs, circles, ellipses, splines, insulation, clouds) and `join_polyline`, `explode`, `vertex`, `convert_spline`, `offset`, `trim_extend`, `filled_region`, `create_group`, `detail_group`, `repeating_detail`, `ungroup`, `group_type`, `linework`, `make_fill_pattern`. Their replies, errors, saved JSON and model rules (in your `check`). Many need walls/doors/floors/rooms to refer to: write them the way the original saves them, or work on projects the original built. The ids and names views get (Section 1, A101…, in the project's language), and what each view element holds, must match the saved files exactly.
I'll start by exploring the codebase and the environment.

| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) 
after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its 
own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer 
walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from 
the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's 
Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are 
subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a 
path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its 
level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen 
from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project 
parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água 
fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's 
language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an 
elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an 
`IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the 
luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and 
`IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 
127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |
| Lightning protection (SPDA) | Air terminals (captores), down conductors (condutores de descida), earthing electrodes (hastes de aterramento), inspection boxes and earthing conductors (the ring or mesh), the vocabulary of NBR 5419; Revit has no such tab, so its tools are BIMCraft's own, on the same runs and fixtures. A down conductor is a run that stands upright down a wall (the same point twice 
and two heights), round in steel or copper or a flat strip; an earthing conductor runs under the level; both belong to a named system. The project starts with a Franklin air terminal in three heights, an earthing rod driven 2.4 or 3 m and a round inspection box, original drawings in the project's language. IFC4 has no lightning protection, so the terminals, rods and boxes are 
`IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` and `InspectionBox`, which a reader can filter on and BIMCraft reads back into a family of its category; the conductors are `IfcCableSegment` `CONDUCTORSEGMENT`, told apart by a `Category` BIMCraft writes. A conductor under the level shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth) |
| Data (lógica, dados e voz) | Data outlets, voice outlets, racks, patch panels, the cable trays of the Electrical tab and structured cabling, the vocabulary of NBR 14565. Cabling is a run like a wire, round, in a named `system` (a link, a network), a Cat6, a Cat6A or an optical cable to start from. The project starts with a data and a voice outlet (a plate with its jacks cut in), a patch panel 
and a floor rack in three sizes, each at the height its type says, original drawings in the project's language, written as `IfcOutlet` (`DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`), `IfcCommunicationsAppliance` (`NETWORKAPPLIANCE`) and, for the rack, which IFC4 has no class for, an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `Rack`, and read back into a family of the same category (an `IfcOutlet` of another 
type is read as a power outlet) |
| Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 
kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands 
as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category. `reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and 
anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end 
to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project, which `reinforce` takes with 
`preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on 
it. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and 
a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a section's cut seen through the concrete. |
| Types | Wall, floor, ceiling, door, window, column, structural column, footing, beam, strip footing, pipe, conduit, cable tray, wire, down conductor, earthing conductor, cable, roof and railing types; editing one changes every element that uses it (a run type's roundness and material too) |
| Materials | A library of materials in each project, as Revit's Material Browser: each with a shading colour, a cut pattern and a surface pattern (solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete or insulation), drawn in code. Wall, floor, roof and ceiling types are built of layers, each a function, a material from the library and a thickness of its own, adding up to the 
type's: a wall's from the exterior in, the others' from the top down. Plans and sections cut each layer and hatch it with its material's cut pattern where it's wide enough to hold it (a drafting pattern, the same on screen and on paper); a floor's top in plan and a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan show their surface pattern at its size in the building; the 3D view shades each layer in its 
material's colour. A material may have a texture over its colour in the 3D view: a pattern drawn in code (brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof tiles, fabric, metal or insulation, each at its real size) or a picture you add (a PNG or a JPEG, kept in the project, at most 1024 px a side, up to 24 of them), laid on every face of what's made of the material at the size you give it, 
turned and moved as you say, by the face's own axes (across a wall, a slab's east and north); the library's materials come with theirs. Paint (PT) lays a material, with its texture, over one face of an element, a wall's exterior or a floor's top, over what its type is made of, as Revit's Paint does. A material, with its picture, can be kept in your Favorites, a file of your own (`favorites.json` 
in your configuration folder, or where `BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES` says) that every project reads; textures show in the 3D view alone (plans and sections keep their patterns), and IFC carries the colour |
| Editing | Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is); move, copy, rotate and mirror, with the walls joined to them stretching to stay joined and doors and windows going with their walls (a mirrored wall runs back the other way, its exterior mirrored); trim or extend two walls to a corner; split a wall, an arc into two arcs; flip 
walls; delete (a wall takes its doors and windows with it, and they their tags; a roof or floor walls are attached to lets them go); undo and redo |

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()
import re, sys
s = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
m = {}
def rep(mo):
    g = mo.group(0)
    if g not in m:
        m[g] = "GUID-%d" % (len(m)+1)
    return m[g]
s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
sys.stdout.write(s)
import json, re, sys
langs = ['en','pt','es','sv','cs','fr','nl','de','it']
out = ['//! The default contents of a new project in each language: what `new` makes, with',
       '//! `@G<n>` standing for a GUID made fresh for each project.',
       '']
for l in langs:
    s = open(f'/tmp/tpl/{l}.bimcraft').read()
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": 0', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m:
            m[g] = '@G%d' % len(m)
        return m[g]
    s = re.sub(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}', rep, s)
    d = json.loads(s)
    mini = json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(',',':'))
    assert '"#' not in mini
    out.append(f'pub const {l.upper()}: &str = r##"{mini}"##;')
open('/workspace/src/templates.rs','w').write('\n'.join(out)+'\n')
