# Structure and the discipline tabs (Plumbing, Electrical, SPDA, Data)

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Structure (`runs.rs`, `structure.rs`; the design for the five discipline tabs is in [docs/disciplines.md](../disciplines.md)). A run
(`model::Run`) is a straight element from `start` to `end` in plan; its `offset` mm over its level is the height of its `justify` line
(top, centre or bottom) at the start, `end_offset` at the end (level when none), `system` the name of the system it is in: a beam, a
strip footing, a pipe (Plumbing), and what the other tabs draw (conduits, cable trays, down conductors, data cabling) as further
`Element` variants over the same struct, as `Door` and `Window` share `Opening`; `model::run_arm!` is the pattern for any of them, so a
place that treats runs alike names no category, and a new category is a line there. Its type is `Types::runs[category][name]`, a `RunType`
(`width` across by `depth` deep, or round, in a `material` of the library). The section is square to the axis, so a sloped run is
`depth / cos θ` deep vertically (`Geom::half`). `runs::Geom` is the one place that knows the geometry (centre line, `footprint`,
`prism` for a rectangle, `tube` for a round one, `z_span`); plans, sections (a prism is cut like any solid; a tube by the plane
through the section's line, `Solid::cuts`: the hull of where its edges cross it, a ring, an ellipse when oblique), 3D, snaps and IFC call
it and know no category. A run's heights are those of its `justify` line, which a beam or a footing has at the top by default and
anything else at the middle (`runs::default_justify`); the desktop keeps each run tool's own justification and offset
(`keep_run_options`). A beam or strip footing can't stand or lean past 75°
(`runs::check`, `may_stand`: what stands is a column; a pipe, a conduit or a conductor may stand, a riser). In plan (`render::stands`) a footing or a run
hangs under the level it is drawn on, its top flush with the view's bottom, and is seen (`seen_below` allows `TOL` for these only,
or a wall of the storey below would show in the plan above); through the cut plane it's cut; over it and under the view range's top
it's dashed; a faint dashed centre line is drawn where it's seen or overhead, which is also where a click picks it. A structural column and an
isolated footing are `Column`s in their own categories (`Element::StructuralColumn`, `Element::Footing`; ask `Element::column()`,
`Model::column_type(e)` and `column_outline(e)`, which take the element, not the column) with types of their own
(`Types::structural_column`, `Types::footing`); a footing is laid down, its `height` its thickness and its `base_offset` putting its
top at the level (the command's `thickness` and `offset`). A floor is `structural` or not, the one flag, and its schedule and IFC say it.
`runs_of` and `stood_of` build what a command would make, so a tool's sketch is the element its click makes. The desktop's
`Tool::Run(category, start)` and `Tool::Stand(category)` serve every category: a tab adds a ribbon button and its rows in
`structure.rs`, `properties.rs` and `lang.rs`, not a tool. The Floor tool makes structural floors while `floor_structural` is set (SB,
the Structure tab's button; every other `set_tool` clears it); CL is the structural column on the Structure tab and the architectural one
elsewhere, as in Revit. IFC writes a run as an extrusion along its own axis (`Step::body_along`, `aim`) of the class and predefined type
the one table `runs::IFC` gives its category (import reads the same table back, `runs::from_ifc`), each structural element with
`LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, a run's system as an `IfcSystem` (named for it, its GlobalIds following the name) the runs in it
are assigned to by an `IfcRelAssignsToGroup`, its `Justification` and `Category` in `BIMCraft_Run`, and its material as an `IfcMaterial`. A beam, a column, a structural column and a
pad footing carry their section on their type, the IFC4 way (`Step::typed_member`, `write_types`): the `IfcBeamType`, `IfcColumnType` or
`IfcFootingType` is related by `IfcRelAssociatesMaterial` to an `IfcMaterialProfileSet` of one `IfcMaterialProfile`, holding the type's
material (a beam type's; a column type has none, so the material is `$`) and its profile, an `IfcRectangleProfileDef` of the width by the
depth or an `IfcCircleProfileDef` of half the width, in millimetres as every length is. Each occurrence is related to an
`IfcMaterialProfileSetUsage` of that set (one for each cardinal point, shared by the occurrences placed by it): a beam's cardinal point is
the line its heights are on, the top (8), the middle (5) or the bottom (2) of its section, a column's and a footing's the middle (5). The
beam has no other material association, so the importer reads a run's material through the usage (`element_material`). The profile
definition (`Step::section_profile`, keyed by `Section`) is written once for a section, and the type's profile and its occurrences' bodies
share it; two types of one name and two sections (a column's and a structural column's) are two type objects. A strip footing, a pipe and
the other runs have no profile set, only the plain material.
Import (`import::run_in`) finds a run's axis as the direction its body's points spread furthest in (power iteration on their
covariance), so a beam rolled about its axis comes in as the box round it; an axis that stands (a riser) has its width along east and
runs up; the justification BIMCraft wrote puts the heights back on the line they were typed at (`Geom::half`), none meaning the middle;
a system comes from the IfcSystem the product is assigned to, and its category from the class and type, or BIMCraft's `Category`
where a class has several; `LoadBearing` makes a column or a floor structural.

**Sizing** is a command with no model behind it, so it needs no connectors: `circuit` (`nbr5410.rs`, its tables in `nbr5410/tables.rs` as NBR 5410:2004 prints them: Tabelas 36 and 37 current capacity for methods A1 to D, 40 and 41 temperature and soil, 42 and 45 grouping, 47, 48 and 58) sizes one 
electrical circuit for copper: the design current from watts or VA, the demand and power factors and the phases at the voltage `system` it is given (it reads nothing from the model), then the smallest section and breaker with I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the 
breakers of NBR NM 60898) and a voltage drop within the limit (4 %, from the conductor's resistance at its working temperature and 0.1 ohm/km), with the neutral and the protective conductor. A section or breaker already chosen is never made smaller. It does not check aluminium, trays (methods E and 
F), several layers, short circuit, harmonics or the conditions of a reduced neutral, and says so; a circuit in the model and a panel schedule come after it. `conduit_fill` (`conduit.rs`, its catalogues in `conduit/tables.rs`) checks a conduit's fill: the conductors of a circuit (phases, neutral, 
protective; by outside diameter) over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two and 40 % for three or more (NBR 5410), and the smallest size of a family that takes them. The dimensions are the makers' own (Amanco Wavin PVC, Elecon steel, Corfio flexible cable), each family 
naming its document, page and address; the inside diameter is derived (outside less twice the wall); a cable the catalogue lacks (EPR, above 240 mm²) leaves the fill pending, never guessed. Trays are not sized. `drain_size` and `vent_size` (`drainage.rs`) size sanitary drains and vents as NBR 8160 
asks, by the fixture units (UHC) they carry, with the standard's own tables: Tabela 3 (the units and smallest drain of each fixture), 5 (branches), 7 (building drains and collectors by slope), 6 (stacks by the building's floors), 8 (branch vents), 2 (vent stacks and headers by the DN served, its 
units and the longest length of each vent DN) and 1 (a trap's longest run to its vent). A drain is never smaller than its fixtures' own drains or than one flowing into it (`min_dn`), and a building drain is DN 100 at least. They are stateless, so none of this needs a pipe network; a network that 
carries the units along the runs comes with connectors. `storm_size` (`storm.rs`) sizes storm drains as NBR 10844 asks: the flow Q = I·A/60 from a rainfall and a roof area, a downpipe by the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses (read curve by curve: the water depth in the gutter, the 
downpipe's length and a sharp-edged or funnel outlet; 70 mm inside at least; off the chart nothing is read) and a horizontal drain by Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, which reproduces its Table 4 within 1 %; 0.5 % slope at least). `water_size` (`water.rs`) sizes a cold water pipe of PVC 
soldável as NBR 5626 asks: the design flow of the fixtures by the method the project chooses (weights, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, or every fixture at once), the smallest DN within 3 m/s, the Darcy-Weisbach head loss over the length and the equivalent length of the fittings, and the pressure left (10 kPa at 
least at a point of use). `hydrant_size` (`hydrant.rs`) sizes hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks: the system type and fire reserve of Tabela 3 by occupation column and built area, the flow of the two most unfavourable jets of Tabela 2's type, and a pipe's speed (5 m/s at 
most), Hazen-Williams head loss (Tabela 1) and the head needed at its start. `load_points` (`loads.rs`) lists what a dwelling's rooms must have as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks: one ceiling lighting point per room (100 VA up to 6 m², 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above) and the general-use 
outlets by the room's kind, which its name says or `kind` gives (a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area and laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room and bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and by perimeter above), with their power (600 VA each for the first 3 
points of a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry and 100 VA after, or for the first 2 by the alternative where those rooms have more than 6 points together; 100 VA a point elsewhere) on the points a room has. It reads the model's rooms (inside the walls' finish) or the rooms it is 
given, and changes nothing. It leaves out the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, where the outlets stand, and the TUE, and says so.

**Electrical settings** (`electrical.rs`) are the tables circuits, panels and connectors will name, as Revit's Electrical Settings: `Voltage` (`nominal`, and the band `min` to `max` a device may read within), `DistributionSystem` (`phases` 1 to 3, `wires` the line conductors and the neutral and not 
the protective one, and the voltages it supplies by name: `l_l` between lines, `l_n` to the neutral, `l_g` to earth, and `ground`, how it is earthed as IEC 60364-1 names it) and `WireType` (`material`, `temperature`, `insulation`, a `note` saying where the ampacities come from, and `sizes`, a row 
for each section with its `ampacity`). Every section is in mm² whatever the project's units; a size a standard gives in AWG or kcmil is converted and keeps its name as `label`. Each is a map of `Model` (`voltages`, `distribution_systems`, `wire_types`), a library entry (`Kind::Voltage`, 
`Kind::DistributionSystem`, `Kind::WireType`, so each has an id and a GUID, comes in with Insert from File and is renamed with `rename_entry`), and has a command that makes, edits, renames and deletes it and, without a `name`, lists it (`voltage`, `distribution_system`, `wire_type`); `inspect` 
lists all three. A system names voltages, so `Model::lib_refs_mut` hands them out (a file holds their GUIDs, a rename follows) and `Model::check` refuses a system that names one the project lacks, saying which and listing the ones it has, and `voltage` refuses to delete one a system supplies; with 
three phases `l_l` must be about root three times `l_n`. `Model::voltage_range`, `system_voltages` and `wire_ampacity` are what circuits will ask: the band of a voltage, the voltages a system supplies (the ones a circuit on it may have) and the ampacity of a section in a wire type's table. A new 
project starts with `data/electrical.json`, data and not code: 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of NBR 5410:2004 Tabelas 36 and 37 (PVC 70 °C and XLPE or EPR 90 °C, seeded from `nbr5410/tables.rs`: method B1, two loaded conductors, a test keeps them equal) and of 
NFPA 70 Table 310.16 (THHN 90 °C, THW 75 °C); their ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked, and one number for a section cannot say how a wire is laid, so a wire type's `note` says. `start_system` and `start_wire` name the ones a new panel or circuit starts with for the project's units 
(Europe's in metric, North America's in feet and inches). None of it goes to IFC: the tables are project data, and what they produce (voltage, current, section) will go in the device's property set once circuits exist. On the desktop, Manage > Electrical Settings (`ui-egui/src/electrical.rs`) is 
one dialog with a tab for each table: rows to add and delete, a voltage chosen from the project's own for each line of a system, and a wire type's table of sections below its fields. It is a draft, applied by OK or Apply as one undo step (`Session::transaction`) through the three commands, in an 
order the core accepts (`renames::plan`, which the other Manage dialogs use, orders each table's renames and deletes; the voltages are made before the systems that name them and taken away after the systems that no longer do). A system's voltages are held by their rows' keys, so one renamed in the 
dialog is still the one named. A blank or repeated name, a voltage a system supplies being deleted, and what the core refuses are said inside the dialog, which stays open. Not yet: circuits, panels and the load schedule, connectors in families.

The discipline tabs after Structure add data to this, no engine code of their own. Plumbing: `pipe` (PI), types in PVC and copper
(`Types::runs["pipe"]`, outside diameters, so a pipe's `width` is its diameter and its schedule says Diameter). Electrical: `conduit`
(CN), `duct` (DU: a rectangular or round duct, written as `IfcDuctSegment`; only a Revit import makes them in practice) `cabletray` (CT, `cable_tray`: the one rectangular run) and `wire` (EW), by their outside size. Lightning protection (NBR 5419):
`downconductor` (DC, may stand: a riser down a wall) and `groundconductor` (GC), two runs of one IFC class that `BIMCraft_Run`'s `Category`
tells apart; an air terminal, an earthing electrode and an inspection box are components of their own family categories, written as
`IfcBuildingElementProxy` of the object type `Category::ifc` names, so the product's name (not its object type) holds `Family:Type` and
import reads it from there. Data (NBR 14565): `cable` (CB, `cabling`), a run like a wire, so a file's `IfcCableSegment` is a wire unless its
`Category` says cable; data and voice outlets (`IfcOutlet` `DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`; one of no type reads as the power outlet,
`Category::from_ifc` taking the first of equals), a patch panel (`IfcCommunicationsAppliance`) and a rack (a proxy of object type `Rack`);
the Cable Tray tool is the Electrical tab's, on the Data tab too. A fixture or a
device is a component of a family whose `family::Category` says what it is (a sanitary fixture, a floor drain, a pipe fitting, a pipe
accessory…); `Category::ifc` is its IFC class, predefined type and, where IFC has no class (lightning protection), the object type a
proxy carries, and `Category::from_ifc` reads the same table back, so a category is one row, in `family.rs`. A family's `kind`
(`Category::kinds`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`… for a sanitary fixture, `floor_drain`… for a drain, `bend`, `tee`… for a fitting, the names the
sizing commands count fixtures by) says which one it is, and `Family::ifc` writes that kind's predefined type in place of the
category's `.NOTDEFINED.`; the import reads it back with `Category::kind_of`, the first kind of a predefined type two share. The starter families are
`fixtures.rs` (original forms, named in the project's language; a fitting or a valve is centred on its pipe, along x, so placing it at the
pipe's height lines them up; a wall device, a board and a luminaire carry their `Mounting Height` in their type, so the Fixture tool
places them at the level and they stand where they hang). The desktop's `mep.rs` has one tool for every fixture and device, `Tool::Fixture(key)`: the families of the
kinds its `FixtureTool` names, listed in its Type Selector and placed as the Component tool places them (`placing` takes the tool's
kinds), and the tabs' ribbon panels; a fixture's two-letter shortcut is in `mep::FIXTURES`, not `SHORTCUTS`, since no command makes
one. Edit Type of a run type also sets whether it is round (a diameter, no depth) and its material.

Reinforcement (`rebar.rs`, `model::Rebar`, `Element::Rebar`, category `rebar`, the `rebar` command; tests in `rebar_tests.rs`). A bar is one
element: a round bar of `diameter` mm (3 to 100) bent along `path` (points in mm, `z` over its level), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless
told), with the `host` it reinforces (a beam, a column, a footing or a floor, held as a `Guid`, and it goes when its host does). A hoop
is a bar whose last point is its first; a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam, is one command with `count` and `step`, which makes one
element for each (IFC has one `IfcReinforcingBar` for each, and a bar schedule counts them). It has no type: the diameter and the grade
are its own, and the bends are sharp, with no hooks, so its length is the sum of its pieces (`rebar::length`) and its weight that
length of steel at 7850 kg/m³ (`rebar::weight_kg`). Nothing checks that it lies inside its host: `reinforce` places bars inside by construction. The schedule of category `rebar` lists Id, Level, Grade, Diameter,
Length, Count, Weight and Host, and grouped by Grade, Diameter and Length with Count and Weight totalled it is a bar schedule. IFC
writes each as an `IfcReinforcingBar` (`SteelGrade`, `NominalDiameter`, `CrossSectionArea`, `BarLength`) with a body of an
`IfcSweptDiskSolid` along an `IfcPolyline`, aggregated (`IfcRelAggregates`) to its host, or contained in its storey when it has none;
import reads the same back, with the host found by the aggregation. The 3D view draws a tube along each straight piece
(`rebar::tubes`, built with a round run's tube), which the concrete round a bar hides: look at bars with their host hidden. A section draws each bar it cuts as a
dot over the host's poché (`render::section_in` keeps them out of the host's pieces, which would swallow them); a plan draws them too (`render::bar_in_plan`).

Importing a structural program's IFC (Eberick, Cype and the like; tests in `eberick_tests.rs`, written by hand, never from anyone's project). Each
product is named by its mark, so a name that is not its type's (BIMCraft names a product by its type, and writes it as its object type too) is its
`Mark` parameter, for the categories in `import::MARKED` (beams, columns, structural columns, footings, strip footings and floors; not stairs,
which BIMCraft calls "Stair"). The single values of every property set that is not BIMCraft's (`BIMCraft_*`, `RoomSeparation`; `Project Parameters`
is read by its names as written) are project parameters named for the property, a character a formula can't say turned into a space
(`parameter_name`: "Cargas de parede (G2)" is "Cargas de parede G2"), lengths in the file's unit made millimetres; `LoadBearing` is left out because
it already makes a column or a floor structural. The cover Eberick sets (`Cobrimento`, `ConcreteCover`) is therefore on the host as a length, for the
rules that will arm it. A run is found in its body as the way it spreads furthest, except where the body is one extruded profile and the extrusion is
not up: then it runs along the extrusion (`Reader::extrusion`), because a beam between two columns can be shallower than it is deep, and its body then
spreads furthest up. A strip footing, a plan outline stood up, is still read by its shape. A landing slab that belongs to no stair is a floor.

Bars by rules (`reinforce.rs`, the `reinforce` command; tests in `reinforce_tests.rs`). The engineer says how many bars, how thick and how far
apart; the module lays them out in the host's own frame (`Frame`: along, across, up) inside the cover and checks that what is asked fits, with the
message saying what to change. It holds geometry and no standard's table: a spacing or a count is never decided here (that is design), and the
clearance between bars (`clearance`, their thickness and at least 20 mm unless told) is the only rule it brings. Parameters are read with serde types
that deny unknown fields (`Row`, `Pitch`, `Stirrup`, `ColumnBars`, `Mesh`, `Grid`), by key, so a key that is not the host's is refused with the host named.
The cover is `{top, bottom, sides}` (Revit's faces: the top and bottom faces of a beam, a footing or a floor, the ends of a column, and all round
the rest) or one number, and where none is given the host's `Cobrimento` or `ConcreteCover` parameter (a length in mm, as the import of an Eberick IFC
leaves it) is the cover. A spacing is the most between bars: `spread` and `stations` place them evenly from end to end, so the count follows the length
(Revit's Maximum Spacing) and `ends` gives closer stirrups in the first and last `length` mm. A stirrup is a closed loop; with `hook` it runs on past
its first corner to a tail turned into the section at each end (`stirrup`). A beam has `bottom` and `top` rows, `stirrup`, `skin` and `anchor`; a
column `bars` (`x` and `y` along each face, corners counted; a round one, `count` round its circle), `stirrup` (a round one's a polygon of 24 sides), `ties`
(across a rectangular section; with `hook` a tail at each end turned toward the other axis) and `anchor`; a footing a `mesh` of two layers with `hook`
turning their ends up (a round one's bars stop at its circle, `half` in `footing`); a floor `bottom` and `top` meshes (`hook` turning their ends up from the
bottom one and down from the top one, square to the slab's top) whose bars stop a cover short of its outline and of its
openings (`chords`, a scan line through the outline and the openings together; a bar parallel to an opening's edge and nearer it than the cover keeps
its cover from the ends only). A sloped floor's layers are measured from its top face, square to it (`off`, and its secant for the height plumb), so the
cover and the thickness are the type's and its bars follow the slope; a mesh on a slope is one plane's bars. Round beams and strip footings are refused. Each bar is a `rebar` element of the host with a `layer`
(`bottom`, `top`, `skin`, `stirrup`, `bars`, `tie`, `mesh x`, `mesh y`, `bottom x`, `top y`, ...); reinforcing a host again replaces its bars that have a layer
and leaves the ones with none, which were drawn by hand, and one command makes up to `rebar::MAX_BARS`. A bar's layer is in the project file and the
schedule (a field a bar schedule may show), not in IFC. What it does not do: bends other than a hook, laps and splices, bars of a round beam, and any check
against a standard. A section shows a bar in its plane as a strip along it and one it crosses as a dot (the cut of the bar's tube, `section_in`); a bar
beyond the cut stays hidden by the concrete it is in.

More of `reinforce`. `hosts` arms a list (`rebar::MAX_HOSTS`, 1000) alike in one command: every host's bars are made before any is replaced, so one that refuses (its refusal names its category and id) arms none, and `rebar::MAX_BARS_ALL` (20000) caps all of them
together. A `hook` on a beam's `bottom` and `top` rows is the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at each end
(a number for both, or `{start, end}`), and on a column's `bars` a leg turned into the section along the way across the face the bar is on
(`{below, above}`); `legs` reads it, with its own words when it is not a length, and a leg that does not stay inside the stirrup (a column's: stop
short of the middle) is refused. The bends are sharp, as every bar's are, and each leg is a piece of the path, so the length and the weight count it.
A `reinforcement_preset` is `reinforce::Preset`, a kind of host (`KINDS`) and the parameters that kind takes, in `Model::reinforcement` and as a library
entry (`Kind::ReinforcementPreset`, so it has an id and a GUID, comes in with Insert from File and is renamed with `rename_entry`); it is checked
for its keys and its size when saved (`Preset::check`, `MAX_PRESETS`) and against a host only when it arms one. `reinforce` with `preset` takes its parameters
and lets any given with it replace them, key by key; a preset of another kind than the host is refused, saying both. Plans: a bar of the plan's level
is drawn from above, solid when the cut plane is over its lowest point and dashed when it is over the plane and under the view range's top, a bar
that stands (a column's) as a dot, and bars that lie on one another (a column's stirrups, one over the next) once.

Bends beyond a hook. `bottom.bent` `{count, angle?, top?}` (`Bent`, `bent_up`) takes `count` of a beam's inner bottom bars (the two at the corners hold the
stirrups and stay straight; the others are picked evenly) and bends them up at each end: along the top face for `top` mm from the end (a fifth of the
length unless told), down a slope of `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) to the bottom row's level and along it. They are on the layer `bent`,
have no hook, count as bottom steel in the check, and are refused where the slopes meet in the middle, where the section is too shallow to rise
in, and where one comes within the clearance of a top bar at the top. `bars.jog` `{by, from_top, slope?}` (`Jog`, `step`, `stepped`) steps a column's
bars `by` mm toward the axis (a corner bar along both faces, a face bar across its own, a round column's radially), the step starting `from_top` mm below
the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told); the points of the bar above the step move with it, including a hook's leg, and
the bars at their new places are checked against one another for the clearance.

The check (`reinforce/norm.rs`). `check` `"NBR 6118"`, with `aggressiveness` (1 to 4) and `fck` (MPa), makes `reinforce` return `notes`: where the bars
made fall short of the usual limits for the kind of host (Table 7.2's cover by class; for a beam the 4 % most, the 0.15 % least up to C30, skin bars over 600 mm
deep, stirrups of 5 mm to a tenth of the width at most min(0.6 d, 300) apart; for a column bars of 10 mm to an eighth of the side, 4 bars or 6 round,
centres at most min(2 sides, 400), 0.4 to 8 % of steel, stirrups of 5 mm or a quarter of the bars' at most min(200, the side, 12 bars) apart; for a floor
bars of at most an eighth of the thickness at most min(2 h, 200) apart). A note never refuses: an engineer may know better, and the bars are made.
It reads only the bars made, so a limit that needs shear, the load or the aggregate is not in it. The numbers are typed from handbooks and course material
that print them, not from the standard's text, which is paid for, and the item numbers are the 2014 edition's at the level of the chapter's item: check
one against a copy before relying on it. The desktop's Check row (Standard, Aggressiveness class, fck) shows the notes inside the dialog, which stays
open, with the bars made, so a field can change and OK remake them.

The Reinforce dialog (`crates/ui-egui/src/reinforce.rs`, Structure > Reinforcement, RF; tests in `tests/reinforce.rs`). It opens on the one beam, column,
structural column, footing or floor selected (anything else says what to select), with the form of its kind (`BEAM`, `COLUMN`, `FOOTING`, `FLOOR`: tables of
groups of fields, each field the path of the parameter it sets, such as `bottom.count`). Every field is text: a count is a whole number, a bar size is mm,
a length is read in the project's units (`Units::parse`); a field left empty is not sent, a group with none filled is left out, and the command is the one
that says what is missing. OK builds the parameters and runs `reinforce` as one undo step; a refusal is the command's own words, shown inside the dialog
(a status box in the view's corner could lie over its buttons) with the dialog left open and the project unchanged, and a field that is not a number is
named before the command is asked. It takes any number of elements selected, of one form (a mixed selection says so), and arms them with one `hosts` command; Remove Bars removes the bars of all. What was typed is kept for the next element of the same form (not in the project, not on disk). The 
Preset row lists the project's presets of the form: choosing one fills the fields (`ReinforceDialog::load`, the reverse of `params`, lengths in the project's units), Save Preset keeps the fields as they are under the name typed (`reinforcement_preset`, the parameters without the hosts), and Delete 
Preset takes the chosen one away; each keeps the dialog open. Remove Bars, shown
when the element has bars the command made (those with a layer), deletes them and leaves the ones drawn by hand. The fields' accessible names are
"Group: Field" (`Bottom bars: Count`), and the cover's is `Cover`, its label having a colon so that no two nodes carry the name.

**Connectors.** A family's `connectors` (`family::Connector`, a list for any discipline; today the electrical device's) say what
a placed device draws: `kind` `power` or `switch`, `system` `power-balanced`, `power-unbalanced` or `switch`, `poles` (1 to 3),
`voltage`, `load_va`, `power_factor` and a `classification`. The numbers are numbers or formulas over the family's parameters, so a
type sets its load (the starter luminaires' `Load` parameter) and an instance parameter lets one component set its own; a
`power-unbalanced` connector's `load_va` may be a list, one load for each pole, and a single number is shared out evenly.
`Family::check` refuses a family of two `power` connectors, a kind and system that don't go together, poles, voltage, power factor
or load out of range for any type, and a load on a switch. A connector is a part (`HasPart`: an id and a GUID, kept by place
while the family is edited), and a family without any reads and places as it always did. A component's `element_json` carries
`connectors` worked out for its type (`Family::connector_values`: `load_va` in all, `load_va_by_phase`), which a circuit will sum;
there are no circuits, panels or fitting-to-pipe joins yet, and the connector holds no position. `Model::warnings` (shown by
`inspect`; `Model::check` stays an error only) says which lighting, outlet or switch family in use holds no connector, so its devices
count as zero load. IFC writes each device with a connector `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` (`NumberOfPoles`, and for a power
connector `PowerFactor` and `RatedVoltage`) and `BIMCraft_Connector` (`System`, `Classification`, `LoadVA`, `LoadVAPhase1`…); IFC
import doesn't read them back.

# Families, forms, materials and textures

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

A family (`Model::families`, `family.rs`) is parameters, types that set them and forms in its own axes: x along a
component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base; a form is a profile in a sketch plane (`xy` swept up, `xz` along y,
`yz` along x), its sizes numbers or formulas, or triangles as a file brings them. A component places a type;
`Model::component_pieces` are its forms where it stands. Plans draw them from above, a form's edges hidden under a higher
form of the same component; sections show them beyond their line and never cut them (a `Solid::Mesh` is cut only where its `cut`
says, as a round run's tube is); the
3D view takes a form's triangles that share an edge and turn under 20° there as one curved surface, so a curve draws no
edge between its facets (`view3d::facets`) and shades smoothly across them, each corner lit by the angle-weighted mean of
its own surface's normals there, so a crease keeps its step (`corner_normals`); IFC writes each form as a closed face set,
triangles turned out, and reads one family per family name the file gives.

A form is swept, or with an `axis` turned about it (`family::revolve`: `from` to `to` degrees, 32 steps to a turn, the profile to
one side of the axis); a `void` cuts the solid forms listed before it (`csg::subtract`: convex polygons in binary space
partitions, built and walked with a worklist rather than recursion and bounded by a `Meter`, so a hostile shape ends in an error;
a cut piece keeps its uncut outline in plan). A family of category `door` or `window` is hosted: its `Width` and `Height` (English
names, whatever the project's language) size the wall's opening, `Sill Height` is a window's default sill, its forms are drawn in
the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it from the wall's middle plane and + toward its
exterior, z up from the sill) and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`; its `symbols` also draw in plan (a door's swing). Its `connectors` say what an electrical device draws ([structure and MEP](structure-and-mep.md)); a family file keeps them. An
`Opening` holds a `family`, or none (one of the project's own types): `Model::opening_dims` gives its size either way
(`opening_type` returns it by value), its flips are mirrors (`opening_local`), and `Element::family()` is the one way to ask what
family a component or an opening is of. Sections show a family opening's forms beyond their line and never cut them.
How a door or a window opens is its family's `operation` (`model::Operation`: swing, double-swing, sliding, double-sliding,
folding, fixed), or for one of the project's own types the type's (`OpeningType::operation`); none, a door swings. IFC writes
it as the door's `OperationType` (`Operation::ifc_door`, its side from `flip_hand`: `SLIDING_TO_RIGHT`) and a window's
`PartitioningType` (two leaves, `DOUBLE_PANEL_VERTICAL`); the import reads a door's back, or its `IfcDoorType`'s (IFC4) or
`IfcDoorStyle`'s (IFC2x3), onto the type it makes. Schedules have it as the `Operation` field, in the project's language. A
window's panel operation (`IfcWindowPanelProperties`, a sliding sash) needs an `IfcWindowType`, which the export doesn't write yet.
A material's `texture` (`texture.rs`) is a pattern drawn in code or a picture of `Model::images` (a PNG or JPEG comes in, is kept
as a PNG of at most 1024 px, its header checked before the decoder makes room for it), laid on a face at its `size` in mm by the
face's own axes (`view3d::basis`: across is level, up goes up it, east and north where it lies flat), sampled per pixel from the
depth buffer, in the 3D view alone, from a mip chain. A triangle carries a skin (`view3d::skin`): in its low 24 bits a texture id (one more than its material's place in the
library), in its high 8 its material's `transparency`; `Scene::new` resolves the textures. A material's `transparency` (percent,
0 to 100, 0 opaque and not written, the starter Glass 70) is how see-through the 3D view draws what is made of it, with no view
override: a layer's skin wins over its element's, paint gives a face its own, and a family-less window's glass takes the Glass
material's. IFC carries it in `IFCSURFACESTYLESHADING`'s second argument (0 opaque to 1 clear, `$` for opaque), read back from a
shading or a rendering. Only the nearest see-through surface is blended, so a glass wall's far face and stacked glass don't
accumulate; plans and sections ignore it. Paint (`paint.rs`) is `{face: material}` in an element's `params` under `Paint`, a reserved
name: a triangle's face is read from its winding, so every solid emits triangles turned out (`Solid::tris`, `prism`), and
`Image::face` says which face a pixel is on. Favorites (`favorites.rs`) are a file of the user's own (`default_path`:
`BIMCRAFT_FAVORITES`, else the configuration folder) with materials and their pictures, families and their materials; they change
a project only through the `favorite` command (`load` never overwrites without `replace`). The desktop's Family Editor
(`editor.rs`) edits text (`FormText`, `ParamText`, ...) and changes the project's family only through a `family` command; its
preview is a scratch `Session` of its own, and it says what's wrong inside the window (the status box, over the view's corner, would lie on its
buttons).

A type of a category or of a family is renamed with `rename_type` (`Model::move_entry` moves it in its map, and `rename_entry` the
library entry and every reference `Model::lib_refs_mut` visits, so it keeps its GUID). A type or a family goes with `delete_type` (one entry, refused while an element uses it, and for the last type of a category or of a family: a
tool needs one to place) and `purge` (every entry of the kinds asked that nothing uses). Use is what `Model::lib_refs_mut` visits, the one place
that names every reference to a library entry: `Model::library_uses` counts them on a copy of the model, `Model::unused_entries` is one pass of
what purge takes out (each category keeps its default's type, else its first; a family that goes takes its types), the command repeats it
for what a pass frees (a family's material, a type's), at most 16 times, on a copy that becomes the model only when it isn't a `dry_run`.
`Model::remove_entry` is the single place that knows where each kind lives. The desktop's Purge Unused window (`purge.rs`) lists a dry run
for the kinds checked and runs the same; the Project Browser's Families lists the system types and has the right-click Delete.

The `family` command works out the whole change before the model is touched (`commands.rs::family`), so reading one costs no undo step
and a family `Model::check` would refuse never enters it. `family {name}` alone reads: the definition with every form's and symbol's `id`
and `GUID`, each type's `values` worked out, and `warnings` — no `model_mut()`, no file. Without `name` it lists the project's families
with their category and how much of each there is; `save` still writes one to a file. `dry_run: true` builds the change it's given
locally and replies `ok`, `warnings`, `changes` (parameters and types added, taken away and changed; forms and symbols replaced, patched
and deleted by id; the rename) instead of doing it; a refusal comes back as an error exactly as it would without it, carrying every error
and warning found, not only the first. One form or symbol is patched by its `id` or `guid` (`form`/`symbol`: its fields merged over what
that one holds, a `null` taking one away, its place, id and GUID kept; `delete_form`/`delete_symbol` to take it away), where `forms` and
`symbols` still replace whole lists — `keep_parts` binds by place, so patching is what leaves the other parts' ids alone. Validation is
`family/validate.rs` (`Family::problems`): every formula read at once (`names`, unknown parameters besides a hosted family's
`Wall Thickness`, syntax errors with the character they stop at), then `Family::check`, plus geometry warnings best worked out around
what doesn't build — a void reaching no solid before it, a form wholly outside its opening, one thicker than its wall, a door's or
window's plan with no symbols — each aggregated as `(in type …)`. `Family::shapes` gives each form's box before any void cuts it, from
the same `solid` `build` uses. `render {family, type, mode}` draws a family on its own: a `Session::new()` of its own holding the
project's materials and images, a wall of `wall_thickness` mm for a hosted family (a floor of its own footprint otherwise) with the type
in it, then `render_view` on that model — `3d`, `plan` (what its symbols draw) or `elevation` (front-on) — and the project keeps no
element and no undo step from it, the way the Family Editor's own preview already worked (`editor.rs::scratch`).


## Plan symbols

A family's `symbols`, of any category, are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes: each is exactly one of a
`line` (up to `MAX_PROFILE` points), an `arc`, a `text` or a `dot`, with `visible` (a yes/no parameter or a formula) for any.
`Family::marks` works them out, for a type's values, as `Mark`s: a `Mark::Line` (an arc as chords of `ARC_STEP` degrees; a
label as a `Mark::Label`, lettered with `font.rs` by `lettering` where it is drawn) or a `Mark::Dot`. A `text` is `{at, height, value, align?}`: capitals `height` mm
tall, `at` the middle of the line, started, centred or ended there (`Align`); `{Parameter Name}` in `value` reads that parameter
(`said_text`: a number as plainly as it reads, a material by its name), an unknown name or an unclosed `{` is refused by
`Family::check`, and the lettered text is at most `MAX_TEXT` characters. `at` is the middle of the line of text vertically, and `align`
sets the horizontal anchor. A `dot` is a `Circle`, drawn solid in ink. Everything
numeric is checked finite and within `MAX_COORD`; a label's height and a dot's radius must be above zero.

`Model::component_marks` places a component's marks (mirrored, then turned and moved) and `Model::opening_marks` an opening's,
and `render::marks` draws them: lines in the category's pen (`BY_CATEGORY`, so Object Styles and Visibility/Graphics apply), dots
as filled discs. Coarse detail leaves them out. A label's anchor is placed with the component (turned, mirrored, moved) but its
letters never are: they are always drawn at 0 degrees in the view, left to right with a horizontal baseline, however the component
stands (the simplest rule; no flipping by quadrant). Symbols are annotation of the component's level: they draw in that level's
plan and its ceiling plan whatever height the component's forms reach (a ceiling light shows its symbols in the floor plan) and
on no other level's; the forms are outlined by the old rule (whole while any of them is between the view's depth and cut plane,
and not in ceiling plans). A component with no forms draws its symbols the same way. IFC export ignores symbols (they are plan notation, not geometry); the Family Editor's Symbols tab lists
all four parts. Library parts: a symbol of any kind has its own id and GUID (`HasPart`, `keep_parts`). A file written with
`text` or `dot` symbols, or symbols on a category other than a door or a window, is read by an older version only with them left
out or refused, so the file format is unchanged.


## Symbol sets

A symbol set (`symbol_set.rs`) is families that are a plan symbol and nothing else, loaded on demand and never part of a new
project: the starter fixtures (`fixtures.rs`) are in every project, and 76 more would crowd every family list. The
`symbol_set {set, names?}` command adds a set's families to the project (the Electrical tab's Symbols > Load AREI Symbols
button runs it); a family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing and an edited family is
never overwritten (`loaded` and `kept` in the reply). Each family has one type, `Standard`, no forms, and the symbols of
`crates/core/data/arei-symbols.json`, in the family `symbols` schema (mm, y up, the origin at the symbol's own origin): a
switch is in category `switch`, a socket in `outlet`, a data socket in `dataoutlet`, a light point or luminaire in `lighting`
and everything else (appliances, consumers, sources, domotics, protection) in `generic`, so the Device and Lighting Fixture
tools list their own kinds and the others are placed with the Component tool. They have no connectors, loads or 3D forms: they
are plan symbols only for now, and a family without a connector raises no warning in `inspect`.

The `arei` set is the graphical symbols of Table 2.23 of the AREI/RGIE (FOD Economie, Book 1), redrawn originally. The names
are those printed in its Dutch and French versions (`name_nl`, `name_fr` in the data), the English ones are working names. The
symbols are drawn at about 30 mm per drawing point, so a socket is about 25 cm wide on a plan. `names` (`en`, `nl`, `fr`) picks
the language of the family names; as given none, a French project gets the French wording, a Dutch project the Dutch
and every other language the English.

# The discipline tabs: design

A client asked for the complementary-project tabs Revit users know: structure (estrutural), plumbing and drainage
(hidrossanitário), electrical (elétrico), lightning protection (SPDA) and data and voice (lógica, dados e voz). This note
is how BIMCraft builds all five with as little new machinery as possible. All five are built, each a follow-up that added data
to what is described here, not new engine code. The rules in [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) apply
to all of it (everything is a command, `Model::check` validates, the core has no UI, clean-room).

## What the five have in common

Look at what each tab draws and there are three shapes, and BIMCraft has two of them already.

| Shape | Examples | What builds it |
|---|---|---|
| A vertical or point thing with a type and a size | columns, footings; sanitary fixtures, panels, luminaires, outlets, racks, air terminals | `Column` (vertical members) and the families with `Component` (devices and fixtures) |
| A straight thing between two points | beams, strip footings; pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays, down conductors, data cabling | **`Run`**, new |
| A slab or a region | structural floors, foundation slabs | `Floor`, with a `structural` flag |

So the new element is one: the run. Everything else is a category added to something that exists.

## (a) The run

`model::Run` is a straight element: from `start` to `end` in plan, at a height over its `level`, of a type with a size.

```
Run { type, level, start, end, offset, end_offset?, justify, system, params }
```

- **Height.** `offset` is the height, over the level, of the run's `justify` line (`top`, `centre` or `bottom`) at the
  start; `end_offset` is the height at the end, and when it is missing the run is level. A sloped run (a drain falling
  1%, a brace) is two offsets. A vertical run (a riser, a down conductor) has the same `start` and `end` and two
  offsets. Beams default to `top` justification, as engineers think of them (top of beam at the top of slab); the pipes
  and cables to come default to `centre`, the commands set it, not the type.
- **Section.** The type's `RunType { width, depth, round, material }`: a rectangle `width` across by `depth` deep, or
  round, `width` across. It is square to the run's axis, as a pipe's or a member's is.
- **Chains.** The command takes `points` and makes one run for each segment, as `wall` does. A fitting, an elbow or a
  tee is not a run: runs that meet butt against each other until the MEP slice joins them (ROADMAP 2.x). A family has
  connectors (`Family::connectors`) for what an electrical device draws; a run and a fitting have none yet.
- **System.** `system` is a name ("Água fria", "Circuito 3", "SPDA 1"). Nothing else about a system is stored: a
  schedule groups and filters by it like any field, and a fixture carries its system as a project parameter named
  `System`, which exists already. Systems are a name, not a registry, because a registry would need rules for renaming,
  deleting and merging that no tab has asked for. (What a system *supplies* is another matter: the project's electrical
  settings keep voltages, distribution systems and wire types as tables, `electrical.rs`, which circuits and panels will
  name; a run's `system` stays a name.)

In plan, a run or a footing is drawn from the level it hangs under: its top is flush with that level, so a beam placed at
the level is seen by that level's plan, which an element whose top is that low would not otherwise be (a plan sees down to
its view depth, which is the level by default); its centre line is dashed, to pick it by; one whose underside is over the cut plane and under the view range's top is
dashed, as a roof's eaves are; one that crosses the cut plane is cut, in poché. A section cuts a rectangular run across its
section, and the 3D view draws it as a sloped prism, or a round one as a tube.

A run is one Rust type serialized under several categories, as `Door` and `Window` share `Opening`. The category is the
`Element` variant, so Visibility/Graphics, schedules, project parameters, phases, view filters and the IFC class all
work per category without a line of per-category machinery. Today: `beam`, `stripfooting`, `pipe`, `duct`, `conduit`, `cabletray`, `wire`, `downconductor`, `groundconductor` and `cable`. A tab adds a variant, a name
in `model::run_arm!` and a row to each table below:

| Category | Tab | Revit's name |
|---|---|---|
| `beam`, `stripfooting` | Structure | Structural Framing, Structural Foundation: Wall |
| `pipe` | Plumbing | Pipe |
| `conduit`, `cabletray`, `wire` | Electrical | Conduit, Cable Tray, Wire |
| `downconductor`, `groundconductor` | SPDA | (none: Revit has no lightning protection) |
| `cable` | Data | Wire / Cable Tray |

Types live in `Types::runs`, a map from category to type name to `RunType`, so a tab adds no field to `Types`. The model
starts with a few (`Beam 200 x 500`…), and the `type` command creates and changes them. Geometry is in `runs.rs`: the
centre line's ends, the footprint in plan, the prism or tube in 3D. The plan, the section, the 3D view, the snaps and
IFC call it and know no category. A rectangular run is a sloped prism, so sections cut it; a round one is a tube mesh, a convex
solid, which a section cuts by the plane through its line (`Solid::cuts`: where the tube's edges cross the plane, their hull, a
ring, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A component's forms, which are not convex, are shown beyond the line and never cut.

## (b) Points and verticals

- **Vertical members.** `Column` (a plan outline, a base, a height) is reused as it is, under two more categories:
  `structuralcolumn` and `footing` (an isolated pad, Revit's Foundation: Isolated, which is a column laid down: its
  `height` is its thickness and its top is at the level). Each has its own types (`Types::structural_column`,
  `Types::footing`, both `ColumnType`).
- **Devices and fixtures.** Placed with the Component machinery from families, by adding `family::Category` values: sanitary
  fixtures (`Plumbing`, exists), electrical equipment and devices, communications devices, lightning terminals. A
  family gives a fixture its forms, parameters and types, and a section never cuts it. A starter library of original
  families goes with each tab and is its own piece of work (ROADMAP 0.8).
- **Slabs.** A structural floor is a `Floor` with `structural: true`. Same category, so the same types, schedule and
  Visibility/Graphics, and IFC writes `Pset_SlabCommon.LoadBearing`.

## (c) Systems and schedules

Every category has an entry in `schedule::OWN`, so Structure gets Beam, Structural Column, Footing and Strip Footing
schedules from the `schedule` command and the Manage tab, with Type, Level, Width, Depth, Length, Offset, System and a
Count. A system's schedule is the schedule of its category, grouped or filtered on `System`: a pipe schedule by system
is a pipe schedule with `System` as a sort-and-group field. No second schedule engine.

## (d) IFC

IFC4 (ISO 16739-1:2018). Class names are checked against the IFC4 and IFC4X3_ADD2 schemas that ship with IfcOpenShell
0.9. Built is the Structure rows.

| BIMCraft | IFC class and predefined type | Built |
|---|---|---|
| `beam` | `IfcBeam` `.BEAM.`; braces `IfcMember` `.BRACE.` | beam (braces are a sloped beam of a brace type: not yet) |
| `structuralcolumn` | `IfcColumn` `.COLUMN.`, with `Pset_ColumnCommon.LoadBearing` | yes |
| `footing` | `IfcFooting` `.PAD_FOOTING.` | yes |
| `stripfooting` | `IfcFooting` `.STRIP_FOOTING.` (a grade beam, baldrame, is `.FOOTING_BEAM.`) | yes |
| structural `floor` | `IfcSlab` `.FLOOR.` (`.BASESLAB.` for a foundation slab) with `Pset_SlabCommon.LoadBearing` | yes |
| `pipe` | `IfcPipeSegment` `.RIGIDSEGMENT.`; fittings `IfcPipeFitting`, valves `IfcValve` | yes |
| sanitary fixtures | `IfcSanitaryTerminal` of the family's `kind` (`wc` `.TOILETPAN.`, `lav` `.WASHHANDBASIN.`, `sink` and `laundry` `.SINK.`, `shower`, `bath`, `bidet`, `urinal`), `.NOTDEFINED.` without one; floor drains `IfcWasteTerminal` `.FLOORTRAP.` (`floor_waste`, `roof_drain` their own); 
fittings by kind (`bend` `.BEND.`, `tee` and `cross` `.JUNCTION.`, `transition`, `coupling` `.CONNECTOR.`) | yes |
| `conduit` | `IfcCableCarrierSegment` `.CONDUITSEGMENT.` | yes |
| `cabletray` | `IfcCableCarrierSegment` `.CABLETRAYSEGMENT.` (`.CABLELADDERSEGMENT.`, which only another tool writes, is read as a tray) | yes |
| `wire`, `cable` | `IfcCableSegment` `.CABLESEGMENT.`, which BIMCraft's `Category` tells apart | yes |
| panels, boards | `IfcElectricDistributionBoard` `.DISTRIBUTIONBOARD.` | yes |
| luminaires | `IfcLightFixture` | yes |
| outlets, switches | `IfcOutlet` (`.POWEROUTLET.`, `.DATAOUTLET.`, `.TELEPHONEOUTLET.`), `IfcSwitchingDevice` (`.TOGGLESWITCH.`) | power outlets and switches |
| data equipment | `IfcCommunicationsAppliance` `.NETWORKAPPLIANCE.` (a patch panel; a router, a switch would be `.ROUTER.`, `.NETWORKAPPLIANCE.`). A rack has no class: an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `Rack`, which a filter finds and an `IfcElectricDistributionBoard` would hide among 
boards | yes |
| `downconductor`, `groundconductor` | `IfcCableSegment` `.CONDUCTORSEGMENT.`, which BIMCraft's `Category` tells apart | yes |
| air terminals, earthing rods, inspection boxes | **no IFC class.** IFC4 and IFC4X3 have none for lightning protection. `IfcBuildingElementProxy` (`.USERDEFINED.`) with `ObjectType` `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` or `InspectionBox`, so a reader can filter on it, and the family and type in its 
name. Surge protection has `IfcProtectiveDevice` `.VARISTOR.`; an `IfcDistributionChamberElement` `.INSPECTIONCHAMBER.` exists for the box but would hide it from a filter on the others | yes |

A run is written as an extrusion along its own axis (`IfcExtrudedAreaSolid`), so a reader gets the profile and the
length and not a mesh. Its system is an `IfcSystem`, named for it, that an `IfcRelAssignsToGroup` assigns the runs in it to;

3	{refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm. It follows what it measures

A ref is {at: [x, y, z]}, a point of the model, or {at, edge: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]]}, a point on an edge, which it measures square to (from a point, to the edge's line; between two parallel edges, how far apart they are). `type` is a dimension type, the aligned one's unless told. Each line becomes a family that runs on into the next tiles' copies of itself; one at a slope that never meets itself again is turned to the simplest slope within 0.25° that does (else the nearest, at most 48 tiles across or up). 92	=== ungroup  label='Ungroup' aliases=['UG'] menu=None

97	
98	=== detail_line  label='Detail Line' aliases=['DL'] menu=None
99	{view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused
100	
101	=== graphics  label='Visibility/Graphics' aliases=[] menu=None
102	{view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)
103	
104	=== section_box  label='Section Box' aliases=[] menu=None
105	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again
106	
107	=== perspective  label='Perspective' aliases=[] menu=None
108	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands
109	
110	=== graphic_display_options  label='Graphic Display Options' aliases=['GD'] menu=None
111	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), edges?: true | false, silhouette?: px, ambient_shadows?: true | false} how a 3D view draws its edges and shadows, as Revit's Graphic Display Options: `edges`, the lines where its surfaces meet in Shaded (on unless turned off; Hidden Line always draws them); `silhouette`, an outline that many pixels wide (a whole number, 0 to 10; 0, the default, for none) round what stands in front of what is further off or of nothing; `ambient_shadows`, soft shadows where faces meet inside a corner (off unless turned on). What is left out stays as it was; with none of them it only says what the view has
112	
113	=== camera  label='Camera' aliases=[] menu=None
114	{eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in
115	
116	=== work_plane  label='Work Plane' aliases=[] menu=None
117	{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level
118	
119	=== filter  label='View Filter' aliases=[] menu=None
120	{name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one
121	
122	=== template  label='View Template' aliases=[] menu=None
123	{name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one
124	
125

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/<area>-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999 via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session) ; `alloc_id()` for element ids (from `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case, from the catalog), snapshots the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (which calls every module's `check(pr)`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step labelled by the command's catalog label (`always_step` hooks force a step even when nothing changed).
- `src/commands/mod.rs` (dispatch: each module's `dispatch(s, cid, p)` is tried in turn), `src/commands/basic.rs` (new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid/delete(basic); `open_path`, `write_atomic`), `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers producing the original's texts: `` `x` in mm is required``, ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9), `src/model.rs` (levels by elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` with the original's errors, `find` by id/GUID, `normalize_guid`), `src/check.rs` (core rules: level/grid; your rules go in your module's `check`).
- Done by others (reuse, don't redo): `src/rvt/` (Revit import; `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a planar-faces tracer), `src/cloud/` (point clouds; `cloud::mirror_refusal(id)` for mirror, scans move/rotate by `at`/`angle`; the original rotates `at` rounding to 0.001 mm), `src/deflate.rs`, `src/inflate.rs`, `src/util.rs`, `src/media/` (pictures, `material`, `favorite`, `library`, `paint`), `src/styles/` (library/settings commands; `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` give new/copied elements their phase/option params — copies must call `stamp_copy`), `src/mcp/`.
- Being written in parallel by others (don't implement these; if you need one, write a minimal private stand-in inside your area and note it): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors, ceilings, shafts, roofs, dormers, rooms, room separators, stairs, ramps, railings, masses and by-face, sketch/edit_boundary/edit_shape/…, flip, show_mass; `src/arch/`, `src/geom/` — including the model rules that refuse a door that no longer fits its wall, an outline that isn't simple, etc.), STRUCTURE (columns, footings, beams, runs, rebar, reinforce, type, family, symbol_set, component, calculators; `src/structure/`), VIEWS (sections, elevations, sheets, view settings, graphics, filters, templates, cameras, text, dimensions, tags, spots, detail lines and their own editing commands, filled regions, groups, linework, make_fill_pattern; `src/views/`), READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, measure, select_by_id, ids_of, filter_selection, and the loader `src/load.rs`; `src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`), IFC-EXPORT (`src/ifc/export*`), IFC-IMPORT (`src/ifc/import*`). Rendering, CAD/DXF, the sample house and the highrise come later.

## How to test
`MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels exactly. Essential trick for you: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`, with walls, doors, rooms, floors, components, detail lines, dimensions, views…), then run both programs as `run in.bimcraft --cmd '<your command>' --save out.bimcraft` — the loader reads the original's files, so you don't depend on the creation commands others are writing. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params` text) and the README; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, every category of element, edge cases, every error and the order of checks).

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't; edits outside your area; what other areas must provide or call (model rules that refusals depend on, etc.).

## YOUR AREA: EDIT (`src/edit/`)
Commands: `modify` (any element's fields as `elements` shows them, `id`/`ids`, level names, merges into objects like `view_range`, `params` (project parameters keyed via `styles::parameters::key_of`), type changes by name, location line changes keeping the wall in place, frozen rooms, patterns…), `move` (walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined — find out exactly which joins count; doors/windows slide; `end` moves one wall end; every category, including views, annotation, scans and CAD imports), `copy` (with hosted doors/windows, stamp_copy), `rotate` (`about`, `angle`, `copy`), `mirror` (`axis`, `copy`; walls run back the other way, doors flip facing; refusals), `corner` (walls, or detail lines incl. arcs; `keep`), `split` (walls incl. arcs with their doors/windows going with their part, and detail lines of any shape), `fillet` (straight walls or detail lines), `align` (`reference`, `line`, `lock`, `to`), `match_properties`, `delete` (cascades: a wall takes its doors/windows and their tags; a view its notes and spots; dimensions lose references and go when left with fewer than two; roofs/floors release attached walls; errors such as `delete: no element 999999`; always an undo step), `insert` (Insert from File: ids/GUID clashes, copies, library by GUID then by name, ` 2` suffixes, `left_out`), `link`, `reload`, `purge` (kinds, dry_run, cascading), `delete_type`, `rename_type`, `autosave`, `recover`. Undo/redo of all of them, and the labels.
