162
===== rebar Rebar [] None
{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule

===== reinforce Reinforce [] None
{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes

===== column Column ['CL'] Architecture > Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

===== structural_column Structural Column ['CL'] None
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

===== footing Isolated Footing ['FI'] None
{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below

===== beam Beam ['BM'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°

===== strip_footing Wall Footing ['FW'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)

===== pipe Pipe ['PI'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")

===== duct Duct ['DU'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")

===== conduit Conduit ['CN'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

===== cable_tray Cable Tray ['CT'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep

===== wire Wire ['EW'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

===== down_conductor Down Conductor ['DC'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to

===== ground_conductor Earthing Conductor ['GC'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)

===== cabling Cabling ['CB'] None
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to

===== type Edit Type [] None
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

===== family Load Family [] Manage > Family Editor
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out

===== symbol_set Load Symbol Set [] None
{set: arei, names?: en|nl|fr} loads a set of families that are plan symbols and nothing else, each of one type `Standard` with no forms: `arei` is the Belgian AREI/RGIE's graphical symbols (Table 2.23: switches, sockets, light points, appliances, sources, domotics, protection), 76 families, switches in the switch category, sockets in outlet, luminaires in lighting and the rest generic. `names` is the language of their names, English, Dutch or French as the source prints them; as given none, French in a French project and English otherwise. A family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing; the reply lists `loaded` and `kept`. Place them as components

===== component Component ['CM'] Architecture > Component
{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

===== circuit Size a Circuit [] None
{load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it

===== conduit_fill Conduit Fill [] None
{section, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, circuits?, reduced_neutral?, family?, size?} the fill of a conduit as NBR 5410 asks, for the conductors of a circuit (its phases, neutral and protective conductor, of `section` mm²) times `circuits` in the same conduit (1): their cross-sections by outside diameter over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two, 40 % for three or more. `family` (pvc-thread, pvc-solder, steel-heavy, steel-rir; pvc-thread) and `size` (its mark, e.g. 3/4"; none: the smallest that fits). The dimensions are the makers' own from their catalogues, each family naming maker, document, page and address; the inside diameter is the outside less twice the wall. The data covers the flexible 750 V PVC cable of 0.5 to 240 mm² only: there is no `insulation` key, and a section above 240 mm² is `pending`, never guessed. `sections_mm2` lists the conductors of one circuit (`circuits` of them are in the conduit). Cable trays are not sized. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== drain_size Size a Sanitary Drain [] None
{units?, fixtures?: {wc?, lav?, sink?, shower?, laundry?}, role?: branch|main|stack, slope?, floors?, min_dn?} the DN of a sanitary drain as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) it carries: `units`, or `fixtures` counted (Tabela 3: a water closet 6 UHC and DN 100, a lavatory 1 and 40, a sink 3 and 50, a shower 2 and 40, a laundry tub 3 and 40; the drain is never smaller than the fixtures' own). `role`: a `branch` (ramal de esgoto, Tabela 5, the default), a `main` (subcoletor or coletor predial, Tabela 7 by `slope`, a fraction, 0.01 by default; DN 100 at least) or a `stack` (tubo de queda, Tabela 6 by the building's `floors`, up to three or more). `min_dn` is the largest drain flowing into it. Replies with the `dn`, what it carries (`capacity`) and the `minimum_dn` the fixtures ask. A blank in the standard's table means not allowed: DN 100 and 150 carry nothing in a building drain at 0.5 %, and a branch or a building drain never borrows the other's table. For a `main` every fixture given counts, where item 5.1.4.2 counts only the largest fixture of each bathroom in a residential building: pass `units` already reduced to follow it. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== vent_size Size a Sanitary Vent [] None
{units, wc?, stack_dn?, length?, trap_dn?} the DN of a sanitary vent as NBR 8160 asks, by the units (UHC) of what it vents: a branch vent (ramal de ventilação, Tabela 8; `wc` says a water closet is in the group), or, with `stack_dn` (the DN of the stack or drain served) and `length` (mm, from its foot to its open end), a vent stack or header (Tabela 2). `trap_dn` adds the longest run from a trap of that DN to its vent (Tabela 1). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== hydrant_size Size Hydrants [] None
{column?: 1-5, area?, type?: 1|2|3|4-40|4-65|5, hydrants?, inside?, nominal?, material?: steel|steel-wet|copper|pvc|pex, length?, rise?} hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks. With `column` (of Tabela 3, by the occupation) and `area` (m², built) it replies the system type and the fire reserve (m³). With `type` (Tabela 2; 4 comes as 4-40 or 4-65 by its nozzle) it replies the design flow, that of the two most unfavourable jets (`hydrants`, 2 by default), and the head at the nozzle; with `inside` (mm) it also replies the speed (5 m/s at most), the Hazen-Williams head loss over `length` (m) of the `material` (Tabela 1: `steel` is black steel in a dry system, C 100, the lowest steel row and the default, `steel-wet` is galvanised or wet, C 120), the head needed at the start of the pipe with its `rise` (mm, up) and, with `nominal` (mm), whether the pipe is big enough (DN 65; DN 50 for types 1 and 2). `length` and `rise` are in millimetres. `need_mca` is the nozzle head + the head loss of the straight pipe + the rise: it leaves out the hose, the fittings and the pressure at the source (`need_covers` says so), and `ok` is only the nozzle head within 100 mca, the speed and the pipe's size (`ok_covers`), not a verdict on the design. A `type` that contradicts `column` and `area` is an error. Notes 1 and 2 of Tabela 3 (a system one type lower in some cases) are not applied. `region` is SP, the only one: this is the São Paulo rule, and no other state's. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== load_points Residential Load Points [] None
{rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish. A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== water_size Size Cold Water Pipes [] None
{fixtures?: {wc, lav, sink, shower, laundry: count}, flow?, method?: weights|sum, dn?, length?, fittings?: {elbow90, elbow45, tee_through, tee_side, gate, globe, check: count}, pressure?, rise?} a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/s), or the design flow of the `fixtures` by the `method` the project chooses: weights (the empirical method, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, never more than the fixtures' own flows; the default) or sum (every fixture at once). The fixture flows and weights are Tigre's (Manual Técnico, page 198), not the standard's; `wc` is the WC with a flush tank only (a flush-valve WC is not in the table here). Without `dn` it replies the smallest DN chosen by speed alone (3 m/s at most; the pressure is not used to choose it); with `dn`, whether that pipe keeps the speed. The head loss is Darcy-Weisbach (Colebrook, PVC at 20 °C) over `length` (mm) plus the equivalent length of the `fittings`; with `pressure` (kPa, dynamic, upstream) and `rise` (mm, up) it replies the pressure left at the end, 10 kPa at least at a point of use, and `ok` covers both; without `pressure` `ok` is the speed alone (`ok_covers` says which). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

===== storm_size Size a Storm Drain [] None
{kind: downpipe|horizontal, area?, rainfall?, flow?, outlet?: edge|funnel, gutter?, length?, slope?, inside?} a storm drain as NBR 10844 asks. The flow is `flow` (L/min), or the rain on `area` (m², as the standard counts a roof) at `rainfall` (mm/h; 150 by default, which the standard allows for up to 100 m² only: above that `rainfall` is required): Q = I·A/60. A `downpipe` (condutor vertical) takes the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses by Q, the water depth in the gutter `gutter` (50 to 100 mm), its `length` (mm, 0.3 m or more) and the gutter's `outlet` (edge: sharp-edged, the default; funnel); 70 mm inside at least. A `horizontal` drain takes Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, PVC only, from the standard's Table 2) at its `slope` (a fraction, 0.005 at least): the inner diameter it needs, and with `inside` (mm) whether that pipe carries the flow. Off the abacuses (more than 150 mm inside) nothing is read. A key that does not apply to the `kind`, or `flow` together with `area`, is an error. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

194	The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you
195	turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor,
196	and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor
197	draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes
198	transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which.
199	
200	## Why BIMCraft
201	
202	- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type
203	  Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO,
204	  RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's
205	  underneath.
206	- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around
207	  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
208	  every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone.
209	- **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with
210	  IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public
211	  specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md):
212	  `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import
213	  its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds
214	  by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read
215	  while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out.
216	- **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to
217	  check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI.
218	- **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on
219	  Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet.
220	- **Free.** MIT OR Apache-2.0, with no account and no subscription.
221	
222	## What works today
223	
224	BIMCraft is in early, fast development. Honest status:
225	
226	| Area | Works today |

The 3D view has a section box, as Revit's: six planes square to the axes that keep what lies between them, the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, turned on and off with BX or its Properties, each face dragged by its grip in the view or typed in Properties, its extents kept while it's off; the levels it doesn't reach are left out. A plan can follow it (Section Box in the plan's Properties): it then shows what the box keeps, cut at the box's top, seen down to its bottom and cropped to its sides, and snaps to a scan where the box's top cuts it |

284	## Quick start
285	
286	The engine and the CLI need Rust 1.90 or later; the desktop app needs 1.95 (egui 0.36).
287	
288	```sh
289	git clone https://github.com/IPedrax/bimcraft
290	cd bimcraft
291	cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample       # opens the sample house
292	```
293	
294	Without a window:
295	
296	```sh
297	cargo build --release
298	./target/release/bimcraft-cli run --sample --save house.bimcraft --save house.ifc --save plan.png
299	```
300	
301	That builds the sample house and saves the project, an IFC4 file and the Level 1 plan:
302	
303	<p align="center">
304	  <img src="docs/images/sample-plan.png" alt="Level 1 of the sample house: grey wall poché, door swings, windows, its furniture seen from above, room tags with areas, grid bubbles, dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation and a note, and the roof's edge dashed overhead" width="100%">
305	</p>
306	
307	`--cmd 'render {"view": "{3D}", "path": "house-3d.png"}'` adds the 3D view (`azimuth` and `elevation` turn it);
308	`render {"view": "Section 1"}` draws the sample's section, `South` (or `North`, `East`, `West`) one of its elevations, and
309	`render {"view": "A102"}` one of its sheets. `--save sheets.pdf` prints every sheet, a page each.
310	
311	A script is one command per line, `id {json params}`, with lengths in millimetres:
312	
313	```text
314	wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000],[0,6000]], "closed": true, "type": "Exterior - 300mm"}
315	door {"at": [2000, 0]}
316	window {"at": [8000, 3000]}
317	room {"point": [4000, 3000], "name": "Living"}
318	floor {}
319	roof {}
320	```
321	
322	A script stops at its first failing line and names it. Through MCP, `script {"text": …, "atomic": true}` runs it all or nothing:
323	a line that fails takes back the lines before it, and one that goes through is a single undo step.
324	
325	```sh
326	bimcraft-cli run --script house.txt --save house.ifc
327	bimcraft-cli convert building.ifc building.bimcraft   # an IFC file from Revit or any BIM tool, as a project
328	bimcraft-cli info house.bimcraft                      # levels, counts, types and warnings
329	bimcraft-cli info building.rvt                        # a Revit file: release, last save, levels, elements by category
330	bimcraft-cli convert building.rvt building.ifc        # a Revit project, imported, then written as IFC4
331	bimcraft-cli convert house.bimcraft plan.svg
332	bimcraft-cli commands                                 # every command and its parameters
333	```

335	## The desktop app
336	
337	`bimcraft [FILE] [--sample]` opens a `.bimcraft` project, imports an `.ifc` file, or starts on the sample house. The layout
338	is Revit's, so it should feel familiar: the Quick Access Toolbar; the ribbon's File, Architecture, Annotate, View and Modify

338	is Revit's, so it should feel familiar: the Quick Access Toolbar; the ribbon's File, Architecture, Annotate, View and Modify
339	tabs, with a green contextual tab (Modify | Place Wall, Modify | Walls) for the tool or the selection; the Options Bar;
340	Properties over the Project Browser; views in tabs with a navigation bar; and the tool's prompt in the status bar. The
341	icons and colours are BIMCraft's own: BIMCraft starts in your system's theme. View > Dark Mode opens a menu for Light, Dark,
342	Dark UI, Light Canvas, or As the System; File > Settings offers the same choices. The choice is saved between sessions.
343	
344	Autosave runs in the background every two minutes while the model has unsaved changes (File > Settings > Files changes
345	the interval or disables it). A saved project's recovery copy is `<project filename>.autosave.bimcraft` beside the project;
346	an untitled project's copy is under the system temporary folder's `bimcraft-autosave` directory. Opening a project with a
347	copy offers **Recover**, **Discard**, or **Postpone**. Recover opens unsaved work, Discard removes the copy, and Postpone
348	protects it for later through File > Recover Autosave. Orphaned untitled copies are offered at startup. Successful Save
349	or an explicit Don't Save removes the current recovery copy, except a postponed copy. See [autosave design](docs/autosave.md).

422	## Drive it from agents, MCP and the CLI
423	
424	`bimcraft-cli mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio, on a model of its own.
425	Add it to Claude Code:
426	
427	```sh
428	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp
429	```
430	
431	or to any MCP client's configuration:
432	
433	```json
434	{ "mcpServers": { "bimcraft": { "command": "/path/to/bimcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
435	```
436	
437	| Tool | What it does |
438	|---|---|
439	| `execute {command, params}` | Any command with JSON parameters |
440	| `script {text, atomic?}` | Several commands, one per line; `atomic`: all or nothing, one undo step |
441	| `list_commands {filter?}` | The catalog, with parameters and shortcuts |
442	| `inspect_model` | Levels, counts, types, warnings and undo history |
443	| `query_elements {category?, level?}` | Elements with derived values: wall length and height, room area, door position |
444	| `schedule {name?, category?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?}` | A schedule's columns, rows and totals; a new one, or one changed, as the command makes it |
445	| `render {view?, ceiling?, width?, height?, azimuth?, elevation?}` | A level's floor plan (or reflected ceiling plan), a section or elevation by name, a sheet by number, or with `view: "{3D}"` the 3D view, as a PNG the agent can look at |
446	| `new_model`, `open`, `save` | Projects; `open` imports `.ifc` files, `save` to `.ifc`, `.svg` or `.png` exports |
447	
448	A command that fails comes back as a tool error saying what to fix (`door: no wall at [4000, 3000] on Level 1`), and it
449	changes nothing.
450	
451	### On the project you have open
452	
453	Start the window with `--control PORT` (`0` for any free port) and an agent can work on the project in front of you instead of
454	a copy of its own: what it makes appears in the window, as an undo step you can take back, and is saved with Ctrl+S.
455	
456	```sh
457	bimcraft --control 0                       # the window says the port; bridge.json beside the favorites holds it and a token
458	claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp --connect
459	```
460	
461	`mcp --connect` takes the port from that file (or `--connect PORT` names it, which must be the window's). The port is on this
462	machine's own address only, a connection that does not say the token in its first line is dropped, and only the user can read
463	the file. The tools are the same, except `new_model` and `open`, which would replace your project: start or open another in
464	the window. The window answers between its frames, so a long command holds the window as it would from a button.
465	
466	File > Settings > Agents opens the same port without `--control` (and again at each start), on a port you choose or any free one,
467	and closes it. With **Allow agents to edit this project** off, an agent only reads your project: it inspects it, reads its schedules,
468	renders its views and exports it to new files (the sheets to PDF among them), and every change it asks for comes back as an error
469	that says so. The view control bar shows the port: off, listening on its number, or how many agents are connected, and read-only.
470	An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
471	for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.

1	# Views: scale, detail and style, and visibility and graphics
2	
3	Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.
4	
5	A view's scale, detail level and visual style are in its `Graphics` (`scale`, `detail`, `style`; the `scale`, `detail` and `visual_style`
6	commands, which the view control bar's menus, Properties' View Scale, Scale Value 1:, Detail Level and Visual Style, and WF, HL and SD run). A
7	view template controls them as groups of their own (`Group::Scale`, `Detail`, `Style`, in `Graphics::resolved`, `check_followed` and the three
8	commands, which refuse what a template controls); `render::scale_of`, `detail_of` and `Look::with` read the value in force, never the view's own, and
9	the bar and Properties show it greyed out, the template named on hover (`controlled_note`). A scale is the n of 1 : n (`graphics::SCALES`);
10	`render::annotation` turns it and the zoom into `Drawing::k`, the factor annotation is drawn at (`Drawing::px`, `Drawing::grow`: annotation is
11	laid out one pixel to the pixel and grown about its anchor), and 1 on a sheet (`draw_at`, `section_at`), where the viewport's scale already
12	sets paper size. Every plan, section and elevation has a scale: one with none of its own is at its project units' default,
13	1 : 100 or 1/8" = 1'-0" (`Units::default_scale`, `Graphics::scale_n`, `graphics::scale_of`), and `scale` refuses null. A viewport
14	placed with no scale takes the view's. The units name the scales and list the ones offered (`Units::scale`, `scales`,
15	`parse_scale`): metric 1 : n; in inches or feet the architect's (12" = 1'-0" to 1/32" = 1'-0") and the engineer's (1" = 10'-0" to
16	1" = 200'-0"), and 1 : n for any other. The Scale menu, Properties, templates and sheets' titles name them so, and a scale is typed
17	as n, 1 : n, or two lengths (`1/4" = 1'-0"`).
18	
19	Background grids are view-owned graphics (`Graphics::background_grid`), controlled by a view template through the
20	`background_grid` group. `graphics` and `template` accept a grid patch (spacing in millimetres, divisions, rotation, two
21	styles and visibility), or null to reset it. `Graphics::resolved` supplies the effective grid, and both the
22	commands and `check_followed` protect template-controlled values. Instance Properties and the bottom view control bar
23	open the view's grid editor; View Templates edits the template's grid. The controls are disabled in a follower, with the
24	template named on hover. Grid snapping is a separate global preference in Manage > Snaps and the bottom grid menu,
25	and is never controlled by a view template. Details: [background grids](desktop.md#background-grids).
26	
27	The view control bar's High Contrast Point Clouds (`footer.rs`, wherever the project or a link holds a scan, in a plan, a section, an elevation
28	and the 3D view) fills the view's `pointcloud` category with one colour, the user's, in one `graphics` command; how it behaves is in
29	[point clouds](point-clouds.md).
30	
31	Paper space and model space. A view's geometry is model millimetres; its annotation and its line weights are millimetres of the paper the
32	view stands for, 1 : n of the model. A sheet is that paper ([`sheet::DENSITY`] px to the mm). On screen, or in an image of a view, `k`
33	says how big the paper is at the zoom: a paper mm is `DENSITY * k` px. A line's weight is a pen (`pen.rs`): 1 to 16, each a width on
34	paper at 1 : 100 from 0.10 to 2 mm (our own steps, not Revit's: what's seen, pen 4, 0.18 mm, and what's cut, pen 10, 0.35 mm), and 0, a hairline, which every output draws as thin as it can whatever the scale
35	and the zoom (a width of 0 in the display list: tiny-skia's hairline, PDF's `0 w`, an SVG pixel with `vector-effect="non-scaling-stroke"`,
36	a pixel on screen). What a pen draws is the project's line weights (`pen::LineWeights`, `Model::line_weights`, the `line_weights`
37	command, Manage > Line Weights in the desktop, `lineweights.rs`): the model's pens 1 to 16 at each of a list of scales, a view taking
38	the column of the scale nearest its own (`LineWeights::at`), and the annotation's at any scale. A project that hasn't set them has
39	our own start for its units (`default_for`: metric or imperial columns, the model's pens wider at finer scales, by the fourth root,
40	and at 1 : 100 the pens' own widths, `Pen::mm`). A drawing keeps each line's pen (`Drawing::pens`, `stroke`), an override sets the pen
41	(`Look::dress`), and the last step of drawing a plan, a section, a sketch or a sheet's own lines sizes each line (`Drawing::weigh`),
42	as annotation where its owner is a dimension, tag, text, spot elevation, grid, level, room or mark (`annotates`), else as the model;
43	a view on a sheet takes the line weights at its viewport's scale. Cut outlines are inked over the poché: `cut_edges` keeps of each
44	outline what isn't against another's on its outer side, so joins stay clean. Where two runs meet (two walls at a corner), `turn_corners` carries each a pixel on round the corner into the other, so the corner is a join inside a line, mitred square, 
45	not two ends with a notch between them; an outline nothing lies against is one closed line (`ink_cut`), no corner of it an end. A column the plan cuts is solid poché: a compound wall's layers (their fills and patterns, and the lines between them) 
46	are cut back to outside its outline (`outside_columns`, `geom::subtract_convex` and `geom::line_outside_convex`, for outlines are convex), so a wall that runs into or through a column shows nothing of itself inside it. PNG, SVG and PDF join a pen's 
47	lines mitred and lettering's round (`Part::mitred`), so a V's point doesn't stick out. A pen is as wide as on the paper however far the view is zoomed (`paper_of`, not clamped as lettering's size is), and a tool's preview draws its pens as the plan 
48	it is in does. The desktop draws a line its pixels at the zoom, at least one (`canvas::on_screen`); Thin Lines draws every line one. A
49	file from before pens (format 3) held weights in pixels of a sheet's drawing, and opens with each the nearest pen (`pens_from_pixels`).
50	Which pen each kind of line draws with is named once, in `pen.rs` (`Pen::CUT`, `Pen::PROJECTION`, `Pen::HEAVY` and the rest), never a number at the draw site: a cut is `Pen::CUT` in plan and in section alike. A category's own lines are its Object 
51	Styles'
52	(`styles.rs`, `Model::object_styles`, the `object_styles` command, Manage > Object Styles in the desktop, `objectstyles.rs`): the
53	draw site marks them `BY_CATEGORY`, and `Drawing::by_category` gives each the cut or the projection pen of its owner's category, by
54	its `Part`, before `Look::dress` puts a view's overrides over them. Marked: what's cut (`cut_edges`, plan and section), what's
55	seen (floors, walls and columns below, roofs, ceilings, runs, components, shafts, masses, stairs' and ramps' edges, railings), a
56	door's or window's family forms and symbols, a door's leaf and swing. The rest keep their own pens, as Revit's subcategories
57	would: a compound element's layer lines, an opening's jambs and glass, a stair's cut line and walk line, a floor's holes. A project
58	holds only the categories set apart from `styles::default_of` (which draws as before: cut pen 10, seen pen 4). What's next on this
59	foundation: annotation categories' object styles and subcategories, viewports as windows onto their views, and printing.
60	
61	Family components are split by category. A component is of its family's category (`graphics::category_of`; `component_category` names
62	each `family::Category`: `furniture`, `casework`, `plumbing`, `drain`, `pipefitting`, `pipeaccessory`, `equipment`, `outlet`, `switch`,
63	`airterminal`, `earthing`, `inspectionbox`, `lighting`, `generic`, `dataoutlet`, `voiceoutlet`, `patchpanel`, `rack`; `graphics::COMPONENTS`),
64	and each is a row of `graphics::MODEL`, so of Visibility/Graphics, Object Styles and `object_styles`: a power plan hides the luminaires
65	and a lighting plan the outlets. A door's or a window's family is placed in a wall as a door or a window and has no row. `component`
66	(`graphics::COMPONENT`) is no row but still a name, for every one of them: `drawn` and `styles::known` accept it, `Graphics::hides` takes
67	a family category as hidden when it is, and `Look::with` lays a category's own override over the one `component` says (hidden if
68	either is), as `styles::inherited` lays an object style over it, so a project from before (a view, a template or Object Styles that
69	names `component`) opens and draws as it did. A view filter and a schedule still name `component`; both pick every family component.
70	The desktop splits `component` into its rows in a dialog's draft (`Graphics::split_component`), so the rows show what the view does and a
71	click shows one again. A new `family::Category` is a compile error in `component_category` until it has its row; the key is the name it
72	goes by in a file (a test compares them), and a new one goes in `MODEL` and `COMPONENTS`, and a name in the desktop's `lang::category`.
73	A new project starts with three plan templates for the electrical disciplines that control the categories alone
74	(`graphics::starter_templates`, named by the project's language through `Language::word`): Electrical Power (luminaires in halftone),
75	Electrical Lighting (outlets hidden) and Electrical Ceiling (the devices that stand on the floor or the wall hidden, luminaires and cable
76	trays kept). A project from before has none. File format 13 is the one that has these rows: a build that reads up to 12 refuses it on
77	opening, with an error about a category, not "saved by a newer BIMCraft".
78	
79	Detail lines and their line styles (`lines.rs`): a `LinePattern` is a freely ordered sequence of 1–32 graphic segments, each length mm
80	on paper, so it reads the same at any scale (`Solid` is none, a name no pattern takes); a `LineStyle` is a pen, a colour and a
81	pattern; both are library entries (`Kind::LinePattern`, `Kind::LineStyle`), so a style names its pattern and a detail line its style
82	by GUID in a file, and a rename (`rename_entry`) follows everywhere. A project starts with ours, named in its language
83	(`lines::patterns`, `lines::styles`); one in use can't be deleted. A `DetailLine` (category `line`, Lines in Visibility/Graphics) is
84	drawn in one view, as a text note is: a level's plan (not its ceiling plan), a section or an elevation, or a sheet, in the view's own
85	terms, and goes with it. `render::detail_line` draws it in its style's pen with the model's line weights, its colour and its
86	pattern's dashes in pixels at the view's paper (`LinePattern::dash`); a repeat under two pixels draws solid. A primitive's dash is
87	any list of on and off lengths (`Prim::Line::dash`), which SVG, PDF, the PNG and the canvas all take. The desktop has Annotate >
88	Detail Line (DL; a line a click, as walls are, chained until Enter or the first point again; the Options Bar's Line Style and
89	Chain; the Draw panel's other shapes, below) and Manage > Line Styles (`linestyles.rs`: styles and patterns on two tabs of one
90	draft, applied as one undo step). Patterns > New Pattern or Edit opens the separate Line Pattern Creator
91	(`linestyles/creator.rs`), with a live straight/curved preview and segment controls, add, reorder and delete. Save Pattern
92	updates the library draft; Cancel Pattern discards just the creator, and the parent Cancel discards the whole draft.
93	Segments are Gap (`space`), Straight (`dash`), Dot (`dot_length`, its reserved length, with a circle exactly the pen width),
94	Offset (`length`, `count` 2–9, `distance` between adjacent lines symmetrically about the centerline), Wave and Zig Zag
95	(`length`, `frequency` in cycles per segment, `amplitude` from centerline), and Text (`length`, `size`, `text`). Text uses
96	bundled IBM Plex Sans on Linux, Windows and macOS, with the annotation font fallback for missing characters. Its size is
97	maximum capital height; it scales uniformly down when its reserved length is shorter than the text. Text is centered on
98	the axis and each glyph rotates with its own curve tangent. `lines/pattern.rs` makes shared stroke/fill geometry for
99	preview, canvas, PNG, SVG and PDF; old alternating dash/space/dot patterns retain native dashes. On canvas and paper,
100	pattern lettering uses the same non-zero contour tessellation as notes, keeping counters transparent during selection
101	and hover as well as ordinary drawing; dots retain their pen-sized polygon rendering. Tiny or excessively dense
102	patterns draw solid with bounded work. Region profiles, snapping, alignment and dimensions use the original centerline.
103	Format 9 adds these segments; older dash/space/dot patterns open unchanged. Next: patterns made from lines drawn in a view.
104	
105	A detail line and a sketch line are any `curves::Curve`: a polyline (straight segments and arcs, each arc's turn in degrees
106	counter-clockwise as a wall's; a line or an arc is one of two points), a circle, an ellipse whole or partial, a spline by its
107	control points (a clamped cubic B-spline, uniform knots unless it holds its own), or a spline through points (a cubic by the
108	distance along them, each end free or leaving along a tangent). In a file and in a command a curve is flat, the fields of its
109	shape (`curves::Fields`; `curve_struct!` makes a type that holds one among its own fields, since serde's `flatten` won't take
110	`deny_unknown_fields`), so an older file's `points` and `closed` read as they did. `Curve::points` draws it with chords no
111	further than `FLAT` from it; `nearest`, `split`, `map` (a move, a turn or a mirror), `handles` and `moved` (grips) and
112	`check` are the rest. Splitting is exact but for a spline through points: a polyline's segment or arc divides, an ellipse's
113	span does, and a control-point spline gets the knot inserted to the degree's multiplicity (Boehm's algorithm) so its halves'
114	control points are the original's; a spline through points becomes two through the original's points on each side and the
115	cut, leaving it along the original's tangent, with points of the original added where it strays most until it is within

117	where it's cut. Commands: `split` (detail lines as walls), `join_polyline` (PJ), `explode` (EX), `fillet` (FL), `corner`
118	(TR, two detail lines as two walls), `trim_extend` (detail lines to a boundary: Revit's Trim/Extend Single and Multiple
119	Elements) and `offset` (OF; `draw::offset` keeps arcs concentric and mitres a polyline's corners). `draw::meet` finds where two
120	lines or arcs cross, run on along their lines or circles, and `draw::trim_to` brings one to it, keeping the part picked.

133	Vertices come and go (`vertex`; Modify | Lines' Add Vertex and Delete Vertex, on sketch lines too): `Curve::with_vertex`
134	cuts a polyline's segment, inserts a knot in a control-point spline (one control point more, the curve exactly as it was)

136	(Convert Spline) turns a spline through points into the same curve by control points, exactly (`fit_to_control`: knots at
137	the points' distances along, a tridiagonal system for the control points with the fitted spline's end conditions), and

140	Revit's Insulation is a detail line with an `insulation` width: `DetailLine::drawn` gives `lines::batt`, a prolate cycloid
141	along its curve (loops the whole width across, `BULGE` times it apart), so it splits, offsets, joins and takes grips as any
142	line does, and follows arcs and splines, which Revit's doesn't. Annotate > Detail > Insulation draws it, its Width on the
143	Options Bar; Properties shows Insulation Width. A revision cloud is the same idea: a detail line with a `cloud` arc length (and
144	a `revision`, any text) that `drawn` turns into scallops (`lines::cloud`, arcs of `SCALLOP` degrees bulging out of a loop
145	whichever way round it was drawn, to the left of an open line). A scallop ends at each corner where the way turns by more
146	than about 25 degrees (so a rectangle's scallops never cut a corner) and, past 1,024 scallops or more corners than that
147	allows, the scallops are even and fewer, each drawn within its share of `MAX_DRAWN` points. A line is a cloud or insulation
148	(`DetailLine::check` refuses both). `revision` is a label: it is kept with the cloud and `elements` lists it, and no
149	schedule reads it yet. Annotate > Detail > Revision Cloud draws one, a rectangle by
150	default; with it a rectangle or a polygon is one cloud round (`curves::join`), and Line is one cloud through the points
151	(`one_line`). `centre_mark` is Revit's Center Mark Visible: a 3 mm cross at each of `Curve::centres`, the Options Bar's Show
152	Centre for new arcs and circles.

154	Linework (`linework`, LW) is Revit's: an edge of a model element drawn in a line style in one plan, or hidden there. The
155	plan's `Graphics::linework` holds each as the element's GUID, the edge's two ends and a style (`None` hidden).
156	`render::edge_at` finds the edge picked: the plan drawn again around the point without its linework, the nearest
157	segment of the element's lines within `LINEWORK_REACH`. `render::linework` restyles, after `Look::dress`, the parts of the
158	element's lines that lie along that edge (collinear within a pixel, over its length), so one face of a wall changes and the
159	rest of its outline doesn't. Picked again, an edge's entry is replaced; `remove` takes out the one nearest the point (the desktop's
160	`<By Category>`), not every edge within reach: both faces of a thin wall are. An entry on an edge the element no longer draws (a
161	wall across a styled face cut it in two) is stale: the drawing still restyles what it overlaps, and where the edge picked has
162	no entry, `remove` takes the nearest stale entry within `LINEWORK_REACH`, one a call, never one on another edge that is
163	drawn (`render::edges_at` lists the edges drawn). A view's linework is checked (`Graphics::check`):
164	at most `MAX_LINEWORK` (2,000) edges, ends within `MAX_COORD`, and a line style the project has. The drawing splits an element's
165	lines along all its edges in one pass (`render::linework`: the cost is the prims plus the edges, not a pass over every prim for
166	each edge). A line style a view's linework uses can't be deleted, and an element's entries go with it.

182	type has it already. A family's own bold and italic faces are taken where it has them; else a variable face is set to
183	`wght` 700, any other is made bold by its outline drawn round heavier (our lettering by heavier strokes), and italic by

185	(`system::FALLBACKS`: Noto Sans CJK, Microsoft YaHei, PingFang…), else drawn as the lettering's question mark.

195	`text::triangles` (strips between every corner's and crossing's height), kept by its points for the frames that draw it again.

613	IFC, and gbXML; the rest of structure (beams, columns, footings and structural floors are in), then MEP (its four tabs are designed in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md)); site and massing; several people editing one model; and signed installers (macOS

615	[docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md): it lists what a file holds (`bimcraft-cli info`) and imports its levels, walls, floors, doors

627	The installer is a short setup wizard. It puts BIMCraft and `bimcraft-cli` for every user in `Program Files\BIMCraft`, or in
628	the folder you pick on its folder page (Change, on any drive), adds BIMCraft to the Start menu, asks whether to put it on the
629	desktop too, opens `.bimcraft` projects in it, and offers it under Open with for `.ifc` files. It needs no Visual C++

634	The portable zip is for a PC where you can't install software: unzip it anywhere (a USB stick will do) and run `bimcraft.exe`.
635	It holds `bimcraft.exe`, `bimcraft-cli.exe`, the licences and this readme, needs no rights and no Visual C++ runtime, and leaves

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/<area>-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`); `alloc_id()`, `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records undo steps (`history()` gives the labels).
- `src/commands/mod.rs` (dispatch), `src/commands/basic.rs` (new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid; `open_path`/`open_project_file` call `crate::load::load`; `info(path)` = inspect + path), `src/commands/params.rs`, `src/model.rs` (levels, `resolve_level`, `find`), `src/check.rs`, `src/inspect.rs` (a stub `inspect` and `elements` — yours now), `src/load.rs` (a permissive loader — yours now).
- Done by others (reuse, don't redo): `src/rvt/` (Revit import; `src/rvt/plan.rs` planar faces, `src/rvt/rooms.rs` room enclosure), `src/cloud/` (point clouds; `cloud::load` is called by the loader, `cloud::left_out(doc)` gives unknown cloud fields for the open reply's `left_out`; `elements` already shows scans), `src/media/` (pictures, materials, favorites, library, paint; ready helpers `media::material::inspect_materials(pr)` and `inspect_images(pr)` give inspect's `materials` and `images`), `src/styles/` (settings commands; `styles::inspect_entries` gives inspect's phases, phase_filters, phase_overrides, option_sets, parameters, voltages, distribution_systems, wire_types, units, project_units, room_area, standard; on open, call `phasing::load` (its `left_out`/`left_out_count` go in the reply), `text::normalize`, `text::sync_library`; rename project parameters with reserved names), `src/deflate.rs` (zlib/deflate byte-identical to the original's flate2 — for .xlsx), `src/mcp/`.
- Being written in parallel by others (don't implement their commands): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors, ceilings, shafts, roofs, rooms, stairs, ramps, railings, masses…; `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`), STRUCTURE (columns, footings, beams, runs, rebar, type, family, component…; `src/structure/`), VIEWS (sections, sheets, graphics, dimensions, tags, detail lines…; `src/views/`), EDIT (modify, move, copy, delete, insert…; `src/edit/`), IFC-EXPORT, IFC-IMPORT. If you need geometry they own (room boundaries for areas, wall joins), write your own inside `src/readers/`.

## How to test
`MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on many inputs. Essential trick for you: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft` — use every kind of element: walls of all location lines and arcs, doors/windows (with families too), floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms (enclosed, unbounded, redundant, frozen, with separators, islands), columns, beams, runs, components, stairs, ramps, railings, masses, views, annotations; `--sample` builds a furnished sample house), then compare `info in.bimcraft`, `run in.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {…}'`, `run in.bimcraft --cmd 'schedule {…}'` between the two programs.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't; edits outside your area; what other areas must provide or call.

## YOUR AREA: READERS (`src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`, `src/load.rs`)
1. `inspect` (and `info <project>` which is inspect plus `path`): every key exactly (counts, levels, types with layer materials by name, families with category/connectors/parameters/types, materials, images, history, warnings such as rooms no longer enclosed, view_templates, view_filters, phases…, wire_types, voltages, path…), for every kind of project.
2. `elements` (`category`, `level`, `limit`, `offset`; `count`/`returned`; every category's fields as stored plus derived values: wall length/thickness/type name/type_guid/room_bounding, room area_m2/perimeter/enclosed/unbounded_height/volume_m3, door/window at/width/height/level, level computation_height, and so on for all categories).
3. `schedule` (every category and `multicategory`, `available`, fields incl. formulas and project parameters, filters with every op, sort/descending, grouped with counts and totals, headings, the built-in Room/Door/Window/Wall/Floor/Level schedules becoming the project's own once changed (saved as schedule elements), `.csv` and `.xlsx` output (xlsx is a zip of XML: match bytes, using `src/deflate.rs`), units).
4. `measure`, `select_by_id`, `ids_of`, `filter_selection`.
5. The loader: what opening a project file does (`open`, `run x.bimcraft`, `info x.bimcraft`, `convert`): serde-style errors for malformed files (e.g. `x is not a BIMCraft project: missing field ...`, `invalid type: ...`, references that aren't GUIDs), filling sections the file lacks from the defaults, canonical ordering, the open reply (`name`, `path`, `left_out`…), the model check on open, older formats if any. Test with files the original saved and with damaged copies of them.
I'll start by exploring the codebase to understand the current state.

203	reach them; `Model::check` holds each to what the same element in a view must be (`annotation_ok`). A placed group is an

205	`commands::transform`, as Move and Rotate take elements), which `render::detail_group` draws, regions under lines and notes,

207	`group_type` renames a type (its groups follow) or deletes it while nothing is of it. A `RepeatingDetail` places a group
208	along a line every `spacing` from its start, each turned along it (at most `MAX_REPEATS`), as Revit's Repeating Detail
209	Component does with a detail component. A view draws every member of every group and repeat in it each time, so
210	`Model::check` caps what one view places: a group counts its type's members, a repeating detail its members once for each
211	repeat, and `MAX_PLACED` (10,000) is the most in a view (measured with the probe `probe_the_cost_of_the_most_hatched_regions_a_view_may_place`,
212	10,000 hatched regions take about 0.1 s to draw at 3 m across and 0.5 s at 30 m across, 2.8 million primitives, on a machine that

302	A 3D view may be seen in perspective, as through a camera, rather than parallel (axonometric): `View3D::perspective`, a `Perspective`
303	with the `lens` it is seen through (its focal length, mm on a 35 mm camera, whose 36 mm of film, `FILM`, is the picture's width; 10 to
304	600 mm, checked in `Model::check`) and `on` or off (off, it keeps its lens), set by the `perspective` command, which makes the default 3D
305	view as `section_box` does; `View3D::lens` is the lens while it's on. The camera is `view3d::Camera` with `lens` set: the eye stands back from
306	the target along the view as far as makes `scale` true at the target (`Camera::eye_distance`, the focal length in px over the scale), so
307	orbit turns it about the target, pan carries both, zoom walks it in (a point on the plane through the target staying under the cursor),
308	`Camera::sized` keeps the eye where it stood as the picture or the lens changes, and `with_eye_elevation` raises or lowers it looking at the
309	same target from as far across the plan. `fit_from` fits a perspective with the eye as far back as puts a ball round what is shown inside
310	the picture's narrower side. `Camera::project` keeps "larger is nearer": in perspective `d² / a - d` for a point `a` mm in front of an eye
311	`d` from the target, as near as a parallel view's at the target and straight across the picture of a plane (it goes as `1 / a`), so the
312	rasterizer's barycentric depths stay exact, and `point_at` turns a pixel and its depth back into the model point (textures, the section
313	box's `Boxed`). What is less than `NEAR` (10 mm) in front of the eye is cut away: a triangle into the one or two its near part makes
314	(`Projector::in_front`, as weights of its corners, so a curve's lighting carries over), a line to its near part (`Camera::in_front`: edges in
315	wireframe, levels' marks, the section box's frame); a point behind the eye projects to no number. A face is lit on the side the eye is on
316	(`Camera::toward`), as the card's `front_facing` is, and how far a line may lie behind a surface and show is a pixel's worth where the
317	line is (`Camera::slack`). `Camera::along` takes, in perspective, the point on the axis nearest the line from the eye through the pointer,
318	so a dragged section box face stays under it. `render` of the 3D view goes through its lens, and `eye_elevation` puts the eye that high. A
319	sheet's 3D viewport stays parallel (its scale is paper's). The card draws perspective too: `View::perspective` gives the shader the
320	focal length, how far the eye is and a depth of `a + b / ahead`, 1 at `NEAR` and 0 past the far side of the mesh (a reversed depth, as
321	precise far off as near), with the same `NEAR` cut by the card's clipping; `Mesh::pick` cuts and projects as the processor does.
322	`picking_the_mesh_in_perspective_finds_what_the_cpu_picture_shows_from_afar_and_from_within` and
323	`the_card_draws_in_perspective_what_the_processor_does_from_afar_and_from_among_the_walls` compare them, from outside and with the eye
324	inside the house (`view3d::inside`).

368	lookups are written again only when they change. A change to how
369	the processor shades, draws an edge or marks a level goes in the shader too: `the_card_draws_what_the_processor_does` and the core's

377	A 3D view's **Graphic Display Options** (Revit's GD) are `View3D::display`, a `view3d::DisplayOptions`: `edges` (on unless turned
378	off; only Shaded leaves them out, as Hidden Line and Wireframe always draw them), `silhouette` (an outline that many px wide, 0 to
379	`MAX_SILHOUETTE`, 10, checked in `Model::check`; 0 for none) and `ambient_shadows` (off unless turned on), set by the

382	draw them alike; a section's picture ignores them. Both come off the opaque depth the rasterizer already has, before a scan's
383	dots are in it, in nearness as `Camera::project` gives it, measured in pixels' worth (`Camera::slack`), so they read the
384	same parallel and in perspective. Ambient shadows (`view3d::ambient`) are a screen-space pass: for each pixel, the pixels
385	across from each other at eight offsets (`AMBIENT`, 4 to 12 px, four lines at two reaches); over a plane the depth runs
386	straight, so their mean is the pixel's own, and only where the surfaces round it rise toward the eye on both sides (a corner,
387	the foot of a wall on a floor) does it darken, by `AMBIENT_DARK` of its light at most; a neighbour more than `AMBIENT_REACH`
388	pixels' worth a pixel off in depth is something else, in front or behind, and counts for nothing, so nothing casts a halo. A
389	silhouette (`view3d::outlines`) is wherever two neighbouring pixels are one on a surface and one on nothing, or on different
390	planes `OUTLINE_GAP` (4) pixels' worth apart in depth: each pixel whose square `width + 1` across (from `width / 2` before it)
391	holds such a pair is drawn in the edge's colour, so a straight outline is exactly `width` px wide. The card does the same in
392	`fs_post` (`ambient`, `outlined`, `worth` in `gpu.wgsl`, the options in the globals' ninth vector, from `Mesh::display`), so
393	no pass is added: `the_card_draws_edges_silhouettes_and_ambient_shadows_as_the_processor_does` compares them. Cast shadows
394	from a sun are not drawn yet. The desktop's dialog (`display.rs`) opens by GD and from the view control bar's Visual Style
395	menu, alike in both looks of the window, and runs the command on the 3D view on screen.

409	chunks back (header, lengths, alignment, the JSON, a box's bounds and volume); the Khronos validator (`npm i gltf-validator`, then

456	families of parallel lines as a PAT file has them (`HatchLine`: an angle, an origin, a spacing across, a shift along, and

458	lines, it fills solid. `fills::strokes` lays a pattern over any outlines with holes (inside an odd number of rings), each line
459	cut to the view's window (what lies past it is never counted or drawn), and gives up rather than draw past a cap: more than

461	dense pattern over an outline of thousands of corners and dots a twentieth of a millimetre apart. A pattern that gives up draws

465	only draws nothing and never trips a cap. `render::filled_region` draws a region's
466	masking (paper), its background and its foreground pattern, then its boundary's sketch lines, each in its own line style

471	its view (`Model::annotation_plan`, so a duplicated plan has its own) and its sketch is a `sketch::SketchLine` list, solved
472	when drawn, any number of outlines; Edit Boundary edits it as any other. Patterns and region types are library entries,
473	renamed with their references (a type follows its patterns, a region its type and line style) and refused deleted while
474	used. The desktop has Annotate > Region (Filled Region, FR, and Masking Region, sketch mode with the type and the line style

476	Annotation Settings > Fill Patterns (`fillpatterns.rs`: the patterns as one draft, each a name, drafting or model and a

478	and a spacing each: a shift only staggers dashes, and dashed patterns are drawn and made with Custom), one made of lines
