482	A custom pattern is made of lines drawn, as pyRevit's Make Pattern makes one (`fills::make`, the `make_fill_pattern` command):
483	the detail lines picked, all of one view, cut to the rectangle between two corners (the tile), each a family that runs on into the
484	next tiles' copies of itself. A line repeats only at a slope `(i W, j H)` of whole tiles (`i`, `j` at most `MAX_STEPS`, 48), so one
485	drawn at another is turned to the simplest such slope within `TURN` (0.25°), else the nearest; its family's dashes are its length
486	and a space to the repeat `L = |(i W, j H)|`, its lines `W H / L` apart, each shifted along by the lattice's other vector
487	`(c W, d H)`, `i d - j c = 1` (Euclid's). A line on the tile's edge and its copy on the opposite one are one family; curves go as
488	their drawn points' chords. A model pattern is as drawn; a drafting one is the drawing on paper at the view's scale, which the
489	pattern keeps (`FillPattern::drawn`, saved with it): turned from one to the other (the dialog's Type, or `fill_pattern`'s `target`
490	without `lines`), it is rescaled (`retargeted`), and the dialog offers Redefine for it where a simple one has Edit Lines, which
491	picks the lines and corners again and keeps its name and type. A pattern holds at most `MAX_FAMILIES`
492	(256) families. In the desktop, New Pattern > Custom hides the dialog while the lines are picked as anything is (Enter, or the
493	right-click menu's Finish), then the corners (`Tool::PatternCorner`), and brings it back with the pattern previewed: OK, Pick
494	Again, Cancel. Esc, another tool or another view brings the dialog back. `pat.rs` reads and writes PAT files (`;%UNITS`,
495	`;%TYPE`, a negative offset stepping the other way; a pattern that can't be one left out with why) for the dialog and for the
496	`import_fill_patterns` and `export_fill_patterns` commands. A PAT file is hostile input: `read` stops after `MAX_PATTERNS`
497	(2,000) patterns and counts the rest, `Read::left_out` names the first `MAX_LEFT_OUT` (100) with `left_out_count` for all, a line
498	is cut at 22 fields and a bad one is echoed to 40 letters, a family whose dashes are all spaces is left out, and a file over
499	`MAX_TEXT` (16 MiB) is refused unread. A byte that isn't UTF-8 is read as the Latin-1 letter with its number, which is right
500	for accents and not for Windows-1252's punctuation at 0x80 to 0x9F. The description after a pattern's name isn't kept. The
501	`import_fill_patterns` command takes the file's `text` up to that size too (a name is limited to 256 letters, a file isn't) and
502	replies with the first 100 `left_out` and `left_out_count`.
503	
504	Edit Type opens a region's Type Properties from either a selected region or an active sketch: select a type, create a
505	new one, duplicate one with its settings, or rename it. Foreground and background each have their own pattern (including
506	None) and color; masking controls whether paper hides geometry underneath. The combined preview shows both layers and
507	a sample line behind them, so masking can be checked before applying. The Patterns tab edits and creates patterns in
508	the same draft. Apply and OK update definitions and the selected instances in one transaction; a type edit affects every
509	region of that type, a duplicate is assigned only to the selected instances or the active sketch, and Cancel discards
510	unapplied work. Duplicate or blank names are refused without replacing another definition. Renames preserve library
511	identity and update the active sketch's type reference. The palette's Type Selector and Edit Type use the same region
512	types as the Options Bar.
513	
514	The instance parameter grid has no second Region Type field: the Type Selector is the type control. Non-masking regions
515	replace model backgrounds while retaining visible cut outlines, cut foreground patterns (including solid foregrounds),
516	and projected model lines. `render/regions.rs` finds the drawing's ink once (the model layer's lines and patterns, less what a
517	later fill covers, so a low wall hidden by a cut wall does not reappear; and a section's or elevation's hidden-line picture as
518	runs of its pixels, which is all the ink an elevation has) and gives each region the part of it in its area: the outline less
519	its holes, inside an odd number of rings, less the masking regions drawn before it. A line is kept where it lies in the area or
520	within half its stroke of it (its pen's width as it will draw, from the owner's object style while the pen is not set yet), so a
521	region edge sketched on a wall face keeps the whole face; Visibility/Graphics weights wider than the object style's are not
522	allowed for. Lines are cut by the rings and the masks as they are, never by boolean operations on polygons (which are cubic in
523	the corners an outline can have): only the model's filled patterns are, by the pieces of the area they reach. The pieces of a
524	polyline that meet stay one line, so its corners keep their joins, and a dashed line's dashes stay where they were (the dashes of
525	the cycle a piece begins in are solid lines of their own). A section's ink belongs to the region that keeps it (`Part::Pattern`),
526	so a sheet's viewport, which keeps what an element owns, has it. A caller that has the section's picture (the desktop's, a sheet's,
527	`section_png`'s) hands it in (`render::section_over`, `section_at_over`), at the view's size or a multiple of it (a screen with more
528	pixels to the point), and the ink is the picture's own pixels, as runs: a row of a pixel's height, and a run of up to two pixels
529	that sits on one of the row above (the edge of a tall wall) joined to it as one vertical line, so 200 walls 20 m tall at 4000 x 2600
530	px are some hundreds of lines and not a million runs. A picture of more than 250,000 runs (noise, not drawings) keeps the first
531	250,000 and the drawing's `notes` say the ink of the last rows is under the region. `render::section` draws a picture of its own
532	when a non-masking region wants one, which costs what the picture does, every call. Masking still hides the model; detail annotation remains above the
533	region. The same display list feeds the desktop, PNG, SVG and sheet viewports.
534	
535	Limits, kept as Revit has them or not yet built: a non-masking region with a solid background hides a room's tag text while its outlines
536	stay (Revit keeps room tags above filled regions: not verified); grids, levels and room fills are drawn before the regions, so a masking
537	region hides them; there is no Bring to Front or Send to Back, a region is over the model and under the annotation, in the order of its
538	id; Move and Rotate carry a region's or a floor's model pattern with it (`pattern_origin`), where Revit may leave a model pattern fixed in
539	the building, and Align moves it; a filled region drawn on a sheet itself is plain annotation over the viewports, so a solid one hides
540	what lies under it (Revit has no regions on sheets).
541	
542	Sketch snapping (`snap::in_sketch`) combines the visible model's wall faces and slab edges, detail lines and existing
543	region boundaries in the active view, and the draft's own lines. It supports endpoints, midpoints (of each segment of a
544	polyline), intersections (where two walls meet is one too), perpendiculars, nearest points and angle guides, the anchors of
545	annotation (a note's insertion point and leader, a tag's head, a dimension's stations, a spot elevation, section and elevation
546	marks, detail groups and repeating details), and a camera's eye and target rather than its mark's body or name, honoring Manage > Snaps
547	and one-point overrides. An element being edited is omitted as a model snap target; its draft supplies the boundary instead.
548	Rectangle and arc previews use the same origin points and Shift constraint as a click. Annotation in another independent view,
549	or hidden by Visibility/Graphics, is excluded. A plan view cuts where its own view range says (`plan_range` of the view, not of its
550	level); a section or an elevation has no plan to snap to, only its own detail lines and regions. Of what the plan builds, the
551	nearest `MAX_OUTLINES` elements within reach have their outlines snapped to (one `walls::Index` for them all), and the nearest
552	`MAX_NEAR` chords are tried against each other. Ceilings snap in a floor plan as well as a ceiling plan, because a snap does not know
553	which of the two the cursor is in, and the members of a detail group are not snap targets.
554	
555	The reference workflows are Autodesk's [fill layers](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2024/ENU/Revit-GetStarted/files/GUID-8A38ADC8-98A6-4A30-BD21-1886F044F6ED.htm),
556	[region editing](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2026/ENU/Revit-DocumentPresent/files/GUID-183D9B1E-6554-4C19-9EA9-B32C8D2A5C9D.htm),
557	and [sketch snaps](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2022/ENU/Revit-Customize/files/GUID-A3947840-1F30-41D7-AF75-B61687952A07.htm).
558	Boundary weights follow each boundary line's style. See also Autodesk's [region masking 
559	behavior](https://www.autodesk.com/support/technical/article/caas/sfdcarticles/sfdcarticles/Filled-Region-with-solid-fill-does-not-cover-all-elements-in-Revit.html).
560	
561	A material's cut and surface may be one of the project's fill patterns (`Material::cut_pattern`, `surface_pattern`, a
562	library reference like a region type's), over the patterns drawn in code (`model::Pattern`), which stay for the materials
563	that name them: `material` takes either name for `cut` and `surface`, and the desktop's material editor lists both. A fill
564	pattern a material shows can't be deleted, and is renamed with it. `render::fill_pattern` draws a fill pattern for a
565	region, a cut layer (its courses along the layer) and a floor's or a ceiling's surface. A model pattern is aligned and
566	rotated as Revit's: a filled region and a floor hold `pattern_origin` and `pattern_angle` (`fills::strokes_placed`), which
567	Move, Rotate and Mirror carry with the element; Align with a pattern line picked second (`render::pattern_line_at`) moves the
568	origin so that line lies on the reference, and Properties shows Pattern Angle. `Model::align_pattern(id, reference, line)` is
569	that arithmetic (the origin moved across by the gap between the two parallel lines, to the micron; the error says when the
570	element has no model pattern, or the lines aren't parallel or have no length), so every front end gets the same answer and
571	sets it with `modify`. `pattern_origin` and `pattern_angle` are in the `modify`, `filled_region` and `floor` command docs, and
572	`elements` shows them for a region and a floor even at their defaults.
573	
574	## Linked models
575	
576	A `Link` element (`link.rs`; commands `link` and `reload`) is another project shown in this one as a reference. The file holds its name, its
577	path, where its origin stands (`at`) and a turn (`angle`); what it read is `Model::loaded`, by path, outside the file (`serde(skip)`), filled by
578	`link`, `reload` and `open` (`relink`, which doesn't follow the links of a linked file). The views draw `link::seen(model)`: the project with
579	each loaded link's built elements (`built`: not its views, sheets, annotation, detail lines, filled regions, detail groups, rooms, grids or links) moved and turned by `commands::transformed`
580	and brought in with `insert::insert_as(.., linked: true)` under ids from `LINKED` up (`ids.rs`), so `link::is_linked(id)` tells them; a level of the
581	link at the height of one of the project's (1 mm) is that level, another comes in named `link: level`. Everything that takes a `&Model` draws and snaps to
582	them without knowing: `Look::with` makes a linked id halftone, and picking never answers one (`Drawing::pick_all`, `in_box`, `Image::pick`,
583	`in_box`, `shows` and `Mesh::pick` leave them out). The commands that make an image (`render`, `save` to svg, png or pdf) draw `seen`; the desktop's
584	`view_model` does, cached by the project's `Arc`. The schedules, `Model::check`, IFC and every command that edits work on the project itself.
585	To do: shared coordinates, a link's graphics overrides and visibility per view, hosting on a linked wall, unloading.
586	
587	## Dimensions
588	
589	A dimension (`Dimension`, the `dimension` command) measures the model as it is, so it follows what it measures. Its `refs` are lines
590	(`Reference {id, face}`: a wall's centre line, faces and ends, a door's or window's centre and jambs, a grid, a straight detail line) or, with
591	`point: start|end`, the point at that end of one (`Model::reference_point`: a wall's centre line ends where its location line does, a face where
592	the outline turns off it, so at the mitred corner; a detail line of any shape at its ends; `reference_points` lists them, `endpoint_at` finds the
593	nearest, `{endpoint: [x, y]}` in a command). `reference_geometry` gives either as a line, a point as a line of no length, and `crossings` lays
594	them along the way the dimension measures (`measured_along`): a linear one's `orient` (horizontal or vertical), else square to its first line,
595	else from its first point to the next elsewhere. `Model::check` refuses a line not parallel to the first, or not square to a linear one's line,
596	and points all in one place. Mirror keeps the end of a line along the element and flips the one across it (`Reference::mirrored`); Flip swaps
597	both. A linear one given no `orient` runs vertical where `at` is east or west of everything it measures, else horizontal; the desktop's Auto
598	(`dims::Placing::kind`) also lays an aligned one where the cursor is among the points (`Orient::follow`), as Archicad does. Radial and diameter
599	dimensions measure round columns, curved walls (centre line or a face) and circles and arcs (`reference_arc`); arc length, a curved wall's or an
600	arc's length along it (`reference_sweep`), all of it or, with two point references after the arc, between them (`Model::arc_span`), its line an arc through `at` round the same centre. `dims::round_at` picks the face nearest a click.
601	
602	Each dimension has a dimension type (`dims.rs`, `Model::dimension_types`, a library entry `Kind::DimensionType`, the `dimension_type` command),
603	Revit's type parameters with lengths in mm on paper: Dimension String Type (continuous, baseline, ordinate), tick mark (diagonal, arrow, open
604	arrow, dot, none) and its size, line and tick pens, colour, dimension line extension, Witness Line Control (gap to element, or fixed to the
605	dimension line with its length), witness line gap and extension, baseline spacing, centre marks, and its text: font (as text types take one,
606	`DimensionType::lettering`), size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, offset, opaque or transparent background, Read Convention, units and
607	rounding (`DimensionType::length`), and the radius and diameter symbols and the equality text. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial`,
608	which aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in, and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial`, which radial and diameter ones do
609	(`dims::default_type`); a file of format 9 gives its dimensions their kind's (`Model::typed_dimensions`). A dimension's own text, Revit's
610	instance values, is a prefix, a suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display, and a segment may have its own over it
611	(`texts`, `SegmentText`, the `dimension_text` command; `Dimension::text` reads one through the other, `dimension_segment_at` finds a segment by a
612	point); `Model::dimension_labels` is what its
613	numbers read (and `elements` shows as `labels`): a baseline string's each from its first reference, an ordinate's each witness line's, the first 0.
614	An aligned or linear dimension may be kept equal (`equal`, Revit's EQ, which also turns its Equality Display on) and have segments
615	locked at a length (`locked`, `Lock`; the `dimension_constraint` command). `constraints::keep` runs in `Session::execute` after every undoable
616	command, before the check: each constrained dimension is solved on its own line (its `stations`, each with its reference), a locked segment tying
617	two stations rigidly and equality tying all its segments to one length (a locked one's, else its ends', which stay where they are, so an inner
618	reference dragged goes back); a run of tied stations stays where what the command moved puts it, else where its first is. What has to move is
619	moved by `commands::move_by`, as `move` moves it, and the dimensions are solved again (`PASSES`) until all hold; where they can't (locked
620	lengths that differ made equal, one element pulled two ways), the command is refused, saying which dimension, and nothing changes.
621	A length typed for a segment (`dimension_value`; in the window, a click on the selected dimension's number, as a temporary
622	dimension's takes one) moves what the segment ends at, its second station's reference, along the dimension by the difference
623	(`move_by`), and a locked segment is locked at it; the other locks then hold or the command is refused. Align with `lock` (Revit's
624	padlock: in the window, the open padlock Align offers on the line it moved) leaves a lock: a dimension of the aligned line's reference
625	and the reference's (`to`, else whatever has a line along it), its one segment locked at 0 and `alignment` set, which
626	`constraints::keep` holds as it holds the others, so the two lines stay on one line whatever either is moved by; one that can't hold
627	with the other locks is refused, and the project is as it was. A lock is drawn by a front end, never on paper (`render/dimensions.rs`
628	draws nothing of it): the window shows each locked segment's shut padlock whether its dimension is selected or not, and each alignment
629	lock's padlock beside where its lines meet, which a click unlocks (deletes). Format 15 holds them; 14 would read one as a dimension of
630	nothing.
631	`render/dimensions.rs` draws them all as the type says (`Ink`: its lines, ticks and witness lines, and its numbers laid out by `crate::text`
632	over the paper where the background is opaque).
633	
634	A 3D view has dimensions of its own (`Element::Dimension3D`, the `dimension_3d` command; `dims3d.rs`), as Revit's aligned dimension in a 3D
635	view: two references (`Ref3`), each a point of the model or a point on an edge (its two ends with it), and a point its line passes through,
636	kept by the view (`view`, a GUID: deleting the view takes them with it) and of a dimension type as a plan's are. Between two points it measures
637	straight from one to the other; to an edge, square to the edge's line, so between two parallel edges it is how far apart they are
638	(`dims3d::ends`). They hold places in space, not references to elements: moving an element leaves them, and `move`, `rotate` and `mirror`
639	take them in plan when they are moved themselves. They draw as marks (`dims3d::marks`, `Mark`: a polyline in the picture's pixels, its width
640	and colour), through any camera and at any paper size (`SCREEN` pixels a paper millimetre on screen, `sheet::DENSITY` on a sheet): a
641	witness line from each end of what it measures to its line, its line, a tick at each end and its number lettered along it in our strokes
642	(`font.rs`), reading from the left, on the side away from what it measures; nothing hides them. `dims3d::paint` paints marks into the
643	processor's picture, which the `render` command does for a 3D view; a sheet draws them as its own lines over the view's picture, so they print
644	in its PDF; the window draws them over the picture on either painter (the card's too) with the theme's ink, the selection's colour when
645	picked. Visibility/Graphics hides them with Dimensions (`category_of`). In the window the Aligned Dimension tool (DI) in the 3D view picks a
646	corner seen within the snap's reach (`Scene::corner_near`), else an edge within a pick's (`Scene::edge_near`, the point of it nearest the
647	cursor), else the point of the face there; after two, a click places the line where it meets the plane through the two that faces the
648	camera most (`dims3d::line_through`), and the status line says how long it is. In Modify a click on a dimension's lines picks it before what
649	the picture shows under them (`dims3d::pick`).

    let _ = (s, cid, p);
    None
}

    let _ = pr;
    Ok(())
}

## Drive it from agents, MCP and the CLI

`bimcraft-cli mcp` serves the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdio, on a model of its own.
Add it to Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp
```

or to any MCP client's configuration:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "bimcraft": { "command": "/path/to/bimcraft-cli", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `execute {command, params}` | Any command with JSON parameters |
| `script {text, atomic?}` | Several commands, one per line; `atomic`: all or nothing, one undo step |
| `list_commands {filter?}` | The catalog, with parameters and shortcuts |
| `inspect_model` | Levels, counts, types, warnings and undo history |
| `query_elements {category?, level?}` | Elements with derived values: wall length and height, room area, door position |
| `schedule {name?, category?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?}` | A schedule's columns, rows and totals; a new one, or one changed, as the command makes it |
| `render {view?, ceiling?, width?, height?, azimuth?, elevation?}` | A level's floor plan (or reflected ceiling plan), a section or elevation by name, a sheet by number, or with `view: "{3D}"` the 3D view, as a PNG the agent can look at |
| `new_model`, `open`, `save` | Projects; `open` imports `.ifc` files, `save` to `.ifc`, `.svg` or `.png` exports |

A command that fails comes back as a tool error saying what to fix (`door: no wall at [4000, 3000] on Level 1`), and it
changes nothing.

### On the project you have open

Start the window with `--control PORT` (`0` for any free port) and an agent can work on the project in front of you instead of
a copy of its own: what it makes appears in the window, as an undo step you can take back, and is saved with Ctrl+S.

```sh
bimcraft --control 0                       # the window says the port; bridge.json beside the favorites holds it and a token
claude mcp add bimcraft -- /path/to/bimcraft-cli mcp --connect
...

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/ifc-export-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs` (`Value`, ordered `Map`, parse/format exactly as serde_json), `src/project.rs` (`Project` = `doc` sections in file order + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (JSON objects as the original saves them) + `library` of `{kind, name, guid}`; elements reference each other and library entries by GUID), `src/session.rs`, `src/commands/basic.rs` (`save` with a `.ifc` path calls `crate::ifc::export::export(&project, path) -> String` and writes it; it should probably return a Result — adjust the hook), `src/model.rs` (levels by elevation etc.), `src/load.rs` (a permissive loader that reads the original's project files).
- Done by others: `src/rvt/` (Revit import, `src/rvt/plan.rs` planar faces), `src/cloud/` (scans: IFC leaves them out), `src/media/`, `src/styles/` (phases/options, parameters), `src/deflate.rs`, `src/inflate.rs`.
- Being written in parallel by others (creation commands for every element, families and their formula engine, readers, editing, IFC import). You don't need them: your input is a project FILE.

## How to test (essential)
Build input projects with the ORIGINAL: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft` (or `--script`), then compare both programs on `convert in.bimcraft out.ifc` with `MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- convert in.bimcraft out.ifc` (it normalises IFC GlobalIds by first appearance as `GID-N`, the timestamp as `<TIMESTAMP>`, GUIDs, and prints SAME or a diff). `/workspace/executable run --sample --save house.bimcraft` gives a rich furnished house. The hidden tests compare exactly; known expected outputs (already normalised) are in `/workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/*.ifc` (attached, circulation, devices, empty, furniture, masses, mep, names, phased_kinds, phasing, roofs, shaped, slabs, structure, walls), `/workspace/assets/test_model_geometry/*.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_mep_runs/mep.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_structure_elements/structure.ifc`, `/workspace/assets/test_structure_reinforce/rebar.ifc`. For each, reconstruct a project that the original exports to exactly that file (read the entities: names, ids in the `Tag` attribute, coordinates, types, psets), keep those reconstruction scripts in /tmp, and make your exporter produce the same bytes from the original's saved project.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; which asset files and which kinds of element export identically; what doesn't and why; edits outside your area.

## YOUR AREA: IFC-EXPORT (`src/ifc/export.rs` and any `src/ifc/export_*.rs`/`src/ifc/geom*` you add)
The IFC4 STEP writer for every element kind the README's "Files" and IFC rows describe: header (FILE_NAME with the project name escaped as STEP strings `\X2\…\X0\`, `\X4\`, quotes; timestamp; `BIMCraft 0.10.0`), units, project/site/building/storeys (and their placements), the exact entity order and numbering, GlobalIds (22-char IFC base64 of each element's GUID, and fresh ones for relationships — find which are derived and which random), real-number formatting (`0.`, `3000.`, `1.E-05`…), walls (swept from their plan outline mitred where they join; arcs in chords; attached to roofs as closed shells; layer sets and usages; Qto quantities gross and net of openings; Pset_WallCommon), openings with doors/windows (and their family forms as IfcTriangulatedFaceSet with styled items and materials — family forms are profiles swept or revolved, voids cutting solids, sizes from formulas over parameters: write the evaluation and tessellation you need, matching the original's triangles exactly), slabs (sloped, shaped, with openings and shafts), coverings, roofs (straight skeleton hips/valleys/ridges, gables, courtyards, extrusion roofs, dormers, joins) as faceted breps, spaces with Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities (room boundaries at centre lines and at faces), columns, structural elements (beams, footings, strip footings, LoadBearing), runs (pipes, ducts, conduits, trays, wires, conductors, cabling) with IfcSystem assignments, components as their IFC classes with predefined types, masses (proxies, lofted face sets, BIMCraft_Mass), stairs/ramps (flights, landings) and railings, rebar (IfcReinforcingBar aggregated to hosts), type objects and IfcRelDefinesByType, materials and colours, project parameters pset, BIMCraft_Phasing and Pset_*Common Status, everything the assets show. Also make `save` return the original's errors for IFC paths it can't write.

use std::process::exit;

pub const VERSION: &str = "0.10.0";

fn usage_exit(prefix: Option<String>) -> ! {
    if let Some(p) = prefix {
        eprint!("{}\n\n", p);
    }
    eprint!("{}", catalog::USAGE);
    exit(1);
}

enum Action {
    Open(String),
    Sample,
    Highrise,
    Cmd(String),
    Script(String),
    Save(String),
}

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
    if args.is_empty() {
        usage_exit(None);
    }
    match args[0].as_str() {
        "--version" | "-V" if args.len() == 1 => {
            println!("bimcraft-cli {}", VERSION);
        }
        "commands" if args.len() == 1 => {
            let v = json::parse(catalog::CATALOG).unwrap();
            println!("{}", v.to_pretty());
        }
        "info" if args.len() == 2 => cmd_info(&args[1]),
        "convert" if args.len() == 3 => cmd_convert(&args[1], &args[2]),
        "run" => cmd_run(&args[1..]),
        "mcp" => commands::mcp_main(&args[1..]),
        _ => usage_exit(None),
    }
}

fn cmd_run(args: &[String]) {

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

803 /workspace/README.md

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.
Phases: what stood before in halftone, what comes down dashed red, what is new as the category draws it. Phasing: phases in order, and phase filters that say how a view shows each status.
Textures: a material's texture at its real size on the faces it lies on: brick in courses, boards, glass. Paint: a material laid over one face, as Revit's Paint does; Remove Paint takes it off.
Family Editor: parameters, types, forms (extrusions, revolves, voids) and a door's or window's plan symbols, with a preview. Materials: a texture from a pattern or a picture of yours, its tile size, and a favorite kept for every project.
Structure: beams, structural columns, isolated and wall footings and structural floors; Revit's Structure tab on one new element, the run (design). Section: a beam is cut across its section, a round run (a pipe, a steel tube) in a ring.
Beam tool: two clicks, or a chain of them, each step a beam; sketched before the click. Beam properties: heights at both ends, justification, and the system it belongs to.
Pipe tool: two clicks, or a chain; centred on its height by default, falling or rising with a second height. Pipe type: its diameter (or width and depth, if it isn't round) and its material.
Section: a pipe is cut in poché along the line, across it in a ring.
Device tool: the Type Selector lists only the families of its kind; Space turns what you place. Cable tray type: a width by a depth, or round, in a material.
Plumbing: the starter fixtures, a pipe falling to a drain and a riser, in 3D with the walls hidden. Electrical: a tray, a board, luminaires and devices at their mounting heights.
Lightning Protection (SPDA): NBR 5419's vocabulary on the same runs and fixtures; Revit has no such tab. SPDA in 3D: terminals, down conductors and the earthing ring and rods.
Data tab: outlets, a rack, a patch panel and cabling, in NBR 14565's words. Data in 3D: a tray, cables dropping to their outlets, a rack.
## Performance sample Start an original 20-storey, 9,521-element tower with `bimcraft --highrise`, or generate a native file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is [`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md) for reproducible core/UI measurements and the remaining optimization work. Private local IFC fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder. The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor, and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which. ## Why BIMCraft

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area; yours is described at the end.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Your code goes in the directories you own (below). Edits elsewhere: only tiny, unavoidable ones (a `pub mod` line, a hook), listed in your report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, e.g. `/tmp/ifc-import-agent/`. Commit only Rust. You may spawn your own sub-agents (worktrees) to parallelise inside your area; integrate and verify their work yourself.

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first; you are in a git worktree)
- `src/json.rs` (`Value`, ordered `Map`, serde_json-exact parse/format; `.sorted()` for replies), `src/project.rs` (`Project::new(lang)` = the default project; `doc` sections in file order, `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (JSON objects in the original's field order), `library` of `{kind, name, guid}` with `lib_add` (ids count down); `alloc_id`), `src/session.rs`, `src/commands/basic.rs` (`open_path`/`open_project_file` route `.ifc` to `crate::ifc::import::import(s, path)` — your entry point in `src/ifc/import.rs`: replace `s.project`, return the reply `run x.ifc` prints, e.g. `{"elements":{"door":1,"level":2,"wall":4},"format":"IFC4","moved":null,"name":"Project","path":"rt.ifc","skipped":[]}`; an Err is printed after `open: `), `src/model.rs`.
- Done by others: `src/rvt/` (the Revit importer: a good model of how an importer builds a project and drops what breaks the model's rules — `src/rvt/drop.rs`, `src/rvt/plan.rs`), `src/cloud/`, `src/media/` (materials, pictures), `src/styles/` (phases and design options: `styles::phasing` for BIMCraft_Phasing; project parameters), `src/deflate.rs`, `src/inflate.rs`.
- Being written in parallel by others: creation commands for every element (ARCH, STRUCTURE), families and their formula engine (STRUCTURE), readers, editing, IFC export (you don't depend on it: the original exports IFC files for you to read).

## How to test (essential)
Make IFC inputs with the ORIGINAL: build projects (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.ifc`, or `--sample`), and also write IFC2x3/IFC4 files by hand in the styles other tools write (Revit-like extrusions of profiles, Breps, triangle meshes, mapped items, local placements nested, IfcMaterialLayerSetUsage, property sets, map coordinates far from the origin, curved walls). Then compare both programs on `run in.ifc`, `run in.ifc --save out.bimcraft` and `convert in.ifc out.bimcraft` with `MINE=<worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f in.ifc -- convert in.ifc out.bimcraft` (normalises GUIDs, uids, prints SAME or a diff); also `info in.ifc`. Known targets: `/workspace/assets/test_cli_info_convert/convert_ifc_to_project.bimcraft` is the expected result of converting an IFC export of a 6000×4000 walled room with a door, a window and a room named Office (rebuild that scenario), and every `.ifc` under `/workspace/assets/test_ifc_export/`, `/workspace/assets/test_model_geometry/`, `/workspace/assets/test_mep_runs/`, `/workspace/assets/test_structure_elements/`, `/workspace/assets/test_structure_reinforce/` is a (GlobalId-normalised) export the tests may import — convert each with both programs and match.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch. Final message: branch and commit; which inputs import identically; what doesn't and why; edits outside your area.

## YOUR AREA: IFC-IMPORT (`src/ifc/import.rs`, `src/ifc/step*.rs`, `src/ifc/import_*.rs`)
A STEP (ISO 10303-21) reader (strings with `\X2\`/`\X4\`/`\S\` escapes, enumerations, nested lists, `$`/`*`, comments, errors on malformed files exactly as the original words them) and the importer the README's "IFC import" row describes: storeys as levels, straight and curved walls with their doors/windows (cut to a roof over them), floors level or sloped and ceilings with holes, rooms (their point inside the space), columns (structural ones by Pset LoadBearing), beams, strip footings, runs (pipes, conduits, trays, wires, conductors, cables: the longest direction and the section square to it, or the extrusion direction; justification and IfcSystem), isolated footings, structural floors, grids, stairs/ramps of straight flights with landings, railings, roofs (flat, sloped all round with gables, courtyards, openings, extrusion), masses (BIMCraft_Mass), openings through slabs as shafts, material layer sets as types' layers with colours, furniture/sanitary/devices/proxies as components of families made of their bodies (a family per family name, a type per type, mirrored types), project parameters from `Project Parameters` and other psets (names cleaned for formulas; Mark from names), BIMCraft_Phasing, walls that nearly meet joined, models at map coordinates moved near the origin (`moved`), and `skipped` listing what was left out and why — all exactly as the original does it.

## Why BIMCraft

- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type
  Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO,
  RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's
  underneath.
- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around
  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
  every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone.
- **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with
  IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public
  specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md):
  `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import
  its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds
  by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read
  while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out.
- **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to
  check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI.
- **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on
  Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet.
...
