results.content:
link : {path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`

wall : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door : {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window : {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

floor : {boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline

ceiling : {point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it

shaft : {boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`

mass : {boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`

room : {point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

room_separator : {points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

rebar : {points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule

column : {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

structural_column : {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

footing : {at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below

beam : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°

strip_footing : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)

pipe : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")

stair : {start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too

ramp : {start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level

railing : {host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are

roof : {level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over `boundary` or else the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces, round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it): flat at `slope` 0, else every edge sloping up at `slope` degrees (30), hips, valleys and ridges where the slopes meet, but the edges in `gables` (edge i runs from point i to the next, the courtyards' edges numbered on after the boundary's) left upright, gable ends; `gable` leaves a rectangle's short ends upright. `slopes`: a slope in degrees (up to 75) for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for an edge that takes `slope`; none, every edge does; the eaves stay level and an edge in `gables` stays upright whatever its slope. A `sketch` line may carry a `slope` for the edges along it. Or with `extrusion` {line: [[x,y],[x,y]], profile: [[along, up],…], from?, to}: its underside's profile in the upright plane through `line`, along it from its start and up from the base, swept square to it from `from` (0) to `to` mm to its left. `openings` are holes through it in plan; with `join`, a roof it runs into, it ends where it meets that one's top

dimension : {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm. It follows what it measures

text : {text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's

spot : {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up

tag : {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

section : {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

elevation : {facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

sheet : {number?, name?, size?: A0|A1|A2|A3|A4} a sheet of paper, landscape (A3 by default), with a title block; numbers run A101, A102…

place : {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

duplicate_view : {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

type : {category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

family : {name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out

component : {family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

filled_region : {sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)

detail_line : {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

camera : {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""probe.py [-m] [-c] [--name x.ifc] FILE...: run `run x.ifc` (or convert with -c, printing the
project's elements and changed sections) on each file with the original (and mine with -m)."""
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import shutil

ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-a269fc74daf28a975/target/release/bimcraft-cli')


def run(exe, path, conv, name):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    shutil.copy(path, os.path.join(d, name))
    args = ['convert', name, 'out.bimcraft'] if conv else ['run', name]
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=300)
    out = p.stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace') + p.stderr.decode('utf-8', 'replace')
    if conv and os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, 'out.bimcraft')):
        r = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/ifc-import-agent/sections.py', os.path.join(d, 'out.bimcraft'), '-e'],
                           capture_output=True)
        out += r.stdout.decode() + r.stderr.decode()
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out.rstrip() + ' [code %d]' % p.returncode


args = sys.argv[1:]
mine = conv = False
name = None
while args and args[0].startswith('-'):
    if args[0] == '-m':
        mine = True
    elif args[0] == '-c':
        conv = True
    elif args[0] == '--name':
        name = args[1]
        args = args[1:]
    args = args[1:]
for f in args:
    nm = name or os.path.basename(f)
    o = run(ORIG, f, conv, nm)
    print('##', f)
    print('orig:', o)
    if mine:
        m = run(MINE, f, conv, nm)
        print('mine:', m)
        print('SAME' if o == m else 'DIFF')

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run a reader command on a project with the original (or mine with -m) and show it readably.
usage: show.py [-m] [-k key1,key2] [-x key,..] project 'cmd {json}'
- for `elements`: one element per line
- for `inspect`: one top-level key per line (skips -x keys)
- otherwise: pretty JSON
"""
import subprocess, sys, os, json
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-acefd841d6568a66c/target/release/bimcraft-cli'
a = sys.argv[1:]
exe = ORIG
skip = {'families', 'wire_types', 'distribution_systems', 'voltages', 'materials', 'phase_filters'}
only = None
while a and a[0] in ('-m', '-x', '-k', '-a'):
    if a[0] == '-m': exe = MINE; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-x': skip = set(a[1].split(',')); a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-a': skip = set(); a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-k': only = set(a[1].split(',')); a = a[2:]
proj, cmd = a[0], a[1]
args = [exe, 'run']
if proj != '-':
    args.append(os.path.abspath(proj))
args += ['--cmd', cmd]

# Translation catalogs

English messages stay in Rust as lookup keys and fallback text. Translations belong in UTF-8 gettext PO files:

| Domain | Template | Language catalogs | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interface | `translations/ui/bimcraft-ui.pot` | `pt.po`, `es.po`, `cs.po`, `fr.po`, `de.po`, `nl.po`, `it.po`, `vi.po`, `zh.po`, `zh_TW.po` | `lang::t`, `lang::tf`, `lang::tc` |
| Project | `translations/project/bimcraft-project.pot` | `pt.po`, `es.po`, `sv.po`, `cs.po`, `fr.po`, `de.po`, `nl.po`, `it.po` | `Language::word`, `Language::translated`, `Language::find` |

Interface and project language remain independent. Settings and project files retain `en`, `pt`, `es`, `sv`, `cs`, `fr`,
`de`, `nl`, `it`, `vi` (Vietnamese, interface only), `zh` and `zh_TW` (Simplified and Traditional Chinese, interface only; the catalog's file name is the code); the project languages after `es` came with file format 11, German and Dutch with 12 and 
Italian with 17, whose steps have nothing to convert. Native language names and locale aliases remain language metadata in Rust. Chinese,
either kind, still needs a system font, and the project's stroke lettering still cannot draw it. Diagnostics returned by the core,
CLI and MCP remain English. Existing project and user-supplied names are never translated in place.

## Translating

Edit the language's `.po` file in a text editor or a gettext-compatible translation editor. Change `msgstr`, keeping
`msgid` and `msgctxt` intact. Keep every `{}` placeholder in the same argument order: `tf` substitutes them sequentially.
Keep deliberate spaces, line breaks and punctuation. Entries may be left unfinished.

```po
#. Prompt shown before closing a changed project.
msgid "Save changes to {}?"
msgstr "¿Guardar los cambios en {}?"
```

An unknown locale, missing message, empty or whitespace-only translation, or entry marked `#, fuzzy` uses English.
Obsolete entries (`#~`) are retained for translators and excluded from the application. Fuzzy entries can remain in a
catalog while awaiting review; remove the flag when the translation is ready. Coverage is reported, not enforced as 100%.
The interface catalog includes translations of shared project terms so that an unfinished interface message falls back
to English directly, without borrowing a translation from another domain.

## Adding or changing English messages

Use `t("English")` for interface labels, `tf("Value {}", &[value])` for sequential substitution, and
`Language::word("English")` for project text. An ambiguous word can use `tc("context", "English")`, which looks up exactly
that `msgctxt`; a translation in another context never satisfies it. Category labels use `category` and `category-plural`
contexts for the existing one/several selection.

The extractor recognizes literal arguments to these functions and the ribbon's button helpers. A label selected through
an enum, table, conditional or other indirect path must be marked where its English literal is defined:

```rust
use bimcraft_i18n::{msg, ui_msg};

let prompt = msg!("Click the wall.");
let category = msg!("category", "Wall");
// In the core or desktop launcher, a label translated only by the interface:
let heading = ui_msg!("Properties");
```

`msg!` and `ui_msg!` return the English literal unchanged. Core `msg!` messages enter the project template and are also
available to interface translators; `ui_msg!` messages enter only the interface template. Markers in the UI enter only
the interface template. Do not mark user data, JSON field keys or arbitrary diagnostics. A `// TRANSLATORS:` comment
immediately before a literal becomes an extracted comment. Templates include source references. Test code is excluded.
The small unnamed English list in `lang.rs` retains historical keys still accepted by translation lookup.

From the repository root:

```sh
cargo i18n extract  # Refresh the English templates only.
cargo i18n update   # Refresh templates and merge all PO files.
cargo i18n check    # Check extraction, PO syntax, duplicate keys and placeholders.
cargo i18n stats    # Report finished translations in each catalog.
```

Run `update` after formatting Rust sources, since references contain line numbers. Merging matches exact English and
context, preserves translator comments, flags and metadata, refreshes developer comments/references, and keeps removed
translations as obsolete entries. Reintroduced messages can recover their obsolete translations. Changed English gets
an empty translation; the tool does not guess one. `check` is part of CI and accepts partial catalogs.

# Shared brief for the STRUCTURE sub-agents (read it all first)

We are reimplementing a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written
in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md, docs in /workspace/docs, especially
/workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md, /workspace/docs/areas/families.md, /workspace/docs/disciplines.md),
as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one
area. Our area is STRUCTURE (`src/structure/`); you own one part of it (your prompt says which files).

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files,
  env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run
  `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Your code goes ONLY in the files/directories your prompt gives you. Do not edit other files (not even
  `src/structure/mod.rs`, `src/structure/common.rs` or other parts' files); if you truly need a change
  elsewhere, write a private stand-in inside your own files and say so in your final report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, under `/tmp/<your-part>-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- Do the work yourself; do not spawn sub-agents.

## The codebase (you are in a git worktree of the repo)
First make sure your worktree has the structure skeleton: `git log --oneline -3` must show the commit
"Structure: module skeleton ..."; if not, run `git merge worktree-agent-ae3ecafdd2ebc3dc0` (the parent's branch).
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`; `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical
  parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are
  printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro, `Value::f/u/i/s`, `kind_name()` (serde's
  "invalid type" wording), `fmt_f64`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section`,
  `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's
  field order, `guid` first) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999
  via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session; `lib_add(kind, name)`); `alloc_id()` for element ids (from
  `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`, `lib_find_guid`. Elements reference
  each other and library entries by GUID. Family parts (forms, symbols, connectors, wall layers) carry their
  own `id` (counting down with the library ids) and `guid` inside the JSON.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case), snapshots
  the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (every module's `check(pr)`; ours is
  `crate::structure::check`, which calls each part's `check`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step
  labelled by the command's catalog label when the project changed (or when the command called
  `crate::structure::common::mark_step()`). `s.now_phase`/`s.now_option`: the phase/option new elements get.
- `src/commands/params.rs`: param readers producing the original's texts (`` `x` in mm is required``,
  ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9). `src/model.rs`: levels by
  elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` (the original's level errors), `find` (element by id or GUID),
  `normalize_guid`, `level_above`. `src/commands/basic.rs`: new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid.
- `src/styles/` (done by others; reuse): `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` (new/copied elements get
  their phase/option params), `styles::parameters::key_of` (project parameter keys), `styles::presets::find`
  (reinforcement presets), `styles::common` (check_keys: "`x` isn't one of its parameters: a, b", opt_name…),
  `styles::electrical` (voltages, distribution systems, wire types). `src/media/` (materials: `media::paint::
  material_ref(pr, name)` gives a material's GUID by name or GUID; favorites; library). `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a
  planar-faces tracer and `src/rvt/rooms.rs` a room-enclosure test.
- Being written in parallel by other agents (don't implement them; if you need one to build a test input,
  build the input project with the ORIGINAL and load it — see below): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors,
  ceilings, roofs, rooms, stairs…), VIEWS, EDIT (modify, move, copy, delete, rename_type, delete_type, purge…),
  READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, and the project-file loader `src/load.rs`, today a plain JSON read that
  is good enough to load the original's files), IFC export/import.

## Our skeleton (`src/structure/`, committed by the parent)
- `mod.rs` (parent's): `dispatch` routes each command id to its part's `run(s, cid, p) -> R<Value>`;
  `check(pr)` calls `types::check`, `members::check`, `family::check`, `component::check`, `rebar::check`,
  `reinforce::check`; `element_view(pr, id, x)` routes per category to `members::element_view`,
  `component::element_view`, `rebar::element_view` — the hook `elements` calls (already wired in
  `src/inspect.rs`, so `elements {"category": ...}` shows what you add); `warnings(pr)` → `family::warnings`.
- `common.rs` (parent's, read-only for you): `R<T>`, `RUN_CATS`, `COLUMN_CATS`, `type_kind(cat)` ("type:beam"),
  `type_path(cat)` (where a category's types live in the file's `types`: structuralcolumn → `structural_column`,
  runs → `runs.<cat>`), `types_of`, `type_of`, `type_guid`, `type_name_of_guid`, `element_type`,
  `add_element(s, e)` (stamps phase/option, allocates the id, inserts; returns the id), `new_guid()`,
  `mark_step()` (make an undo step even if nothing changed).
- `types::default_type(pr, cat)`: the type a new element takes without `type` (a named default when the
  project has it, else the first by name) — owned by the TYPES part; others call it.
- The calculators are already listed as read-only in `src/commands/mod.rs::changes_model` (no undo step, no check).

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>`
runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after
normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or
the diff. E.g. `... cmp.py -- run --cmd 'beam {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]]}' --save out.bimcraft`.
`run` takes several `--cmd` (each may hold several lines, one `ID {json}` per line), `--script FILE`, and
`--save PATH`; replies are printed sorted and compact, one per line; an error prints `line N (id): message` to
stderr with exit 1. Build with `cargo build --release` (fast). The hidden tests do this same kind of comparison
on many inputs, so match replies, error texts (and the order the checks happen in), saved files (field order,
number formatting: `0.0` vs `0`) and undo labels (`inspect` shows `history`) exactly.
Useful trick: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`)
and run both programs on that file (`cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd '…' --save out.bimcraft`) —
our loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params`
text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases,
every error and the order of checks, wrong types for every key: null, string, bool, array, object, negative,
huge, NaN-ish like 1e400). Learn element formats from the original's saved files. Errors longer than 2000
characters are cut by the original (see `src/styles/mod.rs::clip_error`) — check whether that applies to yours.
Write quick regression scripts under /tmp/<part>-agent/ that run many cmp.py cases and report the failures.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (only your files; `git add` them explicitly), with a clear message. Final
message (concise): your branch name and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't (and how widely you
tested it); any stand-ins you wrote for other areas; what other areas must provide or call (public functions you
expose for them, with signatures).

runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after
normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or
the diff. E.g. `... cmp.py -- run --cmd 'beam {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]]}' --save out.bimcraft`.
`run` takes several `--cmd` (each may hold several lines, one `ID {json}` per line), `--script FILE`, and
`--save PATH`; replies are printed sorted and compact, one per line; an error prints `line N (id): message` to
stderr with exit 1. Build with `cargo build --release` (fast). The hidden tests do this same kind of comparison
on many inputs, so match replies, error texts (and the order the checks happen in), saved files (field order,
number formatting: `0.0` vs `0`) and undo labels (`inspect` shows `history`) exactly.
Useful trick: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`)
and run both programs on that file (`cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd '…' --save out.bimcraft`) —
our loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params`
text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases,
every error and the order of checks, wrong types for every key: null, string, bool, array, object, negative,
huge, NaN-ish like 1e400). Learn element formats from the original's saved files. Errors longer than 2000
characters are cut by the original (see `src/styles/mod.rs::clip_error`) — check whether that applies to yours.
Write quick regression scripts under /tmp/<part>-agent/ that run many cmp.py cases and report the failures.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (only your files; `git add` them explicitly), with a clear message. Final
message (concise): your branch name and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't (and how widely you
tested it); any stand-ins you wrote for other areas; what other areas must provide or call (public functions you
expose for them, with signatures).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build cases with the original and compare my export.

usage:
  case.py build NAME            # cases/NAME.txt (a script) -> cases/NAME.bimcraft, cases/NAME.ifc (original)
  case.py cmp NAME [-n LINES]   # convert cases/NAME.bimcraft with mine and the original; diff normalised
  case.py all                   # cmp every case, print SAME/DIFF per case
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, difflib, glob, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
D = '/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases'

def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s

def build(name):
    txt = os.path.join(D, name + '.txt')
    bim = os.path.join(D, name + '.bimcraft')
    ifc = os.path.join(D, name + '.ifc')
    args = [ORIG, 'run']
    if open(txt).read().strip():
        args += ['--script', txt]
    args += ['--save', bim, '--save', ifc]
    p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if p.returncode != 0:
        print('BUILD FAILED', name, p.stderr.strip()[:2000])
        return False
    return True

def export(exe, bim):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='ifcx')
    out = os.path.join(d, 'out.ifc')
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'convert', bim, out], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300)
    s = open(out, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read() if os.path.exists(out) else ''
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return p.returncode, p.stdout, p.stderr, s

def cmp(name, n=40, quiet=False):
    bim = os.path.join(D, name + '.bimcraft')
    if not os.path.exists(bim):
        if not build(name): return False
    a = export(ORIG, bim)
    b = export(MINE, bim)
    x = norm(a[3]).splitlines()
    y = norm(b[3]).splitlines()
    ok = x == y and a[0] == b[0]
    if not ok and not quiet:
        if a[0] != b[0] or a[2] != b[2]:
            print('exit/stderr: orig', a[0], a[2].strip()[:300], '| mine', b[0], b[2].strip()[:300])
        for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x, y, 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:n]:
            print(l[:400])
    return ok

if __name__ == '__main__':
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    if a[0] == 'build':
        for nm in a[1:]: build(nm)
    elif a[0] == 'cmp':
        n = 40
        if '-n' in a:
            i = a.index('-n'); n = int(a[i+1]); del a[i:i+2]
        for nm in a[1:]:
            r = cmp(nm, n)
            print(nm, 'SAME' if r else 'DIFF')
    elif a[0] == 'all':
        names = sorted(os.path.basename(f)[:-4] for f in glob.glob(D + '/*.txt'))
        if len(a) > 1: names = [x for x in names if re.search(a[1], x)]
        same = 0
        for nm in names:
            r = cmp(nm, quiet=True)
            same += r
            print('%-30s %s' % (nm, 'SAME' if r else 'DIFF'))
        print(same, '/', len(names))

MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-a7aa74e0622ce519f/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
D = '/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases'

def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s

def build(name):
    txt = os.path.join(D, name + '.txt')
    bim = os.path.join(D, name + '.bimcraft')
    ifc = os.path.join(D, name + '.ifc')
    args = [ORIG, 'run']
    if open(txt).read().strip():
        args += ['--script', txt]
    args += ['--save', bim, '--save', ifc]
    p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if p.returncode != 0:
        print('BUILD FAILED', name, p.stderr.strip()[:2000])
        return False
    return True

def export(exe, bim):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='ifcx')
    out = os.path.join(d, 'out.ifc')
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'convert', bim, out], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300)
    s = open(out, encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read() if os.path.exists(out) else ''
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return p.returncode, p.stdout, p.stderr, s

def cmp(name, n=40, quiet=False):
    bim = os.path.join(D, name + '.bimcraft')
    if not os.path.exists(bim):
        if not build(name): return False
    a = export(ORIG, bim)
    b = export(MINE, bim)
    x = norm(a[3]).splitlines()
    y = norm(b[3]).splitlines()
    ok = x == y and a[0] == b[0]
    if not ok and not quiet:
        if a[0] != b[0] or a[2] != b[2]:
            print('exit/stderr: orig', a[0], a[2].strip()[:300], '| mine', b[0], b[2].strip()[:300])
        for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x, y, 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:n]:
            print(l[:400])
    return ok

if __name__ == '__main__':
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    if a[0] == 'build':
        for nm in a[1:]: build(nm)
    elif a[0] == 'cmp':
        n = 40
        if '-n' in a:
            i = a.index('-n'); n = int(a[i+1]); del a[i:i+2]
        for nm in a[1:]:
            r = cmp(nm, n)
            print(nm, 'SAME' if r else 'DIFF')
    elif a[0] == 'all':
        names = sorted(os.path.basename(f)[:-4] for f in glob.glob(D + '/*.txt'))
        if len(a) > 1: names = [x for x in names if re.search(a[1], x)]
        same = 0
        for nm in names:
            r = cmp(nm, quiet=True)
            same += r
            print('%-30s %s' % (nm, 'SAME' if r else 'DIFF'))
        print(same, '/', len(names))

| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Schedules | Schedule views of rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, down conductors, earthing conductors, cables, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, as Revit's Schedule/Quantities makes them: the fields chosen and ordered from the category's own (Area, Width, Count…), the project parameters for it and, for components, their families' parameters; calculated fields, formulas over the row's other fields as a family's are (`Area * 120`, `Perimeter * Finish Height / 1e6`); filters (equals, greater than, contains, begins with, has a value…) that every row holds to, comparing values as the schedule shows them; sorting by fields in turn, ascending or descending (the phase fields in the project's order of phases, not by name), and grouped, a row for each set of their values, its count and totals summed; totals under the rows. #!/usr/bin/env python3
"""craft.py base.bimcraft 'python statements on d (the doc) and E (elements dict by int id)' [command]
Writes a crafted copy, opens it with the original (and mine with -b), runs a trivial command, prints the result."""
import json, sys, subprocess, tempfile, os, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-aa380c34464cd9919/target/release/bimcraft-cli'
args = sys.argv[1:]
both = False
if args and args[0] == '-b':
    both = True
    args = args[1:]
base, code = args[0], args[1]
cmd = args[2] if len(args) > 2 else 'level {"elevation": 90000}'
d = json.load(open(base))
E = {int(k): v for k, v in d['elements'].items()}
def guid(i):
    return E[i]['guid']
exec(code)
d['elements'] = {str(k): v for k, v in sorted(E.items())}
def run(exe):
    t = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    json.dump(d, open(os.path.join(t, 'c.bimcraft'), 'w'), indent=2)
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'run', 'c.bimcraft', '--cmd', cmd], cwd=t, capture_output=True)
    shutil.rmtree(t)
    return (p.stdout.decode() + p.stderr.decode()).strip()
o = run(ORIG)
print('O:', o)
if both:
    m = run(MINE)
    print('M:', m)
    print('SAME' if m == o else 'DIFF')

You are a sub-agent of the STRUCTURE agent in a clean-room reimplementation project. FIRST read /tmp/structure-agent/BRIEF.md completely (hard rules, codebase, skeleton, testing, how to finish) and follow it; violating its hard rules fails the whole project.

YOUR PART: MEMBERS. You own `src/structure/members/` only (its `mod.rs`, which the skeleton created as a stub, and any files you add inside that directory, declared from its mod.rs). Scratch work in /tmp/members-agent/.

Implement, matching the original exactly:
1. Commands (all routed to `members::run(s, cid, p)`): `column`, `structural_column`, `footing` (columns: `at`, `type`, `angle`, `level`, `top_level`, `height`, `base_offset`; a footing's `thickness` and `offset`) and the runs `beam`, `strip_footing`, `pipe`, `duct`, `conduit`, `cable_tray`, `wire`, `down_conductor`, `ground_conductor`, `cabling` (`points` chain, `closed`, `type`, `level`, `offset`, `end_offset`, `justify`, `system`; one element per segment; a riser = the same point twice and two heights). Read each spec in `/workspace/executable commands` and the docs (structure-and-mep.md, disciplines.md). Probe every parameter, every error and the order of the checks (wrong types for every key, unknown type names — does the error list the types there are? — types given by GUID, levels by name/id/GUID/plan view, `top_level` below/at the base, zero/negative heights and thicknesses, a chain of one point, repeated points, `closed` with two points, `end_offset` with several segments, slopes past 75° for beams/strip footings vs pipes that may stand, huge numbers, the 1e9 mm limit), the reply (`id` vs `ids`), the saved element JSON (field order, which fields are written when: `end_offset`, `system`, `top_level: null`, `params`), and the undo label. Default type when none is given: call `crate::structure::types::default_type(pr, cat)` (the TYPES part owns and refines it). New elements via `crate::structure::common::add_element` (phase stamping) — verify against the original with `phase {"now": ...}` set.
2. `members::check(pr)`: the model rules for these categories that the original applies after every command (e.g. a beam or strip footing may not stand or lean past 75°; which runs may stand; a column's height; a type or level that must exist…). Find them by provoking refusals through the commands, and — for rules the commands can't reach — by hand-editing an original-made .bimcraft (break one element) and seeing what the original says when a command runs on it or when it opens it (`run in.bimcraft --cmd 'level {"elevation": 9000}'`). Error texts must match exactly.
3. `members::element_view(pr, id, x)`: the derived fields `elements {"category": "beam"}` (etc.) shows for these categories beyond the stored ones (for a beam e.g. `axis`, `length`, `type` as its name, `type_guid`, `width`, `depth`, `round`…; find all, for every category, sloped and standing runs, round and rectangular, each justify; columns and footings too). # Shared brief for the STRUCTURE sub-agents (read it all first)

We are reimplementing a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written
in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md, docs in /workspace/docs, especially
/workspace/docs/areas/structure-and-mep.md, /workspace/docs/areas/families.md, /workspace/docs/disciplines.md),
as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one
area. Our area is STRUCTURE (`src/structure/`); you own one part of it (your prompt says which files).

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files,
  env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run
  `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Your code goes ONLY in the files/directories your prompt gives you. Do not edit other files (not even
  `src/structure/mod.rs`, `src/structure/common.rs` or other parts' files); if you truly need a change
  elsewhere, write a private stand-in inside your own files and say so in your final report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, under `/tmp/<your-part>-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- Do the work yourself; do not spawn sub-agents.

## The codebase (you are in a git worktree of the repo)
First make sure your worktree has the structure skeleton: `git log --oneline -3` must show the commit
"Structure: module skeleton ..."; if not, run `git merge worktree-agent-ae3ecafdd2ebc3dc0` (the parent's branch).
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`; `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps), serde_json-identical
  parse errors and float formatting (`1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies are
  printed with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value), `jobj!{}` macro, `Value::f/u/i/s`, `kind_name()` (serde's
  "invalid type" wording), `fmt_f64`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section`,
  `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's
  field order, `guid` first) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999
  via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session; `lib_add(kind, name)`); `alloc_id()` for element ids (from
  `next_id`); `find_guid`, `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`, `lib_find_guid`. Elements reference
  each other and library entries by GUID. Family parts (forms, symbols, connectors, wall layers) carry their
  own `id` (counting down with the library ids) and `guid` inside the JSON.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command (id or alias, any case), snapshots
  the project, runs it, runs `crate::check::check` (every module's `check(pr)`; ours is
  `crate::structure::check`, which calls each part's `check`), rolls back on any error, records an undo step
  labelled by the command's catalog label when the project changed (or when the command called
  `crate::structure::common::mark_step()`). `s.now_phase`/`s.now_option`: the phase/option new elements get.
- `src/commands/params.rs`: param readers producing the original's texts (`` `x` in mm is required``,
  ``must be a number in mm, got …``, points, text ≤256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9). `src/model.rs`: levels by
  elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` (the original's level errors), `find` (element by id or GUID),
  `normalize_guid`, `level_above`. `src/commands/basic.rs`: new/open/save/undo/redo/level/grid.
- `src/styles/` (done by others; reuse): `styles::phasing::stamp_new`/`stamp_copy` (new/copied elements get
  their phase/option params), `styles::parameters::key_of` (project parameter keys), `styles::presets::find`
  (reinforcement presets), `styles::common` (check_keys: "`x` isn't one of its parameters: a, b", opt_name…),
  `styles::electrical` (voltages, distribution systems, wire types). `src/media/` (materials: `media::paint::
  material_ref(pr, name)` gives a material's GUID by name or GUID; favorites; library). `src/rvt/plan.rs` has a
  planar-faces tracer and `src/rvt/rooms.rs` a room-enclosure test.
- Being written in parallel by other agents (don't implement them; if you need one to build a test input,
  build the input project with the ORIGINAL and load it — see below): ARCH (walls, doors, windows, floors,
  ceilings, roofs, rooms, stairs…), VIEWS, EDIT (modify, move, copy, delete, rename_type, delete_type, purge…),
  READERS (inspect, elements, schedule, and the project-file loader `src/load.rs`, today a plain JSON read that
  is good enough to load the original's files), IFC export/import.

## Our skeleton (`src/structure/`, committed by the parent)
- `mod.rs` (parent's): `dispatch` routes each command id to its part's `run(s, cid, p) -> R<Value>`;
  `check(pr)` calls `types::check`, `members::check`, `family::check`, `component::check`, `rebar::check`,
  `reinforce::check`; `element_view(pr, id, x)` routes per category to `members::element_view`,
  `component::element_view`, `rebar::element_view` — the hook `elements` calls (already wired in
  `src/inspect.rs`, so `elements {"category": ...}` shows what you add); `warnings(pr)` → `family::warnings`.
- `common.rs` (parent's, read-only for you): `R<T>`, `RUN_CATS`, `COLUMN_CATS`, `type_kind(cat)` ("type:beam"),
  `type_path(cat)` (where a category's types live in the file's `types`: structuralcolumn → `structural_column`,
  runs → `runs.<cat>`), `types_of`, `type_of`, `type_guid`, `type_name_of_guid`, `element_type`,
  `add_element(s, e)` (stamps phase/option, allocates the id, inserts; returns the id), `new_guid()`,
  `mark_step()` (make an undo step even if nothing changed).
- `types::default_type(pr, cat)`: the type a new element takes without `type` (a named default when the
  project has it, else the first by name) — owned by the TYPES part; others call it.
- The calculators are already listed as read-only in `src/commands/mod.rs::changes_model` (no undo step, no check).

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] [-i stdin_file] -- <args…>`
runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after
normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids, temp names, IFC GlobalIds and timestamps. Prints SAME or
the diff. E.g. `... cmp.py -- run --cmd 'beam {"points":[[0,0],[5000,0]]}' --save out.bimcraft`.
`run` takes several `--cmd` (each may hold several lines, one `ID {json}` per line), `--script FILE`, and
`--save PATH`; replies are printed sorted and compact, one per line; an error prints `line N (id): message` to
stderr with exit 1. Build with `cargo build --release` (fast). The hidden tests do this same kind of comparison
on many inputs, so match replies, error texts (and the order the checks happen in), saved files (field order,
number formatting: `0.0` vs `0`) and undo labels (`inspect` shows `history`) exactly.
Useful trick: build input projects with the ORIGINAL (`/workspace/executable run --cmd '…' --save in.bimcraft`)
and run both programs on that file (`cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd '…' --save out.bimcraft`) —
our loader reads the original's files. Read each command's spec in `/workspace/executable commands` (its `params`
text) and the README/docs; then probe the original widely (normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases,
every error and the order of checks, wrong types for every key: null, string, bool, array, object, negative,
huge, NaN-ish like 1e400). Learn element formats from the original's saved files. Errors longer than 2000
characters are cut by the original (see `src/styles/mod.rs::clip_error`) — check whether that applies to yours.
Write quick regression scripts under /tmp/<part>-agent/ that run many cmp.py cases and report the failures.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (only your files; `git add` them explicitly), with a clear message. Final
message (concise): your branch name and commit; per command what matches and what doesn't (and how widely you
tested it); any stand-ins you wrote for other areas; what other areas must provide or call (public functions you
expose for them, with signatures).
