# The discipline tabs: design

A client asked for the complementary-project tabs Revit users know: structure (estrutural), plumbing and drainage
(hidrossanitário), electrical (elétrico), lightning protection (SPDA) and data and voice (lógica, dados e voz). This note
is how BIMCraft builds all five with as little new machinery as possible. All five are built, each a follow-up that added data
to what is described here, not new engine code. The rules in [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) apply
to all of it (everything is a command, `Model::check` validates, the core has no UI, clean-room).

## What the five have in common

Look at what each tab draws and there are three shapes, and BIMCraft has two of them already.

| Shape | Examples | What builds it |
|---|---|---|
| A vertical or point thing with a type and a size | columns, footings; sanitary fixtures, panels, luminaires, outlets, racks, air terminals | `Column` (vertical members) and the families with `Component` (devices and fixtures) |
| A straight thing between two points | beams, strip footings; pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays, down conductors, data cabling | **`Run`**, new |
| A slab or a region | structural floors, foundation slabs | `Floor`, with a `structural` flag |

So the new element is one: the run. Everything else is a category added to something that exists.

## (a) The run

`model::Run` is a straight element: from `start` to `end` in plan, at a height over its `level`, of a type with a size.

```
Run { type, level, start, end, offset, end_offset?, justify, system, params }
```

- **Height.** `offset` is the height, over the level, of the run's `justify` line (`top`, `centre` or `bottom`) at the
  start; `end_offset` is the height at the end, and when it is missing the run is level. A sloped run (a drain falling
  1%, a brace) is two offsets. A vertical run (a riser, a down conductor) has the same `start` and `end` and two
  offsets. Beams default to `top` justification, as engineers think of them (top of beam at the top of slab); the pipes
  and cables to come default to `centre`, the commands set it, not the type.
- **Section.** The type's `RunType { width, depth, round, material }`: a rectangle `width` across by `depth` deep, or
  round, `width` across. It is square to the run's axis, as a pipe's or a member's is.
- **Chains.** The command takes `points` and makes one run for each segment, as `wall` does. A fitting, an elbow or a
  tee is not a run: runs that meet butt against each other until the MEP slice joins them (ROADMAP 2.x). A family has
  connectors (`Family::connectors`) for what an electrical device draws; a run and a fitting have none yet.
- **System.** `system` is a name ("Água fria", "Circuito 3", "SPDA 1"). Nothing else about a system is stored: a
  schedule groups and filters by it like any field, and a fixture carries its system as a project parameter named
  `System`, which exists already. Systems are a name, not a registry, because a registry would need rules for renaming,
  deleting and merging that no tab has asked for. (What a system *supplies* is another matter: the project's electrical
  settings keep voltages, distribution systems and wire types as tables, `electrical.rs`, which circuits and panels will
  name; a run's `system` stays a name.)

In plan, a run or a footing is drawn from the level it hangs under: its top is flush with that level, so a beam placed at
the level is seen by that level's plan, which an element whose top is that low would not otherwise be (a plan sees down to
its view depth, which is the level by default); its centre line is dashed, to pick it by; one whose underside is over the cut plane and under the view range's top is
dashed, as a roof's eaves are; one that crosses the cut plane is cut, in poché. A section cuts a rectangular run across its
section, and the 3D view draws it as a sloped prism, or a round one as a tube.

A run is one Rust type serialized under several categories, as `Door` and `Window` share `Opening`. The category is the
`Element` variant, so Visibility/Graphics, schedules, project parameters, phases, view filters and the IFC class all
work per category without a line of per-category machinery. Today: `beam`, `stripfooting`, `pipe`, `duct`, `conduit`, `cabletray`, `wire`, `downconductor`, `groundconductor` and `cable`. A tab adds a variant, a name
in `model::run_arm!` and a row to each table below:

| Category | Tab | Revit's name |
|---|---|---|
| `beam`, `stripfooting` | Structure | Structural Framing, Structural Foundation: Wall |
| `pipe` | Plumbing | Pipe |
| `conduit`, `cabletray`, `wire` | Electrical | Conduit, Cable Tray, Wire |
| `downconductor`, `groundconductor` | SPDA | (none: Revit has no lightning protection) |
| `cable` | Data | Wire / Cable Tray |

Types live in `Types::runs`, a map from category to type name to `RunType`, so a tab adds no field to `Types`. The model
starts with a few (`Beam 200 x 500`…), and the `type` command creates and changes them. Geometry is in `runs.rs`: the
centre line's ends, the footprint in plan, the prism or tube in 3D. The plan, the section, the 3D view, the snaps and
IFC call it and know no category. A rectangular run is a sloped prism, so sections cut it; a round one is a tube mesh, a convex
solid, which a section cuts by the plane through its line (`Solid::cuts`: where the tube's edges cross the plane, their hull, a
ring, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A component's forms, which are not convex, are shown beyond the line and never cut.

## (b) Points and verticals

- **Vertical members.** `Column` (a plan outline, a base, a height) is reused as it is, under two more categories:
  `structuralcolumn` and `footing` (an isolated pad, Revit's Foundation: Isolated, which is a column laid down: its
  `height` is its thickness and its top is at the level). Each has its own types (`Types::structural_column`,
  `Types::footing`, both `ColumnType`).
- **Devices and fixtures.** Placed with the Component machinery from families, by adding `family::Category` values: sanitary
  fixtures (`Plumbing`, exists), electrical equipment and devices, communications devices, lightning terminals. A
  family gives a fixture its forms, parameters and types, and a section never cuts it. A starter library of original
  families goes with each tab and is its own piece of work (ROADMAP 0.8).
- **Slabs.** A structural floor is a `Floor` with `structural: true`. Same category, so the same types, schedule and
  Visibility/Graphics, and IFC writes `Pset_SlabCommon.LoadBearing`.

## (c) Systems and schedules

Every category has an entry in `schedule::OWN`, so Structure gets Beam, Structural Column, Footing and Strip Footing
schedules from the `schedule` command and the Manage tab, with Type, Level, Width, Depth, Length, Offset, System and a
Count. A system's schedule is the schedule of its category, grouped or filtered on `System`: a pipe schedule by system
is a pipe schedule with `System` as a sort-and-group field. No second schedule engine.

## (d) IFC

IFC4 (ISO 16739-1:2018). Class names are checked against the IFC4 and IFC4X3_ADD2 schemas that ship with IfcOpenShell
0.9. Built is the Structure rows.

| BIMCraft | IFC class and predefined type | Built |
|---|---|---|
| `beam` | `IfcBeam` `.BEAM.`; braces `IfcMember` `.BRACE.` | beam (braces are a sloped beam of a brace type: not yet) |
| `structuralcolumn` | `IfcColumn` `.COLUMN.`, with `Pset_ColumnCommon.LoadBearing` | yes |
| `footing` | `IfcFooting` `.PAD_FOOTING.` | yes |
| `stripfooting` | `IfcFooting` `.STRIP_FOOTING.` (a grade beam, baldrame, is `.FOOTING_BEAM.`) | yes |
| structural `floor` | `IfcSlab` `.FLOOR.` (`.BASESLAB.` for a foundation slab) with `Pset_SlabCommon.LoadBearing` | yes |
| `pipe` | `IfcPipeSegment` `.RIGIDSEGMENT.`; fittings `IfcPipeFitting`, valves `IfcValve` | yes |
| sanitary fixtures | `IfcSanitaryTerminal` of the family's `kind` (`wc` `.TOILETPAN.`, `lav` `.WASHHANDBASIN.`, `sink` and `laundry` `.SINK.`, `shower`, `bath`, `bidet`, `urinal`), `.NOTDEFINED.` without one; floor drains `IfcWasteTerminal` `.FLOORTRAP.` (`floor_waste`, `roof_drain` their own); fittings by kind (`bend` `.BEND.`, `tee` and `cross` `.JUNCTION.`, `transition`, `coupling` `.CONNECTOR.`) | yes |
| `conduit` | `IfcCableCarrierSegment` `.CONDUITSEGMENT.` | yes |
| `cabletray` | `IfcCableCarrierSegment` `.CABLETRAYSEGMENT.` (`.CABLELADDERSEGMENT.`, which only another tool writes, is read as a tray) | yes |
| `wire`, `cable` | `IfcCableSegment` `.CABLESEGMENT.`, which BIMCraft's `Category` tells apart | yes |
| panels, boards | `IfcElectricDistributionBoard` `.DISTRIBUTIONBOARD.` | yes |
| luminaires | `IfcLightFixture` | yes |
| outlets, switches | `IfcOutlet` (`.POWEROUTLET.`, `.DATAOUTLET.`, `.TELEPHONEOUTLET.`), `IfcSwitchingDevice` (`.TOGGLESWITCH.`) | power outlets and switches |
| data equipment | `IfcCommunicationsAppliance` `.NETWORKAPPLIANCE.` (a patch panel; a router, a switch would be `.ROUTER.`, `.NETWORKAPPLIANCE.`). A rack has no class: an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `Rack`, which a filter finds and an `IfcElectricDistributionBoard` would hide among boards | yes |
| `downconductor`, `groundconductor` | `IfcCableSegment` `.CONDUCTORSEGMENT.`, which BIMCraft's `Category` tells apart | yes |
| air terminals, earthing rods, inspection boxes | **no IFC class.** IFC4 and IFC4X3 have none for lightning protection. `IfcBuildingElementProxy` (`.USERDEFINED.`) with `ObjectType` `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` or `InspectionBox`, so a reader can filter on it, and the family and type in its name. Surge protection has `IfcProtectiveDevice` `.VARISTOR.`; an `IfcDistributionChamberElement` `.INSPECTIONCHAMBER.` exists for the box but would hide it from a filter on the others | yes |

A run is written as an extrusion along its own axis (`IfcExtrudedAreaSolid`), so a reader gets the profile and the
length and not a mesh. Its system is an `IfcSystem`, named for it, that an `IfcRelAssignsToGroup` assigns the runs in it to;
`BIMCraft_Run` carries what has no attribute: the line its heights are at (`Justification`) and its `Category`, for the classes
that several categories share. One table, `runs::IFC`, gives the class and predefined type of each category, and import reads it
back (`runs::from_ifc`); the same for a family's category (`family::Category::ifc`, `from_ifc`).

## (e) The tabs

Each tab is a ribbon tab with the panels a Revit user expects, built with the `tools` helper the Architecture tab uses.
A tool is a `Tool` value, a click handler, a preview and a tooltip with its shortcut. Shortcuts are Autodesk's published
defaults where there is one; where BIMCraft has already given the letters to something else, the tool gets two others
and says so.

| Tab (EN / PT / ES) | Tools and shortcuts | Brazilian vocabulary |
|---|---|---|
| **Structure** / Estrutura / Estructura | Column CL, Beam BM, Floor (Structural) SB; Foundation: Isolated FI, Wall FW (Revit's FT is Filters here) | pilar, viga, laje, sapata, sapata corrida, baldrame |
| **Plumbing** / Hidrossanitário / Fontanería | Pipe PI, Plumbing Fixture PX, Pipe Fitting PF, Pipe Accessory PA (built) | tubulação, peça sanitária, ramal, prumada, água fria (NBR 5626), esgoto (NBR 8160) |
| **Electrical** / Elétrico / Eléctrico | Conduit CN, Cable Tray CT, Wire EW, Electrical Equipment EE, Lighting Fixture LF, Device DV (built) | eletroduto, eletrocalha, quadro de distribuição, luminária, tomada, circuito (NBR 5410) |
| **Lightning Protection (SPDA)** / SPDA / SPDA | Air Terminal AT, Down Conductor DC, Earthing Electrode EG, Inspection Box IB, Earthing Conductor GC (built) | captor, condutor de descida, haste de aterramento, caixa de inspeção, malha (NBR 5419) |
| **Data** / Lógica, Dados e Voz / Datos y Voz | Data Outlet DT, Voice Outlet VO, Rack RK, Patch Panel PN, Cable Tray CT, Cabling CB (built) | ponto de dados, ponto de voz, rack, patch panel, cabeamento estruturado (NBR 14565) |

The English stays Revit's words; the Portuguese uses the terms the standards use. Revit has no SPDA, so its tools have
no Autodesk shortcut, and take free letters.

## Not in this design, on purpose

Pipe connectors and fittings, auto-routing, sizing, flow and load calculations, circuits and panel schedules (a family's electrical
connectors are in, and give a device its load, and so are the settings: voltages, distribution systems and wire types), analytical
models, rebar, beam systems and trusses. Each is large, none changes the model above, and they come after the five
tabs can draw and schedule their systems (ROADMAP 2.x).

## What a tab adds

Structure was the worked example and the other four followed it; a tab is these steps and no engine code of its own. Each of
the four took a few lines in each of these places, and the tests are rows in two tables.

1. **Core, a run category.** An `Element` variant over `Run` and its name in `model::run_arm!` (every place that treats runs alike
   takes it from there), in `Element::category` and `of_run`, in `RUN_CATEGORIES` and `PARAMETER_CATEGORIES`, in `graphics::MODEL` and
   `paint::faces`; a row in `schedule::OWN`; its default types in `Model::new` (and a material or two in the library) and
   `Model::default_type`; a row in `runs::IFC` (its class and predefined type, both ways); a command with its shortcut (`chain` in
   commands.rs takes the category, so it is a few lines, a row in `ALL` and one in `command_of`). `runs::may_stand` already says a
   riser may stand; `runs::default_justify` is the middle.
2. **Core, a fixture or a device.** A `family::Category` value, in `PLACED`, with its `ifc` row (the class, the predefined type, and
   the object type a proxy carries where IFC has no class); `from_ifc` reads it back. Starter families in `fixtures.rs`, original,
   named through `language.rs`.
3. **Desktop.** A `Tab` variant and a `fn xxx_tab` in `mep.rs`: buttons for `Tool::Run(category, None)` and for the `FIXTURES`
   rows (a `FixtureTool` is a key, the kinds of family it places, its shortcut, its words and its icon); the title in
   `structure::title`; `properties.rs` (`icon`; the run rows and type rows already take any run category); icons in icons.rs; the
   family editor's labels in editor.rs; the Portuguese and Spanish rows in lang.rs (the words each standard uses).
4. **Tests.** A row in `CASES` (the run categories) and `FIXTURES` (the families) of `mep_tests.rs`, which make, refuse, move,
   draw in plan, cut in a section, show in 3D, snap to, schedule, hide, save, write to IFC and read back every category in them;
   and a row in `RUN_TOOLS` and `FIXTURE_TOOLS` of `tests/mep.rs`, which drive each tool, its options, its previews, its shortcut,
   its palette and Edit Type, its languages. The tab itself is a row in the tab and language tables there.

## Honest limits

- Runs that meet butt against each other: no mitre, elbow or tee, and no connectors on them or on a fitting, so a pipe network cannot yet be
  checked for continuity or sized. A fitting or a valve is a component of a family, placed by hand on a pipe's height; nothing
  says a pipe ends on it.
- A run's `system` is a name and an `IfcSystem`, with no rules: nothing checks that a pipe of "Esgoto" meets only pipes of it.
- A fixture or a device is a `component` to Visibility/Graphics and to schedules (the Component schedule has `Family` to group by),
  so a project cannot hide "Plumbing Fixtures" alone. Its family category is there for it; `Element` has no variant for each.
- Two kinds share a predefined type in places (`sink` and `laundry` are both `.SINK.`; `tee` and `cross`, `.JUNCTION.`), and the
  import reads the first back: a laundry tub comes back a sink. A sizing table that tells them apart reads the family's own `kind`.
- A conductor or a conduit under its level (an earthing ring, usually) shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth).
- An inspection box is a proxy, so a filter on the other lightning kinds finds it; `IfcDistributionChamberElement`
  `.INSPECTIONCHAMBER.` is the real class. A patch panel is placed on the wall, not in a rack.
- A section cuts a tube by the plane through its line, which is exact for a convex mesh only; a component's forms are not, and are
  never cut.
- Braces are beams that slope; they will want their own type and `IfcMember`.
- Import finds a run's section as the box round its body in the frame the axis gives it, so a member rolled about its axis
  reads as the box. An upright run comes back running up with its width along east, whichever end it was drawn from.
- The Portuguese and Spanish words are the standards' as the author knows them; no native speaker has read them.

What the foundation's limits were, and is fixed: a section cutting a round run; the `IfcSystem`; a run's justification surviving
an import; Edit Type setting a run type's roundness and material.

1	# Structure and the discipline tabs (Plumbing, Electrical, SPDA, Data)
2	
3	Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.
4	
5	Structure (`runs.rs`, `structure.rs`; the design for the five discipline tabs is in [docs/disciplines.md](../disciplines.md)). A run
6	(`model::Run`) is a straight element from `start` to `end` in plan; its `offset` mm over its level is the height of its `justify` line
7	(top, centre or bottom) at the start, `end_offset` at the end (level when none), `system` the name of the system it is in: a beam, a
8	strip footing, a pipe (Plumbing), and what the other tabs draw (conduits, cable trays, down conductors, data cabling) as further
9	`Element` variants over the same struct, as `Door` and `Window` share `Opening`; `model::run_arm!` is the pattern for any of them, so a
10	place that treats runs alike names no category, and a new category is a line there. Its type is `Types::runs[category][name]`, a `RunType`
11	(`width` across by `depth` deep, or round, in a `material` of the library). The section is square to the axis, so a sloped run is
12	`depth / cos θ` deep vertically (`Geom::half`). `runs::Geom` is the one place that knows the geometry (centre line, `footprint`,
13	`prism` for a rectangle, `tube` for a round one, `z_span`); plans, sections (a prism is cut like any solid; a tube by the plane
14	through the section's line, `Solid::cuts`: the hull of where its edges cross it, a ring, an ellipse when oblique), 3D, snaps and IFC call
15	it and know no category. A run's heights are those of its `justify` line, which a beam or a footing has at the top by default and
16	anything else at the middle (`runs::default_justify`); the desktop keeps each run tool's own justification and offset
17	(`keep_run_options`). A beam or strip footing can't stand or lean past 75°
18	(`runs::check`, `may_stand`: what stands is a column; a pipe, a conduit or a conductor may stand, a riser). In plan (`render::stands`) a footing or a run
19	hangs under the level it is drawn on, its top flush with the view's bottom, and is seen (`seen_below` allows `TOL` for these only,
20	or a wall of the storey below would show in the plan above); through the cut plane it's cut; over it and under the view range's top
21	it's dashed; a faint dashed centre line is drawn where it's seen or overhead, which is also where a click picks it. A structural column and an
22	isolated footing are `Column`s in their own categories (`Element::StructuralColumn`, `Element::Footing`; ask `Element::column()`,
23	`Model::column_type(e)` and `column_outline(e)`, which take the element, not the column) with types of their own
24	(`Types::structural_column`, `Types::footing`); a footing is laid down, its `height` its thickness and its `base_offset` putting its
25	top at the level (the command's `thickness` and `offset`). A floor is `structural` or not, the one flag, and its schedule and IFC say it.
26	`runs_of` and `stood_of` build what a command would make, so a tool's sketch is the element its click makes. The desktop's
27	`Tool::Run(category, start)` and `Tool::Stand(category)` serve every category: a tab adds a ribbon button and its rows in
28	`structure.rs`, `properties.rs` and `lang.rs`, not a tool. The Floor tool makes structural floors while `floor_structural` is set (SB,
29	the Structure tab's button; every other `set_tool` clears it); CL is the structural column on the Structure tab and the architectural one
30	elsewhere, as in Revit. IFC writes a run as an extrusion along its own axis (`Step::body_along`, `aim`) of the class and predefined type
31	the one table `runs::IFC` gives its category (import reads the same table back, `runs::from_ifc`), each structural element with
32	`LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, a run's system as an `IfcSystem` (named for it, its GlobalIds following the name) the runs in it
33	are assigned to by an `IfcRelAssignsToGroup`, its `Justification` and `Category` in `BIMCraft_Run`, and its material as an `IfcMaterial`. A beam, a column, a structural column and a
34	pad footing carry their section on their type, the IFC4 way (`Step::typed_member`, `write_types`): the `IfcBeamType`, `IfcColumnType` or
35	`IfcFootingType` is related by `IfcRelAssociatesMaterial` to an `IfcMaterialProfileSet` of one `IfcMaterialProfile`, holding the type's
36	material (a beam type's; a column type has none, so the material is `$`) and its profile, an `IfcRectangleProfileDef` of the width by the
37	depth or an `IfcCircleProfileDef` of half the width, in millimetres as every length is. Each occurrence is related to an
38	`IfcMaterialProfileSetUsage` of that set (one for each cardinal point, shared by the occurrences placed by it): a beam's cardinal point is
39	the line its heights are on, the top (8), the middle (5) or the bottom (2) of its section, a column's and a footing's the middle (5). The
40	beam has no other material association, so the importer reads a run's material through the usage (`element_material`). The profile
41	definition (`Step::section_profile`, keyed by `Section`) is written once for a section, and the type's profile and its occurrences' bodies
42	share it; two types of one name and two sections (a column's and a structural column's) are two type objects. A strip footing, a pipe and
43	the other runs have no profile set, only the plain material.
44	Import (`import::run_in`) finds a run's axis as the direction its body's points spread furthest in (power iteration on their
45	covariance), so a beam rolled about its axis comes in as the box round it; an axis that stands (a riser) has its width along east and
46	runs up; the justification BIMCraft wrote puts the heights back on the line they were typed at (`Geom::half`), none meaning the middle;
47	a system comes from the IfcSystem the product is assigned to, and its category from the class and type, or BIMCraft's `Category`
48	where a class has several; `LoadBearing` makes a column or a floor structural.
49	
50	**Sizing** is a command with no model behind it, so it needs no connectors: `circuit` (`nbr5410.rs`, its tables in `nbr5410/tables.rs` as NBR 5410:2004 prints them: Tabelas 36 and 37 current capacity for methods A1 to D, 40 and 41 temperature and soil, 42 and 45 grouping, 47, 48 and 58) sizes one electrical circuit for copper: the design current from watts or VA, the demand and power factors and the phases at the voltage `system` it is given (it reads nothing from the model), then the smallest section and breaker with I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) and a voltage drop within the limit (4 %, from the conductor's resistance at its working temperature and 0.1 ohm/km), with the neutral and the protective conductor. A section or breaker already chosen is never made smaller. It does not check aluminium, trays (methods E and F), several layers, short circuit, harmonics or the conditions of a reduced neutral, and says so; a circuit in the model and a panel schedule come after it. `conduit_fill` (`conduit.rs`, its catalogues in `conduit/tables.rs`) checks a conduit's fill: the conductors of a circuit (phases, neutral, protective; by outside diameter) over the conduit's inside, at most 53 % for one cable, 31 % for two and 40 % for three or more (NBR 5410), and the smallest size of a family that takes them. The dimensions are the makers' own (Amanco Wavin PVC, Elecon steel, Corfio flexible cable), each family naming its document, page and address; the inside diameter is derived (outside less twice the wall); a cable the catalogue lacks (EPR, above 240 mm²) leaves the fill pending, never guessed. Trays are not sized. `drain_size` and `vent_size` (`drainage.rs`) size sanitary drains and vents as NBR 8160 asks, by the fixture units (UHC) they carry, with the standard's own tables: Tabela 3 (the units and smallest drain of each fixture), 5 (branches), 7 (building drains and collectors by slope), 6 (stacks by the building's floors), 8 (branch vents), 2 (vent stacks and headers by the DN served, its units and the longest length of each vent DN) and 1 (a trap's longest run to its vent). A drain is never smaller than its fixtures' own drains or than one flowing into it (`min_dn`), and a building drain is DN 100 at least. They are stateless, so none of this needs a pipe network; a network that carries the units along the runs comes with connectors. `storm_size` (`storm.rs`) sizes storm drains as NBR 10844 asks: the flow Q = I·A/60 from a rainfall and a roof area, a downpipe by the inner diameter of the standard's Figure 3 abacuses (read curve by curve: the water depth in the gutter, the downpipe's length and a sharp-edged or funnel outlet; 70 mm inside at least; off the chart nothing is read) and a horizontal drain by Manning at two thirds full (n 0.011, which reproduces its Table 4 within 1 %; 0.5 % slope at least). `water_size` (`water.rs`) sizes a cold water pipe of PVC soldável as NBR 5626 asks: the design flow of the fixtures by the method the project chooses (weights, Q = 0.3 √ΣP, or every fixture at once), the smallest DN within 3 m/s, the Darcy-Weisbach head loss over the length and the equivalent length of the fittings, and the pressure left (10 kPa at least at a point of use). `hydrant_size` (`hydrant.rs`) sizes hydrants and hose reels as IT 22/2025 of the CBPMESP asks: the system type and fire reserve of Tabela 3 by occupation column and built area, the flow of the two most unfavourable jets of Tabela 2's type, and a pipe's speed (5 m/s at most), Hazen-Williams head loss (Tabela 1) and the head needed at its start. `load_points` (`loads.rs`) lists what a dwelling's rooms must have as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks: one ceiling lighting point per room (100 VA up to 6 m², 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above) and the general-use outlets by the room's kind, which its name says or `kind` gives (a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area and laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room and bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and by perimeter above), with their power (600 VA each for the first 3 points of a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry and 100 VA after, or for the first 2 by the alternative where those rooms have more than 6 points together; 100 VA a point elsewhere) on the points a room has. It reads the model's rooms (inside the walls' finish) or the rooms it is given, and changes nothing. It leaves out the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, where the outlets stand, and the TUE, and says so.
51	
52	**Electrical settings** (`electrical.rs`) are the tables circuits, panels and connectors will name, as Revit's Electrical Settings: `Voltage` (`nominal`, and the band `min` to `max` a device may read within), `DistributionSystem` (`phases` 1 to 3, `wires` the line conductors and the neutral and not the protective one, and the voltages it supplies by name: `l_l` between lines, `l_n` to the neutral, `l_g` to earth, and `ground`, how it is earthed as IEC 60364-1 names it) and `WireType` (`material`, `temperature`, `insulation`, a `note` saying where the ampacities come from, and `sizes`, a row for each section with its `ampacity`). Every section is in mm² whatever the project's units; a size a standard gives in AWG or kcmil is converted and keeps its name as `label`. Each is a map of `Model` (`voltages`, `distribution_systems`, `wire_types`), a library entry (`Kind::Voltage`, `Kind::DistributionSystem`, `Kind::WireType`, so each has an id and a GUID, comes in with Insert from File and is renamed with `rename_entry`), and has a command that makes, edits, renames and deletes it and, without a `name`, lists it (`voltage`, `distribution_system`, `wire_type`); `inspect` lists all three. A system names voltages, so `Model::lib_refs_mut` hands them out (a file holds their GUIDs, a rename follows) and `Model::check` refuses a system that names one the project lacks, saying which and listing the ones it has, and `voltage` refuses to delete one a system supplies; with three phases `l_l` must be about root three times `l_n`. `Model::voltage_range`, `system_voltages` and `wire_ampacity` are what circuits will ask: the band of a voltage, the voltages a system supplies (the ones a circuit on it may have) and the ampacity of a section in a wire type's table. A new project starts with `data/electrical.json`, data and not code: 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of NBR 5410:2004 Tabelas 36 and 37 (PVC 70 °C and XLPE or EPR 90 °C, seeded from `nbr5410/tables.rs`: method B1, two loaded conductors, a test keeps them equal) and of NFPA 70 Table 310.16 (THHN 90 °C, THW 75 °C); their ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked, and one number for a section cannot say how a wire is laid, so a wire type's `note` says. `start_system` and `start_wire` name the ones a new panel or circuit starts with for the project's units (Europe's in metric, North America's in feet and inches). None of it goes to IFC: the tables are project data, and what they produce (voltage, current, section) will go in the device's property set once circuits exist. On the desktop, Manage > Electrical Settings (`ui-egui/src/electrical.rs`) is one dialog with a tab for each table: rows to add and delete, a voltage chosen from the project's own for each line of a system, and a wire type's table of sections below its fields. It is a draft, applied by OK or Apply as one undo step (`Session::transaction`) through the three commands, in an order the core accepts (`renames::plan`, which the other Manage dialogs use, orders each table's renames and deletes; the voltages are made before the systems that name them and taken away after the systems that no longer do). A system's voltages are held by their rows' keys, so one renamed in the dialog is still the one named. A blank or repeated name, a voltage a system supplies being deleted, and what the core refuses are said inside the dialog, which stays open. Not yet: circuits, panels and the load schedule, connectors in families.
53	
54	The discipline tabs after Structure add data to this, no engine code of their own. Plumbing: `pipe` (PI), types in PVC and copper
55	(`Types::runs["pipe"]`, outside diameters, so a pipe's `width` is its diameter and its schedule says Diameter). Electrical: `conduit`
56	(CN), `duct` (DU: a rectangular or round duct, written as `IfcDuctSegment`; only a Revit import makes them in practice) `cabletray` (CT, `cable_tray`: the one rectangular run) and `wire` (EW), by their outside size. Lightning protection (NBR 5419):
57	`downconductor` (DC, may stand: a riser down a wall) and `groundconductor` (GC), two runs of one IFC class that `BIMCraft_Run`'s `Category`
58	tells apart; an air terminal, an earthing electrode and an inspection box are components of their own family categories, written as
59	`IfcBuildingElementProxy` of the object type `Category::ifc` names, so the product's name (not its object type) holds `Family:Type` and
60	import reads it from there. Data (NBR 14565): `cable` (CB, `cabling`), a run like a wire, so a file's `IfcCableSegment` is a wire unless its
61	`Category` says cable; data and voice outlets (`IfcOutlet` `DATAOUTLET`, `TELEPHONEOUTLET`; one of no type reads as the power outlet,
62	`Category::from_ifc` taking the first of equals), a patch panel (`IfcCommunicationsAppliance`) and a rack (a proxy of object type `Rack`);
63	the Cable Tray tool is the Electrical tab's, on the Data tab too. A fixture or a
64	device is a component of a family whose `family::Category` says what it is (a sanitary fixture, a floor drain, a pipe fitting, a pipe
65	accessory…); `Category::ifc` is its IFC class, predefined type and, where IFC has no class (lightning protection), the object type a
66	proxy carries, and `Category::from_ifc` reads the same table back, so a category is one row, in `family.rs`. A family's `kind`
67	(`Category::kinds`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`… for a sanitary fixture, `floor_drain`… for a drain, `bend`, `tee`… for a fitting, the names the
68	sizing commands count fixtures by) says which one it is, and `Family::ifc` writes that kind's predefined type in place of the
69	category's `.NOTDEFINED.`; the import reads it back with `Category::kind_of`, the first kind of a predefined type two share. The starter families are
70	`fixtures.rs` (original forms, named in the project's language; a fitting or a valve is centred on its pipe, along x, so placing it at the
71	pipe's height lines them up; a wall device, a board and a luminaire carry their `Mounting Height` in their type, so the Fixture tool
72	places them at the level and they stand where they hang). The desktop's `mep.rs` has one tool for every fixture and device, `Tool::Fixture(key)`: the families of the
73	kinds its `FixtureTool` names, listed in its Type Selector and placed as the Component tool places them (`placing` takes the tool's
74	kinds), and the tabs' ribbon panels; a fixture's two-letter shortcut is in `mep::FIXTURES`, not `SHORTCUTS`, since no command makes
75	one. Edit Type of a run type also sets whether it is round (a diameter, no depth) and its material.
76	
77	Reinforcement (`rebar.rs`, `model::Rebar`, `Element::Rebar`, category `rebar`, the `rebar` command; tests in `rebar_tests.rs`). A bar is one
78	element: a round bar of `diameter` mm (3 to 100) bent along `path` (points in mm, `z` over its level), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless
79	told), with the `host` it reinforces (a beam, a column, a footing or a floor, held as a `Guid`, and it goes when its host does). A hoop
80	is a bar whose last point is its first; a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam, is one command with `count` and `step`, which makes one
81	element for each (IFC has one `IfcReinforcingBar` for each, and a bar schedule counts them). It has no type: the diameter and the grade
82	are its own, and the bends are sharp, with no hooks, so its length is the sum of its pieces (`rebar::length`) and its weight that
83	length of steel at 7850 kg/m³ (`rebar::weight_kg`). Nothing checks that it lies inside its host: `reinforce` places bars inside by construction. The schedule of category `rebar` lists Id, Level, Grade, Diameter,
84	Length, Count, Weight and Host, and grouped by Grade, Diameter and Length with Count and Weight totalled it is a bar schedule. IFC
85	writes each as an `IfcReinforcingBar` (`SteelGrade`, `NominalDiameter`, `CrossSectionArea`, `BarLength`) with a body of an
86	`IfcSweptDiskSolid` along an `IfcPolyline`, aggregated (`IfcRelAggregates`) to its host, or contained in its storey when it has none;
87	import reads the same back, with the host found by the aggregation. The 3D view draws a tube along each straight piece
88	(`rebar::tubes`, built with a round run's tube), which the concrete round a bar hides: look at bars with their host hidden. A section draws each bar it cuts as a
89	dot over the host's poché (`render::section_in` keeps them out of the host's pieces, which would swallow them); a plan draws them too (`render::bar_in_plan`).
90	
91	Importing a structural program's IFC (Eberick, Cype and the like; tests in `eberick_tests.rs`, written by hand, never from anyone's project). Each
92	product is named by its mark, so a name that is not its type's (BIMCraft names a product by its type, and writes it as its object type too) is its
93	`Mark` parameter, for the categories in `import::MARKED` (beams, columns, structural columns, footings, strip footings and floors; not stairs,
94	which BIMCraft calls "Stair"). The single values of every property set that is not BIMCraft's (`BIMCraft_*`, `RoomSeparation`; `Project Parameters`
95	is read by its names as written) are project parameters named for the property, a character a formula can't say turned into a space
96	(`parameter_name`: "Cargas de parede (G2)" is "Cargas de parede G2"), lengths in the file's unit made millimetres; `LoadBearing` is left out because
97	it already makes a column or a floor structural. The cover Eberick sets (`Cobrimento`, `ConcreteCover`) is therefore on the host as a length, for the
98	rules that will arm it. A run is found in its body as the way it spreads furthest, except where the body is one extruded profile and the extrusion is
99	not up: then it runs along the extrusion (`Reader::extrusion`), because a beam between two columns can be shallower than it is deep, and its body then
100	spreads furthest up. A strip footing, a plan outline stood up, is still read by its shape. A landing slab that belongs to no stair is a floor.
101	
102	Bars by rules (`reinforce.rs`, the `reinforce` command; tests in `reinforce_tests.rs`). The engineer says how many bars, how thick and how far
103	apart; the module lays them out in the host's own frame (`Frame`: along, across, up) inside the cover and checks that what is asked fits, with the
104	message saying what to change. It holds geometry and no standard's table: a spacing or a count is never decided here (that is design), and the
105	clearance between bars (`clearance`, their thickness and at least 20 mm unless told) is the only rule it brings. Parameters are read with serde types
106	that deny unknown fields (`Row`, `Pitch`, `Stirrup`, `ColumnBars`, `Mesh`, `Grid`), by key, so a key that is not the host's is refused with the host named.
107	The cover is `{top, bottom, sides}` (Revit's faces: the top and bottom faces of a beam, a footing or a floor, the ends of a column, and all round
108	the rest) or one number, and where none is given the host's `Cobrimento` or `ConcreteCover` parameter (a length in mm, as the import of an Eberick IFC
109	leaves it) is the cover. A spacing is the most between bars: `spread` and `stations` place them evenly from end to end, so the count follows the length
110	(Revit's Maximum Spacing) and `ends` gives closer stirrups in the first and last `length` mm. A stirrup is a closed loop; with `hook` it runs on past
111	its first corner to a tail turned into the section at each end (`stirrup`). A beam has `bottom` and `top` rows, `stirrup`, `skin` and `anchor`; a
112	column `bars` (`x` and `y` along each face, corners counted; a round one, `count` round its circle), `stirrup` (a round one's a polygon of 24 sides), `ties`
113	(across a rectangular section; with `hook` a tail at each end turned toward the other axis) and `anchor`; a footing a `mesh` of two layers with `hook`
114	turning their ends up (a round one's bars stop at its circle, `half` in `footing`); a floor `bottom` and `top` meshes (`hook` turning their ends up from the
115	bottom one and down from the top one, square to the slab's top) whose bars stop a cover short of its outline and of its
116	openings (`chords`, a scan line through the outline and the openings together; a bar parallel to an opening's edge and nearer it than the cover keeps
117	its cover from the ends only). A sloped floor's layers are measured from its top face, square to it (`off`, and its secant for the height plumb), so the
118	cover and the thickness are the type's and its bars follow the slope; a mesh on a slope is one plane's bars. Round beams and strip footings are refused. Each bar is a `rebar` element of the host with a `layer`
119	(`bottom`, `top`, `skin`, `stirrup`, `bars`, `tie`, `mesh x`, `mesh y`, `bottom x`, `top y`, ...); reinforcing a host again replaces its bars that have a layer
120	and leaves the ones with none, which were drawn by hand, and one command makes up to `rebar::MAX_BARS`. A bar's layer is in the project file and the
121	schedule (a field a bar schedule may show), not in IFC. What it does not do: bends other than a hook, laps and splices, bars of a round beam, and any check
122	against a standard. A section shows a bar in its plane as a strip along it and one it crosses as a dot (the cut of the bar's tube, `section_in`); a bar
123	beyond the cut stays hidden by the concrete it is in.
124	
125	More of `reinforce`. `hosts` arms a list (`rebar::MAX_HOSTS`, 1000) alike in one command: every host's bars are made before any is replaced, so one that refuses (its refusal names its category and id) arms none, and `rebar::MAX_BARS_ALL` (20000) caps all of them
126	together. A `hook` on a beam's `bottom` and `top` rows is the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at each end
127	(a number for both, or `{start, end}`), and on a column's `bars` a leg turned into the section along the way across the face the bar is on
128	(`{below, above}`); `legs` reads it, with its own words when it is not a length, and a leg that does not stay inside the stirrup (a column's: stop
129	short of the middle) is refused. The bends are sharp, as every bar's are, and each leg is a piece of the path, so the length and the weight count it.
130	A `reinforcement_preset` is `reinforce::Preset`, a kind of host (`KINDS`) and the parameters that kind takes, in `Model::reinforcement` and as a library
131	entry (`Kind::ReinforcementPreset`, so it has an id and a GUID, comes in with Insert from File and is renamed with `rename_entry`); it is checked
132	for its keys and its size when saved (`Preset::check`, `MAX_PRESETS`) and against a host only when it arms one. `reinforce` with `preset` takes its parameters
133	and lets any given with it replace them, key by key; a preset of another kind than the host is refused, saying both. Plans: a bar of the plan's level
134	is drawn from above, solid when the cut plane is over its lowest point and dashed when it is over the plane and under the view range's top, a bar
135	that stands (a column's) as a dot, and bars that lie on one another (a column's stirrups, one over the next) once.
136	
137	Bends beyond a hook. `bottom.bent` `{count, angle?, top?}` (`Bent`, `bent_up`) takes `count` of a beam's inner bottom bars (the two at the corners hold the
138	stirrups and stay straight; the others are picked evenly) and bends them up at each end: along the top face for `top` mm from the end (a fifth of the
139	length unless told), down a slope of `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) to the bottom row's level and along it. They are on the layer `bent`,
140	have no hook, count as bottom steel in the check, and are refused where the slopes meet in the middle, where the section is too shallow to rise
141	in, and where one comes within the clearance of a top bar at the top. `bars.jog` `{by, from_top, slope?}` (`Jog`, `step`, `stepped`) steps a column's
142	bars `by` mm toward the axis (a corner bar along both faces, a face bar across its own, a round column's radially), the step starting `from_top` mm below
143	the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told); the points of the bar above the step move with it, including a hook's leg, and
144	the bars at their new places are checked against one another for the clearance.
145	
146	The check (`reinforce/norm.rs`). `check` `"NBR 6118"`, with `aggressiveness` (1 to 4) and `fck` (MPa), makes `reinforce` return `notes`: where the bars
147	made fall short of the usual limits for the kind of host (Table 7.2's cover by class; for a beam the 4 % most, the 0.15 % least up to C30, skin bars over 600 mm
148	deep, stirrups of 5 mm to a tenth of the width at most min(0.6 d, 300) apart; for a column bars of 10 mm to an eighth of the side, 4 bars or 6 round,
149	centres at most min(2 sides, 400), 0.4 to 8 % of steel, stirrups of 5 mm or a quarter of the bars' at most min(200, the side, 12 bars) apart; for a floor
150	bars of at most an eighth of the thickness at most min(2 h, 200) apart). A note never refuses: an engineer may know better, and the bars are made.
151	It reads only the bars made, so a limit that needs shear, the load or the aggregate is not in it. The numbers are typed from handbooks and course material
152	that print them, not from the standard's text, which is paid for, and the item numbers are the 2014 edition's at the level of the chapter's item: check
153	one against a copy before relying on it. The desktop's Check row (Standard, Aggressiveness class, fck) shows the notes inside the dialog, which stays
154	open, with the bars made, so a field can change and OK remake them.
155	
156	The Reinforce dialog (`crates/ui-egui/src/reinforce.rs`, Structure > Reinforcement, RF; tests in `tests/reinforce.rs`). It opens on the one beam, column,
157	structural column, footing or floor selected (anything else says what to select), with the form of its kind (`BEAM`, `COLUMN`, `FOOTING`, `FLOOR`: tables of
158	groups of fields, each field the path of the parameter it sets, such as `bottom.count`). Every field is text: a count is a whole number, a bar size is mm,
159	a length is read in the project's units (`Units::parse`); a field left empty is not sent, a group with none filled is left out, and the command is the one
160	that says what is missing. OK builds the parameters and runs `reinforce` as one undo step; a refusal is the command's own words, shown inside the dialog
161	(a status box in the view's corner could lie over its buttons) with the dialog left open and the project unchanged, and a field that is not a number is
162	named before the command is asked. It takes any number of elements selected, of one form (a mixed selection says so), and arms them with one `hosts` command; Remove Bars removes the bars of all. What was typed is kept for the next element of the same form (not in the project, not on disk). The Preset row lists the project's presets of the form: choosing one fills the fields (`ReinforceDialog::load`, the reverse of `params`, lengths in the project's units), Save Preset keeps the fields as they are under the name typed (`reinforcement_preset`, the parameters without the hosts), and Delete Preset takes the chosen one away; each keeps the dialog open. Remove Bars, shown
163	when the element has bars the command made (those with a layer), deletes them and leaves the ones drawn by hand. The fields' accessible names are
164	"Group: Field" (`Bottom bars: Count`), and the cover's is `Cover`, its label having a colon so that no two nodes carry the name.
165	
166	**Connectors.** A family's `connectors` (`family::Connector`, a list for any discipline; today the electrical device's) say what
167	a placed device draws: `kind` `power` or `switch`, `system` `power-balanced`, `power-unbalanced` or `switch`, `poles` (1 to 3),
168	`voltage`, `load_va`, `power_factor` and a `classification`. The numbers are numbers or formulas over the family's parameters, so a
169	type sets its load (the starter luminaires' `Load` parameter) and an instance parameter lets one component set its own; a
170	`power-unbalanced` connector's `load_va` may be a list, one load for each pole, and a single number is shared out evenly.
171	`Family::check` refuses a family of two `power` connectors, a kind and system that don't go together, poles, voltage, power factor
172	or load out of range for any type, and a load on a switch. A connector is a part (`HasPart`: an id and a GUID, kept by place
173	while the family is edited), and a family without any reads and places as it always did. A component's `element_json` carries
174	`connectors` worked out for its type (`Family::connector_values`: `load_va` in all, `load_va_by_phase`), which a circuit will sum;
175	there are no circuits, panels or fitting-to-pipe joins yet, and the connector holds no position. `Model::warnings` (shown by
176	`inspect`; `Model::check` stays an error only) says which lighting, outlet or switch family in use holds no connector, so its devices
177	count as zero load. IFC writes each device with a connector `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` (`NumberOfPoles`, and for a power
178	connector `PowerFactor` and `RatedVoltage`) and `BIMCraft_Connector` (`System`, `Classification`, `LoadVA`, `LoadVAPhase1`…); IFC
179	import doesn't read them back.

results.content:
| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |
| Lightning protection (SPDA) | Air terminals (captores), down conductors (condutores de descida), earthing electrodes (hastes de aterramento), inspection boxes and earthing conductors (the ring or mesh), the vocabulary of NBR 5419; Revit has no such tab, so its tools are BIMCraft's own, on the same runs and fixtures. A down conductor is a run that stands upright down a wall (the same point twice and two heights), round in steel or copper or a flat strip; an earthing conductor runs under the level; both belong to a named system. The project starts with a Franklin air terminal in three heights, an earthing rod driven 2.4 or 3 m and a round inspection box, original drawings in the project's language. IFC4 has no lightning protection, so the terminals, rods and boxes are `IfcBuildingElementProxy` of object type `LightningTerminal`, `EarthingRod` and `InspectionBox`, which a reader can filter on and BIMCraft reads back into a family of its category; the conductors are `IfcCableSegment` `CONDUCTORSEGMENT`, told apart by a `Category` BIMCraft writes. A conductor under the level shows in a plan whose view range reaches it (its View Depth) |
| `column` | CL | `at`, `type?`, `angle?`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `height?`, `base_offset?` |
| `structural_column` | CL | as `column`, in its own category and types |
| `reinforcement_preset` | | `name?`, `kind?` (beam, column, footing, floor), `params?` (what `reinforce` takes, but the host), `rename?`, `delete?`: a named set of parameters, kept in the project; no `name` lists them |
| `voltage` | | `name?`, `nominal?` (volts), `min?`, `max?` (the band a device may read within; 10 per cent either way unless given), `rename?`, `delete?`: a voltage of the electrical settings; one a distribution system supplies cannot be deleted; no `name` lists them |
| `distribution_system` | | `name?`, `phases?` (1, 2, 3), `wires?` (the line conductors and the neutral), `l_l?`, `l_n?`, `l_g?` (names of voltages; "" takes one away), `ground?` (TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT, IT), `rename?`, `delete?`: a distribution system of the electrical settings; a voltage the project lacks is refused; no `name` lists them |
| `wire_type` | | `name?`, `material?` (copper, aluminium), `temperature?` (°C), `insulation?`, `note?`, `sizes?` (`[{section, ampacity, label?}]`, mm² and amperes, which replaces the table), `rename?`, `delete?`: a wire type of the electrical settings; no `name` lists them |
| `reinforce` | | `host` (a beam, a column, a footing or a floor) or `hosts` (a list), `preset?`, `cover?`, `grade?`, `grade_stirrup?`, `clearance?`, and by host: `bottom`, `top`, `stirrup`, `skin`, `anchor` (beam), `bars`, `stirrup`, `ties`, `anchor` (column), `mesh` (footing), `bottom`, `top` (floor), `check?`, `aggressiveness?`, `fck?`: bars by rules, as `rebar` elements on layers, and notes from the check |
| `footing` | FI | `at`, `type?`, `thickness?` (400), `offset?` (its top over the level, 0), `angle?`, `level?`: an isolated footing |
| `beam` | BM | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (the height of its `justify` line over the level at its start, 0), `end_offset?` (at its end, for one segment: it slopes), `justify?` (`top`, `centre`, `bottom`), `system?`: a beam for each segment |
| `pipe` | PI | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (the height of its `justify` line over the level at its start, 0), `end_offset?` (at its end, for one segment: it falls or rises, or stands if the two points are one), `justify?` (`centre` by default), `system?`: a pipe for each segment |
| `conduit` | CN | as `pipe`: a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment, round |
| `cable_tray` | CT | as `pipe`, its type a `width` across by a `depth` deep: a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment |
| `wire` | EW | as `pipe`: a wire (condutor) for each segment, round; its `system` the circuit |
| `down_conductor` | DC | as `pipe`: a down conductor (condutor de descida) for each segment; the same point twice and two heights stand it upright |
| `ground_conductor` | GC | as `pipe`: an earthing conductor (the ring or mesh), usually under the level (a negative `offset`) |
| `cabling` | CB | as `pipe`: structured cabling for each segment, round; its `system` the link or the network |
| `strip_footing` | FW | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (its top over the level, 0), `system?`: a footing under a wall for each segment |

arguments.prompt:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent; I own `src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`, `src/load.rs`, and I'm delegating the LOADER part of my area to you.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/loader-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c ... | ...`). Write Python scripts to files in /tmp/loader-agent/ and run them with `python3 /tmp/loader-agent/script.py` instead (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Your task: the loader — what opening a project file does
Make our program behave exactly like the original whenever it reads a `.bimcraft` project file: `bimcraft-cli info x.bimcraft`, `bimcraft-cli run x.bimcraft --cmd ...` (the open reply printed first), `run --cmd 'open {"path":"x.bimcraft"}'`, `bimcraft-cli convert x.bimcraft y.bimcraft`, and saving after opening (`run x.bimcraft --save y.bimcraft` must write the same file the original writes, modulo GUIDs/uid normalisation). Files: `src/load.rs` (entry point; currently a permissive stub) and a new directory `src/readers/file/` for your modules (add `pub mod file;` to `src/readers/mod.rs` — I may edit that file too, so keep your edit to that one line). You may edit `src/commands/basic.rs`'s `open_project_file` (and `info`) for the open reply / error wording; list any other edit outside your files in your report.

### The codebase (read these first; you're in a git worktree of the repo)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting, `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies print sorted, as serde_json::Value), `kind_name()` (serde's "invalid type" wording: `integer `5``, `string "a"`, `floating point `1.5``, `sequence`, `map`...), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`). `Project::new("en")` builds a new project from `src/templates.rs` (what the original's `new` makes).
- `src/commands/basic.rs`: `open_project_file` (reads, parses, calls `crate::load::load`, then `crate::cloud::check`), `info`. `src/main.rs`: `info`, `convert`, `run` (prints the open reply sorted+compact; errors print `open: <message>` and exit 1).
- Already done by others, to reuse and call from the loader (don't redo): `crate::cloud::load(&mut Project)` and `crate::cloud::left_out(&Value)` (point-cloud sections and elements; it currently runs inside `load`), `crate::styles::phasing::load(&mut Project) -> Result<Vec<String>, String>` (phases, phase_filters, phase_overrides, option_sets: returns the left_out pointers of those sections), `crate::styles::text::normalize` and `crate::styles::text::sync_library` (text and dimension types), and styles' checks (`crate::styles::check`, `crate::check::check` is the whole model check run after commands). grep `src/styles/` and `src/media/` for other `load`/`normalize`/`left_out`-like helpers before writing your own for those sections (line patterns, fill patterns, region types, materials/images, parameters, electrical settings, reinforcement presets...). Read `src/styles/phasing.rs` `load` to see the style used.
- Build: `cargo build --release` in your worktree. Compare tool: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] -- <args…>` runs both programs in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uid, temp names. Prints SAME or a diff. E.g. `cmp.py -f /tmp/loader-agent/x.bimcraft -- info x.bimcraft`, `cmp.py -f x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --save y.bimcraft`, `cmp.py -f x.bimcraft -- convert x.bimcraft y.bimcraft`.
- Note: `inspect`/`elements` output (and so `info`'s body) is being rewritten by me in parallel — don't chase differences in derived values in `info`'s output; judge the loader by: the error messages (exact), the open reply (`run x.bimcraft` first line), and the file saved after opening (`run x.bimcraft --save y.bimcraft`, `convert`). For a file that opens, the saved file must match the original's byte for byte after normalisation.

### What I've observed so far (verify and extend; don't trust blindly)
- Errors read `open: <path> is not a BIMCraft project: <serde-style message>` for malformed/mistyped files, and `open: <path>: <model check message>` when the file deserialises but breaks a model rule (e.g. `open: m.bimcraft: wall 100002: type `2020bf8b-...` doesn't exist (there are: Exterior - 300mm, Generic - 200mm, Interior - 100mm)`, `wall 100002 points at element 100000 by its id, not its GUID`). `info` prints the same messages. JSON syntax errors carry serde_json's line/column (`EOF while parsing a value at line 2 column 0`; `src/json.rs` already produces these).
- The original seems to parse to a JSON value, then: process `elements` first (a map; `` `abc` isn't an element id``; each element `element 100000: <msg>`; elements are an internally tagged enum `Element` on `category` with 49 variants: `level, grid, wall, floor, ceiling, shaft, mass, door, window, room, roomseparator, dimension, dimension3d, tag, section, elevation, sheet, viewport, column, structuralcolumn, footing, beam, stripfooting, pipe, duct, conduit, cabletray, wire, downconductor, groundconductor, cable, rebar, component, stair, ramp, railing, roof, text, line, region, detailgroup, repeatingdetail, spot, schedule, view3d, planview, link, pointcloud, cadimport` — an unknown one gives `unknown variant `foo`, expected one of `level`, `grid`, ...`; a non-object `invalid type: integer `5`, expected internally tagged enum Element`; `[]` → `missing field `category``), then `library` (must be a map if present), then `format` (``format` must be a whole number``; above 17: `it was saved by a newer BIMCraft (file format 18; this one reads up to 17): update BIMCraft to open it`), then deserialises `struct Model` (36 fields; an array root says `invalid length 1, expected struct Model with 36 elements`, so serde's seq form works too — `[17,"a"]` → `invalid length 2`; scalars → `invalid type: integer `5`, expected struct Model`). `{}` gives `invalid type: null, expected a map` (elements missing). Map keys are visited in SORTED order (serde_json Map is a BTreeMap there): with two bad fields, the alphabetically first one's error is reported. Required: `elements`, `name`, `uid` (u64), `next_id`, `types` (with required `wall`, `floor`, `door`, `window`, `column`, `roof`, `ceiling`, `railing`); missing sections are filled from defaults (a file without `materials` gets the materials its types reference, made grey `[200,200,200]`; without `families`, `{}`), the library is rebuilt/resynced from the sections (entries added/removed: e.g. family-parameter entries go when families go).
- Element fields: `guid` optional (a new one is made), wrong ones: `` `a` is not a GUID (xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx) or an id``, `5 is an id, not a GUID`; number fields `invalid type: string "a", expected f64`; level `view_range` optional (written back as `{"top":null,"cut":1200.0,"bottom":0.0,"depth":0.0}`); wall `height`/`base_offset` default 0.0, door `flip_hand` default false — everything is written back in struct order with defaults filled. Unknown fields are ignored and reported: the open reply becomes `{"left_out":["/elements/100000/foo","/bar","/types/wall/Generic - 200mm/zz"],"left_out_count":3,"name":"Project","path":"p.bimcraft"}` (JSON pointers; elements first, then the rest in sorted visiting order; without any, just `{"name","path"}`). Check whether left_out is capped/truncated when long, and the `~0`/`~1` escaping.

### Method (suggested)
1. Build a corpus of project files with the ORIGINAL covering every element category and every optional field: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' ... --save x.bimcraft` (`/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `--sample` builds a furnished sample house; `run --script file.txt` runs one command per line). Use every option of every command (walls with arc/location/attach_top/attach_base/room_bounding, doors/windows with families, floors with openings/slope/structural, roofs of every kind (extrusion, gables, slopes), rooms frozen, stairs with landings and railings, ramps, components with params, masses with top/lean, dimensions of every kind, tags, text with runs and leaders, spots, sections, elevations, sheets, viewports, schedules, 3D views/cameras, plan views (duplicate_view), detail lines of every shape, filled regions, detail groups, repeating details, links, point clouds, CAD imports, rebar, project parameters (`parameter`), view filters/templates, phases, design options, materials with textures, images (pictures)...).
2. Write a schema explorer (Python) that takes a valid file and for each field of each element/section: deletes it (required → `missing field`; optional → what default gets written back on save, or whether it is omitted), replaces it with values of other JSON types (records serde's `expected ...` wording: `f64`, `a string`, `a boolean`, `u32`, `a sequence`, `struct X`, `a map`, `unknown variant`, `invalid length`...), and adds unknown candidate fields (a field NOT reported in `left_out` is a known optional field — use this to find optional fields that aren't written by default). Record field order as written on save. Then implement the schemas in Rust (a small serde-like layer over `Value`: typed field readers producing the exact messages, defaults, struct-order writers, `left_out` collection).
3. Reference checks done on open (GUIDs that must name existing elements/types/materials/families, id-vs-GUID, the model check's messages), and what the original repairs silently. Library resync rules (ids, which kinds, kept GUIDs).
4. Older formats: try `format` values below 17 with otherwise current files (and absent `format`) and see whether anything is migrated or refused.
5. Damaged copies of real files: truncated JSON, wrong types deep inside types/materials/families/elements, duplicate keys, huge numbers, negative ids, NaN-like values, non-UTF-8 bytes, empty file, BOM, etc. Match the original's messages exactly.

### API to keep
- Keep `pub fn crate::load::load(v: Value) -> Result<Project, String>` working (others call it: insert, link, recover), and add what you need for the open reply's `left_out` (e.g. `pub fn load_report(v: Value) -> Result<(Project, Vec<String>), String>`), wiring `open_project_file` to print `left_out`/`left_out_count`. Keep the "is not a BIMCraft project:" vs model-check message split exact.
- Don't implement inspect/elements/schedules or any modelling command; don't edit other agents' modules (src/arch, src/structure, src/views, src/edit, src/ifc, src/styles, src/media, src/cloud, src/rvt, src/mcp) — call their public functions instead; if one of them is wrong for loading, describe the problem in your report rather than editing it.

## Finish
Commit your work on your worktree branch (commit messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: the branch name and commit; what matches the original and what doesn't (with concrete examples of remaining differences); the public API you added; every edit outside `src/load.rs` and `src/readers/file/`. Be thorough: the hidden tests compare outputs on many inputs, including files the original saved and damaged copies of them.
