arguments.description: Implement modify command
arguments.prompt:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I own the EDIT area (`src/edit/`) and delegate to you the command `modify`.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Edit ONLY `src/edit/modify.rs` (you may add new files `src/edit/modify_*.rs` and their `pub mod` lines in `src/edit/mod.rs`). Nothing else in the repo. Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/edit-modify/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell commands it can't verify (loops, heredocs, `cd` outside the worktree, `$(...)` feeding python): write Python scripts to files in /tmp and run them as `python3 /tmp/edit-modify/x.py`.

## Setup
You are in a git worktree. First make sure your HEAD contains commit 89ee1af ("Editing: module skeleton"): `git log --oneline -3`; if not, `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-a76b15059404997b3`. Build with `cargo build --release` (about 15 s).

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical float formatting (`1000.0`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies are printed sorted by main.rs: just return the Value), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order — key order matters, files are compared byte for byte after normalising GUIDs) + `library` (`{kind, name, guid}`: `type:wall`, `material`, `family`, `parameter`, `phase`, …). Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID. `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` resolves the command, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records an undo step labelled by the catalog label (`modify` always makes a step, even unchanged: already wired in `src/edit/mod.rs::always_step`).
- `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers with the original's texts), `src/model.rs` (`resolve_level`, `level_param` with the original's errors for levels by name/id), `src/edit/common.rs` (`ids_param` — `ids`, else `id`, with the original's errors `no element 5` / `"x" is not an element id or GUID` —, `resolve`, `element_view(s, id)` = the element as `elements` shows it, `r3`).
- `src/styles/parameters.rs` (`key_of(pr, name)`: the GUID an element's `params` keys a project parameter by; `check_value`), `src/styles/phasing.rs` (`set_param`/`remove_param` keep `params` where the original puts it; `Phase Created`, `Phase Demolished`, `Design Option` params; its `check` already validates them after the command).
- Other areas are being written in parallel and are empty stubs now: ARCH (walls, doors, rooms, floors… and the model rules such as "a door must fit its wall", "an outline must be simple"), VIEWS, READERS (`elements` view — `src/inspect.rs::elements` is a minimal version now), STRUCTURE. Don't implement their commands or their model rules; if a refusal of the original comes from such a model rule (after the change), list it in your report. Your command must work on project files made by the ORIGINAL.

## How to test
Build input projects with the original: `/workspace/executable run --cmd 'wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0]]}' --script s.txt --save in.bimcraft`. A fixture with one element of most categories is `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft` (made from `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.txt`; `python3 /tmp/edit-agent/dump.py file [ids|categories]` dumps elements). `/tmp/edit-agent/lib.py` has `run(cmds, src=file, exe=...)` → (code, replies, stderr, project dict) and `/tmp/edit-agent/probe.py in.bimcraft 'modify {...}'` prints the reply and the element diff; import/use them, but don't edit files under /tmp/edit-agent. To compare with yours: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd 'modify {…}' --save out.bimcraft` prints SAME or the diff (exit code, stdout, stderr, files). The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels must match exactly.

## Your command: `modify`
Spec (`/workspace/executable commands`): "{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); … A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it". README: "Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is)"; frozen rooms keep their boundary; `params` (project parameters, `modify {id, params: {name: value}}`, a null takes one away); into a field that is an object (a level's `view_range`) they merge; components' `params` merge (a null back to the family's).
What I've seen: one id → the reply is the element as `elements` shows it (use `common::element_view`); several → `{"modified": [ids]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `{"modified": []}`. Unknown fields give serde's text per category, e.g. `modify: element 100014: unknown field `name`, expected one of `type`, `level`, `at`, `angle`, `top_level`, `height`, `base_offset`, `params`, `room_bounding`` — the lists per category (level, wall, door/window, room, floor, ceiling, roof, column/structuralcolumn/footing, beam/stripfooting/pipe…, stair, ramp, railing, shaft, mass, roomseparator, grid, component, line, text, dimension, tag, spot, section/elevation, sheet; find the others: plan views, sheets' viewports, schedules, cameras, filled regions, groups, point clouds, CAD imports, rebar…) come from `modify {"id": X, "zzz": 1}`. Work out for each category: value validation and its error texts (wrong types, ranges, unknown names: types by name or GUID, levels by name or id, styles…), how the value is stored (names → GUIDs, defaults removed or kept, key order when a field is added), what `elements` shows vs what the file holds, merges, nulls, the order of checks over several ids (all or nothing), what `modify` changes beside the field (a wall's `location` change keeps the wall in place by moving its line by the offset between the two location lines, computed from its type's layers; a type change of a wall with a non-centre location line; `height` vs `top_level`; a room's `frozen` keeps its boundary — that needs the room's boundary from the walls, ARCH's room solver: do a private stand-in only if simple, else report), and which follow-on effects happen (doors of a wall whose start/end change: do their offsets change?). Prioritise what tests most likely hit: walls, doors, windows, rooms, levels, floors, columns, components, text, detail lines, dimensions, params, names, types; then the rest.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (message ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: your branch name and commit; per category what matches (tested with cmp.py) and what doesn't; anything in `common.rs` you would want shared; what other areas must provide (model rules the original refuses after a modify, the `elements` view…).

- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` resolves the command, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records an undo step labelled by the catalog label when the project changed (`corner` that changes nothing makes no step, I saw).

"arc": 90}`, `door {"at": [2000,0]}`, `detail_line {"start": [0,0], "end": [4000,0]}`, `detail_line {"points": [[0,0],[1000,0],[1000,1000]], "arcs": [0, 90]}`, circles, ellipses, splines by `control` and by `fit` — see `/workspace/executable commands`). A fixture with one element of most categories is `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft` (`python3 /tmp/edit-agent/dump.py file [ids|categories]` dumps elements). `/tmp/edit-agent/lib.py` has `run(cmds, src=file, exe=...)` → (code, replies, stderr, project dict) and `/tmp/edit-agent/probe.py in.bimcraft 'split {...}'` prints the reply and the element diff; use them, but don't edit files under /tmp/edit-agent. ## Your commands
- `corner` (TR): "{ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep". Seen: `corner {"ids": [100002, 100003]}` on two walls already meeting at (8000,0) replies `{"corner": [8000.0, 0.0]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `corner: `ids` takes two walls`.
- `split` (SL): "{id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`". Seen: on a wall → `{"ids": [100002, 100036]}`; `split {"id": 5}` → `split: 5 is not a wall`; `{}` → `split: `id`, a wall or a detail line, is required`. Arcs walls split into two arcs.

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent; I own `src/readers/`, `src/inspect.rs`, `src/load.rs`, and I'm delegating the LOADER part of my area to you.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/loader-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c ... | ...`). Write Python scripts to files in /tmp/loader-agent/ and run them with `python3 /tmp/loader-agent/script.py` instead (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Your task: the loader — what opening a project file does
Make our program behave exactly like the original whenever it reads a `.bimcraft` project file: `bimcraft-cli info x.bimcraft`, `bimcraft-cli run x.bimcraft --cmd ...` (the open reply printed first), `run --cmd 'open {"path":"x.bimcraft"}'`, `bimcraft-cli convert x.bimcraft y.bimcraft`, and saving after opening (`run x.bimcraft --save y.bimcraft` must write the same file the original writes, modulo GUIDs/uid normalisation). Files: `src/load.rs` (entry point; currently a permissive stub) and a new directory `src/readers/file/` for your modules (add `pub mod file;` to `src/readers/mod.rs` — I may edit that file too, so keep your edit to that one line). You may edit `src/commands/basic.rs`'s `open_project_file` (and `info`) for the open reply / error wording; list any other edit outside your files in your report.

### The codebase (read these first; you're in a git worktree of the repo)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting, `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (command replies print sorted, as serde_json::Value), `kind_name()` (serde's "invalid type" wording: `integer `5``, `string "a"`, `floating point `1.5``, `sequence`, `map`...), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`). `Project::new("en")` builds a new project from `src/templates.rs` (what the original's `new` makes).
- `src/commands/basic.rs`: `open_project_file` (reads, parses, calls `crate::load::load`, then `crate::cloud::check`), `info`. `src/main.rs`: `info`, `convert`, `run` (prints the open reply sorted+compact; errors print `open: <message>` and exit 1).
- Already done by others, to reuse and call from the loader (don't redo): `crate::cloud::load(&mut Project)` and `crate::cloud::left_out(&Value)` (point-cloud sections and elements; it currently runs inside `load`), `crate::styles::phasing::load(&mut Project) -> Result<Vec<String>, String>` (phases, phase_filters, phase_overrides, option_sets: returns the left_out pointers of those sections), `crate::styles::text::normalize` and `crate::styles::text::sync_library` (text and dimension types), and styles' checks (`crate::styles::check`, `crate::check::check` is the whole model check run after commands). grep `src/styles/` and `src/media/` for other `load`/`normalize`/`left_out`-like helpers before writing your own for those sections (line patterns, fill patterns, region types, materials/images, parameters, electrical settings, reinforcement presets...). Read `src/styles/phasing.rs` `load` to see the style used.
- Build: `cargo build --release` in your worktree. Compare tool: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd] -- <args…>` runs both programs in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uid, temp names. Prints SAME or a diff. E.g. `cmp.py -f /tmp/loader-agent/x.bimcraft -- info x.bimcraft`, `cmp.py -f x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --save y.bimcraft`, `cmp.py -f x.bimcraft -- convert x.bimcraft y.bimcraft`.
- Note: `inspect`/`elements` output (and so `info`'s body) is being rewritten by me in parallel — don't chase differences in derived values in `info`'s output; judge the loader by: the error messages (exact), the open reply (`run x.bimcraft` first line), and the file saved after opening (`run x.bimcraft --save y.bimcraft`, `convert`). For a file that opens, the saved file must match the original's byte for byte after normalisation.

### What I've observed so far (verify and extend; don't trust blindly)
- Errors read `open: <path> is not a BIMCraft project: <serde-style message>` for malformed/mistyped files, and `open: <path>: <model check message>` when the file deserialises but breaks a model rule (e.g. `open: m.bimcraft: wall 100002: type `2020bf8b-...` doesn't exist (there are: Exterior - 300mm, Generic - 200mm, Interior - 100mm)`, `wall 100002 points at element 100000 by its id, not its GUID`). `info` prints the same messages. JSON syntax errors carry serde_json's line/column (`EOF while parsing a value at line 2 column 0`; `src/json.rs` already produces these).
- The original seems to parse to a JSON value, then: process `elements` first (a map; `` `abc` isn't an element id``; each element `element 100000: <msg>`; elements are an internally tagged enum `Element` on `category` with 49 variants: `level, grid, wall, floor, ceiling, shaft, mass, door, window, room, roomseparator, dimension, dimension3d, tag, section, elevation, sheet, viewport, column, structuralcolumn, footing, beam, stripfooting, pipe, duct, conduit, cabletray, wire, downconductor, groundconductor, cable, rebar, component, stair, ramp, railing, roof, text, line, region, detailgroup, repeatingdetail, spot, schedule, view3d, planview, link, pointcloud, cadimport` — an unknown one gives `unknown variant `foo`, expected one of `level`, `grid`, ...`; a non-object `invalid type: integer `5`, expected internally tagged enum Element`; `[]` → `missing field `category``), then `library` (must be a map if present), then `format` (``format` must be a whole number``; above 17: `it was saved by a newer BIMCraft (file format 18; this one reads up to 17): update BIMCraft to open it`), then deserialises `struct Model` (36 fields; an array root says `invalid length 1, expected struct Model with 36 elements`, so serde's seq form works too — `[17,"a"]` → `invalid length 2`; scalars → `invalid type: integer `5`, expected struct Model`). `{}` gives `invalid type: null, expected a map` (elements missing). Map keys are visited in SORTED order (serde_json Map is a BTreeMap there): with two bad fields, the alphabetically first one's error is reported. Required: `elements`, `name`, `uid` (u64), `next_id`, `types` (with required `wall`, `floor`, `door`, `window`, `column`, `roof`, `ceiling`, `railing`); missing sections are filled from defaults (a file without `materials` gets the materials its types reference, made grey `[200,200,200]`; without `families`, `{}`), the library is rebuilt/resynced from the sections (entries added/removed: e.g. family-parameter entries go when families go).
- Element fields: `guid` optional (a new one is made), wrong ones: `` `a` is not a GUID (xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx) or an id``, `5 is an id, not a GUID`; number fields `invalid type: string "a", expected f64`; level `view_range` optional (written back as `{"top":null,"cut":1200.0,"bottom":0.0,"depth":0.0}`); wall `height`/`base_offset` default 0.0, door `flip_hand` default false — everything is written back in struct order with defaults filled. Unknown fields are ignored and reported: the open reply becomes `{"left_out":["/elements/100000/foo","/bar","/types/wall/Generic - 200mm/zz"],"left_out_count":3,"name":"Project","path":"p.bimcraft"}` (JSON pointers; elements first, then the rest in sorted visiting order; without any, just `{"name","path"}`). Check whether left_out is capped/truncated when long, and the `~0`/`~1` escaping.

### Method (suggested)
1. Build a corpus of project files with the ORIGINAL covering every element category and every optional field: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' ... --save x.bimcraft` (`/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `--sample` builds a furnished sample house; `run --script file.txt` runs one command per line). Use every option of every command (walls with arc/location/attach_top/attach_base/room_bounding, doors/windows with families, floors with openings/slope/structural, roofs of every kind (extrusion, gables, slopes), rooms frozen, stairs with landings and railings, ramps, components with params, masses with top/lean, dimensions of every kind, tags, text with runs and leaders, spots, sections, elevations, sheets, viewports, schedules, 3D views/cameras, plan views (duplicate_view), detail lines of every shape, filled regions, detail groups, repeating details, links, point clouds, CAD imports, rebar, project parameters (`parameter`), view filters/templates, phases, design options, materials with textures, images (pictures)...).
2. Write a schema explorer (Python) that takes a valid file and for each field of each element/section: deletes it (required → `missing field`; optional → what default gets written back on save, or whether it is omitted), replaces it with values of other JSON types (records serde's `expected ...` wording: `f64`, `a string`, `a boolean`, `u32`, `a sequence`, `struct X`, `a map`, `unknown variant`, `invalid length`...), and adds unknown candidate fields (a field NOT reported in `left_out` is a known optional field — use this to find optional fields that aren't written by default). Record field order as written on save. Then implement the schemas in Rust (a small serde-like layer over `Value`: typed field readers producing the exact messages, defaults, struct-order writers, `left_out` collection).
3. Reference checks done on open (GUIDs that must name existing elements/types/materials/families, id-vs-GUID, the model check's messages), and what the original repairs silently. Library resync rules (ids, which kinds, kept GUIDs).
4. Older formats: try `format` values below 17 with otherwise current files (and absent `format`) and see whether anything is migrated or refused.
5. Damaged copies of real files: truncated JSON, wrong types deep inside types/materials/families/elements, duplicate keys, huge numbers, negative ids, NaN-like values, non-UTF-8 bytes, empty file, BOM, etc. Match the original's messages exactly.

### API to keep
- Keep `pub fn crate::load::load(v: Value) -> Result<Project, String>` working (others call it: insert, link, recover), and add what you need for the open reply's `left_out` (e.g. `pub fn load_report(v: Value) -> Result<(Project, Vec<String>), String>`), wiring `open_project_file` to print `left_out`/`left_out_count`. Keep the "is not a BIMCraft project:" vs model-check message split exact.
- Don't implement inspect/elements/schedules or any modelling command; don't edit other agents' modules (src/arch, src/structure, src/views, src/edit, src/ifc, src/styles, src/media, src/cloud, src/rvt, src/mcp) — call their public functions instead; if one of them is wrong for loading, describe the problem in your report rather than editing it.

## Finish
Commit your work on your worktree branch (commit messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: the branch name and commit; what matches the original and what doesn't (with concrete examples of remaining differences); the public API you added; every edit outside `src/load.rs` and `src/readers/file/`. Be thorough: the hidden tests compare outputs on many inputs, including files the original saved and damaged copies of them.
I'll start by exploring the codebase and environment.

You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I own the EDIT area (`src/edit/`) and delegate to you the command `modify`.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Edit ONLY `src/edit/modify.rs` (you may add new files `src/edit/modify_*.rs` and their `pub mod` lines in `src/edit/mod.rs`). Nothing else in the repo. Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/edit-modify/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell commands it can't verify (loops, heredocs, `cd` outside the worktree, `$(...)` feeding python): write Python scripts to files in /tmp and run them as `python3 /tmp/edit-modify/x.py`.

## Setup
You are in a git worktree. First make sure your HEAD contains commit 89ee1af ("Editing: module skeleton"): `git log --oneline -3`; if not, `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-a76b15059404997b3`. Build with `cargo build --release` (about 15 s).

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical float formatting (`1000.0`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies are printed sorted by main.rs: just return the Value), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order — key order matters, files are compared byte for byte after normalising GUIDs) + `library` (`{kind, name, guid}`: `type:wall`, `material`, `family`, `parameter`, `phase`, …). Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID. `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` resolves the command, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records an undo step labelled by the catalog label (`modify` always makes a step, even unchanged: already wired in `src/edit/mod.rs::always_step`).
- `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers with the original's texts), `src/model.rs` (`resolve_level`, `level_param` with the original's errors for levels by name/id), `src/edit/common.rs` (`ids_param` — `ids`, else `id`, with the original's errors `no element 5` / `"x" is not an element id or GUID` —, `resolve`, `element_view(s, id)` = the element as `elements` shows it, `r3`).
- `src/styles/parameters.rs` (`key_of(pr, name)`: the GUID an element's `params` keys a project parameter by; `check_value`), `src/styles/phasing.rs` (`set_param`/`remove_param` keep `params` where the original puts it; `Phase Created`, `Phase Demolished`, `Design Option` params; its `check` already validates them after the command).
- Other areas are being written in parallel and are empty stubs now: ARCH (walls, doors, rooms, floors… and the model rules such as "a door must fit its wall", "an outline must be simple"), VIEWS, READERS (`elements` view — `src/inspect.rs::elements` is a minimal version now), STRUCTURE. Don't implement their commands or their model rules; if a refusal of the original comes from such a model rule (after the change), list it in your report. Your command must work on project files made by the ORIGINAL.

## How to test
Build input projects with the original: `/workspace/executable run --cmd 'wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0]]}' --script s.txt --save in.bimcraft`. A fixture with one element of most categories is `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft` (made from `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.txt`; `python3 /tmp/edit-agent/dump.py file [ids|categories]` dumps elements). `/tmp/edit-agent/lib.py` has `run(cmds, src=file, exe=...)` → (code, replies, stderr, project dict) and `/tmp/edit-agent/probe.py in.bimcraft 'modify {...}'` prints the reply and the element diff; import/use them, but don't edit files under /tmp/edit-agent. To compare with yours: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd 'modify {…}' --save out.bimcraft` prints SAME or the diff (exit code, stdout, stderr, files). The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels must match exactly.

## Your command: `modify`
Spec (`/workspace/executable commands`): "{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); … A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it". README: "Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is)"; frozen rooms keep their boundary; `params` (project parameters, `modify {id, params: {name: value}}`, a null takes one away); into a field that is an object (a level's `view_range`) they merge; components' `params` merge (a null back to the family's).
What I've seen: one id → the reply is the element as `elements` shows it (use `common::element_view`); several → `{"modified": [ids]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `{"modified": []}`. Unknown fields give serde's text per category, e.g. `modify: element 100014: unknown field `name`, expected one of `type`, `level`, `at`, `angle`, `top_level`, `height`, `base_offset`, `params`, `room_bounding`` — the lists per category (level, wall, door/window, room, floor, ceiling, roof, column/structuralcolumn/footing, beam/stripfooting/pipe…, stair, ramp, railing, shaft, mass, roomseparator, grid, component, line, text, dimension, tag, spot, section/elevation, sheet; find the others: plan views, sheets' viewports, schedules, cameras, filled regions, groups, point clouds, CAD imports, rebar…) come from `modify {"id": X, "zzz": 1}`. Work out for each category: value validation and its error texts (wrong types, ranges, unknown names: types by name or GUID, levels by name or id, styles…), how the value is stored (names → GUIDs, defaults removed or kept, key order when a field is added), what `elements` shows vs what the file holds, merges, nulls, the order of checks over several ids (all or nothing), what `modify` changes beside the field (a wall's `location` change keeps the wall in place by moving its line by the offset between the two location lines, computed from its type's layers; a type change of a wall with a non-centre location line; `height` vs `top_level`; a room's `frozen` keeps its boundary — that needs the room's boundary from the walls, ARCH's room solver: do a private stand-in only if simple, else report), and which follow-on effects happen (doors of a wall whose start/end change: do their offsets change?). Prioritise what tests most likely hit: walls, doors, windows, rooms, levels, floors, columns, components, text, detail lines, dimensions, params, names, types; then the rest.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (message ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: your branch name and commit; per category what matches (tested with cmp.py) and what doesn't; anything in `common.rs` you would want shared; what other areas must provide (model rules the original refuses after a modify, the `elements` view…).

189:file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is
261:| Revit files (read only; the command line and the desktop) | A Revit `.rvt` or `.rfa` file of release 2015 to 2027 (checked on Autodesk's sample projects of 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026, and the Snowdon Towers files) is read by a reader of its own, `crates/rvt`, ported in part from [rvt-rs](https://github.com/DrunkOnJava/rvt-rs) and fenced by [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md). `info` shows its release, build and document GUID, the last save (the saver's name when worksharing records it, and the path it was saved to; shown by `info`, never written into a project or an IFC file), the title, the levels with their names and elevations, and the number of elements in each `BuiltInCategory`, how many of them are placed instances. `run x.rvt`, `convert x.rvt out.ifc` and the MCP server's `open` import the file as a new project: its levels, straight and curved walls with their compound layers and materials (the exterior on the side the file's flip says), floors and ceilings from their sketches (holes and separate loops included), doors and windows in the walls that hold them, columns, rooms with their numbers and names, and roofs (by footprint, those that rise coming in level, and ones by extrusion whose profile is straight lines in a plane square to an axis and whose box the profile and the type's thickness reproduce to a millimetre), converted from feet to millimetres and checked by `Model::check`. Only what a record says is read, and the reply says what is not. Where the record's own box gives a stand-in (a curtain wall as the plane of its box, a sloped or stepped floor, ceiling or roof level at the bottom of its box, a sketch that closes nothing as the footprint of its box, a column as the rectangle of its box) the element comes in as that stand-in and a note in `skipped` says what was not read of it; that is an approximation, and it is not counted as read whole. Anything else the reader cannot decode (a roof by extrusion that is not a straight-line profile, a skylight, a room no walls enclose, stairs, groups, families) is left out and listed in the reply's `skipped` as `N kinds left out, why`. In the desktop, File > Open, the system's open event (Finder, Open With) and a file named on the command line take a `.rvt`: the window stays alive while a box says "Opening a Revit file", asks about unsaved changes first as for any file, and the project that comes in is new and unsaved (Save asks for a `.bimcraft` name; nothing is written back to the `.rvt`, and it is not in File > Open Recent). The status box says how many elements came in and how many were left out, and File > Revit import report lists what came in by category and the notes of what was left out, grouped by cause with their ids. A build without the reader has no `.rvt` option and says why. Joins are BIMCraft's own, and a door's swing is not read. Checked against rvt-rs's own IFC export of the same files, the imported walls, floors, ceilings, openings, columns and roofs agree to a fraction of a millimetre (walls differ where a join is a butt there and a mitre here). A file is read under limits (its size, its streams, what each inflates to) and a damaged or hostile one is an error that says what is wrong. Nothing is taken from inside the file (families, templates, icons) for BIMCraft's own content. Builds that include the reader are Apache-2.0 (see License); `--no-default-features` leaves it out |
263:| Files | `.bimcraft` projects (JSON, file format 12: every save is 12, so an earlier build refuses even a plain project saved by this one, saying it is from a newer BIMCraft); IFC4 export with storeys, walls swept up from their plan outline (mitred where they join, an arc in short chords) or, attached to a roof, as closed shells, walls, floors, roofs and ceilings with their material layer sets (each material with its colour), slabs (sloped ones as closed shells), ceilings as coverings, spaces and columns, walls, slabs, doors and windows with their `Qto_*BaseQuantities` (a wall's side area and volume gross and less its openings, a slab's area and volume less its openings), beams (`IfcBeam`), footings (`IfcFooting`), pipes (`IfcPipeSegment`), conduits, cable trays and wires (`IfcCableCarrierSegment`, `IfcCableSegment`) and structural columns and floors, each along its own axis and, if structural, with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, the runs of a system assigned to an `IfcSystem` of its name, stairs and ramps as their flights, landings and railings (each railing with its rail's top line as its axis), roofs as closed shells of flat faces (hip, gable, shed or flat), openings that cut the walls and hold the doors and windows, an opening for each slab, ceiling and roof a shaft passes through, masses as building element proxies of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set), and components as furniture, sanitary or waste terminals, pipe fittings, valves, distribution boards, outlets, switching devices, communications appliances, light fixtures or proxies, named `Family:Type` as Revit names them, each form a closed face set in its material's colour, each element's values of the project parameters in a `Project Parameters` property set (dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations belong to views, and stay out of it), and each element's phase and design option in a `BIMCraft_Phasing` property set: its `Phase Created` is always named in it, the first phase too (said to be implied, for another tool to read; a door or window says only what it holds, as one with no phase follows its wall), `Phase Demolished` and `Design Option` where it holds them, and the project's phases in order, with the phase filters, overrides and option sets it changed, in one on the project, and, as IFC says it, its `Status` in its `Pset_*Common` (`EXISTING`, `DEMOLISH`, `NEW` or `TEMPORARY`, for another tool to filter the work by); a project that uses none of it writes none |

results.content: 106: 153: 177: 202:- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type 229:| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do | 236:| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category | 246:| Editing | Modify any field, of one element or many in one step (a wall put on another location line stays where it is); move, copy, rotate and mirror, with the walls joined to them stretching to stay joined and doors and windows going with their walls (a mirrored wall runs back the other way, its exterior mirrored); trim or extend two walls to a corner; split a wall, an arc into two arcs; flip walls; delete (a wall takes its doors and windows with it, and they their tags; a roof or floor walls are attached to lets them go); undo and redo | 256:| Project parameters | Values of your own that each element of their categories holds (text, numbers, lengths, yes or no, unset a no), as Revit's project parameters are: set in Properties or with `modify`, shown, filtered and sorted in schedules and read by their formulas, and written to IFC in a `Project Parameters` property set and read back from it; renamed, schedules follow; taken off a category, its elements and schedules lose them | 265:| Desktop | Revit's layout: ribbon tabs with a contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Type Properties, the Project Browser and views in tabs; a plan and a reflected ceiling plan per level that pan and zoom, sections and elevations, a 3D view that orbits, and sheets; tools for walls (straight or arcs, on the location line picked), doors, windows, columns, roofs by footprint (and Gable Edge, to stand a roof's edge upright) and by extrusion, dormers, floors (and a floor's slope arrow), ceilings, shaft openings, sketch mode (Edit Boundary on a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft, and Boundary Line or Sketch Ceiling for a new one: lines, rectangles, arcs and Pick Walls, sketch lines with ids of their own picked by click or box and moved by their grips, Finish Edit Mode saying what's wrong and marking the lines; in the 3D view, Edit Boundary sketches on the element's own plane, and Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft sketch on the view's Work Plane: a level from the list, a surface or three points picked on the model (snapping to corners), each with an offset, at any angle; walls, beams and braces, columns and structural columns, footings, pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays and components draw in the 3D view on the level face under the cursor, snapping as a plan does, a run climbing from one face to another; they need it horizontal), masses (and floors, walls and roofs from them), stairs and ramps (run by run, turning at landings), railings, rooms, levels, grids, dimensions (aligned, angular, radial), spot elevations, text, detail lines, filled and masking regions, tags, sections and elevations; Flip, Attach Top/Base and Detach Top/Base for walls; a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's layers in Type Properties, and the project's materials in Manage > Materials; project parameters in Manage > Project Parameters, and their values in Properties; schedules from View > Schedules, their fields, filters, sorting and totals in Schedule Properties; the Component tool, families and their types in the Type Selector, the Project Browser and Type Properties, a component's own parameters in Properties, and Load Family; Crop View with grips to drag a crop region's edges, and the view range in Properties; project units, metric or feet and inches; Revit's selection (click, Ctrl, Shift, Tab, window and crossing boxes); dragging and the Modify panel (Align, Offset, Mirror, Split, Move, Copy, Rotate, Trim/Extend to Corner) and its Phasing panel (Demolish); Paint and Remove Paint on its Geometry panel, for the 3D view; typed lengths and temporary dimensions; undo and redo; open, save and export; a light and a dark theme; English, Portuguese or Spanish. The Manage tab has the Materials window (with textures and pictures), the Favorites, Object Styles, Annotation Settings (Line Weights, Line Styles, Line Patterns and Fill Patterns, a fill pattern simple or made of detail lines picked in a plan and the tile between two corners), and the Family Editor (New Family, Edit Family) | 338:is Revit's, so it should feel familiar: the Quick Access Toolbar; the ribbon's File, Architecture, Annotate, View and Modify 339:tabs, with a green contextual tab (Modify | Place Wall, Modify | Walls) for the tool or the selection; the Options Bar; 353:| Draw walls | Wall (WA), click points: each click builds a wall from the point before, one undo step each; Enter or Esc ends the chain, and a click back on its start closes it. Ends snap to wall ends and location lines; Shift keeps a segment square. The Draw panel draws a Line, or a Start-End-Radius Arc: its start, its end, then a point it passes through. The Options Bar sets the height (up to a level, or unconnected), the Location Line (the line of the wall you click along) and Chain. A wall's exterior is to your left as you go, so draw clockwise for walls that face out | 354:| Flip, attach walls | Select walls, and Modify \| Walls has Flip (or Space) to turn their exterior side round about their location line, Attach Top/Base to pick a roof or a floor for their tops (or, as the Options Bar says, their bases) to follow, and Detach Top/Base. Properties shows their Location Line (pick another and the wall stays where it is) and whether they're attached | 365:| Roof the building | Roof, in a plan: click inside the walls, and a roof goes on the level above, over their outline and past their faces, whatever its shape, and open over a courtyard: a loop of walls standing free inside the others, with no room in it; its hips and valleys show before you click. The Options Bar sets the slope (0° for a flat roof), the overhang, and gable ends for a rectangle. You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I own the EDIT area (`src/edit/`) and delegate to you the commands `corner`, `split` and `fillet`.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Edit ONLY `src/edit/corner.rs`, `src/edit/split.rs`, `src/edit/fillet.rs` (you may add files `src/edit/curves.rs` or `src/edit/ops_*.rs` for shared geometry, with their `pub mod` lines in `src/edit/mod.rs`). Nothing else in the repo. Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/edit-ops/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell commands it can't verify (loops, heredocs, `cd` outside the worktree, `$(...)` feeding python): write Python scripts to files in /tmp and run them as `python3 /tmp/edit-ops/x.py`.

## Setup
You are in a git worktree. First make sure your HEAD contains commit 89ee1af ("Editing: module skeleton"): `git log --oneline -3`; if not, `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-a76b15059404997b3`. Build with `cargo build --release` (about 15 s).

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical float formatting (`1000.0`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies are printed sorted by main.rs: just return the Value), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order — key order matters, files are compared byte for byte after normalising GUIDs) + `library` (`{kind, name, guid}`); `alloc_id()` for new element ids; `find_guid`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID (a door's `host` is its wall's GUID, a dimension's `refs[].id`, a tag's `host`, a line's `view` and `style`).
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` resolves the command, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records an undo step labelled by the catalog label when the project changed (`corner` that changes nothing makes no step, I saw).
- `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers with the original's texts: `` `at` [x, y] is required``, ``must be a point [x, y] in mm, got …``), `src/edit/common.rs` (`ids_param` — `ids`, else `id`, with the original's errors —, `resolve`, `r3` rounding to 0.001 mm, which the original does on computed coordinates — check where), `src/styles/phasing.rs` (`stamp_copy(pr, s.now_phase, s.now_option, &mut e)`: what a new element made from another gets of the session's phase/option — find out whether a split's new part gets it).
- Other areas are being written in parallel and are empty stubs now: ARCH (walls, doors, rooms…, and model rules such as "a door must fit its wall"), VIEWS (detail lines and their own commands offset/trim_extend/join_polyline/explode/vertex/convert_spline, dimensions, tags), READERS. Don't implement their commands or their model rules; if a refusal of the original comes from such a model rule (after the change), list it in your report. Your commands must work on project files made by the ORIGINAL.

## How to test
Build input projects with the original: `/workspace/executable run --script s.txt --save in.bimcraft` (e.g. `wall {"points": [[0,0],[8000,0],[8000,6000]]}`, `wall {... "arc": 90}`, `door {"at": [2000,0]}`, `detail_line {"start": [0,0], "end": [4000,0]}`, `detail_line {"points": [[0,0],[1000,0],[1000,1000]], "arcs": [0, 90]}`, circles, ellipses, splines by `control` and by `fit` — see `/workspace/executable commands`). A fixture with one element of most categories is `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft` (`python3 /tmp/edit-agent/dump.py file [ids|categories]` dumps elements). `/tmp/edit-agent/lib.py` has `run(cmds, src=file, exe=...)` → (code, replies, stderr, project dict) and `/tmp/edit-agent/probe.py in.bimcraft 'split {...}'` prints the reply and the element diff; use them, but don't edit files under /tmp/edit-agent. To compare with yours: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd 'split {…}' --save out.bimcraft` prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels must match exactly.

## Your commands
- `corner` (TR): "{ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep". Seen: `corner {"ids": [100002, 100003]}` on two walls already meeting at (8000,0) replies `{"corner": [8000.0, 0.0]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `corner: `ids` takes two walls`.
- `split` (SL): "{id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`". Seen: on a wall → `{"ids": [100002, 100036]}`; `split {"id": 5}` → `split: 5 is not a wall`; `{}` → `split: `id`, a wall or a detail line, is required`. Arcs walls split into two arcs.
- `fillet` (FL): "{ids: [a, b], radius} rounds the corner where two straight detail lines, or two straight walls, meet (or would, extended) with an arc of `radius` mm, in the first's line style or of the first's type: each is cut back to the arc (a wall's doors and windows stay where they stand in plan, as in `corner`, and only their offset along the wall changes)". Seen: two walls → `{"id": 100036, "ids": [100002, 100003]}`; `{"ids": []}` → `fillet: `ids` is two detail lines`.
For each: every error and the order of checks (wrong categories, same id twice, parallel lines, lines of different views, walls on different levels, `at` off the element, radius too big…), what happens to the doors and windows of a wall (offsets recomputed so they stand where they stood in plan; a door on the part split off moves to the new wall, its `host` changing), to other walls joined at the trimmed/extended ends (walls whose end is within 1 mm of another wall's end or line count as joined — find out whether corner/split/fillet stretch them), to dimensions and tags referring to a split wall or line, to the new element's fields (a copy of the original's fields, key order, GUID, `stamp_copy`?), the rounding of the results (r3?), arcs (walls with `arc`, detail lines with `through`/`arc`/`arcs`/`centre`…), and undo labels (`Trim/Extend to Corner`, `Split`, `Fillet Arc`; whether an unchanged result makes a step). Prioritise walls and straight detail lines; then arcs; then polylines, circles, ellipses and splines.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (message ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: your branch name and commit; per command what matches (tested with cmp.py) and what doesn't; what other areas must provide (model rules behind refusals…).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""q.py [-x exe] [-f in.bimcraft] [-s] cmd1 cmd2 ... : run the original on a script (one command per arg);
prints replies and with -s the final elements (walls/doors/windows/lines etc compactly)."""
import json, sys, subprocess, tempfile, shutil, os
exe = '/workspace/executable'
a = sys.argv[1:]
src = None
show = False
cats = None
while a and a[0].startswith('-'):
    if a[0] == '-x': exe = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': src = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-s': show = True; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-c': cats = a[1].split(','); show = True; a = a[2:]
    else: break
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='q')
args = [exe, 'run']
if src:
    shutil.copy(src, os.path.join(d, 'in.bimcraft'))
    args.append('in.bimcraft')
script = '\n'.join(a) + '\n'
open(os.path.join(d, 's.txt'), 'w').write(script)
args += ['--script', 's.txt', '--save', 'out.bimcraft']
p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True)
print('code', p.returncode)
for l in p.stdout.splitlines():
    if l.startswith('{"format":"bimcraft"'): continue
    print('>', l[:3000])
if p.stderr:
    print('ERR', p.stderr.strip()[:3000])
if show and os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, 'out.bimcraft')):
    B = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, 'out.bimcraft')))
    for k, v in B['elements'].items():
        c = v.get('category')
        if cats and c not in cats: continue
        if not cats and c in ('level',): continue
        v = dict(v); v.pop('guid', None)
        for f in ('level', 'top_level', 'type', 'host', 'view', 'style'):
            if f in v and isinstance(v[f], str) and len(v[f]) == 36: v[f] = '<g>'
        print(k, json.dumps(v, ensure_ascii=False)[:1500])
shutil.rmtree(d)
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-agent')
from lib import *
for g in [1.0, 1.001, 1.2, 1.5, 1.9]:
    c, r, e, p = run(['wall {"points": [[0,0],[4000,0]]}', 'wall {"points": [[%r,0],[4000,3000]]}' % (4000 + g), 'move {"ids": [100002], "by": [0, 1000]}'])
    print('gap', g, e)
    show(p, 'wall', ['start', 'end'])

44:{boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline
53:## edit_shape | Modify Sub Elements
78:{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen
134:{text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's
176:{name, kind?: text|number|length|yesno, categories?: [wall|floor|ceiling|roof|door|window|room|column|component|stair|ramp|railing|mass, …], rename?, delete?: true} a project parameter, as Revit's Manage > Project Parameters makes one: a value of its kind each element of its categories may have of its own, set with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}` (lengths in mm, yes or no as true or false). Off a category, that category's elements lose their values of it; deleted, every element does; renamed, they follow it. `inspect` lists them
182:{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)
185:## modify | Modify
238:{sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)
292:{name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides
296:{set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)

{set: arei, names?: en|nl|fr} loads a set of families that are plan symbols and nothing else, each of one type `Standard` with no forms: `arei` is the Belgian AREI/RGIE's graphical symbols (Table 2.23: switches, sockets, light points, appliances, sources, domotics, protection), 76 families, switches in the switch category, sockets in outlet, luminaires in lighting and the rest generic. `names` is the language of their names, English, Dutch or French as the source prints them; as given none, French in a French project and English otherwise. A family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing; the reply lists `loaded` and `kept`. Place them as components
## component | Component
{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)
## flip | Flip
{ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are
## modify | Modify
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it
## match_properties | Match Properties
{from: id, ids: [id,…]} gives the elements in `ids` the type of `from` (and, for components, its family), as Revit's Match Properties does; only elements of `from`'s category take it, the rest come back in `skipped`. Returns {modified, skipped}
## align | Align
{id, reference: [[x,y],[x,y]], line: [[x,y],[x,y]], lock?: true, to?: id} aligns an element's picked line with a reference in plan: turns by the smaller angle about the picked line's midpoint, then moves it onto the reference, keeping its size. Doors and windows slide along their host wall; they cannot turn independently. With `lock`, Revit's padlock: the line and the reference (of element `to`, else whatever has a line along it) are kept on one line after every command, as a locked dimension keeps its length; refused when that can't hold with the other locks. Returns {aligned, angle, by, line} (the picked line where it went), and the lock's id
## dimension_value | Dimension Value
{id, value, segment?} types a length into an aligned or a linear dimension's segment (the first unless told), as a click on its number does: what the segment ends at (its second reference, as the dimension runs west to east or south to north) moves along the dimension so the segment is `value` mm; a locked segment is locked at it, and the other locks hold, or it is refused. Returns {id, moved, by}
## move | Move
{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall moves
## copy | Copy

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.

import os
D = '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-ae7e467313951842e/src/views/'
mods = {
    'sections': ('Sections and elevations: `section`, `elevation` (the four building elevations, `facing`, `at`).', True, True, False),
    'sheets': ('Sheets and what is placed on them: `sheet`, `place` (viewports; schedules and the 3D view come to be as first placed).', True, True, False),
    'plans': ('Plans: `crop`, `duplicate_view` (plan views: duplicate, detailing, dependent).', True, True, False),
    'view3d': ('3D views: `section_box`, `perspective`, `graphic_display_options`, `camera`, `work_plane`.', True, True, False),
    'graphics': ("A view's graphics: `graphics` (Visibility/Graphics), `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`.", True, False, False),
    'filters': ('View filters: `filter`.', True, False, True),
    'templates': ('View templates: `template`.', True, False, True),
    'dims': ('Dimensions: `dimension` (aligned, linear, angular, radial, diameter, arc length).', True, True, False),
    'dims3d': ('Dimensions in a 3D view: `dimension_3d`.', True, True, False),
    'constraints': ("A dimension's constraints, text and value: `dimension_constraint`, `dimension_text`, `dimension_value`.", True, False, False),
    'notes': ('Text notes: `text`.', True, True, False),
    'tags': ('Tags: `tag`.', True, True, False),
    'spots': ('Spot elevations and slopes: `spot`, `spot_slope`.', True, True, False),
    'linework': ('Linework: `linework` (an edge of an element drawn in a line style in one plan).', True, False, False),
    'curves': ("A detail line's curve: polylines with arcs, circles, ellipses, splines; points drawn, bounds, ends, moves.", False, False, False),
    'lines': ('Detail lines: `detail_line` (lines, polylines with arcs, circles, ellipses, splines, insulation, clouds).', True, True, False),
    'lineedit': ('Editing detail lines: `join_polyline`, `explode`, `vertex`, `convert_spline`, `offset`, `trim_extend`.', True, False, False),
    'regions': ('Filled regions: `filled_region`.', True, True, False),
    'groups': ('Detail groups: `create_group`, `detail_group`, `repeating_detail`, `ungroup`, `group_type`.', True, True, True),
    'makepat': ('Fill patterns made of detail lines: `make_fill_pattern`.', True, False, False),
}
for m, (doc, cmd, ev, insp) in mods.items():
    p = D + m + '.rs'
    if os.path.exists(p):
        continue
    out = ['//! ' + doc, '']
    out.append('#![allow(unused_imports)]')
    out.append('')
    out.append('use super::common::*;')
    out.append('use crate::json::Value;')
    out.append('use crate::project::Project;')
    out.append('use crate::session::Session;')
    out.append('')
    if cmd:
        out += ['/// Runs the commands of this part.',
                'pub fn run(s: &mut Session, cid: &str, p: &Value) -> R<Value> {',
                '    let _ = (s, p);',
                '    Err(format!("{}: not supported here", cid))',
                '}', '',
                '/// The model rules of this part, checked after every command.',
                'pub fn check(pr: &Project) -> R<()> {',
                '    let _ = pr;',
                '    Ok(())',
                '}', '']

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I own the EDIT area (`src/edit/`) and delegate to you the commands `insert`, `link`, `reload`, `autosave` and `recover`.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only.
- Edit ONLY `src/edit/insert.rs`, `src/edit/link.rs`, `src/edit/autosave.rs` (you may add files `src/edit/insert_*.rs` with their `pub mod` lines in `src/edit/mod.rs`, and add your commands to `always_step` / your module's `check` call there). Nothing else in the repo; if you need a hook elsewhere (e.g. the loader reading links when a project opens), describe it precisely in your report instead. Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/edit-files/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell commands it can't verify (loops, heredocs, `cd` outside the worktree, `$(...)` feeding python): write Python scripts to files in /tmp and run them as `python3 /tmp/edit-files/x.py`.

## Setup
You are in a git worktree. First make sure your HEAD contains commit 89ee1af ("Editing: module skeleton"): `git log --oneline -3`; if not, `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-a76b15059404997b3`. Build with `cargo build --release` (about 15 s).

## The codebase (read the relevant parts first)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`, `insert_sorted`), serde_json-identical parse errors and float formatting (`1000.0`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies are printed sorted by main.rs: just return the Value), `jobj!{}`.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`, `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field order — key order matters, files are compared byte for byte after normalising GUIDs) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`; ids count down from 999999 via `alloc_lib_id`, never reused in a session); `alloc_id()` for element ids; `find_guid`, `lib_find`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name`. Elements reference each other and library entries by GUID; library parts (a type's layers, a family's forms) have ids/GUIDs too.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` resolves the command, snapshots, runs, runs `crate::check::check`, rolls back on error, records an undo step labelled by the catalog label when the project changed (`autosave` is a read-only command; `recover` is a history command that starts a new history: see `commands::changes_model`/`is_history_cmd`).
- `src/commands/basic.rs` (`open_project_file`, `open_path`, `cmd_save`, `write_atomic` — tempfile-and-rename as the original writes), `src/load.rs` (the loader, READERS' area: `crate::load::load(Value) -> Result<Project, String>`), `src/commands/params.rs` (param readers with the original's texts), `src/edit/common.rs` (`ids_param`, `resolve`, `strict_guid`).
- Other areas, written in parallel, are mostly empty stubs: ARCH, STRUCTURE, VIEWS, READERS (`elements`, the loader), IFC-IMPORT (`src/ifc/import.rs`: `.ifc` input for insert/link — call what exists and report what you need from them). `src/styles/` (done: line styles/patterns, fill patterns, region types, text/dimension types, parameters, phasing) and `src/media/` (materials, pictures, families' favorites) are done: reuse their helpers for library sections. Your commands must work on project files made by the ORIGINAL.

## How to test
Build projects with the original: `/workspace/executable run --script s.txt --save a.bimcraft` (walls, doors, rooms, floors, components, detail lines, dimensions, materials, types, families, parameters, views…; `/workspace/executable commands` lists every command). A fixture with one element of most categories is `/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft` (`python3 /tmp/edit-agent/dump.py file` dumps elements). `/tmp/edit-agent/lib.py` has `run(cmds, src=file, files=[...], exe=...)` → (code, replies, stderr, project dict); use it, don't edit files under /tmp/edit-agent. To compare with yours: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f a.bimcraft -f b.bimcraft -- run a.bimcraft --cmd 'insert {"path": "b.bimcraft"}' --save out.bimcraft` (it copies the -f files into fresh temp dirs, runs both, and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written, GUIDs normalised by first appearance). The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: replies, error texts, saved files and undo labels must match exactly.

## Your commands (specs from `/workspace/executable commands`)
- `insert` (Insert from File): "{path, ids?: [id, …]} elements of another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) brought into this one: those `ids` names (their ids there), else all of them, and what they point at that this project hasn't (a level they stand on is this project's of the same name, where it has one). Each keeps its id unless this project has that id, and its GUID unless this project has that GUID: then it's a copy, with a GUID of its own (the same file inserted into itself is copied whole). What they point at among themselves follows them. A name or a number taken here gets ` 2`, ` 3`…; types, families, materials and parameters this project hasn't come by name, and so do the line styles (with their line patterns), fill patterns, filled region types and detail groups a detail line, a filled region or a group uses. Returns `ids` {there: here}, `copies`, `library`, `left_out`". README: the library is matched by GUID, then by name.
- `link` (LK): "{path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited … It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`". Find how a link is stored (an element? a `links` top-level section — see `TOP_ORDER`), what `elements`/`inspect` show of it, what a missing/broken file gives, relative paths (relative to the project's file, `s.path`), what opening a project with links prints/does (a hook in the loader/open: describe it).
- `reload`: "{id?} read the file of the link `id`, or of every link, again … Returns `reloaded` (the names) and `failed` ({name, error})". Seen: `reload {}` → `{"failed": [], "reloaded": []}`; `reload {"id": 5}` → `reload: element 5 is not a link`.
- `autosave`: "{path} atomically write a recovery snapshot, keeping the project path and undo history". Seen: `{}` → `autosave: `path` is required`.
- `recover` (Recover Autosave): "{path, project?} open and validate a recovery snapshot; Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it". Seen: `{}` → `open: `path` is required` (note the `open:` prefix).
For each: every error and the order of checks, the replies, what is written (byte for byte: autosave's file vs save's), undo/history effects (`inspect`'s `history`), ids/GUID clashes, ` 2` suffixes for names and numbers (levels, rooms' numbers, marks, sheets, views…), what is `left_out` and why, inserting the same file into itself, and `ids` given. Prioritise autosave/recover and insert of .bimcraft files, then link/reload.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (message ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: your branch name and commit; per command what matches (tested with cmp.py) and what doesn't; hooks needed outside src/edit (exactly where and what); what other areas must provide.

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.
