An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.

## Commands

| Command | Shortcut | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `autosave` | | `path`: atomically write a native recovery snapshot without changing the project path or undo history |
| `recover` | | `path`, `project?`: validate and open a recovery snapshot; later Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it |
| `wall` | WA | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `top_offset?` (mm above `top_level`, negative below it), `height?`, `base_offset?`, `arc?` (degrees each turns, counter-clockwise), `location?` (`centre`, `core-centre`, `exterior-finish`, `interior-finish`, `exterior-core`, `interior-core`), `attach_top?`, `attach_base?` (a roof or a floor), `room_bounding?` (false: rooms run past it, as Revit's Room Bounding off; `modify` turns it on and off) |
| `door` | DR | `at`, or `wall` and `offset?`; `type?`, `family?` (a door family's `type`, its first by default), `mark?`, `flip_facing?`, `flip_hand?` |
| `window` | WN | as `door`, plus `sill?` (a family's `Sill Height` by default) |
| `sketch` | | `lines` ([[[x, y], [x, y]], …]; an arc [[x, y], [x, y], [x, y]], its ends then a point it passes through): solves a sketch without making anything, the loops it closes into (outlines and their holes) and their area, or every problem with the lines it's about: ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line that crosses itself too), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc or a circle is cut into chords): past 200,000 of them it is refused at once |
| `edit_boundary` | | `id` (a floor, a ceiling, a roof by footprint or a shaft), `sketch?`: its outline and holes redrawn as one sketch, a line sent back with its `id` keeping it; without `sketch`, the lines it has now, each with its id once it has one |
| `floor` | | `boundary?` (else the walls of the level) or `sketch?` (lines, in any order, solved into its outline and openings), `openings?` (holes in it, inside it and apart; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it), `level?`, `type?`, `offset?` (its top above the level), `slope?` (degrees) and `arrow?` (its tail and head: it rises from the tail toward the head), `structural?` (a floor that carries load, as Revit's Floor: Structural). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof`, `shaft`, `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` hold to it too, saying which edges); a saved file that has one still opens. Its model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (set with `modify`) |
| `ceiling` | | `point` (in a room: out to its walls' faces, open round the walls standing free inside it), `boundary` or `sketch`, `openings?` (holes in it, inside it and apart), `level?`, `type?`, `offset?` (its underside above the level, 2600) |
| `shaft` | | `boundary` or `sketch`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `height?`, `base_offset?`: a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs on its way |
| `room` | RM | `point`, `name?`, `number?`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `limit_offset?`, `base_offset?`, `frozen?` (keeps its boundary: it isn't found from the walls again) |
| `room_separator` | | `points` [[x, y], …], `level?`, `closed?`: room separation lines, one per segment, that bound rooms where there is no wall (an open plan) and nothing else |
| `column` | CL | `at`, `type?`, `angle?`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `height?`, `base_offset?` |
| `structural_column` | CL | as `column`, in its own category and types |
| `reinforcement_preset` | | `name?`, `kind?` (beam, column, footing, floor), `params?` (what `reinforce` takes, but the host), `rename?`, `delete?`: a named set of parameters, kept in the project; no `name` lists them |
| `voltage` | | `name?`, `nominal?` (volts), `min?`, `max?` (the band a device may read within; 10 per cent either way unless given), `rename?`, `delete?`: a voltage of the electrical settings; one a distribution system supplies cannot be deleted; no `name` lists them |
| `distribution_system` | | `name?`, `phases?` (1, 2, 3), `wires?` (the line conductors and the neutral), `l_l?`, `l_n?`, `l_g?` (names of voltages; "" takes one away), `ground?` (TN-S, TN-C, TN-C-S, TT, IT), `rename?`, `delete?`: a distribution system of the electrical settings; a voltage the project lacks is refused; no `name` lists them |
| `wire_type` | | `name?`, `material?` (copper, aluminium), `temperature?` (°C), `insulation?`, `note?`, `sizes?` (`[{section, ampacity, label?}]`, mm² and amperes, which replaces the table), `rename?`, `delete?`: a wire type of the electrical settings; no `name` lists them |
| `reinforce` | | `host` (a beam, a column, a footing or a floor) or `hosts` (a list), `preset?`, `cover?`, `grade?`, `grade_stirrup?`, `clearance?`, and by host: `bottom`, `top`, `stirrup`, `skin`, `anchor` (beam), `bars`, `stirrup`, `ties`, `anchor` (column), `mesh` (footing), `bottom`, `top` (floor), `check?`, `aggressiveness?`, `fck?`: bars by rules, as `rebar` elements on layers, and notes from the check |
| `footing` | FI | `at`, `type?`, `thickness?` (400), `offset?` (its top over the level, 0), `angle?`, `level?`: an isolated footing |
| `beam` | BM | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (the height of its `justify` line over the level at its start, 0), `end_offset?` (at its end, for one segment: it slopes), `justify?` (`top`, `centre`, `bottom`), `system?`: a beam for each segment |
| `pipe` | PI | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (the height of its `justify` line over the level at its start, 0), `end_offset?` (at its end, for one segment: it falls or rises, or stands if the two points are one), `justify?` (`centre` by default), `system?`: a pipe for each segment |
| `conduit` | CN | as `pipe`: a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment, round |
| `cable_tray` | CT | as `pipe`, its type a `width` across by a `depth` deep: a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment |
| `wire` | EW | as `pipe`: a wire (condutor) for each segment, round; its `system` the circuit |
| `down_conductor` | DC | as `pipe`: a down conductor (condutor de descida) for each segment; the same point twice and two heights stand it upright |
| `ground_conductor` | GC | as `pipe`: an earthing conductor (the ring or mesh), usually under the level (a negative `offset`) |
| `cabling` | CB | as `pipe`: structured cabling for each segment, round; its `system` the link or the network |
| `strip_footing` | FW | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `offset?` (its top over the level, 0), `system?`: a footing under a wall for each segment |
| `stair` | | `start`, `end?` or `angle?` (the way it climbs), `level?`, `top_level?`, `height?`, `width?`, `riser?` (the most each riser may rise), `tread?`, `landings?` ([{`at`, `turn`}]: after `at` risers, the next run going on (0), turned left or right (90, -90), or back beside it (180, -180)), `railings?` |
| `ramp` | | `start`, `end?` or `angle?`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `height?`, `width?`, `slope?` (percent, 8.33), `landings?` (`at` mm up), `railings?` |
| `railing` | | `host` (a stair or a ramp) and `side?` (`left` or `right`; both by default), or `path`, `level?`, `base_offset?`; `type?` |
| `roof` | | `level?` (the one above the lowest), `offset?`, `boundary?` (else the walls of the level below) or `sketch?` (its outline and courtyards), `courtyards?` (holes in it with eaves of their own, inside it and apart; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it), `overhang?`, `slope?` (0 is flat), `slopes?` (a slope in degrees for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for the roof's `slope`), `gables?` (edges left upright, edge i from point i to the next, a courtyard's numbered on after the boundary's), `gable?` (a rectangle's short ends), `extrusion?` (`line`, `profile` of `[along, up]` points, `from?`, `to`: swept across to the line's left), `openings?`, `join?` (a roof it ends against), `type?` |
| `dormer` | | `host` (a roof), `at` (on its slope: the front wall's middle), `width?`, `height?` (over the roof at the front), `slope?`, `window?` (a window type), `type?` (its walls') |
| `dimension` | DI | `refs` (each `{id, face?, point?}`: a wall's `centre`, `left` or `right` face, `start` or `end`; a door's or window's `centre`, or its jamb at the `start` or `end` side; a grid's line; with `point: start|end` that line's end; or a point on one, or `{endpoint: [x, y]}`), `at`, `level?`, `kind?` (`aligned`, `linear` with `orient?` horizontal or vertical, `angular` between two lines that meet, `radial` and `diameter` on what is round, `arc_length` along a curved wall or an arc), `type?`, `prefix?`, `suffix?`, `above?`, `below?`, `replace?`, `equality?` |
| `dimension_constraint` | | `id`, `equal?`, `locked?: [segment, …]`: keep an aligned or linear dimension's segments equal (EQ) or locked at their lengths; what it measures to then moves with what a command moves, or the command is refused |
| `dimension_text` | | `id`, `segment?`, `prefix?`, `suffix?`, `above?`, `below?`, `replace?`: a dimension's text, or with `segment` (0 west to east, as `labels` lists them) one segment's own |
| `dimension_type` | | `name?`, `like?`, `rename?`, `delete?` and Revit's type parameters (`string`, `tick`, `tick_size`, `line_pen`, `tick_pen`, `color`, `line_extension`, `witness`, `witness_length`, `witness_gap`, `witness_extension`, `baseline_spacing`, `centre_mark`, `font`, `text_size`, `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor`, `text_offset`, `background`, `read`, `units`, `decimals`, `radius_symbol`, `diameter_symbol`, `equality_text`): create, edit, rename or delete a dimension type; without `name`, lists them |
| `tag` | TG | `ids?` (without them, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`), `label?` (the field it shows: any of its category's schedule fields), `level?`, `category?`, `offset?`, `leader?` |
| `text` | TX | `text`, `at` (its top left), `view?` (a level's plan by default; a section, an elevation, or a sheet by number), `size?` (mm on paper, 2.5), `angle?`, `leader?` |
| `spot` | EL | `at`, `view?`, `host?`: in a plan, the top of what stands there; in a section or an elevation, the point's height |
| `section` | CR | `start`, `end` (it looks to the left of the line), `depth?`, `name?` |
| `elevation` | | `facing?` (north, south, east or west: the side it shows), `at?`, or `start` and `end`; none of them: the four building elevations |
| `sheet` | | `number?` (A101, A102… by default), `name?`, `size?` (A0 to A4; A3 by default) |
| `place` | | `sheet` (its number), `view` (a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name: Room Schedule, `{3D}`…), `at?` (mm on the paper), `scale?` (100 for 1 : 100), `azimuth?` and `elevation?` for the 3D view |
| `delete_type` | | `category` and `type`, or `family`, or `family` and `type`: deletes a type of a category, a family, or one of a family's types; refused while an element uses it (it says how many) and for the last type of a category or of a family |
| `rename_type` | | `category` and `type`, or `family` and `type`, and `name`: renames a type of a category or one of a family's types; what's of it and what names it follow, and it keeps its GUID; refused for a name another type of it has |
| `purge` | PU | `kinds?` (`type`, `family`, `material`, `picture`, `filter`, `template`; types and families by default), `dry_run?`: takes out what nothing uses, again for what that frees; a category keeps a type and a family a type; `dry_run` lists what would go |
| `duplicate_view` | DP | `view` (a plan: a level's or a plan view's name or id), `mode?` (`duplicate`, `detailing`, `dependent`), `name?`: a new plan view of the same level; `detailing` copies the annotation in it, `dependent` follows its parent's range and graphics |
| `crop` | | `view`, `region?` (two corners: plan mm, or along a section and up), or `null` to uncrop; none: to what the view shows |
| `scale` | | `view?`, `scale?` (the n of 1 : n, 1 to 100000; 1 : 100, or 1 : 96 in feet and inches, until set): a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, the paper it stands for, which sizes its annotation and its line weights; a viewport placed with no `scale` takes it; without `scale`, what the view has |
| `detail` | | `view?`, `detail?` (`coarse`, `medium` or `fine`): how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts; without `detail`, what the view has |

42:as annotation where its owner is a dimension, tag, text, spot elevation, grid, level, room or mark (`annotates`), else as the model;
235:symbols, medium its patterns (`cut_layer`, a floor's `surface`), fine draws as before. In the 3D view `Look::style` picks how
239:A view's graphics (`graphics.rs`; `Level`, `Section` and `View3D` each hold `graphics`) hide and override by category, by view
243:sections, `cut_outlines`, `seen_below`, `view3d::Scene::picture`) and `look.dress` recolours the finished `Drawing` by owner and
246:(`Model::view_templates`), for a kind of view (`ViewKind`: plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; `from` sets it, none is any),
250:Instances and the framing of sections and 3D views take what `Look` shows too. A level's ceiling plan is its plan's view;
254:A 3D view sketches on its work plane (`workplane.rs`), as Revit's Work Plane > Set and more: `View3D::work_plane`, a `WorkPlane` on a
256:`offset` mm along its normal; with none, the lowest level (`Model::work_plane`). `WorkPlane::resolve` gives it as a `workplane::Frame`,
257:a point and a unit normal, at any angle, upright too: three points along a line are refused (`workplane::through`, facing up unless
259:that stays plan lines raised onto it (none for an upright one); `Frame::axes` are its level and up directions. The `work_plane` command
260:sets it (making the default 3D view, as `section_box` does), moves the plane as it is given only `offset`, or, given nothing, clears it;
261:deleting its level clears it too. `workplane::host` is the level what is made on it stands on: the highest at or below the plane, else
262:the lowest; a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft is made only on a level one (`workplane::is_level`, the desktop's check). The scene
263:says what a work plane is picked from: `Scene::face_at`, the face under a pixel (where, which way toward the camera, and the element's
265:look shows and inside its section box.
266:`Camera::on_slope` finds the point of such a plane under a pixel, `Camera::at_depth` a pixel's point at a depth, and the 3D pictures
269:A 3D view may be cut to a section box (fork issue 1), as Revit's Section Box: `View3D::section_box`, a `SectionBox` of six planes
270:square to the axes from `min` to `max`, `on` or off (off, it keeps its extents), set by the `section_box` command (which makes the
271:default 3D view, as `graphics` does, and with no extents fits the box round `Model::model_box`, `SECTION_BOX_ROOM` clear of it), and
272:checked in `Model::check` (usable numbers, `MIN_SECTION_BOX` between the planes on each axis). `Look::of` carries a view's box while
273:it's on (`Look::section_box`; `with_section_box` puts another in, for a box being dragged), and `Scene::picture` cuts to it: the view
281:from it) and `Camera::along` (how far, mm, a drag on the picture moves a point along an axis; none for an axis pointing at the camera).
282:A plan may follow the box (`section_box` on a `Level` or a `PlanView`, set by `modify`; a dependent view follows its parent's,
283:`Model::plan_box`; Duplicate View copies it): while the default 3D view's box is on, the plan shows what the box keeps, its range
297:A 3D view may be seen in perspective, as through a camera, rather than parallel (axonometric): `View3D::perspective`, a `Perspective`
298:with the `lens` it is seen through (its focal length, mm on a 35 mm camera, whose 36 mm of film, `FILM`, is the picture's width; 10 to
299:600 mm, checked in `Model::check`) and `on` or off (off, it keeps its lens), set by the `perspective` command, which makes the default 3D
300:view as `section_box` does; `View3D::lens` is the lens while it's on. The camera is `view3d::Camera` with `lens` set: the eye stands back from
301:the target along the view as far as makes `scale` true at the target (`Camera::eye_distance`, the focal length in px over the scale), so
303:`Camera::sized` keeps the eye where it stood as the picture or the lens changes, and `with_eye_elevation` raises or lowers it looking at the
304:same target from as far across the plan. `fit_from` fits a perspective with the eye as far back as puts a ball round what is shown inside
305:the picture's narrower side. `Camera::project` keeps "larger is nearer": in perspective `d² / a - d` for a point `a` mm in front of an eye
309:(`Projector::in_front`, as weights of its corners, so a curve's lighting carries over), a line to its near part (`Camera::in_front`: edges in
310:wireframe, levels' marks, the section box's frame); a point behind the eye projects to no number. A face is lit on the side the eye is on
311:(`Camera::toward`), as the card's `front_facing` is, and how far a line may lie behind a surface and show is a pixel's worth where the
312:line is (`Camera::slack`). `Camera::along` takes, in perspective, the point on the axis nearest the line from the eye through the pointer,
313:so a dragged section box face stays under it. `render` of the 3D view goes through its lens, and `eye_elevation` puts the eye that high. A
314:sheet's 3D viewport stays parallel (its scale is paper's). The card draws perspective too: `View::perspective` gives the shader the
317:`picking_the_mesh_in_perspective_finds_what_the_cpu_picture_shows_from_afar_and_from_within` and

steps.message:
Read /tmp/views-tools/BRIEF.md first and follow it (hard rules, base commit, how to test, how to finish).

YOUR PART (GRAPHICS): the commands `graphics`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style` (in `src/views/graphics.rs`), `filter` (in `src/views/filters.rs`, with `inspect_entries` for the project's view filters) and `template` (in `src/views/templates.rs`, with `inspect_entries` for the view templates). Implement each file's `run` and `check` (the model rules for a view's graphics: categories, overrides, filters applied, phases, options, layers, background grids, templates followed and what they control; the view filters and the view templates). Other sub-agents do, in parallel: section/elevation/sheet/place/crop/duplicate_view; section_box/perspective/graphic_display_options/camera/work_plane/dimension_3d/spots; dimensions; text/tag/linework; detail lines; regions and groups. Don't do theirs.

Observed so far (verify; there's much more to find):
- `graphics {}` (reads; the lowest level's plan) → `{"background_grid":{"divisions":[5,5],"main":{"color":[230,230,230],"enabled":false,"pen":0},"rotation":0.0,"spacing":[1000.0,1000.0],"sub":{"color":[245,245,245],"enabled":false,"pen":0},"visible":true},"categories":{},"controlled":[],"detail":"fine","elements":{},"filters":[],"hidden":[],"hidden_elements":[],"layers":{},"name":"Level 1","options":{},"phase":null,"phase_filter":null,"scale":null,"template":null,"view":100000,"visual_style":"shaded"}`. On `{3D}` before it exists, the same with `"name":"{3D}","view":null` (reading makes nothing); a change makes it (`common::ensure_default_3d`). Sections and elevations take graphics too.
- After `graphics {"hide":["walls"],"categories":{"doors":{"halftone":true}}}`, `filter {"name":"F1","categories":["walls"]}` (→ `{"categories":["wall"],"matches":[100002,100003,100004,100005],"name":"F1","rules":[]}`), `graphics {"filters":[{"filter":"F1","halftone":true}]}`, `scale {"view":"Level 1","scale":50}` (→ `{"name":"Level 1","scale":50.0,"view":100000}`) and `detail {"view":"Level 1","detail":"coarse"}` (→ `{"detail":"coarse","name":"Level 1","view":100000}`), the level is saved with `"graphics":{"categories":{"door":{"halftone":true},"wall":{"hidden":true}},"filters":[{"filter":<view-filter guid>,"halftone":true}],"scale":50.0,"detail":"coarse"}` after its `view_range`, and the project with `"view_filters":{"F1":{"categories":["wall"]}}` and a library entry `{"kind":"view-filter","name":"F1","guid"}`. `scale {}` reads `{"name":"Level 1","scale":100.0,"view":100000}`. The 3D view's style is saved `"graphics":{"style":"wireframe"}`.
- `template {"name":"T1","from":"Level 1"}` → `{"background_grid":{…},"categories":{"door":{"halftone":true},"wall":{"hidden":true}},"controls":["categories","filters","range","phase","options","scale","detail","style","background_grid"],"detail":"fine","filters":[{"filter":"F1","halftone":true}],"hidden":["wall"],"kind":"plan","layers":{},"name":"T1","options":{},"phase":null,"phase_filter":null,"scale":null,"view_range":{"bottom":0.0,"cut":1200.0,"depth":0.0,"top":null},"views":[],"visual_style":"shaded"}`; saved in `view_templates` as `"T1":{"kind":"plan","controls":[…],"graphics":{"categories":{…},"filters":[{"filter":<guid>,"halftone":true}]},"view_range":{"top":null,"cut":1200.0,"bottom":0.0,"depth":0.0}}` with a `view-template` library entry. A new project has three (Electrical Ceiling, Electrical Lighting, Electrical Power: `{"kind":"plan","controls":["categories"],"graphics":{"categories":{…}}}`).
- Errors seen: "graphics: Room Schedule isn't a plan, a section, an elevation or a 3D view", "graphics: wall 100002 isn't a plan, a section, an elevation or a 3D view", "graphics: no view named `A101`" (sheets aren't found by number here), "graphics: `view`: 12345 is not a view", "scale: {3D} isn't a plan, a section or an elevation; only those have one", "detail: {3D} isn't …", "visual_style: Level 1 isn't a 3D view; only those have a visual style", "filter: a new filter needs `categories`, [\"walls\", \"doors\"…]", "template: there's no view template `x`; make one with `from` (a view), or `controls` (there are: Electrical Ceiling, Electrical Lighting, Electrical Power)". `graphics {"foo":1}` is NOT refused.
- `inspect` lists `view_filters` and `view_templates` with names where the file has GUIDs: implement `inspect_entries` in filters.rs and templates.rs.
- `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options` (design options) in graphics and templates are the styles agent's phases (`crate::styles::phasing`: `check_view_graphics`, names ↔ GUIDs of `phase`, `phase-filter`, `option-set`, `design-option` library entries); fill patterns of foreground/background overrides are styles' `fill_patterns`. Read `src/styles/phasing.rs` for how they're kept and checked (it already checks a view's or a template's `graphics.phase`/`phase_filter`/`options` in the model check).
- A filter's `matches` and its `rules` are a schedule filter's (the fields of the category's schedule; ops equals… has-no-value): READERS writes schedules in parallel; write the stand-in you need (fields and values for each category: probe the original's `schedule` command, e.g. `schedule {"category":"wall"}` and its `available` fields).
- A dependent plan view (a `planview` with `parent`, made by `duplicate_view {"mode":"dependent"}`) refuses graphics/scale/detail naming its parent; a view following a template refuses what the template controls; `template` with `rename`, `like`, `kind`, `controls`, `view_range`, `delete`, `reset`, and views following it (`views` in the reply; `controlled` in graphics). `visual_style` on the 3D view and camera views. Category names "in any case, singular or plural" (walls → wall), subcategories (roomreference, roomseparator), family component categories (furniture, casework, plumbing… see the docs), `layers` of CAD drawings, `background_grid`.

results.content:
Instances and the framing of sections and 3D views take what `Look` shows too. A level's ceiling plan is its plan's view;
transparency shows in 3D only. A surface is seen through as much as the greater of its material's `transparency` (`Tri::alpha`, in
plain views too) and the view's override for its element (not in a plain view); both painters take it from `Tri::alpha`.

A 3D view sketches on its work plane (`workplane.rs`), as Revit's Work Plane > Set and more: `View3D::work_plane`, a `WorkPlane` on a
`level` (a GUID, in `visit_refs!`), through three `points`, or on a `surface` picked on the model (a point and a normal), each moved
`offset` mm along its normal; with none, the lowest level (`Model::work_plane`). `WorkPlane::resolve` gives it as a `workplane::Frame`,
a point and a unit normal, at any angle, upright too: three points along a line are refused (`workplane::through`, facing up unless
upright), and `Model::check` resolves it. `Frame::over_plan` is it as a `walls::Plane` over the plan, as a floor's top is, for a sketch
that stays plan lines raised onto it (none for an upright one); `Frame::axes` are its level and up directions. The `work_plane` command
sets it (making the default 3D view, as `section_box` does), moves the plane as it is given only `offset`, or, given nothing, clears it;
deleting its level clears it too. `workplane::host` is the level what is made on it stands on: the highest at or below the plane, else
the lowest; a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft is made only on a level one (`workplane::is_level`, the desktop's check). The scene
says what a work plane is picked from: `Scene::face_at`, the face under a pixel (where, which way toward the camera, and the element's
triangles in its plane), and `Scene::corner_near`, the corner within so many pixels that nothing nearer hides, both of what the view's
look shows and inside its section box.
`Camera::on_slope` finds the point of such a plane under a pixel, `Camera::at_depth` a pixel's point at a depth, and the 3D pictures
say what point of the model a pixel shows (`Image::point`, from the depth the processor's picture now keeps; `gpu::Mesh::point`).

A 3D view may be cut to a section box (fork issue 1), as Revit's Section Box: `View3D::section_box`, a `SectionBox` of six planes
square to the axes from `min` to `max`, `on` or off (off, it keeps its extents), set by the `section_box` command (which makes the
default 3D view, as `graphics` does, and with no extents fits the box round `Model::model_box`, `SECTION_BOX_ROOM` clear of it), and
checked in `Model::check` (usable numbers, `MIN_SECTION_BOX` between the planes on each axis). `Look::of` carries a view's box while
it's on (`Look::section_box`; `with_section_box` puts another in, for a box being dragged), and `Scene::picture` cuts to it: the view
is square on, so `Boxed` turns a pixel and its depth into a model point with one sum, and `raster` keeps a pixel only where that point
is in the box (a triangle wholly past one plane is passed over first), `dots` a scan's point only where it is, and the wireframe each
edge as far as it runs inside (`within`, Liang and Barsky's clipping). What it cuts away isn't drawn, so it isn't picked; the edge
where a cut face meets paper is drawn as any edge is, and cut faces aren't capped yet. A level whose plane is above or below the box is
left out, and the rest are cut to its sides. A section's picture has its own clip and ignores the box. The card doesn't cut yet:
`Mesh::new` refuses a boxed view, and the processor draws it. Its grips are the core's: `box_grips` (the middle of each face: west,
east, south, north, bottom, top), `box_edges`, `move_box_face` (a face moved along its axis to 10 mm, stopping short of the face across
from it) and `Camera::along` (how far, mm, a drag on the picture moves a point along an axis; none for an axis pointing at the camera).
A plan may follow the box (`section_box` on a `Level` or a `PlanView`, set by `modify`; a dependent view follows its parent's,
`Model::plan_box`; Duplicate View copies it): while the default 3D view's box is on, the plan shows what the box keeps, its range
from the box's bottom up to its top, where it cuts (`Model::shown_range`), and its crop the box's sides, within its own crop if it has
one (`Model::shown_crop`). What a plan draws and snaps to reads those; `plan_range` and `crop_of` stay the plan's own, which commands
(dimensions, joins, Duplicate View) and Properties use. A ceiling plan keeps its own range.
Visibility/Graphics lists each tab's categories alphabetically by their translated display names. Projection and cut pattern
cells edit independent foreground and background overrides, using the project's fill patterns (including imported PAT patterns),
colours and a combined preview. Unchecked layers inherit; `<None>` explicitly hides a layer. OK/Apply submits the draft as one
`graphics` command; Clear Overrides clears only that cell. Annotation categories expose projection patterns for filled regions.
Styles hold `foreground` and `background` as optional `{pattern: name | null, color: [r,g,b]}` layers, alongside the existing
`fill` colour. Element, filter and category precedence resolves each layer separately. Plans, reflected ceiling plans, section
cuts and regions draw the layers with the same bounded pattern renderer as filled region types; the pattern's drafting/model
target sets its scale. Pattern references follow library renames, save as GUIDs, and prevent deletion while used by a view or
template. The 3D renderer continues to use the solid `fill` colour for shading; it does not draw hatch patterns.

A 3D view may be seen in perspective, as through a camera, rather than parallel (axonometric): `View3D::perspective`, a `Perspective`
with the `lens` it is seen through (its focal length, mm on a 35 mm camera, whose 36 mm of film, `FILM`, is the picture's width; 10 to
600 mm, checked in `Model::check`) and `on` or off (off, it keeps its lens), set by the `perspective` command, which makes the default 3D
view as `section_box` does; `View3D::lens` is the lens while it's on. The camera is `view3d::Camera` with `lens` set: the eye stands back from
the target along the view as far as makes `scale` true at the target (`Camera::eye_distance`, the focal length in px over the scale), so
orbit turns it about the target, pan carries both, zoom walks it in (a point on the plane through the target staying under the cursor),
`Camera::sized` keeps the eye where it stood as the picture or the lens changes, and `with_eye_elevation` raises or lowers it looking at the
same target from as far across the plan. `fit_from` fits a perspective with the eye as far back as puts a ball round what is shown inside
the picture's narrower side. `Camera::project` keeps "larger is nearer": in perspective `d² / a - d` for a point `a` mm in front of an eye
`d` from the target, as near as a parallel view's at the target and straight across the picture of a plane (it goes as `1 / a`), so the
rasterizer's barycentric depths stay exact, and `point_at` turns a pixel and its depth back into the model point (textures, the section
box's `Boxed`). What is less than `NEAR` (10 mm) in front of the eye is cut away: a triangle into the one or two its near part makes
(`Projector::in_front`, as weights of its corners, so a curve's lighting carries over), a line to its near part (`Camera::in_front`: edges in
wireframe, levels' marks, the section box's frame); a point behind the eye projects to no number. A face is lit on the side the eye is on
(`Camera::toward`), as the card's `front_facing` is, and how far a line may lie behind a surface and show is a pixel's worth where the
line is (`Camera::slack`). `Camera::along` takes, in perspective, the point on the axis nearest the line from the eye through the pointer,
so a dragged section box face stays under it. `render` of the 3D view goes through its lens, and `eye_elevation` puts the eye that high. A
sheet's 3D viewport stays parallel (its scale is paper's). The card draws perspective too: `View::perspective` gives the shader the
focal length, how far the eye is and a depth of `a + b / ahead`, 1 at `NEAR` and 0 past the far side of the mesh (a reversed depth, as
precise far off as near), with the same `NEAR` cut by the card's clipping; `Mesh::pick` cuts and projects as the processor does.
`picking_the_mesh_in_perspective_finds_what_the_cpu_picture_shows_from_afar_and_from_within` and
`the_card_draws_in_perspective_what_the_processor_does_from_afar_and_from_among_the_walls` compare them, from outside and with the eye
inside the house (`view3d::inside`).

A 3D view may have a **camera of its own**, as Revit's Camera tool makes one: `View3D::camera`, a `ViewCamera` holding the model
point its `eye` stands at and the `target` it looks at (both `[x, y, z]` mm), with the view's `perspective` on. The `camera` command
makes a new named view from an eye and a target (the eye never on the target, checked in `Model::check`), gives one to an existing
view (the default `{3D}` among them, made by name as `perspective` makes it), or, with a `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or
`lens`, reads one back (`null` eye and target for a view with no camera yet — reading makes nothing). A view that already has a
camera keeps the point a change leaves out, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that; a view without one needs both.
`view3d::Camera::at` builds the render camera from the
eye, target and lens, its azimuth and elevation the direction from the eye to the target and `scale` the focal length over the
distance, so `Camera::eye` is exactly the eye given; `view3d::camera_of` does the same for a view and a scale, for a sheet's 3D
viewport. On the desktop the Camera tool (View tab) clicks an eye then a target in a plan, each at a height over it from the Options
Bar, and opens the new view: `BimApp::active_3d` is the 3D view the 3D tab shows (a camera view by id, or none for the default),
`BimApp::open_3d` sets it (and resets the on-screen camera, so the view stands from its own camera), the Project Browser lists every
3D view under 3D Views. Properties (`camera.rs`, `BimApp::camera_properties`) is one panel bound to a view: the 3D tab passes the
view it shows, and a camera view picked on a plan passes the picked one, so both show the same Name, Eye, Target and Focal Length
and edit it the same way (`camera` for the camera, `modify` for the name). Graphics, phasing and the section box stay with the view
on screen (`graphic_view`), not with a camera view picked on a plan: its mark shows its camera, its project parameters and its
phase. A camera view shows no Azimuth or Elevation: those
(`View3D::azimuth`, `View3D::elevation`) only frame a 3D view **without** a camera on a sheet (`sheet::framing`, `camera_of`), so a
view on a sheet whose view has a camera shows its name alone. A camera edit while its view is on screen drops the on-screen
camera (`Orbit::camera`), so the next frame stands the view from the model and the settled hand has nothing old to write back. A
camera view's mark is drawn on its level's plan
(`render::camera_mark`, the level from `Model::camera_level`): a symbol at its eye, a dashed line to what it looks at, pickable so a right
click opens the view (`Action::OpenView`) or a double click does. Orbiting, panning or zooming a camera view writes its eye and target back
once the hand and the wheel have let it be (`view3d` reads the on-screen `Camera::eye` back into the view), so leaving it and returning comes
back to where it was left. A camera moved elsewhere — its mark dragged on a plan, a command, undo — moves the view already showing
it: `Orbit::built` holds the camera the picture was built from, and a difference with the model's means the picture stands from the
model anew instead of its old camera being written back over the move; a floating window, drawn while the hand works in another
view, writes nothing.

sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-files')
from r import *

exe = MINE if len(sys.argv) > 1 else ORIG
small = '/tmp/edit-files/fx/small.bimcraft'

    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True)
    print('$', label or ' '.join(args)[:200], '->', p.returncode)
    for l in p.stdout.splitlines():
        if l.startswith('{"counts"'):
            dd = json.loads(l)
            print('   inspect history', dd['history'], 'counts', dd['counts'], 'warnings', dd.get('warnings'), 'path', dd.get('path'))

sh(d, ['run', 'sub/q.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'reload {"id": "x"}'])
sh(d, ['run', 'sub/q.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'reload {"id": [100002]}'])
sh(d, ['run', 'sub/q.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'reload {"id": 100002.5}'])
sh(d, ['run', 'sub/q.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'reload {"id": -1}'])
sh(d, ['run', 'sub/q.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'reload {"ids": [100002]}'])
sh(d, ['run', 'sub/q.bimcraft', '--cmd', 'reload {"id": null}'])
g = [k for k, v in json.load(open(d + '/sub/q.bimcraft'))['elements'].items() if v['category'] == 'link']
gg = json.load(open(d + '/sub/q.bimcraft'))['elements'][g[1]]['guid']

# Brief for the VIEWS sub-agents (read all of it first)

You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler
written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md), as a new Rust program built only from observed
behaviour. Many agents work in parallel, each owning one area. The VIEWS area (views and annotation,
`src/views/`) is owned by the agent that launched you; it split the area between several sub-agents.
Your part is given in your prompt. Do it fully and exactly; don't do the other parts.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it ONLY by running it (args, stdin,
  files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete
  it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Edit only the files your prompt gives you. You may add child modules of your own files
  (`src/views/dims.rs` may say `pub mod geom;` for `src/views/dims/geom.rs`). Do NOT edit
  `src/views/mod.rs`, `src/views/common.rs`, `src/views/model.rs` or anything outside `src/views/`; if you
  need a change there, copy what you need into your own files and say so in your final report.
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in your own `/tmp/views-<yourpart>/`.
  Commit only Rust (your files). Don't write report/summary .md files into the repo.
- Never use bare `git stash`. Don't push. Don't touch other worktrees or branches but your own.

## Your worktree and base
You run in your own git worktree. FIRST run `git log --oneline -3`: your branch must contain commit
`9de3863` ("Views: the constraints hook…", after "Views: the module's skeleton…"). If it doesn't, run `git merge 9de3863` (or, in a fresh
clean worktree, `git reset --hard 9de3863`). Build with `cargo build --release --offline`
(about 15 s); the binary is `<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli`.

## The codebase (read the parts you need)
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`; `insert_sorted` for BTreeMap-like maps; `Value::f`,
  `Value::u`, `Value::s`; `jobj!{"k" => v, …}`), serde_json-identical parse errors and float
  formatting (`1000.0`, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()`. Command replies are printed
  with keys sorted (as serde_json::Value), so a reply's key order doesn't matter; a saved element's
  field order DOES (match the original's saved files exactly).
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections in file order; `insert_top`, `section_mut`,
  `TOP_ORDER`) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object in the original's field
  order) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}` entries; ids count down from 999999 via
  `alloc_lib_id`, shared with the "parts" elements and types hold, e.g. a region's sketch lines
  `{id, guid, start, end}`, never reused in a session). `alloc_id()` for element ids; `find_guid`,
  `ids_of(cat)`, `lib_find(kind,name)`, `lib_guid`, `lib_name(guid)`, `lib_add`. Elements reference each
  other and library entries by GUID (`crate::rand::guid()` makes one).
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute(cmd, params)`: resolves the command, snapshots the project, runs
  it, then runs `crate::check::check` (which calls every module's `check(pr)`, ours via
  `src/views/mod.rs::check`, which calls your file's `check`), rolls back on any error, and records an
  undo step labelled by the command's catalog label when the project changed (call
  `crate::views::mark_step()` in a command that must make a step even unchanged).
- `src/commands/params.rs`: param readers with the original's texts (`` `x` in mm is required``,
  `` `x` must be a number in mm, got … ``, points, text ≤ 256 chars; |mm| ≤ 1e9). Many commands have
  texts of their own: always probe.
- `src/model.rs`: levels by elevation, `resolve_level`/`level_param` with the original's errors (`tag`
  and `dimension` take `level`), `find` by id/GUID, `normalize_guid`, `level_of_view`.
- `src/styles/` (done by another agent): line patterns/styles, fill patterns, filled region types,
  text types, dimension types, line weights, object styles, units, phases, phase filters, design
  options, project parameters. Library kinds: `line-style`, `fill-pattern`, `filled-region-type`,
  `text-type`, `dimension-type`, `view-filter`, `view-template`, `detail-group`, `phase`,
  `phase-filter`, `type:wall`… `styles::common` has colour/pen readers, `check_keys` (the original's
  "`foo` isn't one of its parameters: a, b, c", listing them in the original's order),
  `styles::phasing::check_view_graphics` checks a view's phase/phase filter/options.
- `src/views/` (ours): `mod.rs` dispatches each command to its file's `run(s, cid, p)`, calls each
  file's `check(pr)` after every command, `element_view(pr, id, x)` (what the `elements` command shows
  of an element beyond its saved fields: e.g. a section's `length` and `looking`, a dimension's
  `values` and `labels`, a text's `type` by name and `level`, a line's `shape`, `length`, `style` by
  name; `elements` is done by READERS and calls this hook for our categories), and
  `inspect_entries` (what `inspect` lists of view filters, templates, detail groups).
  `common.rs`: `find_view` / `view_param` (a view by id or name: "`view`: X is not a view", "no view
  named `X`"), `default_plan` (lowest level), `default_3d` / `ensure_default_3d` (the `{3D}` view as
  the original makes it), `r3` (round to the micron, as the original keeps worked-out points),
  `cat_id` ("wall 100002"), field readers, `word(pr, [en, pt, es, sv, cs, fr, nl, de, it])`.
  `model.rs`: a stand-in for model geometry: wall type, thickness, core, location line → centre line
  (exterior face = LEFT of start→end), faces, arc walls (`arc` degrees CCW), base/top heights, plan
  outlines of walls/floors/columns, vector helpers. ARCH and STRUCTURE (walls, doors, floors…, in
  `src/arch/`, `src/geom/`, `src/structure/`) are being written in parallel by others, so the model
  commands (`wall`, `door`, `floor`, `room`, `column`…) do NOT work in our binary yet: write what you need
  of their geometry yourself (in your files), the way the original's saved files and replies show it.

## How to test
`MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py [-f file_to_copy_into_cwd]
[-i stdin_file] -- <args…>` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code,
stdout, stderr and every file written, after normalising GUIDs (`GUID-N` by first appearance), uids,
temp names and timestamps. Prints SAME or the diff. The hidden tests do the same kind of comparison on
many inputs, so match replies, error texts, saved files (field order, number formatting) and undo
labels exactly.
- Build input projects with the ORIGINAL and run both programs on them (our loader reads the original's
  files as they are): `/workspace/executable run --cmd 'wall {"points":[[0,0],[10000,0],[10000,6000],[0,6000]],"closed":true}' --cmd 'door {"wall":100002,"offset":2000}' --save /tmp/views-x/in.bimcraft`,
  then `cmp.py -f /tmp/views-x/in.bimcraft -- run in.bimcraft --cmd '…' --save out.bimcraft`.
- `/tmp/views-tools/p.py [-m] [-f in.bimcraft] -- run …` runs one program (`-m`: ours, with MINE set)
  and prints its output and the elements (and changed top-level sections) of each .bimcraft it saved.
- `/tmp/views-tools/each.py [-b] [-f in.bimcraft] [-s 'setup cmd']… cmds.txt` runs each line of
  cmds.txt (a command, or several joined by ` ;; `) in a fresh run of the original (`-b`: of both,
  marking SAME/DIFF; `-m`: ours). Set `SCRATCH=/tmp/views-<yourpart>` for its temp dirs. The harness
  refuses shell loops and `cd … &&` chains: write command files and run the tools on them.
- `/workspace/executable commands` prints every command's spec (`params`); read yours, and
  `/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md` (and the README's command table) for what they mean.
- Probe widely: normal cases, every optional parameter, edge cases, every error and the ORDER of the
  checks (which error wins when two things are wrong), what the model check refuses after the command
  ("text 100013: view3d 100008 isn't a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet": category, id, text,
  no command prefix), names in every project language (`new {"language":"pt"}`…: en pt es sv cs fr nl
  de it), the saved JSON of every element and section you make, `elements {"category":…}` output for
  your categories, `undo`/`redo` after your commands (labels), and that a refused command changes
  nothing. Numbers the original works out are usually rounded to the micron (3 decimals).
- Write regression checks for yourself as command files you can re-run with `each.py -b`.

## Finish
Commit your work on your worktree branch (`git add src/views/… && git commit`), message ending with
`Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Final message (to the agent that launched
you): your branch name and last commit; per command, what matches the original and what doesn't
(be honest and specific); what you needed but couldn't write (in shared files or other areas); any
functions you expose for others (e.g. for `delete`, `move`, `elements`).

The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card (File > Settings > Performance; off until asked for: `BimApp::card`, `settings.json`'s
`gpu_3d`). `view3d::gpu::Mesh` is the triangles a view shows as f32 vertices relative to the middle of what is drawn (millimetres far
from the origin would overflow f32), each with its colour, normal, face normal, plane, element and texture; the textures' mip levels as
words (`Skin`; `Mesh::lookups` gives the level a zoom looks up, as `Sampler::level_for` does); and a bounding volume hierarchy built on
the first pick. Surfaces seen through come after the opaque ones (`Mesh::clear_from`), each element's transparency in its `Owner` (an element whose layers differ in transparency has an `Owner` for each).
`Mesh::new` refuses, with a reason, what the card doesn't draw (hidden line, wireframe, more than `MAX_TRIS`), and the processor draws those as before, and sections and sheets always. `Mesh::pick` is `Image::pick` without a picture: the
same projection and barycentric test for triangles (the nearest seen through where it is nearer than the nearest opaque one), and for levels the same `LevelMarks` that `Scene::picture` draws (`level_marks`: one
definition of a level's lines and head). The desktop's `gpu.rs` and `gpu.wgsl` draw it in passes into a texture egui shows like the
processor's picture: the opaque surfaces (lit as `picture` lights them, textured as `Sampler::at` looks up), those seen through (the
nearest in front of the opaque depth, in targets of their own), then an edge wherever the opaque plane changes between a pixel and the one
to its right or below, else the surface tinted halfway where selected, with what is seen through blended over it, and the levels' lines
where nothing opaque nearer hides them. What changes between pictures is the camera and the lines; the owners' tints and the textures'
lookups are written again only when they change. A change to how
the processor shades, draws an edge or marks a level goes in the shader too: `the_card_draws_what_the_processor_does` and the core's
`picking_the_mesh_finds_what_the_cpu_picture_shows` compare them (and, seen through,
`the_card_draws_what_the_view_sees_through_as_the_processor_does` and `picking_through_what_the_view_sees_through_finds_what_the_cpu_picture_shows`), and skip on a machine with no graphics adapter. The card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12: on OpenGL wgpu panics in the shader compiler for what the shaders read (a depth texture; buffers in a vertex shader), so `Gpu::new` refuses it, and puts whatever else a compiler stops at under `catch_unwind`.
The card is made the first time it is wanted (`Card::ready`: compiling its shaders is not a start's cost), and one that can't be made says why on the Performance page.
A device error is caught
in the card's own error scopes, never left to wgpu's handler (which ends the program), and hands the view to the processor for good.

A 3D view's **Graphic Display Options** (Revit's GD) are `View3D::display`, a `view3d::DisplayOptions`: `edges` (on unless turned
off; only Shaded leaves them out, as Hidden Line and Wireframe always draw them), `silhouette` (an outline that many px wide, 0 to
`MAX_SILHOUETTE`, 10, checked in `Model::check`; 0 for none) and `ambient_shadows` (off unless turned on), set by the
`graphic_display_options` command (GD; it makes the default 3D view as `section_box` does, keeps what is left out, and with
nothing given reads them back). `Look::of` carries them (`Look::display`), so the desktop, a sheet's 3D viewport and `render`
draw them alike; a section's picture ignores them. Both come off the opaque depth the rasterizer already has, before a scan's
dots are in it, in nearness as `Camera::project` gives it, measured in pixels' worth (`Camera::slack`), so they read the
same parallel and in perspective. Ambient shadows (`view3d::ambient`) are a screen-space pass: for each pixel, the pixels
across from each other at eight offsets (`AMBIENT`, 4 to 12 px, four lines at two reaches); over a plane the depth runs
straight, so their mean is the pixel's own, and only where the surfaces round it rise toward the eye on both sides (a corner,
the foot of a wall on a floor) does it darken, by `AMBIENT_DARK` of its light at most; a neighbour more than `AMBIENT_REACH`
pixels' worth a pixel off in depth is something else, in front or behind, and counts for nothing, so nothing casts a halo. A
silhouette (`view3d::outlines`) is wherever two neighbouring pixels are one on a surface and one on nothing, or on different
planes `OUTLINE_GAP` (4) pixels' worth apart in depth: each pixel whose square `width + 1` across (from `width / 2` before it)
holds such a pair is drawn in the edge's colour, so a straight outline is exactly `width` px wide. The card does the same in
`fs_post` (`ambient`, `outlined`, `worth` in `gpu.wgsl`, the options in the globals' ninth vector, from `Mesh::display`), so
no pass is added: `the_card_draws_edges_silhouettes_and_ambient_shadows_as_the_processor_does` compares them. Cast shadows
from a sun are not drawn yet. The desktop's dialog (`display.rs`) opens by GD and from the view control bar's Visual Style
menu, alike in both looks of the window, and runs the command on the 3D view on screen.

The 3D scene can be exported as glTF 2.0 binary, for Blender and other viewers (`gltf.rs`: `save` to a `.glb`, which the CLI's `--save` and
`convert` and the MCP server reach too, and File > Export > 3D Scene as glTF in both profiles). It writes the triangles of `Scene::facets`,
the ones the processor's picture and the card's mesh are made of, as the default 3D view shows them (`Look::of_3d`): its phase and phase
filter, its design options, what Visibility/Graphics hides, and the colours and transparency it paints, linked models included
(`extras.linked`). A section box on that view is not applied, the whole of each element shown is written, and neither are textures, edges,
levels, point clouds or the camera. There is a node and a mesh for each element, the node named by the element's id with its `id`, `guid`
and `category` in `extras`, and a primitive in the mesh for each colour the element is shaded in (a compound wall has one for each layer).
A primitive's material is the scene's sRGB colour in linear light, as glTF's base colour is, blended with alpha `1 - clearness` where the view
sees through the surface (a mass is, by default), and always double sided, as the scene draws both sides of every surface. Positions are in
metres, turned and not mirrored: east stays x, up becomes y and north becomes -z, so the winding is kept. Curved surfaces keep their smooth
normals, vertices that agree in position and normal are shared within a primitive, and a triangle with no area is left out. A scene past
`gltf::MAX_TRIS` (the card's limit) is refused with how many triangles there are, and an empty one with what to show. The tests read the
chunks back (header, lengths, alignment, the JSON, a box's bounds and volume); the Khronos validator (`npm i gltf-validator`, then
`validateBytes`) reports no errors, warnings or hints on the sample house and on the 20-storey tower of `run --highrise`.

The 3D view works round what is under the cursor, on both painters. What a pick finds has a point: `view3d::Surface` is the
element, the model point where the line of sight through the pixel meets the surface the picture shows there, and its normal turned
toward the camera. The processor's picture finds it from the triangle its pixel holds (`Scene::surface_in`), the card's mesh from
the triangle its pick finds (`Mesh::surface`), and on a level's mark it is the level's plane; `orbit.rs`'s `Picker::surface` asks
whichever drew the picture on screen. A drag orbits round the surface's point under the pointer where it began
(`Camera::orbit_about` turns the whole camera about it, so the point keeps its pixel, in perspective too), round the target where
nothing is; the wheel zooms toward it (`Camera::zoom_about` closes the target and the eye in on it), and with nothing under the
cursor zooms about the cursor as before. `the_surface_under_a_pixel_is_the_same_through_the_mesh_as_the_picture_and_an_orbit_or_a_zoom_about_it_keeps_it_there`
checks the two painters agree, and `tests/working3d.rs` drives it in both profiles, on the card where the machine has one.

The 3D view's tools draw on a **work plane**, as Revit's (`workplane.rs`): `work_plane` takes the surface under the cursor and,
for a face that is level and turned up (a floor's top, a flat roof's, a level's plane), gives the level its points go on (the face's
element's own level, a level's plane that level, else the highest level at or below it) and the offset over it, to the micron;
with nothing under the cursor, the lowest level's plane, the ground. A face that isn't level, or is turned down, gives none, and
the status line says what the tool draws on. Every drawing tool takes its points so in the 3D view (`orbit.rs`'s `aim`), and each
point snaps as its level's plan snaps (`snap3d`: `snap::snap` on the plane's level, from the points the tool has picked, Shift squaring
the step, within the snap's points as the plane is foreshortened there; else the nearest 10 mm). The Wall tool (WA): the first
point's plane holds for the rest of the chain, whatever the cursor passes over, and each wall goes through `place` as in a plan, with
`base_offset` from `Orbit::wall_base`, which `wall_params` reads while the 3D view places a point. A run's tool (beams, wall footings,
pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays, wires, conductors, cabling) takes each end on the face it is clicked on, so a run from a floor's
top to a wall's or a column's top climbs (`place_run_lifted`: `offset` and `end_offset` over the start's level, the Options Bar's
offset over each): that is a brace; where nothing is under the cursor, its end stays on its start's plane. Column (CL), Structural
Column and Isolated Footing stand on the face (`place_column`, `place_stand_lifted`: `base_offset`, or a footing's top `offset`, its
height over the level), and Component (CM) and the MEP fixtures run `component` with that level and offset. `Orbit::plane` keeps the
last point clicked and its plane, which a chain or a run's end takes only while it is the tool's own point before. The point under the
cursor is drawn as a plan's snap, naming what it snapped to (a free point: Nearest, of the element whose face it is), with the wall
or run from the point before and its length. Where neither a level face nor the ground meets the line of sight, the tool says what
it needs (`needs_face`, by the tool's title). Floor and Ceiling sketch on the view's work plane (below), which may be set on a level
face picked on the model.

A level's own plan is the level (its `view_range`, `crop` and `graphics` are the level's); every other plan of it is an `Element::PlanView`
(Revit's Duplicate View: `duplicate_view`, which only plans take). A plan has a key: the level's id, or a plan view's. `Model::plan_level` says
which level a key shows, and everything that draws or measures the model takes that level (`draw_plan`, `plan_shows`, the canvas's tools), while
what is the view's own takes the key: its graphics (`graphics_of`), view range (`view_range_of`, which a template may control), crop (`crop_of`)
and annotation. Annotation says which view it is in: a note or a spot elevation by `view`, a dimension or a tag by an optional `view` beside its
`level` or its host (none: the level's own plan), and `Model::annotation_in` asks whether a plan draws it. A command that takes a `level` takes a
plan view too (`plan_param`): what is built stands on its level, what is dimensioned or tagged is in the view. A dependent view (`parent`) follows
its parent's view range and graphics (`plan_source`; `graphics`, `scale`, `detail` and `visual_style` refuse it, naming the parent), has a crop
of its own and draws its parent's annotation as well as its own. Deleting a view deletes what is annotated in it and its dependents; a level
takes its plan views with it. A project that has none writes the same file as before. A plan's own name, lettered at its bottom left, is in the drawings that make an image (`plan`, `ceiling_plan`: `titled`), not in the window's (`draw`, `draw_ceiling`) or a sheet's (`draw_at`), where the tab and the viewport's title say it. The desktop: View > Duplicate View, DP, and the Project
Browser's right-click, which also has Delete for a plan view; `Sheet::Plan` and `Sheet::Ceiling` hold the key.

import zlib, struct, sys
def png(path, w, h, color):
    raw = b''.join(b'\x00' + bytes(color) * w for _ in range(h))
    def chunk(t, d):
        c = struct.pack('>I', len(d)) + t + d
        return c + struct.pack('>I', zlib.crc32(t + d) & 0xffffffff)
    data = b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + chunk(b'IHDR', struct.pack('>IIBBBBB', w, h, 8, 2, 0, 0, 0)) + chunk(b'IDAT', zlib.compress(raw)) + chunk(b'IEND', b'')
    open(path, 'wb').write(data)

"""ftall.py fixture out.txt [ids...]: run ft.py for one element per category (or the given ids)."""
import json, sys, subprocess
src = sys.argv[1]; out = sys.argv[2]; ids = sys.argv[3:]
A = json.load(open(src))
if not ids:
    seen = set()
    for k, v in A['elements'].items():
        c = v.get('category')
        if c in seen: continue
        seen.add(c); ids.append(k)
with open(out, 'w') as f:
    for i in ids:
        p = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/edit-modify/ft.py', src, i], capture_output=True, text=True)
        f.write(p.stdout + p.stderr)
        f.flush()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run each command line of a file (or stdin) separately on the original (and optionally mine).
usage: each.py [-m] [-b] [-f in.bimcraft] [-s 'setup cmd']... < cmds.txt
  -m: run mine instead; -b: run both and mark differences; -f: open this project first.
Each line: a command `id {json}` (or several separated by ' ;; ')."""
import os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, re
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ['MINE'] if 'MINE' in os.environ else '/nonexistent-set-MINE'
G = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
a = sys.argv[1:]
exes = [ORIG]
infile = None
setup = []
both = False
while a:
    if a[0] == '-m': exes = [MINE]; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-b': exes = [ORIG, MINE]; both = True; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': infile = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-s': setup.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    else: break
src = open(a[0]) if a else sys.stdin
lines = [l.rstrip('\n') for l in src if l.strip() and not l.startswith('#')]
def norm(s):
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m) + 1)
        return m[g]
    return G.sub(rep, s)
same = 0
for l in lines:
    outs = []
    for exe in exes:
        d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='e', dir=os.environ.get('SCRATCH'))
        args = [exe, 'run']
        if infile:
            shutil.copy(infile, d)
            args.append(os.path.basename(infile))
        for s in setup:
            args += ['--cmd', s]
        for c in l.split(' ;; '):
            args += ['--cmd', c]
        p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
        shutil.rmtree(d)
        o = p.stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip().split('\n')
        o = [x for x in o if x][-1:] if (infile or setup) else o
        outs.append(norm(('OUT ' + '\n    '.join(o) if any(o) else '') + (' ERR ' + p.stderr.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip() if p.stderr else '') + ' [%d]' % p.returncode))
    if both:
        if outs[0] == outs[1]:
            same += 1
            print('SAME', l[:150])
        else:
            print('DIFF', l)
            print('  orig:', outs[0])
            print('  mine:', outs[1])
    else:
        print('>>', l)
        print('  ', outs[0])
if both:
    print('%d/%d same' % (same, len(lines)))

import json, os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, re

ORIG = '/workspace/executable'

a = sys.argv[1:]
exe = ORIG
files = []
full = False
while a and a[0] != '--':
    if a[0] == '-m': exe = MINE; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-F': full = True; a = a[1:]
    else: break
if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='p', dir=os.environ.get('SCRATCH'))
for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
p = subprocess.run([exe] + a, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=300)
print('STDOUT:', p.stdout.decode())
print('STDERR:', p.stderr.decode())
print('EXIT:', p.returncode)
base = json.load(open('/tmp/views-tools/new.bimcraft'))
for f in sorted(os.listdir(d)):

        dd = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, f)))
        print('=== file', f)
        for k, v in dd.items():

            elif k in ('uid', 'library'):

            elif full or k not in base or G.sub('G',json.dumps(base[k])) != G.sub('G',json.dumps(v)):

        bl = {(e['kind'], e['name']) for e in base['library'].values()}
        for id, e in lib.items():

The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands. 247:| Snaps and the ruler | Points picked while drawing stick to what the plan has there, as Revit's snaps do: the ends, middles and centres of walls (an arc's too), grids and components, the centres of columns, structural columns and footings with the corners and edge middles of their outlines (a round one's four quadrants), so a wall can start flush with a column's edge, and the corners of floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; where two straight walls or grids cross; the foot of the perpendicular from the last point to a straight wall or grid; and a wall's centre line, so a wall drawn onto it meets it. It also sticks to the anchors of notes, dimensions, tags, spot elevations, section and elevation marks, detail groups and repeating details; a camera's mark gives its eye and target, never the body, lens or name it is drawn with. Each shows its own marker and its name. A direction from the last point sticks to multiples of an angle (5°, 15°, 30°, 45° or 90°; 15° by default), from east and from the line before it, so corners come out exact, sharp ones too: a dashed guide shows it, and where it crosses a wall or grid the point lands there. The line being drawn carries a ruler: graduations at round lengths, its length and its angle (at the corner it turns once there's a line before it, drawn as an arc). Manage > Snaps switches each snap and sets the angle steps, and Revit's SE, SM, SI, SC, SP and SN take one snap alone for the next point (SO none, SS back); Measure (ME) lays a ruler between two snapped points and reads its length, parts and angle; the `measure` command does the same. Each plan, section and elevation has a background grid, a main grid and a subgrid with their own spacing, divisions, colours and pens, turned by an angle, kept in the view's graphics and controlled by its template; Grid snapping (Manage > Snaps, or the grid menu in the view control bar) lands a free point on its crossings | 248:| Annotation | Aligned dimensions between parallel references, one segment or a chain: wall faces, centre lines and ends, door and window centres and jambs, grids; and between endpoints (a wall's ends and its faces' corners, a line's or a grid's ends, a jamb's), aligned along them or linear, horizontal or vertical, as the cursor lies or the Options Bar says (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them); angular dimensions between two lines that meet, radial and diameter ones on round columns, curved walls, circles and arcs, and arc length ones along a curved wall or an arc; all measuring the model as it is, so they follow what they measure (a change that would turn a reference out of parallel with the others is refused). In a 3D view, aligned dimensions between two points or edges of the model (square to an edge), kept by the view and drawn over it, on either painter and on the sheets that hold it. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. Dimension types, as Revit's type parameters: continuous, baseline or ordinate strings, diagonal, arrow, open arrow or dot ticks, pens, colour, the dimension and witness lines' extensions, gaps and control, and the numbers' font, size, lettering, offset, background, read convention, units and rounding; a dimension's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display (EQ). Tags on any element showing its type, a door's or window's mark, a room's name or any field of its schedule, going where their doors and windows go, with or without a leader; tag everything not tagged yet in one go. Text notes in plans, sections, elevations and on sheets, at any angle, over several lines, with a leader, of a text type (font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour and a border: any font the system has, Arial by default, which a look-alike such as Liberation Sans stands in for where it isn't installed, or IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono or our single-stroke lettering; any script a font on the system has, CJK included), written and rewritten on the canvas (Shift+Enter breaks a line), and with Override Formatting, parts of them bold, italic or underlined whatever their type; spot elevations reading the top of what they stand on in plan (a floor, a roof's slope, a stair's tread), or the height of a point in a section | 249:| Views | A floor plan per level with Revit's view range: cut at its cut plane (1200 mm up by default), what lies below seen from it down to the bottom, faint beyond it down to the view depth, and roofs overhead up to the top: wall poché with clean joins at any angle, compound walls' layers, hatched with their materials' cut patterns where they're wide enough (else lighter where they aren't structure), door swings, window glass, room tags, grid bubbles, dimensions, door and window tags; PNG and SVG, which letter the view's name at the plan's bottom left (the window letters it too, over the canvas and on the screen only, which File > Settings can hide; a viewport on a sheet has its own title). Sections and elevations along any line: the cut in poché (a roof's along its slope, a compound wall's, floor's, roof's or ceiling's with its layers), what lies beyond in hidden line, levels named with their heights, grids; the four building elevations in one go; their marks on every plan; PNG. Crop regions on plans and sections: the view shows only what's inside, grids stopping at its edge with their bubbles. A reflected ceiling plan per level: its walls cut at 2300 mm (over the doors, through the windows), looking up at the ceilings, their tiles and the shafts through them, and at the beams and columns over the cut up to the ceilings, in projection (one over a ceiling is hidden by it). A 3D view, from any angle: walls with their doors and windows cut out, slabs and ceilings with their shafts cut out, columns, stairs and roofs, door leaves and glass, shaded (each layer in its material's colour), with an edge wherever faces meet, but none between the facets of a curve (a curved wall's, a round form's, an imported mesh's where its triangles turn less than 20°), which shades smoothly across them; PNG. A plan or a section always has a scale, 1 : n (1 : 100, or 1/8" = 1'-0" in feet and inches, until set): it stands for paper at that scale, and its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, marks, dimension ticks) and its line weights are that paper's, so on screen a line is as thick as it would print at the zoom (at least a pixel; Thin Lines draws all of them one). A line weight is a pen, 1 to 16, or 0, a hairline, the thinnest line the screen, a PNG or a printer draws, at any scale and zoom; what pens 1 to 16 draw is the project's Line Weights (Manage > Line Weights, as Revit's): the model's pens at each of a list of scales, a view taking the nearest scale's, and the annotation's (dimensions, tags, text, grids, levels, marks) at any scale, edited by scale, added and deleted, applied as one undo step and saved with the project. Which pen each model category draws its own lines in, cut and seen, is the project's Object Styles (Manage > Object Styles, as Revit's), in every plan and section, a view's Visibility/Graphics over them. Detail lines draw in one view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet) in a line style: a pen, a colour and a line pattern, its freely ordered gaps, straight strokes, dots, centered parallel offsets, waves, zigzags and text in mm on paper so it reads the same at any scale; the Line Pattern Creator previews straight or curved paths and letters text with bundled IBM Plex Sans, while geometry and dimensions keep the centerline (Manage > Line Styles, styles and patterns made, changed, renamed and deleted as one undo step; a project starts with Thin, Medium and Wide Lines, a Hairline, Hidden, Centre and Overhead Lines). A cut wall's outline is inked over its poché, and not across where walls join. A plan or a section has a detail level too: coarse (what it cuts in one poché, an opening as its gap and jambs), medium (a compound element's layers and an opening's leaf, swing and glass) or fine, as it has always drawn (the layers' patterns too); the 3D view has a visual style: shaded, hidden line (paper-white faces with their edges, what a face hides staying hidden) or wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). A viewport takes its view's scale; a sheet keeps annotation at paper size. A view fitted into an image (a PNG, Zoom to Fit) leaves as much room round it as its annotation takes at its scale, which grows with the scale, so 1 : 500 doesn't cut its grid bubbles or level names off. A level can have more plans than its own, as Revit's Duplicate View makes them (`duplicate_view`, DP): each a plan view with its own view range, crop and graphics and its own dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations over the same model; with detailing it starts with its source's annotation; a dependent view follows its parent's view range and graphics (scale and detail too), has a crop of its own, and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. They go on sheets, take view templates and have ceiling plans as levels do. Sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet. The 3D view is parallel (axonometric) or in perspective, as through a camera: picked from Projection in its Properties (or `perspective`), seen through a lens of a focal length typed there, from an eye raised or lowered to a height typed there, and orbited, panned, zoomed, picked and edited as ever, on the processor or the graphics card. The Camera tool (`camera`) makes a view of its own, as Revit's does: an eye and a target are clicked in a plan (each at a height over it, typed in the Options Bar), and a named 3D view in perspective opens looking from the eye at the target; it is listed under 3D Views in the Project Browser, opens from its own camera, and its name, eye, target and lens are read and changed in Properties, whether it is open or its mark on the plan is picked (`camera` reads or changes one too, by name or id; a view with no camera shows the azimuth and elevation it is framed by on a sheet instead). The camera shows on its level's plan as a mark at its eye with a line to what it looks at: it is picked there and opened by its right-click menu (or a double click), and its eye and target follow the mouse as the view is orbited, panned or zoomed, so leaving the view and coming back stands it where it was left. The 3D view has a section box, as Revit's: six planes square to the axes that keep what lies between them, the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, turned on and off with BX or its Properties, each face dragged by its grip in the view or typed in Properties, its extents kept while it's off; the levels it doesn't reach are left out. steps.message:
Read /tmp/views-tools/BRIEF.md first and follow it (hard rules, base commit, how to test, how to finish).

YOUR PART (DIMS): the commands `dimension` (in `src/views/dims.rs`, with the `dimension` element's `element_view` and `check`) and `dimension_constraint`, `dimension_text`, `dimension_value` (in `src/views/constraints.rs`, which also has `keep(pr)`: run after every command that changes the model, before the check, already wired into `Session::execute` through `crate::views::keep`; it solves each constrained dimension and moves what it measures to, or refuses the command saying which dimension can't be kept). Other sub-agents do, in parallel: views, sheets, crops; 3D views, dimension_3d, spots; graphics, filters, templates; text/tag/linework; detail lines; regions and groups. Don't do theirs.

Observed so far (verify; there's much more to find):
- On a closed 10000 x 6000 box of Generic - 200mm walls (ids 100002 south, 100003 east, 100004 north, 100005 west), `dimension {"refs":[{"id":100005},{"id":100003}],"at":[5000,3000]}` → `{"id":100008,"values":[10000.0]}`, saved `{"guid","category":"dimension","level":<level guid>,"kind":"aligned","refs":[{"id":<wall guid>,"face":"centre"},{"id":<wall guid>,"face":"centre"}],"at":[5000.0,3000.0],"type":<dimension-type guid>}`; `elements` adds `"labels":["10000"]`, `"values":[10000.0]` and `"type":"Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial"` (by name; `elements` is READERS' and calls our `element_view`).
- Faces: an Exterior - 300mm wall (layers exterior first: finish 100, thermal 50, structure 140, finish 10) drawn west→east at y=0, with refs right, left, centre and a grid at y=1000, measures [150,150,X] (refs sorted south to north): X = 850 (location centre), 1000 (exterior-finish: the exterior face is the LEFT one), 700 (interior-finish), 780 (core-centre), 850 (exterior-core), 710 (interior-core). `centre` is the wall's centre line, not its location line. `src/views/model.rs` has these (thickness, core, centre line, faces, arc walls).
- "dimension 100002: a dimension measures between 2 to 10000 references" (model check after the command; `dimension {"refs":[],…,"foo":1}` isn't refused for `foo`). "dimension: no level or plan view named `Nope` (the levels are: Level 1, Level 2)" (`crate::model::level_param`).
- A door is saved `{"guid","category":"door","type":<guid>,"host":<wall guid>,"offset":2000.0,"sill":0.0,"mark":"1","flip_facing":false,"flip_hand":false}` (`offset` of its middle along its wall from the wall's start, its width from `types.door[<type name>].width`; windows alike); a grid `{"guid","category":"grid","name","start","end"}`; a detail line `{"guid","category":"line","view":<view guid>,"style":<guid>,"start","end"}` (or `points`+`arcs`+`closed`, `start`+`end`+`arc`, `centre`+`radius` (a circle), `centre`+`radii`+`angle`+`span`, `control`, `fit`); a round column `{"category":"column","type":…,"at",…}` of a type with `"round":true`; a curved wall has `"arc": degrees`.
- Refs (see `/workspace/executable commands` for `dimension`, and the Dimensions section of `/workspace/docs/areas/views-and-graphics.md`): wall centre/left/right/start/end, door/window centre and jambs, grids, straight detail lines and their ends, `point: start|end` (a face's end where the outline turns off it: at the mitred corner of joined walls — so you need how walls join at corners: probe), points [x, y] on those lines, `{endpoint: [x, y]}` (within 100 mm); kinds aligned, linear (`orient`), angular, radial, diameter, arc_length; `type`; `prefix`, `suffix`, `above`, `below`, `replace`, `equality` (README's table); the reply's `values`; what the model check refuses (lines not parallel, not square to a linear one's line, points all in one place, references that went away); its `labels` as the dimension type's units/rounding say (units are styles' `units` command).
- dimension_text (segment texts), dimension_constraint (`equal`, `locked` segments; keep after every command), dimension_value (moves what the segment ends at along the dimension: walls, grids, doors/windows along their wall, detail lines — write those moves yourself in your files, as the original's `move` would move them, and learn what it saves).
- Walls, doors, grids are made by other areas (ARCH, the core's `grid` works in our binary); build inputs with the original.
