229:| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
230:| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
231:| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
233:| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
234:| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
235:| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
248:| Annotation | Aligned dimensions between parallel references, one segment or a chain: wall faces, centre lines and ends, door and window centres and jambs, grids; and between endpoints (a wall's ends and its faces' corners, a line's or a grid's ends, a jamb's), aligned along them or linear, horizontal or vertical, as the cursor lies or the Options Bar says (Auto, Aligned, Horizontal, Vertical; Space steps them); angular dimensions between two lines that meet, radial and diameter ones on round columns, curved walls, circles and arcs, and arc length ones along a curved wall or an arc; all measuring the model as it is, so they follow what they measure (a change that would turn a reference out of parallel with the others is refused). In a 3D view, aligned dimensions between two points or edges of the model (square to an edge), kept by the view and drawn over it, on either painter and on the sheets that hold it. A dimension's number takes a typed length and moves what it measures; locked segments show their padlocks always; Align leaves a padlock that keeps the two lines aligned after every change, refusing one the other locks can't hold with. Dimension types, as Revit's type parameters: continuous, baseline or ordinate strings, diagonal, arrow, open arrow or dot ticks, pens, colour, the dimension and witness lines' extensions, gaps and control, and the numbers' font, size, lettering, offset, background, read convention, units and rounding; a dimension's own prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display (EQ). Tags on any element showing its type, a door's or window's mark, a room's name or any field of its schedule, going where their doors and windows go, with or without a leader; tag everything not tagged yet in one go. Text notes in plans, sections, elevations and on sheets, at any angle, over several lines, with a leader, of a text type (font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, colour and a border: any font the system has, Arial by default, which a look-alike such as Liberation Sans stands in for where it isn't installed, or IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono or our single-stroke lettering; any script a font on the system has, CJK included), written and rewritten on the canvas (Shift+Enter breaks a line), and with Override Formatting, parts of them bold, italic or underlined whatever their type; spot elevations reading the top of what they stand on in plan (a floor, a roof's slope, a stair's tread), or the height of a point in a section |
265:| Desktop | Revit's layout: ribbon tabs with a contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type Selector and Type Properties, the Project Browser and views in tabs; a plan and a reflected ceiling plan per level that pan and zoom, sections and elevations, a 3D view that orbits, and sheets; tools for walls (straight or arcs, on the location line picked), doors, windows, columns, roofs by footprint (and Gable Edge, to stand a roof's edge upright) and by extrusion, dormers, floors (and a floor's slope arrow), ceilings, shaft openings, sketch mode (Edit Boundary on a floor, a ceiling, a roof or a shaft, and Boundary Line or Sketch Ceiling for a new one: lines, rectangles, arcs and Pick Walls, sketch lines with ids of their own picked by click or box and moved by their grips, Finish Edit Mode saying what's wrong and marking the lines; in the 3D view, Edit Boundary sketches on the element's own plane, and Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft sketch on the view's Work Plane: a level from the list, a surface or three points picked on the model (snapping to corners), each with an offset, at any angle; walls, beams and braces, columns and structural columns, footings, pipes, ducts, conduits, cable trays and components draw in the 3D view on the level face under the cursor, snapping as a plan does, a run climbing from one face to another; they need it horizontal), masses (and floors, walls and roofs from them), stairs and ramps (run by run, turning at landings), railings, rooms, levels, grids, dimensions (aligned, angular, radial), spot elevations, text, detail lines, filled and masking regions, tags, sections and elevations; Flip, Attach Top/Base and Detach Top/Base for walls; a wall, floor, roof or ceiling type's layers in Type Properties, and the project's materials in Manage > Materials; project parameters in Manage > Project Parameters, and their values in Properties; schedules from View > Schedules, their fields, filters, sorting and totals in Schedule Properties; the Component tool, families and their types in the Type Selector, the Project Browser and Type Properties, a component's own parameters in Properties, and Load Family; Crop View with grips to drag a crop region's edges, and the view range in Properties; project units, metric or feet and inches; Revit's selection (click, Ctrl, Shift, Tab, window and crossing boxes); dragging and the Modify panel (Align, Offset, Mirror, Split, Move, Copy, Rotate, Trim/Extend to Corner) and its Phasing panel (Demolish); Paint and Remove Paint on its Geometry panel, for the 3D view; typed lengths and temporary dimensions; undo and redo; open, save and export; a light and a dark theme; English, Portuguese or Spanish. The Manage tab has the Materials window (with textures and pictures), the Favorites, Object Styles, Annotation Settings (Line Weights, Line Styles, Line Patterns and Fill Patterns, a fill pattern simple or made of detail lines picked in a plan and the tile between two corners), and the Family Editor (New Family, Edit Family) |
376:| Align, trim, split, offset | Align (AL): hover to highlight an edge or centre line, pick the reference, then the target edge. It turns and moves walls, columns, components, slabs, roofs, structural/MEP runs and detail geometry onto the reference in one undo step; hosted doors and windows slide along their wall. While sketching, align sketch lines to model edges or other sketch lines; joined endpoints follow, with sketch undo until Finish. Trim/Extend to Corner (TR): pick two walls on the parts to keep. Split Element (SL): click a wall where to cut it. Offset (OF): point to a wall, and a copy goes to the cursor's side at the Options Bar's distance |
398:| Materials | Manage > Materials: the project's library. Pick a material, or New for another, and set its name, colour, cut pattern and surface pattern; Delete takes one out that no layer uses. A layer picks its material from the library. Texture picks a pattern drawn in code, or Picture… a PNG or JPEG file from your disk, for the 3D view; its tile's width and height, angle and offset follow; Save to Favorites keeps the material, and Favorites… opens them |

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Probe the original: p.py [-f infile] [-m] -- run args...
Runs in a fresh temp dir; prints stdout/stderr/exit and, for each .bimcraft written,
the elements (and top-level sections that differ from a new project's)."""
import json, os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, re
G=re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ['MINE'] if 'MINE' in os.environ else '/nonexistent-set-MINE'
a = sys.argv[1:]
exe = ORIG
files = []
full = False
while a and a[0] != '--':
    if a[0] == '-m': exe = MINE; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-F': full = True; a = a[1:]
    else: break
if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='p', dir=os.environ.get('SCRATCH'))
for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
p = subprocess.run([exe] + a, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=300)
print('STDOUT:', p.stdout.decode())
print('STDERR:', p.stderr.decode())
print('EXIT:', p.returncode)
base = json.load(open('/tmp/views-tools/new.bimcraft'))
for f in sorted(os.listdir(d)):
    if f.endswith('.bimcraft') and f not in [os.path.basename(x) for x in files]:
        dd = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, f)))
        print('=== file', f)
        for k, v in dd.items():
            if k == 'elements':
                for id, e in v.items():
                    print(' ', id, json.dumps(e, ensure_ascii=False))
            elif k in ('uid', 'library'):
                continue
            elif full or k not in base or G.sub('G',json.dumps(base[k])) != G.sub('G',json.dumps(v)):
                if k in ('format','name','next_id','units','language'):
                    print(' top', k, json.dumps(v))
                else:
                    print(' top', k, json.dumps(v, ensure_ascii=False)[:3000])
        # library entries not in a new project's kinds
        lib = dd.get('library', {})
        bl = {(e['kind'], e['name']) for e in base['library'].values()}
        for id, e in lib.items():
            if (e['kind'], e['name']) not in bl:
                print('  lib', id, json.dumps(e, ensure_ascii=False))
shutil.rmtree(d)
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run each command line of a file (or stdin) separately on the original (and optionally mine).
usage: each.py [-m] [-b] [-f in.bimcraft] [-s 'setup cmd']... < cmds.txt
  -m: run mine instead; -b: run both and mark differences; -f: open this project first.
Each line: a command `id {json}` (or several separated by ' ;; ')."""
import os, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, re
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ['MINE'] if 'MINE' in os.environ else '/nonexistent-set-MINE'
G = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
a = sys.argv[1:]
exes = [ORIG]
infile = None
setup = []
both = False
while a:
    if a[0] == '-m': exes = [MINE]; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-b': exes = [ORIG, MINE]; both = True; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': infile = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-s': setup.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    else: break
src = open(a[0]) if a else sys.stdin
lines = [l.rstrip('\n') for l in src if l.strip() and not l.startswith('#')]
def norm(s):
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m) + 1)
        return m[g]
    return G.sub(rep, s)
same = 0
for l in lines:
    outs = []
    for exe in exes:
        d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='e', dir=os.environ.get('SCRATCH'))
        args = [exe, 'run']
        if infile:
            shutil.copy(infile, d)
            args.append(os.path.basename(infile))
        for s in setup:
            args += ['--cmd', s]
        for c in l.split(' ;; '):
            args += ['--cmd', c]
        p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
        shutil.rmtree(d)
        o = p.stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip().split('\n')
        o = [x for x in o if x][-1:] if (infile or setup) else o
        outs.append(norm(('OUT ' + '\n    '.join(o) if any(o) else '') + (' ERR ' + p.stderr.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip() if p.stderr else '') + ' [%d]' % p.returncode))
    if both:
        if outs[0] == outs[1]:
            same += 1
            print('SAME', l[:150])
        else:
            print('DIFF', l)
            print('  orig:', outs[0])
            print('  mine:', outs[1])
    else:
        print('>>', l)
        print('  ', outs[0])
if both:
    print('%d/%d same' % (same, len(lines)))

7:view template controls them as groups of their own (`Group::Scale`, `Detail`, `Style`, in `Graphics::resolved`, `check_followed` and the three
20:`background_grid` group. `graphics` and `template` accept a grid patch (spacing in millimetres, divisions, rotation, two
97:patterns draw solid with bounded work. Region profiles, snapping, alignment and dimensions use the original centerline.
194:Detail groups (`groups.rs`) are Revit's: `create_group` (GP) makes the detail lines, filled regions and text notes given,
195:all of one view, into a group type (`Model::detail_groups`) holding them as `Member`s about the middle of them, in no
196:view, and puts one `DetailGroup` element in their place. Members are parts (`HasPart`, `parts_now`): each has its own id
197:and GUID, and their line styles and region types are library references like an element's (`lib_refs_mut`), so renames
198:reach them; `Model::check` holds each to what the same element in a view must be (`annotation_ok`). A placed group is an
199:origin, an angle and `mirrored`; `groups::placed` gives its members as elements of its view (through
200:`commands::transform`, as Move and Rotate take elements), which `render::detail_group` draws, regions under lines and notes,
201:all owned by the group, so it picks, moves, rotates and mirrors as one. `ungroup` (UG) puts those elements back in the view;
202:`group_type` renames a type (its groups follow) or deletes it while nothing is of it. A `RepeatingDetail` places a group
203:along a line every `spacing` from its start, each turned along it (at most `MAX_REPEATS`), as Revit's Repeating Detail
204:Component does with a detail component. A view draws every member of every group and repeat in it each time, so
205:`Model::check` caps what one view places: a group counts its type's members, a repeating detail its members once for each
206:repeat, and `MAX_PLACED` (10,000) is the most in a view (measured with the probe `probe_the_cost_of_the_most_hatched_regions_a_view_may_place`,
207:10,000 hatched regions take about 0.1 s to draw at 3 m across and 0.5 s at 30 m across, 2.8 million primitives, on a machine that
212:(it still reads the right way round) and turns with the group's angle. The file holds a group's members as elements, and
214:(`/detail_groups/<name>/members/<i>/element/...`). Deleting a line style that a filled region or a group's member is drawn in
215:is refused with the region's or the group's name. On the desktop, Annotate > Detail has Detail Group, Repeating Detail and
216:Create Group, and the right-click menu has Create Group and Ungroup.
218:A project with any of this (line styles and patterns, fill patterns, region types, detail lines, regions, groups, repeating
247:controls groups of the views that follow it (categories, filters, a plan's view range through
290:`graphics` command; Clear Overrides clears only that cell. Annotation categories expose projection patterns for filled regions.
293:cuts and regions draw the layers with the same bounded pattern renderer as filled region types; the pattern's drafting/model
448:Fill patterns, filled region types and filled regions (`fills.rs`) follow line patterns and styles. A `FillPattern` is
458:only draws nothing and never trips a cap. `render::filled_region` draws a region's
460:(`SketchLine::style`, a library reference as the region's is) else the region's, or not at all (`invisible`, or a region
462:lines picked take it at once. A plan draws its regions after the model and before the annotation, in a loop of their own (sections
463:and sheets likewise), so a masking region hides the walls under it but not the note on it. A `FilledRegion` is annotation of
465:when drawn, any number of outlines; Edit Boundary edits it as any other. Patterns and region types are library entries,
466:renamed with their references (a type follows its patterns, a region its type and line style) and refused deleted while

results.content:
(`text::remap`: the common start and end keep theirs, what came in takes the format before it). `text::layout` lays a note out
in mm on paper (lines `LINE_PITCH` sizes apart, each character's place and width), which `render::note` draws (each letter a
`Prim::Fill` of rings filled by the non-zero rule, our lettering and Plex Mono's bold as lines, underlines as lines; `Part::Text`)
and which the desktop's editor reads for its caret, its selection and a click's place (`Layout::caret`, `boxes`, `index_at`;
`Drawing::note_frame` turns layout mm into the drawing's pixels and back). The canvas fills a letter, holes and all, from
`text::triangles` (strips between every corner's and crossing's height), kept by its points for the frames that draw it again.
A file of format 7 has notes with a `size`: reading it gives each a type of that size (`Model::typed_notes`), and `Model::check`
refuses a `size` left on one. A note holds up to `MAX_NOTE` (4,000) characters and `MAX_RUNS` (1,000) runs.

Detail groups (`groups.rs`) are Revit's: `create_group` (GP) makes the detail lines, filled regions and text notes given,
all of one view, into a group type (`Model::detail_groups`) holding them as `Member`s about the middle of them, in no
view, and puts one `DetailGroup` element in their place. Members are parts (`HasPart`, `parts_now`): each has its own id
and GUID, and their line styles and region types are library references like an element's (`lib_refs_mut`), so renames
reach them; `Model::check` holds each to what the same element in a view must be (`annotation_ok`). A placed group is an
origin, an angle and `mirrored`; `groups::placed` gives its members as elements of its view (through
`commands::transform`, as Move and Rotate take elements), which `render::detail_group` draws, regions under lines and notes,
all owned by the group, so it picks, moves, rotates and mirrors as one. `ungroup` (UG) puts those elements back in the view;
`group_type` renames a type (its groups follow) or deletes it while nothing is of it. A `RepeatingDetail` places a group
along a line every `spacing` from its start, each turned along it (at most `MAX_REPEATS`), as Revit's Repeating Detail
Component does with a detail component. A view draws every member of every group and repeat in it each time, so
`Model::check` caps what one view places: a group counts its type's members, a repeating detail its members once for each
repeat, and `MAX_PLACED` (10,000) is the most in a view (measured with the probe `probe_the_cost_of_the_most_hatched_regions_a_view_may_place`,
10,000 hatched regions take about 0.1 s to draw at 3 m across and 0.5 s at 30 m across, 2.8 million primitives, on a machine that
is not busy, in a dev build (the core is built at opt-level 2 there) and in release alike, and up to 0.29 s and 1.10 s in the dev
build on a busy one; the 200,000 it once allowed took 6 s and 30 million primitives). A placed member that is a huge circle costs
more (the probe `probe_the_cost_of_placed_members_that_are_huge_circles`: 8,192 points each, about 0.2 ms to draw and 3 to 5 ms to
rasterize, 8 ms on a busy machine), so a view at the cap of them can take a minute or more to render; the cap stays. A member note keeps its own angle under a pure mirror
(it still reads the right way round) and turns with the group's angle. The file holds a group's members as elements, and
`Model::read` leaves out of them what this build doesn't know, as it does for any element
(`/detail_groups/<name>/members/<i>/element/...`). Deleting a line style that a filled region or a group's member is drawn in
is refused with the region's or the group's name. On the desktop, Annotate > Detail has Detail Group, Repeating Detail and
Create Group, and the right-click menu has Create Group and Ungroup.

A project with any of this (line styles and patterns, fill patterns, region types, detail lines, regions, groups, repeating
details, sketches) needs file format 6, and every file is saved as 6 now, with or without any of it: a build that reads up to 5
would fail on one with a serde error, so 6 makes it say that the file is from a newer BIMCraft (even for a plain project). Nothing
in a file of 5 changes, so `Model::migrate` has no step for 5 to 6.

The Options Bar's Offset puts a line, an arc or a polyline beside the points clicked; a rectangle, a polygon or a circle grows
by it as a whole (`grown`, its corners joined), and a spline or an ellipse takes none (`Shape::offsets`). Modify's Offset takes
ellipses and splines too, as a spline through points within `FIT_TOL` of the true offset (`curves::offset_fit`), refused where
it would fold over itself. While a shape is drawn its numbers can be typed (`draw::numbers`, `reading`, `typed`): a rectangle's
width and height (Tab between them, the canvas taking the Tab from egui's focus), a circle's or a polygon's radius, the third
point's radius, angle or reach; anything else typed is a length toward the cursor, as a line's, in sketch mode too. The canvas
labels them as they read (`shape_dimensions`). A spline or a polyline finishes with Enter, a double click or the right-click
menu's Finish Drawing; Fillet Arc previews the arc nearest the cursor and its radius, Offset a dashed ghost of the copy, and
----
and annotation. Annotation says which view it is in: a note or a spot elevation by `view`, a dimension or a tag by an optional `view` beside its
`level` or its host (none: the level's own plan), and `Model::annotation_in` asks whether a plan draws it. A command that takes a `level` takes a
plan view too (`plan_param`): what is built stands on its level, what is dimensioned or tagged is in the view. A dependent view (`parent`) follows
its parent's view range and graphics (`plan_source`; `graphics`, `scale`, `detail` and `visual_style` refuse it, naming the parent), has a crop
of its own and draws its parent's annotation as well as its own. Deleting a view deletes what is annotated in it and its dependents; a level
takes its plan views with it. A project that has none writes the same file as before. A plan's own name, lettered at its bottom left, is in the drawings that make an image (`plan`, `ceiling_plan`: `titled`), not in the window's (`draw`, `draw_ceiling`) or a sheet's (`draw_at`), where the tab and the viewport's title say it. The desktop: View > Duplicate View, DP, and the Project
Browser's right-click, which also has Delete for a plan view; `Sheet::Plan` and `Sheet::Ceiling` hold the key.

Fill patterns, filled region types and filled regions (`fills.rs`) follow line patterns and styles. A `FillPattern` is
families of parallel lines as a PAT file has them (`HatchLine`: an angle, an origin, a spacing across, a shift along, and
dashes, a space negative and a dot 0), drafting (mm on paper, so the same at any scale) or model (mm in the building); no
lines, it fills solid. `fills::strokes` lays a pattern over any outlines with holes (inside an odd number of rings), each line
cut to the view's window (what lies past it is never counted or drawn), and gives up rather than draw past a cap: more than
50,000 strokes, or more work than `fills::MAX_WORK` (a line tried against every edge, a dash stepped over), which bounds a
dense pattern over an outline of thousands of corners and dots a twentieth of a millimetre apart. A pattern that gives up draws
none of its lines and says so in `Drawing::notes` (`the fill pattern of element 100012 has more lines than a view can hold at
this scale`), which the `render` command returns as `notes` for plans and sheets; a front end can show them. `FillPattern::check`
wants a dash (a dot, 0, is one), a space and a pattern at least `MIN_SPACING` long in a family's dashes, so a list of spaces
only draws nothing and never trips a cap. `render::filled_region` draws a region's
masking (paper), its background and its foreground pattern, then its boundary's sketch lines, each in its own line style
(`SketchLine::style`, a library reference as the region's is) else the region's, or not at all (`invisible`, or a region
of invisible lines with none of its own); in sketch mode the Options Bar's Line Style is what the lines drawn take, and the
lines picked take it at once. A plan draws its regions after the model and before the annotation, in a loop of their own (sections
and sheets likewise), so a masking region hides the walls under it but not the note on it. A `FilledRegion` is annotation of
its view (`Model::annotation_plan`, so a duplicated plan has its own) and its sketch is a `sketch::SketchLine` list, solved
when drawn, any number of outlines; Edit Boundary edits it as any other. Patterns and region types are library entries,
renamed with their references (a type follows its patterns, a region its type and line style) and refused deleted while
used. The desktop has Annotate > Region (Filled Region, FR, and Masking Region, sketch mode with the type and the line style
in the Options Bar), Properties (the Type Selector above the instance fields, Line Style with invisible lines), and Manage >
Annotation Settings > Fill Patterns (`fillpatterns.rs`: the patterns as one draft, each a name, drafting or model and a
swatch; one of whole lines (Simple Lines, `FillPattern::whole_lines`) edited line by line with Edit Lines (an angle, an origin
and a spacing each: a shift only staggers dashes, and dashed patterns are drawn and made with Custom), one made of lines
redefined from lines (Redefine, as wide as Edit Lines), any other (dashed, imported or a starter's) kept as it came, and Import and Export of PAT files at the right, Replace imported by same name saying what an import does
with a name the list has; region types are edited from a region with Edit Type, on the same draft).

A custom pattern is made of lines drawn, as pyRevit's Make Pattern makes one (`fills::make`, the `make_fill_pattern` command):
the detail lines picked, all of one view, cut to the rectangle between two corners (the tile), each a family that runs on into the
next tiles' copies of itself. A line repeats only at a slope `(i W, j H)` of whole tiles (`i`, `j` at most `MAX_STEPS`, 48), so one
drawn at another is turned to the simplest such slope within `TURN` (0.25°), else the nearest; its family's dashes are its length
and a space to the repeat `L = |(i W, j H)|`, its lines `W H / L` apart, each shifted along by the lattice's other vector
`(c W, d H)`, `i d - j c = 1` (Euclid's). A line on the tile's edge and its copy on the opposite one are one family; curves go as
their drawn points' chords. A model pattern is as drawn; a drafting one is the drawing on paper at the view's scale, which the
pattern keeps (`FillPattern::drawn`, saved with it): turned from one to the other (the dialog's Type, or `fill_pattern`'s `target`
without `lines`), it is rescaled (`retargeted`), and the dialog offers Redefine for it where a simple one has Edit Lines, which
picks the lines and corners again and keeps its name and type. A pattern holds at most `MAX_FAMILIES`
(256) families. In the desktop, New Pattern > Custom hides the dialog while the lines are picked as anything is (Enter, or the
right-click menu's Finish), then the corners (`Tool::PatternCorner`), and brings it back with the pattern previewed: OK, Pick
Again, Cancel. Esc, another tool or another view brings the dialog back. `pat.rs` reads and writes PAT files (`;%UNITS`,
`;%TYPE`, a negative offset stepping the other way; a pattern that can't be one left out with why) for the dialog and for the
`import_fill_patterns` and `export_fill_patterns` commands. A PAT file is hostile input: `read` stops after `MAX_PATTERNS`
(2,000) patterns and counts the rest, `Read::left_out` names the first `MAX_LEFT_OUT` (100) with `left_out_count` for all, a line
is cut at 22 fields and a bad one is echoed to 40 letters, a family whose dashes are all spaces is left out, and a file over
`MAX_TEXT` (16 MiB) is refused unread. A byte that isn't UTF-8 is read as the Latin-1 letter with its number, which is right
for accents and not for Windows-1252's punctuation at 0x80 to 0x9F. The description after a pattern's name isn't kept. The
`import_fill_patterns` command takes the file's `text` up to that size too (a name is limited to 256 letters, a file isn't) and
replies with the first 100 `left_out` and `left_out_count`.

Edit Type opens a region's Type Properties from either a selected region or an active sketch: select a type, create a
new one, duplicate one with its settings, or rename it. Foreground and background each have their own pattern (including
None) and color; masking controls whether paper hides geometry underneath. The combined preview shows both layers and
a sample line behind them, so masking can be checked before applying. The Patterns tab edits and creates patterns in
the same draft. Apply and OK update definitions and the selected instances in one transaction; a type edit affects every
region of that type, a duplicate is assigned only to the selected instances or the active sketch, and Cancel discards
unapplied work. Duplicate or blank names are refused without replacing another definition. Renames preserve library
identity and update the active sketch's type reference. The palette's Type Selector and Edit Type use the same region
types as the Options Bar.

The instance parameter grid has no second Region Type field: the Type Selector is the type control. Non-masking regions
replace model backgrounds while retaining visible cut outlines, cut foreground patterns (including solid foregrounds),
and projected model lines. `render/regions.rs` finds the drawing's ink once (the model layer's lines and patterns, less what a
later fill covers, so a low wall hidden by a cut wall does not reappear; and a section's or elevation's hidden-line picture as
runs of its pixels, which is all the ink an elevation has) and gives each region the part of it in its area: the outline less
its holes, inside an odd number of rings, less the masking regions drawn before it. A line is kept where it lies in the area or
within half its stroke of it (its pen's width as it will draw, from the owner's object style while the pen is not set yet), so a
region edge sketched on a wall face keeps the whole face; Visibility/Graphics weights wider than the object style's are not
allowed for. Lines are cut by the rings and the masks as they are, never by boolean operations on polygons (which are cubic in
the corners an outline can have): only the model's filled patterns are, by the pieces of the area they reach. The pieces of a
polyline that meet stay one line, so its corners keep their joins, and a dashed line's dashes stay where they were (the dashes of
the cycle a piece begins in are solid lines of their own). A section's ink belongs to the region that keeps it (`Part::Pattern`),
so a sheet's viewport, which keeps what an element owns, has it. A caller that has the section's picture (the desktop's, a sheet's,
`section_png`'s) hands it in (`render::section_over`, `section_at_over`), at the view's size or a multiple of it (a screen with more
pixels to the point), and the ink is the picture's own pixels, as runs: a row of a pixel's height, and a run of up to two pixels
that sits on one of the row above (the edge of a tall wall) joined to it as one vertical line, so 200 walls 20 m tall at 4000 x 2600
px are some hundreds of lines and not a million runs. A picture of more than 250,000 runs (noise, not drawings) keeps the first
250,000 and the drawing's `notes` say the ink of the last rows is under the region. `render::section` draws a picture of its own
when a non-masking region wants one, which costs what the picture does, every call. Masking still hides the model; detail annotation remains above the
region. The same display list feeds the desktop, PNG, SVG and sheet viewports.

Limits, kept as Revit has them or not yet built: a non-masking region with a solid background hides a room's tag text while its outlines
stay (Revit keeps room tags above filled regions: not verified); grids, levels and room fills are drawn before the regions, so a masking
region hides them; there is no Bring to Front or Send to Back, a region is over the model and under the annotation, in the order of its
id; Move and Rotate carry a region's or a floor's model pattern with it (`pattern_origin`), where Revit may leave a model pattern fixed in
the building, and Align moves it; a filled region drawn on a sheet itself is plain annotation over the viewports, so a solid one hides
what lies under it (Revit has no regions on sheets).

Sketch snapping (`snap::in_sketch`) combines the visible model's wall faces and slab edges, detail lines and existing
region boundaries in the active view, and the draft's own lines. It supports endpoints, midpoints (of each segment of a
polyline), intersections (where two walls meet is one too), perpendiculars, nearest points and angle guides, the anchors of
annotation (a note's insertion point and leader, a tag's head, a dimension's stations, a spot elevation, section and elevation
marks, detail groups and repeating details), and a camera's eye and target rather than its mark's body or name, honoring Manage > Snaps
and one-point overrides. An element being edited is omitted as a model snap target; its draft supplies the boundary instead.
Rectangle and arc previews use the same origin points and Shift constraint as a click. Annotation in another independent view,
or hidden by Visibility/Graphics, is excluded. A plan view cuts where its own view range says (`plan_range` of the view, not of its
level); a section or an elevation has no plan to snap to, only its own detail lines and regions. Of what the plan builds, the
nearest `MAX_OUTLINES` elements within reach have their outlines snapped to (one `walls::Index` for them all), and the nearest
`MAX_NEAR` chords are tried against each other. Ceilings snap in a floor plan as well as a ceiling plan, because a snap does not know
which of the two the cursor is in, and the members of a detail group are not snap targets.

The reference workflows are Autodesk's [fill layers](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2024/ENU/Revit-GetStarted/files/GUID-8A38ADC8-98A6-4A30-BD21-1886F044F6ED.htm),
[region editing](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2026/ENU/Revit-DocumentPresent/files/GUID-183D9B1E-6554-4C19-9EA9-B32C8D2A5C9D.htm),
and [sketch snaps](https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/2022/ENU/Revit-Customize/files/GUID-A3947840-1F30-41D7-AF75-B61687952A07.htm).
Boundary weights follow each boundary line's style. See also Autodesk's [region masking behavior](https://www.autodesk.com/support/technical/article/caas/sfdcarticles/sfdcarticles/Filled-Region-with-solid-fill-does-not-cover-all-elements-in-Revit.html).

library reference like a region type's), over the patterns drawn in code (`model::Pattern`), which stay for the materials
that name them: `material` takes either name for `cut` and `surface`, and the desktop's material editor lists both. A fill

rotated as Revit's: a filled region and a floor hold `pattern_origin` and `pattern_angle` (`fills::strokes_placed`), which

element has no model pattern, or the lines aren't parallel or have no length), so every front end gets the same answer and
sets it with `modify`. `pattern_origin` and `pattern_angle` are in the `modify`, `filled_region` and `floor` command docs, and
`elements` shows them for a region and a floor even at their defaults.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()
USAGE:
  bimcraft-cli run [FILE] [--sample | --highrise] [--cmd 'ID {json}']… [--script FILE]… [--save PATH]…
      Open FILE (a .bimcraft project, or an .ifc or Revit .rvt file to import) or start empty, then in order: build the sample house, run
      commands and scripts (one `ID {json}` per line), save. --save writes by extension:
      .bimcraft (the project), .ifc (IFC4), .glb (the 3D view's scene as glTF), .svg or .png (the lowest level's plan).
      --highrise builds an original 20-storey performance sample (about 10,000 elements).
  bimcraft-cli info FILE         levels, element counts, types and warnings of a project or an IFC file; of a Revit .rvt or
                                 .rfa file, its release, last save, levels and element counts by category
  bimcraft-cli convert IN OUT    a project, an IFC file or a Revit .rvt file to .ifc, .glb, .svg, .png or .bimcraft
  bimcraft-cli commands          every command and its parameters
  bimcraft-cli mcp [--read-only] [FILE | --connect [PORT]]
                                 an MCP server on stdio, for agents: on a headless project of its own (FILE, opened first, or an
                                 empty one), or with --connect on the project open in a window whose control port is open
                                 (`bimcraft --control PORT` or File > Settings > Agents; without PORT, the last one). With
                                 --read-only the agent may read the project, never change it or write over its file
  bimcraft-cli --version         the release

"""Walk an element struct's fields in serde's sequence form: ["category", f0, f1, ...].
usage: elwalk.py CATEGORY [prefix_json] [extra candidates json...]
Prints, for each position, the errors of the probes, and picks the first that passes."""
import sys, json, re, os
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/loader-agent')
from lib import *

cat = sys.argv[1]
prefix = json.loads(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else []
extra = [json.loads(x) for x in sys.argv[3:]]
G = "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001"
probes = [True, "zz", 5, -5, 1.5, [], {}, None, [1.0, 2.0], [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], G, "centre", [[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0]]] + extra
TPL = '{"elements":{"100000":@}}'


def attempt(arr):
    text = TPL.replace('@', json.dumps([cat] + arr))
    code, msg, saved = open_file(text, save=False)
    msg = msg.replace('open: x.bimcraft is not a BIMCraft project: ', '')
    return msg


i = len(prefix)
quiet = os.environ.get('QUIET')
while True:
    valid = None; found = False
    lines = []
    for pr in probes:
        msg = attempt(prefix + [pr])
        if not msg.startswith('element 100000: '):
            ok = True
        else:
            m = re.match(r'element 100000: invalid length (\d+), expected', msg)
            ok = bool(m and int(m.group(1)) > i)
        lines.append(f'    {json.dumps(pr)} -> {msg}')
        if ok and not found:
            valid = pr; found = True
    msg = attempt(prefix)
    print(f'[{i}] without it: {msg}')
    exp = set()
    for l in lines:
        m = re.search(r'expected (.*)$', l)
        if m and 'invalid length' not in l:
            exp.add(m.group(1))
    print('    expected:', ' | '.join(sorted(exp)))
    if not quiet:
        for l in lines:
            print(l)
    if not found:
        print('no valid probe; stopping. prefix =', json.dumps(prefix))
        break
    print('    -> using', json.dumps(valid))
    prefix.append(valid)
    i += 1
    if i > 80:
        break

results.content:
A level's own plan is the level (its `view_range`, `crop` and `graphics` are the level's); every other plan of it is an `Element::PlanView`
(Revit's Duplicate View: `duplicate_view`, which only plans take). A plan has a key: the level's id, or a plan view's. `Model::plan_level` says
which level a key shows, and everything that draws or measures the model takes that level (`draw_plan`, `plan_shows`, the canvas's tools), while
what is the view's own takes the key: its graphics (`graphics_of`), view range (`view_range_of`, which a template may control), crop (`crop_of`)
and annotation. Annotation says which view it is in: a note or a spot elevation by `view`, a dimension or a tag by an optional `view` beside its
`level` or its host (none: the level's own plan), and `Model::annotation_in` asks whether a plan draws it. A command that takes a `level` takes a
plan view too (`plan_param`): what is built stands on its level, what is dimensioned or tagged is in the view. A dependent view (`parent`) follows
its parent's view range and graphics (`plan_source`; `graphics`, `scale`, `detail` and `visual_style` refuse it, naming the parent), has a crop
of its own and draws its parent's annotation as well as its own. Deleting a view deletes what is annotated in it and its dependents; a level
takes its plan views with it. A project that has none writes the same file as before. A plan's own name, lettered at its bottom left, is in the drawings that make an image (`plan`, `ceiling_plan`: `titled`), not in the window's (`draw`, `draw_ceiling`) or a sheet's (`draw_at`), where the tab and the viewport's title say it. The desktop: View > Duplicate View, DP, and the Project
Browser's right-click, which also has Delete for a plan view; `Sheet::Plan` and `Sheet::Ceiling` hold the key.

| Visibility and graphics | What each view hides, and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does, for each plan, section, elevation and 3D view: whole categories left out (walls, doors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels in a section…), or single elements; lines and fills overridden by category, by element and by view filter: a colour, weight and dash for what the view cuts and for what it sees (a plan's below its cut plane, the annotation; in 3D, and in a section beyond its line, the edges' colour), the cut's poché colour or a 3D view's surface colour (a weight is a pen, 0 a hairline at any scale), halftone (halfway to the paper) and, in 3D, transparency, where what lies behind shows through and a click still picks the element (halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can't take its category's away). A hidden door or window leaves its opening in the wall, and snaps, Tag All, Select All and a view's framing take what it shows. View filters pick elements out by rules, a schedule filter's (a field of the category, how to compare it, a value, project parameters among the fields), on the categories chosen; a view applies them in order, the first prevailing where they disagree, and one that hides hides whatever the others say; an element's own override beats the filters', and those beat the category's. View templates keep a view's categories, filters, phase, design options, scale, detail level, visual style and, for a plan, view range under a name, for other views to follow: what a template controls isn't the view's to change, and changed, every view following it follows. A project's filters and templates are saved with it; sheets print each view as its graphics say |
| Visibility/Graphics | View > Visibility/Graphics (VV, VG) opens the active view's dialog, a table as Revit's: a row for each model category (searched by name, with All, None and Invert, and Object Styles… for what isn't overridden), its visibility, then Projection/Surface Lines, Patterns and Transparency, Cut Lines and Patterns, each cell showing what it overrides (the line as it draws, the fill's colour, the percent) and opening its own small dialog (lines: a colour, weight and dash, each with a box that turns it on; patterns: a fill colour; transparency, seen in 3D; Clear Overrides), Halftone a box in the row, and Detail Level, By View until a category can have its own; the Annotation Categories have their lines and halftone; Filters applies the project's filters in order, each a row alike, with Add, Remove, Up and Down; Elements lists what's hidden or overridden one by one. Design Options picks which option of each set the view shows (the primary unless it chooses). OK and Apply send what changed as one `graphics` command, one undo step; Cancel drops it. A view that follows a view template shows what the template controls, and leaves it be |
| Hide in View | Select, then Modify > View: Hide Element (EH) leaves the elements out of the view, Hide Category (VH) every category the selection is of, Override Graphics (EO) opens Visibility/Graphics on its Elements tab with the selection added. Unhide Elements (EU) opens that tab, with what's hidden; tick a box to bring it back |
| Scale, detail level, visual style | The view control bar's first buttons. In a plan, a section or an elevation, Scale lists 1 : 1 to 1 : 1000, or in a project in feet and inches the architect's scales (12" = 1'-0" to 1/32" = 1'-0") and the engineer's (1" = 10'-0" to 1" = 200'-0"), and takes any other typed in Custom, as n, 1 : n or `1/4" = 1'-0"` (every view has one: 1 : 100, or 1/8" = 1'-0" in feet and inches, until it is given another, and its annotation and line weights are the paper's at that scale); Detail Level picks Coarse, Medium or Fine. In the 3D view, Visual Style picks Shaded, Hidden Line or Wireframe; WF, HL and SD do too, as in Revit. Its menu ends with Graphic Display Options (GD, as Revit's): Show Edges, Silhouettes (none, or an outline 1 to 10 px wide round what stands against what is behind) and Show Ambient Shadows (soft shadows where faces meet), drawn alike on the processor and on the graphics card. Each is one undo step, saved with the project, and in a sheet's viewport the view draws as it says. A view's Properties have the same: View Scale (the scales the Scale menu lists), Scale Value 1: (a typed scale) and Detail Level, or in the 3D view Visual Style. A view that follows a view template that controls one shows the template's value, greyed out, with the template's name on hover |
| Filters, view templates | View > Filters (FT): New makes a view filter; tick its categories and add rules as a schedule's filter has them. View > View Templates (VT), as Revit's: the templates on the left, on a tab for each kind of view (Plan, Elevation/Section, 3D), with New from This View (a template of the view open), Duplicate, Rename and Delete under them; on the right the one picked, a table of Parameter, Value and Include: its view scale, detail level and visual style, its V/G Overrides, V/G Filters and Design Options (Visibility/Graphics on the template), its view range, phase and phase filter, its background grids, each ticked under Include for the views following it to take. OK and Apply send each template's changes as one command; Cancel drops them. A view's Properties name its template on a button that opens the same dialog, <None> first, to pick the one it follows |
| `purge` | PU | `kinds?` (`type`, `family`, `material`, `picture`, `filter`, `template`; types and families by default), `dry_run?`: takes out what nothing uses, again for what that frees; a category keeps a type and a family a type; `dry_run` lists what would go |
| `scale` | | `view?`, `scale?` (the n of 1 : n, 1 to 100000; 1 : 100, or 1 : 96 in feet and inches, until set): a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, the paper it stands for, which sizes its annotation and its line weights; a viewport placed with no `scale` takes it; without `scale`, what the view has |
| `detail` | | `view?`, `detail?` (`coarse`, `medium` or `fine`): how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts; without `detail`, what the view has |
| `visual_style` | | `view?` (`{3D}`), `style?` (`shaded`, `hidden_line` or `wireframe`): how a 3D view draws its surfaces; the default 3D view comes to be as it is first changed; without `style`, what the view has |
| `graphic_display_options` | GD | `view?` (`{3D}`), `edges?`, `silhouette?` (px, 0 to 10), `ambient_shadows?`: Revit's Graphic Display Options for a 3D view: its edges on or off in Shaded, a silhouette that wide round what stands against what is behind, soft shadows where faces meet; what is left out stays; with none, what the view has |
| `graphics` | | `view?` (a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or `{3D}`), `hide?` and `show?` ([categories]: walls, rooms, grids, levels…), `hide_elements?` and `show_elements?` ([ids]), `categories?` and `elements?` ({category or id: override}; an override is {`hidden?`, `projection?` and `cut?` ({`color?`, `weight?` (a pen: 0 a hairline at any scale, 1 to 16 from 0.10 to 2 mm on paper at 1 : 100), `dash?` (`solid`, `dashed`, `dotted`), `fill?`}), `halftone?`, `transparency?` (percent, seen in 3D)}, merged into the last, null takes it away), `filters?` ([{`filter`, plus an override's fields}, …], the first prevailing), `template?` (a view template's name, or null), `phase?` and `phase_filter?` (names, or null), `options?` ({set: option, null takes the choice away}), `reset?`: what a view hides and how it draws the rest; none of them: the view's settings as they are |
| `filter` | | `name`, `categories?` (any a schedule can be of), `rules?` ([{`field`, `op`, `value`}, …] as a schedule's `filters`), `delete?`: a view filter, and the ids it picks out; a view applies it with `graphics` |
| `template` | | `name`, `from?` (a view to take the categories, filters, a plan's view range, scale, detail level and visual style from, and its kind), `like?` (a template to copy), `kind?` (`plan`, `section`, `3d`, null for any), `rename?`, `controls?` ([`categories`, `filters`, `range`, `phase`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `style`]), `view_range?`, `scale?`, `detail?`, `visual_style?`, the changes `graphics` makes to a view's categories, filters, phase and options, `delete?`: a view template, for views to follow with `graphics {template}`; a view that follows one that controls the scale, the detail level or the visual style can't set it (`scale`, `detail` and `visual_style` refuse) |

results.content:
and edits, the selection staying as it is: `BimApp::palette_ids` is the selection narrowed to it, and the palette's subject, the Type
Selector, Edit Type (from the palette, the ribbon or the right-click menu) and every edit the palette sends read it, never the selection.
`palette_filter` keeps the selection it was picked for, so a new selection starts it over.

View Templates (`templates.rs`). VT and View > View Templates open it as Revit's does, in the look Type Properties has: on the left a tab for each
kind of view (`ViewKind`: Plan, Elevation/Section, 3D; a template of no kind is on every tab), the templates of the one showing, and Duplicate…,
Rename… and Delete, with New from This View… (enabled on the tab of the active view's kind) under them, each opening a Name row; they run at once
(`template` with `like`, `rename`, `delete`, `from`). On the right the template picked: a table of Parameter, Value and Include, its rows the groups
its kind holds (`ViewKind::groups`), each group's Include box named for the group. Its settings edit a draft (`TemplatesDialog::drafts`, one per
template, kept through Duplicate and Rename); OK and Apply send each template's difference as one `template` command, Cancel drops them.
V/G Overrides, V/G Filters and Design Options open Visibility/Graphics on the template's draft (`VgDialog::for_template`: no Elements tab nor a
drawing's layers, which are a view's own; its OK puts the categories, filters and options back in the draft), View Range a small dialog of
its four offsets, and Background Grids the grid editor. A view's Properties name its template on a button (`properties::wide_button`, as wide as the drop-downs, as Edit… is), which
opens the same dialog as Assign View Template: <None> first, the view's kind's tab showing, and OK also sets the template the view follows.

Visibility sets (`BimApp::visibility_sets`, `templates.rs`, the same in both profiles) are view templates, switched from the view control bar: no
Dimension Type Properties (`dimtypes.rs`), and Properties edits its prefix, suffix, text above and below, Replace With Text and Equality Display.
A double click on one of its numbers opens Dimension Text for that segment (`DimensionTextDialog`). Selected, an aligned or linear one shows
a padlock under each segment and, over a string of two or more, EQ past its end (`dimension_constraints`): a click locks or unlocks, or makes
it equal or not.

## Background grids

Each plan, section and elevation keeps its canvas grid in its `Graphics::background_grid`, saved with the project, copied
with independent view duplicates, and edited through the undoable `graphics` command. Reflected ceiling plans use their
plan key's graphics, like their scale and other view settings; dependent plans follow their parent's graphics.
The Graphics group in a view's instance properties has a Background Grids Edit… button. The grid menu beside Temporary
Hide/Isolate (the glasses) keeps Show grids, independent Main grid and Subgrid checkboxes, Grid snapping and Grid settings….
The editor uses a draft: Apply/OK save one undo step, Cancel discards unapplied changes. File > Settings has no grid page;
application settings files from the earlier global implementation no longer affect views.

View templates can control Background Grids as a group (`Group::BackgroundGrid`, JSON `background_grid`), for plans and
elevations and sections. New from This View copies the effective grid. View Templates has a Background Grids row whose Edit… opens
the grid editor on the template's draft (`open_template_background_grid`; its OK hands the grid back, the templates' OK sends it). Followers use the
template's values and gray out their instance Edit button, bottom menu grid settings and any open editor; removing template
control restores each view's own grid. The engine rejects bypasses through `graphics` and `modify` too.

`core::background_grid` owns the lattice geometry, shared by painting and snapping. Both lattices start at the fixed view
origin (0, 0), with one counter-clockwise rotation in degrees. Main spacing X/Y is entered in the project's actual units;
subgrid divisions X/Y divide that spacing independently. Each grid has its own colour and pen (0–16), with default colours [230,230,230] for main and [245,245,245] for subgrid,
following the project's line weights and the Thin Lines display toggle. Main lines take precedence over coincident subgrid lines.
Dense subgrids disappear below four screen pixels; main grids thin by whole multiples without moving the origin. Drawing
is bounded to 4096 lines. Section/elevation textures expose empty paper behind the model while retaining opaque model faces.
Grids are canvas aids; they do not create elements or appear in sheet/export drawings.

Grid snapping is a global application preference (`BimApp::grid_snapping`, saved as `Settings::grid_snapping`), available
in Manage > Snaps and the bottom grid menu. It is not part of view graphics or view templates: the checkbox stays editable
when a template controls the active view's grid, and changing it creates no project undo step. New/Open retain the setting.
It uses intersections of the active view's enabled subgrid, or main grid when the subgrid is disabled; with neither enabled,
there is nothing to snap to. Show grids only controls display: snapping can remain on while the grid is hidden. Object snaps, one-point snap overrides and Shift
constraints keep priority; grid snapping replaces the free-point fallback and automatic angle guides. Sections and
elevations snap annotation placement in their local horizontal/height coordinates. Model validation rejects invalid
spacing, divisions, pens or rotation, and commands roll back the whole edit.

results.content:
import_cad : {path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given) or origin (its origin on `at`); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out

cad_layers : {id, hide?: [layer, …], show?: [layer, …], view?} a CAD import's layers, each with its colour and linetype and whether it's shown; `hide` and `show` change which it shows in every view, or with `view` in that view only (its Visibility/Graphics, by the drawing's name)

show_mass : {view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's

room : {point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

section : {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

elevation : {facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

duplicate_view : {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

family : {name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out

component : {family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

modify : {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

delete : {ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted

purge : {kinds?: [type|family|material|picture|filter|template, …], dry_run?} takes out what nothing uses, again for what that leaves unused: types and families unless `kinds` says; a category keeps a type and a family a type; with `dry_run` it lists what would go and changes nothing

schedule : {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; none, every built one but rooms, levels and masses), with the fields they share (Category, Family, Type, Level, Count, Width, Height, Length, Thickness, Area: a wall's length by its height, a door's width by its height; Material: its type's structure layer's, a run's type's, a family's), each empty where its category has none; `category` alone reads its own (Room Schedule, Door Schedule, Window Schedule, Wall Schedule, Floor Schedule, Level Schedule, each the project's once changed). `fields`: its columns, in order, each a field's name (`available` lists them: its category's own, Count, project parameters, a component's family's parameters) or {name, formula?, kind?: number|length|area|yesno, heading?, total?}; with a formula, a calculated field worked out from the row's other fields as a family's formulas are (lengths in mm, areas in m²; `Area * 120`); `total` sums it in a totals row. `filters`: [{field, op: equals|not-equals|greater|greater-or-equal|less|less-or-equal|contains|not-contains|begins-with|not-begins-with|ends-with|not-ends-with|has-value|has-no-value, value}, …], the elements all of them keep (text in any case, numbers as the schedule shows them, an unset yes or no as no). `sort`: [field or {field, descending?}, …], in turn (its first column unless it says; Phase Created and Phase Demolished in the project's order of phases, a phase never demolished after the last); `grouped`, a row for each set of the sort fields' values: Count and totals summed, and a field whose values differ left empty. Each one given replaces the last; `fields: []` goes back to its category's

camera : {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in

library : {kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too

elements : {category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do
