results.content:
place : {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

type : {category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

material : {name, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], transparency?: 0-100, cut?, surface?, texture?: {kind?, size?: [w, h], angle?, offset?: [x, y], path?, image?} | null, rename?, delete?: true} a material of the project's library, created or changed: its colour in shaded 3D views, its `transparency` there (percent of what lies behind it that shows through, 0 opaque; the starter Glass has 70), the pattern its cut shows in plans and sections (where a layer is wide enough to hold it), and the one its surfaces show at its size in the building (a floor's top in plan, a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan). Patterns: none, solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete, insulation, or the name of one of the project's fill patterns (see `fill_pattern`), kept while the material shows it and renamed with it. Its `texture` is what its surfaces look like in the 3D view, over its colour, a tile of it `size` mm across and up, turned `angle` degrees and moved `offset` mm: a pattern drawn in code, `kind` brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof, fabric, metal or insulation (at its natural size unless `size` says); or `image`, a picture: the PNG or JPEG file at `path`, taken into the project (up to 1024 px a side, 24 pictures), or one the project holds (`image`, its id from `inspect`); null takes the texture away. `rename` renames it, the layers using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no layer uses it. `inspect` lists the library and the pictures

parameter : {name, kind?: text|number|length|yesno, categories?: [wall|floor|ceiling|roof|door|window|room|column|component|stair|ramp|railing|mass, …], rename?, delete?: true} a project parameter, as Revit's Manage > Project Parameters makes one: a value of its kind each element of its categories may have of its own, set with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}` (lengths in mm, yes or no as true or false). Off a category, that category's elements lose their values of it; deleted, every element does; renamed, they follow it. `inspect` lists them

family : {name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away

symbol_set : {set: arei, names?: en|nl|fr} loads a set of families that are plan symbols and nothing else, each of one type `Standard` with no forms: `arei` is the Belgian AREI/RGIE's graphical symbols (Table 2.23: switches, sockets, light points, appliances, sources, domotics, protection), 76 families, switches in the switch category, sockets in outlet, luminaires in lighting and the rest generic. `names` is the language of their names, English, Dutch or French as the source prints them; as given none, French in a French project and English otherwise. A family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing; the reply lists `loaded` and `kept`. Place them as components

component : {family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

line_pattern : {name?, segments?: [{dash: mm} | {space: mm} | "dot" | {dot_length: mm} | {offset: {length, count, distance}} | {wave: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {zigzag: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {text: {length, size, text}}, …], rename?, delete?: true} a line pattern of the project's: 1–32 freely ordered graphic segments, each 0.05–100 mm long on paper, so it reads the same at any scale. Offsets have 2–9 lines spaced symmetrically; frequency is cycles per segment, 0.1–100; amplitude and spacing are mm. Text uses bundled IBM Plex Sans, size is maximum capital height (shrinks to fit length), 1–256 single-line characters, following the curve. All graphics preserve the centerline. A project starts with Dash, Long Dash, Dot, Dash Dot, Hidden and Centre; Solid is a line with none. `rename` renames it, the line styles using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no style uses it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern

line_style : {name?, pen?, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], pattern?: name | "Solid", rename?, delete?: true} a line style of the project's, as Revit's: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) its lines draw in, their colour (black unless told) and their line pattern. A new one needs `pen`; one changed keeps what it isn't given. A project starts with Hairline, Thin Lines, Medium Lines, Wide Lines, Hidden Lines, Centre Lines and Overhead Lines. `rename` renames it, the lines drawn in it following; `delete` takes it away, while no line is drawn in it. Without `name`, it lists every style

fill_pattern : {name?, target?: drafting|model, lines?: [{angle, spacing, origin?: [x, y], shift?, dashes?: [mm, -mm, …]}, …], drawn?: scale | null, rename?, delete?: true} a fill pattern of the project's, as Revit's (and a PAT file's): families of parallel lines, each at `angle` degrees through `origin`, its lines `spacing` apart and each `shift` along from the last, whole or dashed (`dashes`: a dash's length, a space's as a negative one, 0 a dot); no lines, it fills solid. A drafting pattern's lengths are mm on paper, the same at any scale; a model pattern's mm in the building. A project starts with Solid fill, Diagonal Up and Down, Crosshatch, Diagonal Crosshatch, Horizontal, Vertical, Sand, Brick 225 x 75 and Tile 300. `rename` renames it, the region types filling with it following; `delete` takes it away while no type uses it. `drawn` is the scale (1 : n, its n) of the view one made of lines (`make_fill_pattern`) was drawn in: such a one given a new `target` and no `lines` is rescaled, a drafting one being the drawing on paper at that scale; null forgets it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern

filled_region_type : {name?, foreground?: pattern | null, foreground_color?, background?: pattern | null, background_color?, masking?, rename?, delete?: true} a filled region type of the project's: its foreground pattern over its background one, each in its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), over the paper when `masking` (it hides what's under it). A new one starts with none. A project starts with Solid Black, Diagonal Up, Crosshatch, Sand, Brick and Masking. `rename` renames it, its regions following; `delete` takes it away while no region is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

filled_region : {sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)

create_group : {ids, name?} a detail group made of detail lines, filled regions and text notes of one view, as Revit's Create Group: they become type `name`'s members (Group 1, 2… unless told), and one group of it takes their place, its origin the middle of them. Place it again with detail_group; ungroup gives its members back. Returns {id, name}

detail_group : {type, at: [x,y], angle?, mirrored?, view?} a detail group of type `type` placed in a view (the lowest plan by default): its members drawn with their origin at `at`, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, mirrored across their x axis first when `mirrored`. Move, copy, rotate and mirror take it whole

repeating_detail : {type, start: [x,y], end: [x,y], spacing, mirrored?, view?} detail group `type` repeated along the line from `start` to `end`, every `spacing` mm from `start` (at most 2000 of them), each turned along the line, as Revit's Repeating Detail Component: brick coursing, blocking, batt ties. A view draws up to 10000 group members in all (a repeat places each member of the type again), so a type of 100 members repeats up to 100 times. Returns {id, count}

ungroup : {id} the members of detail group `id` as detail lines, filled regions and text notes of its view again, where it drew them; the group goes, its type stays. Returns {ids}

group_type : {name?, rename?, delete?: true} a detail group type: `rename` renames it, its groups following; `delete` takes it away while none of it is placed. Without `name`, it lists each with its members and how many are placed

detail_line : {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

schedule : {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; none, every built one but rooms, levels and masses), with the fields they share (Category, Family, Type, Level, Count, Width, Height, Length, Thickness, Area: a wall's length by its height, a door's width by its height; Material: its type's structure layer's, a run's type's, a family's), each empty where its category has none; `category` alone reads its own (Room Schedule, Door Schedule, Window Schedule, Wall Schedule, Floor Schedule, Level Schedule, each the project's once changed). `fields`: its columns, in order, each a field's name (`available` lists them: its category's own, Count, project parameters, a component's family's parameters) or {name, formula?, kind?: number|length|area|yesno, heading?, total?}; with a formula, a calculated field worked out from the row's other fields as a family's formulas are (lengths in mm, areas in m²; `Area * 120`); `total` sums it in a totals row. `filters`: [{field, op: equals|not-equals|greater|greater-or-equal|less|less-or-equal|contains|not-contains|begins-with|not-begins-with|ends-with|not-ends-with|has-value|has-no-value, value}, …], the elements all of them keep (text in any case, numbers as the schedule shows them, an unset yes or no a

camera : {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in

filter : {name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one

template : {name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one

phase : {name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides

option : {set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)

results.content:
level | {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

grid | {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

wall | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

floor | {boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline

room | {point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

column | {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

roof | {level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over `boundary` or else the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces, round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it): flat at `slope` 0, else every edge sloping up at `slope` degrees (30), hips, valleys and ridges where the slopes meet, but the edges in `gables` (edge i runs from point i to the next, the courtyards' edges numbered on after the boundary's) left upright, gable ends; `gable` leaves a rectangle's short ends upright. `slopes`: a slope in degrees (up to 75) for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for an edge that takes `slope`; none, every edge does; the eaves stay level and an edge in `gables` stays upright whatever its slope. A `sketch` line may carry a `slope` for the edges along it. Or with `extrusion` {line: [[x,y],[x,y]], profile: [[along, up],…], from?, to}: its underside's profile in the upright plane through `line`, along it from its start and up from the base, swept square to it from `from` (0) to `to` mm to its left. `openings` are holes through it in plan; with `join`, a

dimension | {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 1

text | {text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's

spot | {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up

tag | {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

copy | {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

rotate | {ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

mirror | {ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

filled_region | {sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)

create_group | {ids, name?} a detail group made of detail lines, filled regions and text notes of one view, as Revit's Create Group: they become type `name`'s members (Group 1, 2… unless told), and one group of it takes their place, its origin the middle of them. Place it again with detail_group; ungroup gives its members back. Returns {id, name}

detail_line | {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 

schedule | {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; none, every built one but rooms, levels and masses), with the fields they share (Category, Family, Type, Level, Count, Width, Height, Length, Thickness, Area: a wall's length by its height, a door's width by its height; Material: its type's structure layer's, a run's type's, a family's), each empty where its category has none; `category` alone reads its own (Room Schedule, Door Schedule, Window Schedule, Wall Schedule, Floor Schedule, Level Schedule, each the project's once changed). `fields`: its columns, in order, each a field's name (`available` lists them: its category's own, Count, project parameters, a component's family's parameters) or {name, formula?, kind?: number|length|area|yesno, heading?, total?}; with a formula, a calculated field worked out from the row's other fields as a family's formulas are (lengths in mm, areas in m²; `Area * 120`); `total` sums it in a totals row. `

results.content:
undo | Undo | {count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default)

redo | Redo | {count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default)

level | Level | {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

grid | Grid | {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

wall | Wall | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door | Door | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window | Window | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

column | Column | {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

structural_column | Structural Column | {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

duplicate_view | Duplicate View | {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

flip | Flip | {ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

modify | Modify | {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

copy | Copy | {ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

rotate | Rotate | {ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

mirror | Mirror | {ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

corner | Trim/Extend to Corner | {ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep

offset | Offset | {id, distance, toward: [x, y], copy?} a detail line drawn again `distance` mm beside itself on the side `toward` is, arcs round the same centres, an ellipse or a spline as a spline through points within 0.05 mm of the true offset (which Revit can't): a copy (the default), or with `copy` false moved

trim_extend | Trim/Extend Single Element | {boundary, ids: [id, …], keep: [[x, y], …]} trims or extends each detail line of `ids` (lines and arcs) to where it meets `boundary` (a detail line, a wall's location line or a grid), keeping the part of each its `keep` point is on: Revit's Trim/Extend Single Element, and Multiple Elements with several

split | Split | {id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`

join_polyline | Join into Polyline | {ids: [id, …]} joins detail lines of one view, lines, arcs and polylines that meet end to end, into one polyline in the first's line style (closed when they come round); the first keeps its id, the rest are deleted, and a dimension that measured one of the rest loses that reference (and is deleted, left with fewer than two): the reply's `notes` say which

vertex | Add/Delete Vertex | {id, at: [x, y], delete?} a detail line (a polyline, or a spline of either kind) with a vertex more where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points gains a control point and keeps its shape exactly), or with `delete` one fewer: the corner, control point or point passed through nearest `at`; `at` is within 100 mm of the line (of a vertex, to delete one), or it is refused

explode | Explode Polyline | {id} takes a detail line that is a polyline apart into a line or an arc for each segment, in its view and style; the first keeps its id. Revit has no shortcut for it: EX is ours, PX being the Plumbing Fixture's on the desktop

delete | Delete | {ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted

detail_line | Detail Line | {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

elements | Elements | {category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

wall : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door : {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

dimension : {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 1

text : {text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's

text_type : {name?, font?, size?, bold?, italic?, underline?, width_factor?, color?, border?, border_offset?, border_pen?, like?, rename?, delete?: true} a text type of the project's: its `font`, any the system has, or one BIMCraft carries (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, BIMCraft Lettering: single-stroke capitals); Arial, the default, letters on any system (where it isn't installed, Liberation Sans, Arimo, Helvetica or the like stands in, else IBM Plex Sans), and a font a file names that this system hasn't is stood in for likewise. Its capitals' height on paper (`size`, mm, 2.5 for a new one), bold, italic and underlined or not (a family's own bold and italic faces where it has them), `width_factor` (1: as the font draws it), its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), and whether a border is drawn round its notes, `border_offset` mm on paper out from their text (where a leader starts too; 1), in pen `border_pen` (0 to 16; 1). A new one starts as `like` says, or as 2.5mm Arial. A project starts with 2.5mm, 3.5mm and 5mm. `rename` renames it, its notes following; `delete` takes it away while no note is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type, the fonts this system has, and the font that letters each type here (`drawn_with`)

dimension_type : {name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, …values} a dimension type of the project's, as Revit's type parameters, lengths mm on paper. Graphics: `string` continuous|baseline|ordinate (Dimension String Type; baseline lines `baseline_spacing` apart, 7), `tick` diagonal|arrow|open_arrow|dot|none, `tick_size` (2), `line_pen` and `tick_pen` (0 to 16; 4 and 7), `color` ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b]), `line_extension` past the outer witness lines (0.8), `witness` gap_to_element|fixed (Witness Line Control), `witness_length` when fixed (5), `witness_gap` off what it measures (0.6), `witness_extension` past the dimension line (0.8), `centre_mark` on radial and diameter ones. Text: `font` (as text types take; Arial), `text_size` (2.5), `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor` (1), `text_offset` off the line (1), `background` opaque|transparent, `read` up_then_left|up_then_right (Read Convention), `units` (mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in; null for the project's) and `decimals` (0 to 6; null as the units show), `radius_symbol` (R), `diameter_symbol` (Ø), `equality_text` (EQ). A new one starts as `like` says, else as the default. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial` (aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in it) and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial` (radial and diameter ones). `rename` renames it, its dimensions following; `delete` takes it away while no dimension is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

spot : {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up

tag : {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

modify : {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

## family | Load Family
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out
## symbol_set | Load Symbol Set
## type | Edit Type
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)
## material | Materials

import math
S = (2000.0, -3000.0)
E = (2000.0, 3000.0)
th = 73.739795292
# centre from chord and arc
def centre_of(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(t / 2)
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    # left normal
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    d = c / 2 / math.tan(t / 2)
    return (mx + nx * d, my + ny * d), r
C, r = centre_of(S, E, th)
print('centre', C, 'r', r)
a0 = math.atan2(S[1] - C[1], S[0] - C[0])
a1 = math.atan2(E[1] - C[1], E[0] - C[0])
P = (3000.0, 0.0)
ap = math.atan2(P[1] - C[1], P[0] - C[0])
print('a0', math.degrees(a0), 'a1', math.degrees(a1), 'ap', math.degrees(ap))
print('cand1 th - (ap-a0)', th - math.degrees(ap - a0))
print('cand2 a1-ap', math.degrees(a1 - ap))
print('cand2b deg(a1)-deg(ap)', math.degrees(a1) - math.degrees(ap))
ch = math.hypot(E[0] - P[0], E[1] - P[1])
print('cand3 2asin', math.degrees(2 * math.asin(ch / 2 / r)))
# intersection of y=0 with circle
x = C[0] + math.sqrt(r * r - C[1] ** 2)

import math
S = (2000.0, -3000.0)
E = (2000.0, 3000.0)
th = 73.739795292
target = 36.86989764599999


def centre_a(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(t / 2)
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    d = c / 2 / math.tan(t / 2)
    return (mx + nx * d, my + ny * d), r


def centre_b(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / (2 * math.sin(t / 2))
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    h = math.sqrt(max(r * r - c * c / 4, 0))
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    return (mx + nx * h, my + ny * h), r


def centre_c(S, E, th_deg):
    t = math.radians(th_deg)
    dx, dy = E[0] - S[0], E[1] - S[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(t / 2)
    mx, my = (S[0] + E[0]) / 2, (S[1] + E[1]) / 2
    nx, ny = -dy, dx
    k = 0.5 / math.tan(t / 2)
    return (mx + nx * k, my + ny * k), r


for name, cf in (('a', centre_a), ('b', centre_b), ('c', centre_c)):
    C, r = cf(S, E, th)
    for P in ((3000.0, 0.0),):
        sx, sy = P[0] - C[0], P[1] - C[1]
        ex, ey = E[0] - C[0], E[1] - C[1]
        a_s = math.atan2(sy, sx)
        a_e = math.atan2(ey, ex)
        a0 = math.atan2(S[1] - C[1], S[0] - C[0])
        cands = {
            'ae-as': math.degrees(a_e - a_s),
            'deg diff': math.degrees(a_e) - math.degrees(a_s),
            'atan2(cross,dot)': math.degrees(math.atan2(sx * ey - sy * ex, sx * ex + sy * ey)),
            'acos': math.degrees(math.acos((sx * ex + sy * ey) / (math.hypot(sx, sy) * math.hypot(ex, ey)))),
            'th-(as-a0)': th - math.degrees(a_s - a0),
            'th-deg': th - (math.degrees(a_s) - math.degrees(a0)),
            '2asin': math.degrees(2 * math.asin(math.hypot(E[0] - P[0], E[1] - P[1]) / 2 / r)),
            '2asin b': math.degrees(2 * math.asin(math.hypot(E[0] - P[0], E[1] - P[1]) / (2 * r))),
            '2atan': None,
        }
        # bulge: sagitta via midpoint of arc
        ch = math.hypot(E[0] - P[0], E[1] - P[1])
        mid = ((P[0] + E[0]) / 2, (P[1] + E[1]) / 2)
        dm = math.hypot(mid[0] - C[0], mid[1] - C[1])
        sag = r - dm
        cands['4atan(sag/half)'] = math.degrees(4 * math.atan(sag / (ch / 2)))
        cands['2atan2(half,dm)'] = math.degrees(2 * math.atan2(ch / 2, dm))
        for k, v in cands.items():
            if v is not None:
                print(name, k, repr(v), 'MATCH' if v == target else '')

250:Instances and the framing of sections and 3D views take what `Look` shows too. A level's ceiling plan is its plan's view;
286:(dimensions, joins, Duplicate View) and Properties use. A ceiling plan keeps its own range.
292:`fill` colour. Element, filter and category precedence resolves each layer separately. Plans, reflected ceiling plans, section
545:`MAX_NEAR` chords are tried against each other. Ceilings snap in a floor plan as well as a ceiling plan, because a snap does not know
section Section {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

elevation Elevation {facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

sheet Sheet {number?, name?, size?: A0|A1|A2|A3|A4} a sheet of paper, landscape (A3 by default), with a title block; numbers run A101, A102…

place Place View {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

crop Crop View {view, region?: [[x, y], [x, y]] | null} crops a level's plan to the region's south-west and north-east corners (plan mm), or a section or an elevation to its bottom left and top right (along its line from its start, and up: its line then runs between them, and the notes in it stay put); null uncrops it; without a region, it crops to what the view shows now

duplicate_view Duplicate View {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Cop

render Render {family?, type?, mode?: 3d|plan|elevation, wall_thickness?, view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, a sheet's number, or {3D}, ceiling?, width?, height?, path?, azimuth?, elevation?, eye_elevation?} a family on its own with `family` — its `type` (the first by default) standing in a model of its own, in a wall `wall_thickness` mm thick (200) if it's a door's or a window's, nothing of this project's touched or left behind: `3d` (as seen from the south-east), `plan` (what its symbols draw) or `elevation` (front-on, as seen from the north), a PNG as `pngBase64` or at `path`. Without

schedule Schedule {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; 

camera Camera {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). level | Level | {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

grid | Grid | {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

wall | Wall | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core

section | Section | {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

elevation | Elevation | {facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

sheet | Sheet | {number?, name?, size?: A0|A1|A2|A3|A4} a sheet of paper, landscape (A3 by default), with a title block; numbers run A101, A102…

place | Place View | {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

duplicate_view | Duplicate View | {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Cop

schedule | Schedule | {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…];

section_box | Section Box | {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off an

a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the
boundary it has when frozen, both ways it can be measured (`Room::kept`, given after the command that froze it by
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it

import json, sys, subprocess, os, tempfile, shutil
# usage: badfiles.py base.bimcraft eid variants.json [cmd]
# variants: list of [label, {field: value or "__DEL__"}]
base, eid, varfile = sys.argv[1:4]
extra = sys.argv[4] if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 'level {"elevation":9000}'
exe = os.environ.get('EXE', '/workspace/executable')
variants = json.load(open(varfile))
d0 = json.load(open(base))
for label, changes in variants:
    d = json.loads(json.dumps(d0))
    e = d['elements'][eid]
    for k, v in changes.items():
        if k.startswith('@top.'):
            d[k[5:]] = v
            continue
        if v == '__DEL__':
            e.pop(k, None)
        else:
            e[k] = v
    t = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp/views-notes')
    f = os.path.join(t, 'x.bimcraft')
    json.dump(d, open(f, 'w'), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    p = subprocess.run([exe, 'run', f, '--cmd', extra], capture_output=True, cwd=t)
    out = p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')[-1][:200]
    err = p.stderr.decode().strip()[:300]
    print('%-28s %s %s' % (label, ('OUT ' + out) if not err else '', ('ERR ' + err) if err else ''))
    shutil.rmtree(t)
