arguments.prompt:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/walls-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/walls-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters`, `room_area`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`, `type:beam`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type` (named `Family: Type`), `family-parameter`, `text-type`, `line-style`, `dimension-type`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `normalize_guid`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading, e.g. all rooms of a level), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type` (a category's type by GUID → name and definition in `types`), `family`, `family_type`, `material_name`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator), `slabs::view` (floor, ceiling, roof, shaft, mass; plus `slabs::attached_height(cx, wall_id)` for walls attached to roofs/floors), `parts::view` (doors, windows, components, columns, runs, stairs…), `notes::view` (levels, annotation, views…), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, floors, roofs, rooms… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/walls-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"room"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: WALLS — `src/readers/walls/` (`walls::view` for wall, room, roomseparator)
Every field `elements` shows for walls, rooms and room separators, exactly, for every kind of project. Observed so far (verify everything):
- wall: the stored fields plus `type` (the type's name instead of its GUID), `type_guid`, `thickness` (the type's), `length` (straight: start–end distance; an arc wall with `"arc": 90` and a 4000 chord shows `length` 4442.882938000001 — unrounded, odd digits: find the exact formula — and `radius` 2828.43, rounded), `room_bounding` (true unless stored false), `height` (the stored one, or worked out to `top_level`+`top_offset`; for walls with `attach_top`/`attach_base` call `crate::readers::slabs::attached_height(cx, id)` — another sub-agent implements it; use its value when Some). Check every location line (`location` stored only when not centre: core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core, interior-core), compound types with layers (`Exterior - 300mm`), flipped walls (`flip` command), `top_offset`, `top_level` null (unconnected), walls by face (`wall_by_face` on a mass), walls on upper levels, walls joined/trimmed (`corner`, `split`), and any other derived field the original adds.
- room: `area_m2`, `perimeter_m` (rounded to hundredths), `enclosed`, `unbounded_height`, `volume_m3` (area × height, rounded), `shares_space_with` (redundant rooms), and whatever else appears (frozen rooms keep a boundary in the file — see what they show). The boundary is worked out at reading time from the room's stored `point`: room-bounding walls on its level that the level's `computation_height` (1200 unless set) cuts, room separation lines (category `roomseparator`, whatever their height), room-bounding columns and structural columns (a 400×400 column inside takes 0.16 m² off and adds 1.6 m of perimeter), free-standing islands (a loop of walls inside a room not joined to its walls) subtracted; measured at the walls' centre lines (`room_area` absent or `centre`) or at their faces (`"room_area": "finish"`: a 4000×6000 centre-line bay between `Exterior - 300mm` walls and a 100 mm interior wall gives 21.66 m² and perimeter 19.0). Unenclosed rooms: area 0, perimeter 0, `enclosed` false (they sit as a 1000 mm square); two rooms in one space: the later one is unbounded, with `shares_space_with` (the other's id). Find the rules for: T-junctions, crossing walls, walls that don't quite meet (gaps, overshoots), overlapping walls, arcs (exact or tessellated? match the digits), walls of different thickness meeting, location lines other than centre (is a centre-line area at the wall's centre or its location line?), room separators crossing walls, columns half inside walls, rotated and round columns, walls whose base/height doesn't reach the computation height (base_offset, low walls, walls from lower levels reaching up), walls with room_bounding false, columns with room_bounding false, `room_area` finish with layered types, rooms on Level 2, `top_level`/`limit_offset`/`base_offset` → `unbounded_height` (2700 = 3000 − 300 to the level above by default; Not Bounded: 2500?), frozen rooms (`frozen` true, `modify {id, frozen}`).
- roomseparator: `length`.
Expose for other readers (I'll wire them later), correct and documented: `pub fn room_loops(cx: &Ctx, room_id: u64) -> Option<Vec<Vec<[f64; 2]>>>` (the room's boundary as the original works it out, outer loop first, then holes; None when unbounded) and `pub fn wall_footprint(cx: &Ctx, wall_id: u64) -> Vec<[f64; 2]>` (its outline in plan, joins applied if you work them out).
Performance: work each level's rooms out once per reading (`cx.cached`); projects can have hundreds of walls and rooms.
Prioritise what typical scripts make (rectangles, L-shapes, subdivided plans with interior walls, T-junctions, separators, columns, finish areas, exterior layered walls, unbounded and redundant rooms) before exotic geometry, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/walls/`.

steps.message:
The IFC importer is done and committed: 21 of the 22 target IFC files import identically. The exception is `phasing.ifc`, which differs in one place I couldn't fix (below).

**Branch and commit:** `worktree-agent-a269fc74daf28a975`, last commit `096e843`. The working tree is clean.

**What imports identically.** I compared outputs after numbering GUIDs by order of appearance, on `run`, `run --save` and `convert`:
- **Asset files:** 21 of 22 match, across `test_ifc_export` (except `phasing.ifc`), `test_model_geometry`, `test_mep_runs`, `test_structure_elements` and `test_structure_reinforce`.
- **`info in.ifc`:** every key the import decides matches on all 22 files, including `path`, which is now `null` for an imported project as in the original.
- **Probe files:** 1054 of the 1077 files I generated match outright. Of the rest, 16 differ only in parameter order (same cause as `phasing.ifc`) and the others are the known cases listed below.

This session's work was mostly roof rules, all now matching the original on my probes:
- A roof is "one slope all round" only when every sloped face lies in the plane rising from an eave.
- A roof swept along one profile takes its profile from its top, lowered by the roof's depth. If the lowered pieces don't meet within 0.5 mm, the original either imports it as a shaped flat roof (when it is nowhere thinner than under its highest point) or skips it with "its underside steps up or down".
- A roof whose top falls to drains inside it imports as shaped.
- A roof type of zero or negative thickness stops the import: "open: X.ifc: roof type `…` thickness must be above zero, got …".
- Roofs made of stacked layers now get an outline instead of "it has no body".

**What doesn't match, and why:**
- **`phasing.ifc`:** only the order of keys inside elements' `params` maps differs, so this target asset fails every time, not by chance. The original's GUIDs are not random on import: they come from a generator seeded by the file's bytes (one changed byte changes them all), and `params` is sorted by those GUIDs. My GUIDs are random, so the order differs. I tried several common hash and random-generator combinations and couldn't identify it. The same cause explains the other probe files that differ only in parameter order. Earlier I had written this off as "random noise in both programs"; that was wrong.
- **`info`:** the `families`, `images`, `materials`, `types`, `view_filters`, `view_templates` and `warnings` keys are missing. They come from the inspect reader, which is outside my area.
- **One rotated-room probe:** two candidate triangles for the room's point have equal area in floating point, and the original breaks the tie the other way. No area formula or start vertex I tried explains every case.
- **Roofs placed at far map coordinates:** the original's floating-point error registers extra roof types. These were already failing before this session.

**Edits outside my area:**
- `src/commands/basic.rs`, `info()`: the reported `path` is now the session's own file instead of the argument, so it is `null` for an imported IFC (2 lines).
- `src/ifc/mod.rs`: only `pub mod` lines for my modules.

My probe scripts and generated files are in `/tmp/ifc-import-agent/`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Arc wall with a door, moved freely: collect old/new arcs, offsets."""
import sys, json, random, subprocess, tempfile, shutil, os
random.seed(21)
samples = []
for i in range(40):
    a = [float(random.randint(-6000, 6000)), float(random.randint(-6000, 6000))]
    b = [float(random.randint(-6000, 6000)), float(random.randint(-6000, 6000))]
    arc = random.choice([30.0, 60.0, 90.0, -45.0, 120.0, -90.0, 17.5])
    off = float(random.randint(700, 1500))
    by = [round(random.uniform(-500, 500), 1), round(random.uniform(-500, 500), 1)]
    cmds = ['wall {"points": [%s, %s], "arc": %s}' % (json.dumps(a), json.dumps(b), json.dumps(arc)), 'door {"wall": 100002, "offset": %s}' % json.dumps(off), 'move {"ids": [100002], "by": %s}' % json.dumps(by)]
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(d, 's.txt'), 'w').write('\n'.join(cmds) + '\n')
    p = subprocess.run(['/workspace/executable', 'run', '--script', 's.txt', '--save', 'x.bimcraft'], cwd=d, capture_output=True, text=True)
    if p.returncode == 0:
        e = json.load(open(os.path.join(d, 'x.bimcraft')))['elements']
        samples.append({'a': a, 'b': b, 'arc': arc, 'off': off, 'by': by, 'a2': e['100002']['start'], 'b2': e['100002']['end'], 'new': e['100003']['offset']})
    shutil.rmtree(d)
json.dump(samples, open('/tmp/edit-agent/t79.json', 'w'))
print(len(samples))

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/walls-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/walls-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters`, `room_area`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`, `type:beam`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type` (named `Family: Type`), `family-parameter`, `text-type`, `line-style`, `dimension-type`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `normalize_guid`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading, e.g. all rooms of a level), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type` (a category's type by GUID → name and definition in `types`), `family`, `family_type`, `material_name`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator), `slabs::view` (floor, ceiling, roof, shaft, mass; plus `slabs::attached_height(cx, wall_id)` for walls attached to roofs/floors), `parts::view` (doors, windows, components, columns, runs, stairs…), `notes::view` (levels, annotation, views…), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, floors, roofs, rooms… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/walls-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"room"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: WALLS — `src/readers/walls/` (`walls::view` for wall, room, roomseparator)
Every field `elements` shows for walls, rooms and room separators, exactly, for every kind of project. Observed so far (verify everything):
- wall: the stored fields plus `type` (the type's name instead of its GUID), `type_guid`, `thickness` (the type's), `length` (straight: start–end distance; an arc wall with `"arc": 90` and a 4000 chord shows `length` 4442.882938000001 — unrounded, odd digits: find the exact formula — and `radius` 2828.43, rounded), `room_bounding` (true unless stored false), `height` (the stored one, or worked out to `top_level`+`top_offset`; for walls with `attach_top`/`attach_base` call `crate::readers::slabs::attached_height(cx, id)` — another sub-agent implements it; use its value when Some). Check every location line (`location` stored only when not centre: core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core, interior-core), compound types with layers (`Exterior - 300mm`), flipped walls (`flip` command), `top_offset`, `top_level` null (unconnected), walls by face (`wall_by_face` on a mass), walls on upper levels, walls joined/trimmed (`corner`, `split`), and any other derived field the original adds.
- room: `area_m2`, `perimeter_m` (rounded to hundredths), `enclosed`, `unbounded_height`, `volume_m3` (area × height, rounded), `shares_space_with` (redundant rooms), and whatever else appears (frozen rooms keep a boundary in the file — see what they show). The boundary is worked out at reading time from the room's stored `point`: room-bounding walls on its level that the level's `computation_height` (1200 unless set) cuts, room separation lines (category `roomseparator`, whatever their height), room-bounding columns and structural columns (a 400×400 column inside takes 0.16 m² off and adds 1.6 m of perimeter), free-standing islands (a loop of walls inside a room not joined to its walls) subtracted; measured at the walls' centre lines (`room_area` absent or `centre`) or at their faces (`"room_area": "finish"`: a 4000×6000 centre-line bay between `Exterior - 300mm` walls and a 100 mm interior wall gives 21.66 m² and perimeter 19.0). Unenclosed rooms: area 0, perimeter 0, `enclosed` false (they sit as a 1000 mm square); two rooms in one space: the later one is unbounded, with `shares_space_with` (the other's id). Find the rules for: T-junctions, crossing walls, walls that don't quite meet (gaps, overshoots), overlapping walls, arcs (exact or tessellated? match the digits), walls of different thickness meeting, location lines other than centre (is a centre-line area at the wall's centre or its location line?), room separators crossing walls, columns half inside walls, rotated and round columns, walls whose base/height doesn't reach the computation height (base_offset, low walls, walls from lower levels reaching up), walls with room_bounding false, columns with room_bounding false, `room_area` finish with layered types, rooms on Level 2, `top_level`/`limit_offset`/`base_offset` → `unbounded_height` (2700 = 3000 − 300 to the level above by default; Not Bounded: 2500?), frozen rooms (`frozen` true, `modify {id, frozen}`).
- roomseparator: `length`.
Expose for other readers (I'll wire them later), correct and documented: `pub fn room_loops(cx: &Ctx, room_id: u64) -> Option<Vec<Vec<[f64; 2]>>>` (the room's boundary as the original works it out, outer loop first, then holes; None when unbounded) and `pub fn wall_footprint(cx: &Ctx, wall_id: u64) -> Vec<[f64; 2]>` (its outline in plan, joins applied if you work them out).
Performance: work each level's rooms out once per reading (`cx.cached`); projects can have hundreds of walls and rooms.
Prioritise what typical scripts make (rectangles, L-shapes, subdivided plans with interior walls, T-junctions, separators, columns, finish areas, exterior layered walls, unbounded and redundant rooms) before exotic geometry, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/walls/`.

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.

import sys, json, math, itertools
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-agent')
from fma import fma
S = json.load(open('/tmp/edit-agent/t79.json'))
PI = math.pi
def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1])
def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1])
def mul(a, k): return (a[0]*k, a[1]*k)
def L(d): return math.sqrt(fma(d[0], d[0], d[1]*d[1]))
def geom(a, b, deg):
    t = math.radians(deg); ch = sub(b, a); cl = L(ch)
    r = cl / 2.0 / abs(math.sin(t / 2.0))
    m = mul(add(a, b), 0.5); n = mul((-ch[1], ch[0]), 1/cl); d = cl / 2.0 / math.tan(t / 2.0)
    c = add(m, mul(n, d))
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1]-c[1], a[0]-c[0])
    return c, r, a0, t
def point_at(a, b, deg, s):
    c, r, a0, t = geom(a, b, deg)
    ang = a0 + math.copysign(1, t) * s / r
    return (c[0] + r*math.cos(ang), c[1] + r*math.sin(ang))
score = {}
for s in S:
    a, b, deg, off, by, a2, b2, want = tuple(s['a']), tuple(s['b']), s['arc'], s['off'], tuple(s['by']), tuple(s['a2']), tuple(s['b2']), s['new']
    p = add(point_at(a, b, deg, off), by)
    c, r, a0, t = geom(a2, b2, deg)
    cands = {}
    ang = math.atan2(p[1]-c[1], p[0]-c[0])
    da = (ang - a0) * math.copysign(1, t)
    x = da
    while x < -PI: x += 2*PI
    while x > 1.5*PI: x -= 2*PI
    cands['mine'] = x * r
    da2 = (ang - a0)
    while da2 < -PI: da2 += 2*PI
    while da2 > PI: da2 -= 2*PI
    cands['norm_pi'] = abs(da2) * r
    va = sub(a2, c); vp = sub(p, c)
    cr = va[0]*vp[1] - va[1]*vp[0]; dt = va[0]*vp[0] + va[1]*vp[1]
    th = math.atan2(cr, dt) * math.copysign(1, t)
    cands['atan2cd'] = th * r
    cands['atan2cd_rem'] = (th % (2*PI)) * r
    # unit vectors
    ka = 1/L(va); kp = 1/L(vp); ua = mul(va, ka); up = mul(vp, kp)
    th2 = math.atan2(ua[0]*up[1]-ua[1]*up[0], ua[0]*up[0]+ua[1]*up[1]) * math.copysign(1, t)
    cands['atan2u'] = th2 * r
    cands['acos'] = math.acos(max(-1, min(1, ua[0]*up[0]+ua[1]*up[1]))) * r
    # offset kept: translation only
    cands['kept'] = off
    for k, v in cands.items():
        score[k] = score.get(k, 0) + (v == want)
print(len(S), score)

## Performance sample

Start an original 20-storey, 9,521-element tower with `bimcraft --highrise`, or generate a native
file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is
[`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md)

fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder.

The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you
turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor,
and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor
draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes
transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which.

## Why BIMCraft

- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type

  underneath.
- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around

The goal is to reimplement the closed `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 behaviour exactly (replies, error texts and their order, saved JSON field order/number formatting, undo labels) by observing the original.

   BRIEF.md hard rules (must keep obeying):
   - "The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it ONLY by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`."
   - "No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates)."
   - "Edit only the files your prompt gives you. You may add child modules of your own files … Do NOT edit `src/views/mod.rs`, `src/views/common.rs`, `src/views/model.rs` or anything outside `src/views/`; if you need a change there, copy what you need into your own files and say so in your final report."
   - "Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in your own `/tmp/views-<yourpart>/`. Commit only Rust (your files). Don't write report/summary .md files into the repo."
   - "Never use bare `git stash`. Don't push. Don't touch other worktrees or branches but your own."
   - Finish: commit on the worktree branch (`git add src/views/… && git commit`), message ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`. Final message to the launching agent: branch name and last commit; per command what matches and what doesn't (honest, specific); what I needed but couldn't write (shared files/other areas); functions I expose for others (e.g. for delete, move, elements).
   - Also: the harness refuses complex shell commands (loops with shell variables, some `cd … &&`/heredoc chains, `$(…)`); write Python scripts into files under /tmp/views-notes and run them.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Rust std-only codebase; `crate::json::Value` (insertion-ordered Map, `.sorted()`, `to_compact`, `kind_name`, `fmt_f64`), `Project` (elements BTreeMap, library, `alloc_id`, `lib_guid`, `find_guid`), `Session` runs command then `crate::check::check` (rolls back on error), `crate::views::mark_step()` for undo step even unchanged.
   - Original's serde-like param parsing: objects visited in sorted key order (serde_json BTreeMap) → I sort params (`p.clone().sorted()`) in my run().
   - Errors >2000 chars clipped "… (N more characters)" for command errors (not model-check errors).
   - Linework picking: plan re-drawn round `at` at 0.05 px/mm, centre 500 px, f32 pixel coords; px = f32((x−at.x)·0.05+500), py = f32((at.y−y)·0.05+500); back-transform (q−500)/0.05+at; nearest segment within 10 px (200 mm), strict `<` tie-break in draw order; stored entries r3-rounded; detail lines/regions return exact model coords.
   - glam-like normalize (v × 1/len, len = sqrt(dot)).
   - Wall outlines with joins: endpoint joins ≤1.0 mm (mitre, angular sort, per-wall rejection when corner extension > thickest wall thickness → square cap through location endpoint), T/butt when end lies in host band, middle point = location endpoint; hidden spans via 1 mm outward probe inside other cut solids (walls + cut columns); stubs of 20 mm (1 px) only along other runs' endpoints; arc chord rule max(ceil(θ/2acos(1−1/r)), ceil(|θ°|/5)).
   - Schedule-like value formatting by project units for tag labels.
   - Room boundary via planar face tracing of wall centre lines/separators, finish-face inset, minus columns (union) by probe-based piece Green's theorem.

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/slabs-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/slabs-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters`, `room_area`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`, `type:floor`, `type:roof`, `type:ceiling`…, `material`, `family`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `level_above`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type` (a category's type by GUID → name and definition in `types`), `family`, `material_name`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator — another sub-agent), `slabs::view` (YOURS: floor, ceiling, roof, shaft, mass), `parts::view` (doors, windows, components, columns, runs, stairs… — another), `notes::view` (levels, annotation, views… — another), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, floors, roofs, rooms… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/slabs-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"roof"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: SLABS — `src/readers/slabs/` (`slabs::view` for floor, ceiling, roof, shaft, mass; `slabs::attached_height`)
Every field `elements` shows for floors, ceilings, roofs, shafts and masses, exactly, for every kind of project; and the height `elements` gives a wall attached to a roof or a floor. Observed so far (verify everything):
- floor: stored fields plus `type` (name), `type_guid`, `thickness`, `area_m2`, `volume_m3`, `top` ([0.0, 0.0] for a flat floor — find what it is), `pattern_origin` [0,0] and `pattern_angle` 0 (defaults when not stored). Check openings, shafts through it (are they subtracted?), sloped floors (`slope`, `arrow`), structural floors, shaped floors (`edit_shape`, `add_point`, `add_split_line`, `falls`, `reset_shape`: points and split lines), layered floor types (`type` command with `layers`), floors made by `floor_by_face`/`mass_floors`, floors on upper levels, `offset`.
- ceiling: `type`, `type_guid`, `thickness`, `grid`, `area_m2` (with openings).
- roof: `type`, `type_guid`, `area_m2` (the sample house's roof shows 93.79 for a 11300×8300 boundary at 30°: find what area it is — plan, sloped, minus something?), `outline`, `ridge` (5107.33 in the sample, 4789.79 for a 9200×7200 30° hip roof at Level 2 (3000): the ridge's height, from where?), and what else appears for flat roofs, gables (`gables`, `gable`), per-edge `slopes`, courtyards, openings, extrusion roofs (`extrusion`), `join`, dormers (`dormer`), `roof_by_face`, shaped flat roofs, `offset`, roofs made over walls (no boundary given: the walls' faces plus overhang — the boundary is stored by the command, so you read it).
- shaft: `area_m2`, `height`, `top_level`, `base_offset`.
- mass: `area_m2`, `gross_floor_area_m2`, `levels` (ids of the levels it crosses), `volume_m3`, `height`, `top_level`, lofted (`top`) and leaning (`lean`) masses ("Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly").
- attached walls: `pub fn attached_height(cx: &Ctx, wall: u64) -> Option<f64>` — a wall with `attach_top` (a roof's or a floor's GUID) has its top following that roof's/floor's underside "where it's over the wall" (and `attach_base`: its base standing on a floor's top). `elements` then shows a `height` other than the stored one: in the sample house (`/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/sample.bimcraft`, made by `run --sample`), wall 100007 (x=0, y 0→7000) under a 30° hip roof shows `height` 3173.21 while the file says 3000. Find the rule (the highest point over its length? its middle? rounded to hundredths?) for hip, gable, flat, sloped and extrusion roofs, floors above (attach_top to a floor), `attach_base`, walls partly outside the roof, arc walls, walls whose level differs from the roof's. Return None for walls attached to nothing (the walls module then keeps the stored height). Check also whether attaching changes anything else in a wall's view.
Expose too: `pub fn top_at(cx: &Ctx, id: u64, at: [f64; 2]) -> Option<f64>` (the absolute height of the top surface of a floor or roof at a plan point, None outside it — the spot elevation reader will want it), and anything else general you build (roof surface planes, polygon areas).
Prioritise what typical scripts make (floors from walls, rectangular and L-shaped hip/gable/flat roofs over walls, ceilings from rooms, simple masses) before exotic shapes, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/slabs/`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""batch.py script first last n [jobs]: runs script seed n for each seed in parallel, printing
the seeds that differ (with their output)."""
import subprocess, sys
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
script, a, b, n = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3]), sys.argv[4]
jobs = int(sys.argv[5]) if len(sys.argv) > 5 else 8
def one(s):
    out = subprocess.run(['python3', '/tmp/views-dims/' + script, str(s), n], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    return s, out
bad = 0
with ThreadPoolExecutor(jobs) as ex:
    for s, out in ex.map(one, range(a, b + 1)):
        first = out.strip().split('\n')[0] if out.strip() else ''
        line = [l for l in out.split('\n') if l.startswith('seed')]
        ok = False
        if line:
            parts = line[0].split()
            if len(parts) >= 3 and '/' in parts[2]:
                x, y = parts[2].split('/')
                ok = x == y
            elif 'build failed' in out:
                ok = True
        else:
            ok = 'build failed' in out
        if not ok:
            bad += 1
            print(out.strip()[:3000])
            print('----')
print('batch', a, b, 'bad', bad)
EOF

| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
| Ceilings | In the room around a point, out to its walls' faces (Revit's automatic ceiling) and open round any walls standing free inside it (a courtyard's loop, a core), or along a boundary, open through any openings inside it; their underside 2600 mm up by default, their type's thickness over it; types with square tiles, which the reflected ceiling plan draws, stopping at the openings |
| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/parts-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/parts-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:door`, `type:beam`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type` (named `Family: Type`), `family-parameter` (named `Family: Parameter`), …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `level_above`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type` (a category's type by GUID → name and definition in `types`, e.g. `types.door`, `types.runs.beam`), `family` (name and definition in `families`), `family_type`, `material_name`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator — another sub-agent), `slabs::view` (floors, ceilings, roofs, shafts, masses — another), `parts::view` (YOURS), `notes::view` (levels, annotation, views… — another), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, families, components, stairs… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/parts-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"door"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: PARTS — `src/readers/parts/` (`parts::view` for door, window, component, column, structuralcolumn, footing, beam, stripfooting, pipe, duct, conduit, cabletray, wire, downconductor, groundconductor, cable, rebar, stair, ramp, railing)
Every field `elements` shows for these categories, exactly, for every kind of project. Observed so far (see `big1.bimcraft` and `sample.bimcraft`; verify everything and complete):
- door/window of a project type: `at` (the point on the host wall's location line at `offset` from its start — check arc walls, flipped walls, walls with other location lines), `width`, `height` (the type's), `level` (the host's), `type` (the type's name) and `type_guid`, `sill`, `mark`, flips. Of a family (`family` GUID, `type` a `family-type` GUID): `family` (its name), `family_guid`, `type` (the family type's name, `900 x 2100`; check whether there's a `type_guid`), `operation` (the family's: swing, double-swing, …), `values` (every family parameter worked out for this element: the type's values over the parameters' defaults, formulas evaluated, material parameters as the material's name, plus `Wall Thickness` — the host's thickness), `width`/`height` from `Width`/`Height`. Families loaded with `family` (custom parameters, formulas, instance parameters, yes/no, angles, materials; door/window families with `Sill Height`).
- component: `family`, `family_guid`, `type`, `values` (instance `params` over the type's over the defaults), `height` (find how: the family's forms' top? its `Height`?), `connectors` for electrical families (see the catalog's `family` entry: connectors with `load_va` formulas, poles, voltage, power factor, classification), mirrored, offset, angle, components on upper levels, symbol-only families (`symbol_set`), hosted components if any.
- The family formula language (the catalog's `family` entry): `+ - * / ^`, comparisons `< > = <= >=`, `if`, `and`, `or`, `not`, `min`, `max`, `abs`, `sqrt`, `round`, `roundup`, `rounddown`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan` (degrees), parameter names with spaces, lengths in mm; yes/no parameters; how values print (floats, materials by name, yes/no as booleans?, angles), errors in formulas (what a view shows then). Make it a reusable module with `pub fn family_values(cx: &Ctx, element_id: u64) -> Option<crate::json::Map>` (the `values` of a door/window/component) — the schedule reader will use it for family parameter fields.
- column/structuralcolumn: `type`, `type_guid`, `width`, `depth`, `round` (the type's), `height` (to `top_level` or as stored), `room_bounding` (default true), `base_offset`, `angle`, `top_level`. footing: `height` (its thickness), `base_offset` (−thickness when its top is at the level), `width`/`depth`/`round`.
- beam/stripfooting/pipe/duct/conduit/cabletray/wire/downconductor/groundconductor/cable (runs): `type`, `type_guid`, `width`, `depth`, `round` (the type's), `length` (3D), `axis` (3D end points from the level's elevation, `offset`/`end_offset`, `justify` (top/centre/bottom) and the depth: a 500 deep beam on Level 2 (3000) justified top shows axis z 2750 — the centre line?), `justify`'s default, `system`, risers (start = end with `end_offset`), sloped beams, `closed` chains.
- rebar: `length`, `weight_kg` (steel at 7850 kg/m³: Ø10 × 1000 mm = 0.617), `path` (3D, z over the level), hosted rebar (`host`), `count`/`step` sets, closed hoops, bars made by `reinforce`.
- stair: `end`, `length`, `riser_height` (176.47 = 3000/17 rounded), `risers`, `runs` ([[start, end], …] per run), `height`, `top_level`, landings and turns (`landings: [{at, turn}]`), angle, railings made with it (`railings: true`).
- ramp: `end`, `length`, `runs`, `slope`, landings.
- railing: `type`, `type_guid`, `height` (the type's), `path`; railings hosted on a stair or ramp (`railing {host, side}` or `stair {..., railings: true}`): the path the original works out along its sides (50 mm in from the edges, climbing with it), `base_offset`.
Prioritise what typical scripts make (doors/windows of types and the default families, the default furniture/plumbing/lighting families, columns, beams, pipes, straight stairs, ramps, railings) before exotic cases, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/parts/`.
