## What works today

BIMCraft is in early, fast development. Honest status:

| Area | Works today |
|---|---|
| Datums | Levels with elevations, each a plane over its extent (a rectangle in plan; by default the model's, a metre past it): sections and elevations draw a level where they see its extent, and the 3D view outlines its plane (its far two edges, all four when selected), hidden behind what's in front, its name lettered on a head past the far edges' right end, a click on either picking it; selected, its ends in a section or an elevation and the middles of its plane's edges in 3D are grips that drag its extent; grids that name themselves 1, 2, 3… or A, B, C… |
| Walls | Chains of walls, straight or curved (each turning `arc` degrees), on any of Revit's six location lines (the wall's or its core's centre line, a finish or a core face, exterior or interior); compound types with layers (structure, substrate, thermal, membrane, finish) from the exterior in, the exterior being to the left of start to end, so walls drawn clockwise face out; joins at any angle, mitred, three or more walls sharing a node, a wall ending on another stopped at its face, and sharp corners squared off; base level and offset; the top at a level or an unconnected height (by default, up to the next level), or attached to the underside of a roof or a floor (a base, onto one), following it where it's over the wall; flip, as Revit's arrows do |
| Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |
| Floors | A boundary you give, open through any openings inside it, or the outline of the walls on the level, open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and floored over); the top at the level or a height offset from it, or sloped along a slope arrow (from its tail, where it's at the offset, rising so many degrees toward its head, as Revit's slope arrow does), as thick as its type across the slope; walls attached to one follow it; in plan, its openings, the slope arrow and its slope |
| Ceilings | In the room around a point, out to its walls' faces (Revit's automatic ceiling) and open round any walls standing free inside it (a courtyard's loop, a core), or along a boundary, open through any openings inside it; their underside 2600 mm up by default, their type's thickness over it; types with square tiles, which the reflected ceiling plan draws, stopping at the openings |
| Massing | A mass is an outline extruded from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, as Revit's conceptual mass is, in its own category (`mass`) that Visibility/Graphics hides (Show Mass, MH, does it for a view in one step): dashed in plan where the cut plane passes through it and in a section where the line cuts it (outlined, not filled), a see-through solid in 3D. Give it a `top` outline with as many points as its footprint (twin for twin, the same way round) and it is lofted straight between the two, or a `lean` (the footprint moved sideways for its top: a sloped mass); the plan then draws the outline at the height it cuts, the section the line where it cuts the skin, 3D a closed skin of triangles, and area, perimeter and volume, per level too, come from the cross sections between the outlines, exactly. `mass_floors` makes a floor at each level it crosses, outlined as the mass is there; the floors hold their mass and level, so running it again updates them instead of doubling them (`prune` deletes the ones on levels the mass no longer crosses; without it they are listed as `stale`). `wall_by_face` (on faces that stand plumb), `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` (on the top outline) make a wall on each edge, and a floor and a roof on its top face, and remember their mass and face: `update_by_face` (UF) rebuilds them from the mass as it is now, as Revit's Update to Face does, and refuses the lot, naming each, when a face is gone. The `massfloor` schedule has a row for each level each mass crosses (floor area, perimeter, and the volume up to the next level or the mass's top, to sum into gross floor area and volume); the `mass` schedule one row for each mass. IFC writes a mass as a building element proxy of object type `Mass` (a lofted one as a closed face set, with a `BIMCraft_Mass` property set that says how its corners pair up), and reads one back; a mass with a courtyard in it, or whose outline changes from base to top with no such set, is left out and listed. Masses take the project parameters, phases and design options as other elements do, and move, copy, mirror and rotate with them. What a mass made is ordinary in a copy, after a split, in IFC and once its mass is deleted |
| Shaft openings | A hole along an outline from a level (and an offset) up to the next level, a level or a height, cut through every floor, ceiling and roof it reaches into: in 3D, sections, areas and IFC; in plan, its outline and a cross where the plan cuts it, and the hole in a floor seen below |
| Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |
| Rooms | Placed at a point, bounded by the walls and room separation lines around it, and following them when they change; free-standing islands (a shaft) are subtracted; area and perimeter at the wall centre line, or at the walls' faces (`room_area`, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations); IFC spaces carry `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities`, gross at the centre lines and net at the faces; Revit's Upper Limit, Limit Offset and Base Offset, with Unbounded Height and Volume; frozen rooms keep their boundary and are never recalculated; walls and columns bound rooms while their Room Bounding is on, at the level's Computation Height; two rooms can't share a space (the later is redundant, unbounded); unbounded rooms sit as a 1 m square; Rooms > Reference (the cross) and Room Separation Lines are subcategories; rooms show in 3D as see-through solids when selected, or all of them when a 3D view shows the category |
| Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |
| Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |
| Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |
| Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |

An agent's own side can ask the same: `bimcraft-cli mcp --connect --read-only`, or `bimcraft-cli mcp --read-only house.bimcraft`
for a headless server that opens the file and then only reads it.

## Commands

| Command | Shortcut | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `autosave` | | `path`: atomically write a native recovery snapshot without changing the project path or undo history |
| `recover` | | `path`, `project?`: validate and open a recovery snapshot; later Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it |
| `wall` | WA | `points`, `closed?`, `type?`, `level?`, `top_level?`, `top_offset?` (mm above `top_level`, negative below it), `height?`, `base_offset?`, `arc?` (degrees each turns, counter-clockwise), `location?` (`centre`, `core-centre`, `exterior-finish`, `interior-finish`, `exterior-core`, `interior-core`), `attach_top?`, `attach_base?` (a roof or a floor), `room_bounding?` (false: rooms run past it, as Revit's Room Bounding off; `modify` turns it on and off) |
| `door` | DR | `at`, or `wall` and `offset?`; `type?`, `family?` (a door family's `type`, its first by default), `mark?`, `flip_facing?`, `flip_hand?` |
| `window` | WN | as `door`, plus `sill?` (a family's `Sill Height` by default) |
| `sketch` | | `lines` ([[[x, y], [x, y]], …]; an arc [[x, y], [x, y], [x, y]], its ends then a point it passes through): solves a sketch without making anything, the loops it closes into (outlines and their holes) and their area, or every problem with the lines it's about: ends no other line meets, lines that intersect or overlap (a line that crosses itself too), three or more lines at a point. A sketch is solved as the straight pieces its lines are drawn with (an arc or a circle is cut into chords): past 200,000 of them it is refused at once |
| `edit_boundary` | | `id` (a floor, a ceiling, a roof by footprint or a shaft), `sketch?`: its outline and holes redrawn as one sketch, a line sent back with its `id` keeping it; without `sketch`, the lines it has now, each with its id once it has one |
| `floor` | | `boundary?` (else the walls of the level) or `sketch?` (lines, in any order, solved into its outline and openings), `openings?` (holes in it, inside it and apart; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it), `level?`, `type?`, `offset?` (its top above the level), `slope?` (degrees) and `arrow?` (its tail and head: it rises from the tail toward the head), `structural?` (a floor that carries load, as Revit's Floor: Structural). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof`, `shaft`, `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` hold to it too, saying which edges); a saved file that has one still opens. Its model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (set with `modify`) |
| `ceiling` | | `point` (in a room: out to its walls' faces, open round the walls standing free inside it), `boundary` or `sketch`, `openings?` (holes in it, inside it and apart), `level?`, `type?`, `offset?` (its underside above the level, 2600) |

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/notes-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/notes-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `text_types`, `dimension_types`, `line_styles`, `units`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type`, `text-type`, `line-style`, `dimension-type`, `filled-region-type`, `fill-pattern`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `normalize_guid`, `find` (an element by id or GUID). `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers with the original's error wording.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)` works something out once per reading), `r2` (round to hundredths), lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type`, `family`, `family_type`, `material_name`, `lib_name_of`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command (category/level/limit/offset filters, done) and `element_view(cx, id)`: clones the stored element, adds `id`, and hands it to the module owning its category: `walls::view` (wall, room, roomseparator — another sub-agent), `slabs::view` (floors, ceilings, roofs, shafts, masses — another), `parts::view` (doors, windows, components, columns, runs, stairs, railings — another), `notes::view` (YOURS), `crate::cloud::element_view` (point clouds, done). `schedule/` (another sub-agent) — provides `crate::readers::schedule::field_display(cx, id, field) -> Option<String>` (a field's value as a schedule cell shows it; a stub in your build). `file/` — the project-file loader (done: it validates and canonicalises files on open, so every field is present with its default). `src/styles/` (done by another agent) owns text types, dimension types, line styles, units — read their code for the type definitions and defaults.
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, dimensions, tags, sheets, views… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet. So build every input project with the ORIGINAL and test reading it: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/notes-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house with dimensions, tags, a note, a spot, a section, elevations, sheets and viewports). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. You can also edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'elements {"category":"dimension"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: every value must match exactly (floats to the last digit: find the original's exact formulas and rounding — it reports some values rounded to hundredths, others unrounded).
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: NOTES — `src/readers/notes/` (`notes::view` for level, grid, dimension, dimension3d, tag, text, spot, section, elevation, sheet, viewport, schedule, view3d, planview, line, region, detailgroup, repeatingdetail, link, cadimport; and the commands `select_by_id`, `ids_of`, `measure`: `notes::cmd_select_by_id`, `cmd_ids_of`, `cmd_measure`)
Every field `elements` shows for these categories, exactly, and the three commands' replies and errors. Observed so far (verify everything and complete):
- level: `computation_height` (1200 unless stored), `view_range`, `extent`, anything else; grid: as stored?
- dimension: `type` (the dimension type's name), `values` (mm), `labels` (the text as drawn, `10300`: with the project's `units` (the `units` command: mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in) and the dimension type's settings — see `src/styles/text.rs` for dimension types), for every `kind` (aligned, linear, angular, radial, diameter, arc_length) and every reference: a wall's centre/left/right faces (`face`; they depend on the wall type's thickness, its location line, flips), start/end, a door's/window's centre and jambs, grids, detail lines, points (`point`, `endpoint`); `dimension_text` (prefix, suffix, above, below, replace), `dimension_constraint` (equal, locked), `dimension_value`, `dimension_3d`.
- tag: `at` (the host's point plus `offset`: a door/window at its point on the host wall, a room at its point, walls, columns, components, floors…), `text` (a door's/window's mark, a room's name, else the type's name; with `label`, the field as its category's schedule shows it → call `crate::readers::schedule::field_display(cx, id, label)` — implemented by the schedule sub-agent; in your build it returns None, so test label tags only for what you can verify and note the rest), `level`, `leader`.
- text: `type` (name), `size` (the text type's), `level` (the view's level, for a note in a plan), notes in sections/elevations/sheets, leaders, runs.
- spot: `elevation` (the height of the top of the host at `at` — a floor's top, a pipe's top…; write your own top-of-host heights for now), `level`; spot_slope's fields.
- section/elevation: `length`, `looking` (the unit vector to the left of start→end), `depth`, crop; note: one elevation's start y came out in `elements` as …1904 where the file had …1902 (`big1.bimcraft`, elevations made by `elevation {}`) — find why (recomputed from something?).
- sheet: `paper` ([420, 297] for A3), `viewports` (their ids); viewport: `size` (the view's extent on paper at its scale: a plan's extent of what it shows (`big1` gives [615.6, 254.4] for Level 1 at 1:100), a section's, an elevation's, a schedule's table size, the 3D view's…), `title` (the view's name).
- view3d (cameras, section boxes, perspective), planview (`duplicate_view`: view_range, dependent views), schedule elements (as stored?), line (detail lines: `length`, `shape`, `style` (name) for lines, arcs, circles, ellipses, splines, polylines, insulation, revision clouds), region (`area_m2`, `type`/`line_style` names, sketch, pattern), detail groups and repeating details (`create_group`, `detail_group`, `repeating_detail`), links (`link`), CAD imports (`import_cad` with a small DXF you write).
- `select_by_id {text}` (ids, GUIDs with/without dashes and braces, IFC GlobalIds, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons, lines: `ids` found, each once, in order; `missing`; `plan` and `extent` [[x, y], [x, y]] — the plan that shows them and where: this needs each element's extent in plan, for every category), `ids_of {ids}` (`id`, `guid`, `ifc` GlobalId — the GUID compressed into IFC's 22-character base64 —, `category`, `name` or type/number/mark), `measure {from, to}` (`length`, `dx`, `dy`, `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise). Match their errors exactly (try every bad input).
Prioritise what typical scripts make (dimensions between walls/grids, tags of doors/windows/rooms, notes, spot elevations on floors, sections, elevations, sheets with plans placed, detail lines) before exotic cases, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the public functions others can call (e.g. a plan-extent function for any element); any edit outside `src/readers/notes/`.

9 | Doors, windows | Hosted in walls: place one at a point on the wall (`at`), or by wall and offset; marks number themselves, on in the series they are in (`P1`, `P2` → `P3`; `J-09` → `J-10`) and kept through IFC as the doors' and windows' tags; flip facing and hand; refused when they don't fit their wall or overlap. Of one of the project's own types (a width, a height, a sill), or of a family of their own: a new project comes with a single door, a double door, a sliding door, a fixed window, a casement window and a sliding window, each saying how it opens (swing, double swing, sliding, double sliding, folding or fixed, which IFC's operation types and the schedules carry), and more load from `.json` files. A family's forms (frame, leaf, handle, sashes, panes) are drawn in the opening, its `Width` and `Height` size the hole in the wall, its `Sill Height` is a window's sill, its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, and its plan symbols (a door's swing) go with it as it flips; sections show them beyond their line, never cut |

14 | Columns, stairs, roofs | Columns of rectangular or round types, turned to any angle, from their level up to the next (or a height, or a level); cut in plan, in poché. Stairs from a start point toward an end point, in as many risers as keep each at most 180 mm, treads 280 mm deep, up to the next level: one straight run, or runs with a landing between each two (as deep as the stair is wide) after so many risers, the next run going on straight, turning left or right, or coming back beside the last; in plan, their risers up to the cut line and the rest dashed, landings over the cut plane dashed, and the walk line marked UP (DN from the level above). Roofs on a level and an offset from it, by footprint: flat, or over any outline every edge sloping up at one slope, or at a slope of its own, until the slopes meet, in hips, valleys and ridges (its straight skeleton), but the edges left upright as gable ends; round courtyards too, holes in the footprint whose edges are eaves like the outline's (or gables); by default over the walls of the level below, 500 mm past their faces, at 30°, and open over each loop of them standing free inside, a courtyard (a loop joined to the outer walls, or with a room in it, is rooms, and roofed over). Or by extrusion: a profile drawn along a line, swept across. Openings through them, and a roof that runs into another (a dormer's) ends where it meets that one's top. Dormers: walls standing on a roof's slope under a gable roof of their own, with a window in front, the roof open under them. In plan, their ridges, hips and valleys, and from the level below their edge dashed overhead |

16 | Ramps, railings | Ramps from a start point toward an end point at a slope (8.33%, 1 in 12, by default) up to a level or a height, in one run or turning at landings as stairs do, solid down to their level; in plan, their outline, dashed over the cut plane, and the walk line. Railings down a side of a stair or a ramp, 50 mm in from its edge, climbing with it and going wherever it goes, or along a path on a level; a rail at their type's height over what they run along, and balusters their type's spacing apart; in plan, their line, dashed over the cut plane |

17 | Structure | Beams, structural columns, isolated footings, wall (strip) footings and structural floors, Revit's Structure tab on the design in [docs/disciplines.md](docs/disciplines.md). A beam, or a wall footing, is a **run**: a straight element from one point to another, of a type with a section (`width` across by `depth` deep, or round) made of a material of the library, at a height over its level (the height of its top, middle or bottom line at each end, so it can slope up to 75°), in a named `system`; a chain of points makes one for each step. A structural column is a column of its own category and types; an isolated footing is a column laid down, its top at the level by default and as thick as `thickness`. A floor says it is `structural`. In plan a run hangs under its level (seen from it, with its centre line dashed to pick it by), crosses the cut plane (in poché) or lies overhead (dashed); a section cuts a rectangular run across its section, and the 3D view draws a sloped prism or, round, a tube; snaps find their ends and middles. Each has a schedule (Id, Type, Level, Length, Width, Depth, with System to group a schedule by), a place in Visibility/Graphics, project parameters and phases, and its IFC class: IfcBeam, IfcColumn, IfcFooting (`PAD_FOOTING`, `STRIP_FOOTING`) and IfcSlab, each with `LoadBearing` in its `Pset_*Common`, swept along its own axis; IFC import reads them back, taking a column or slab whose `Pset_*Common` says it carries load as structural |

18 | Plumbing | Pipes, plumbing fixtures, pipe fittings and pipe accessories, Revit's Plumbing & Piping panel on the same **run** the Structure tab uses. A pipe is round (its `width` its outside diameter) in PVC or copper, at a height over its level at each end (a drain falls, a riser stands upright: the same point twice and two heights), its line the middle unless told, in a named `system` (Água fria, Esgoto) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem` its pipes are assigned to. A section cuts a pipe in a ring (the poché of a circle, an ellipse when the line is oblique). A fixture is a component of a family whose category says what it is: the project starts with a basin, a WC, a bathtub, a kitchen sink, a shower, a floor drain, elbows, tees and a gate valve, original drawings in the project's language, written to IFC as `IfcSanitaryTerminal`, `IfcWasteTerminal` (`FLOORTRAP`), `IfcPipeFitting` and `IfcValve` and read back into a family of the same category. A family says which fixture or fitting it is (`kind`: `wc`, `lav`, `sink`, `laundry`, `shower`, `bath`…, `floor_drain`, `bend`, `tee`…), which IFC writes as its predefined type (a WC `TOILETPAN`, a basin `WASHHANDBASIN`, an elbow `BEND`) and the import reads back; the starter families say theirs. Fittings and valves are centred on their pipe, so placing one at the pipe's height lines them up; there are no connectors yet |

19 | Electrical | Conduits, cable trays, wires, distribution boards, outlets and switches and luminaires, Revit's Electrical panel on the same run and the same fixtures. A conduit (eletroduto) and a wire are round, a cable tray (eletrocalha) a width by a depth, each at a height over its level at each end (a riser stands upright), in a named `system` (a circuit: Circuito 3) that IFC carries as an `IfcSystem`. The project starts with PVC and steel conduits, perforated trays in three sizes and copper wires, and a distribution board (12, 24 and 36 circuits), a ceiling and a recessed luminaire, an outlet and a switch, each at the mounting height its type says (an outlet's 300, 1100 or 2100 mm to its centre; a luminaire hung from the slab), original drawings in the project's language, the luminaires, outlets and switches carrying connectors (voltage, poles, a load for each type, per phase on a three-phase outlet; `inspect` warns of a device without one), written as `IfcCableCarrierSegment` (`CONDUITSEGMENT`, `CABLETRAYSEGMENT`; a `CABLELADDERSEGMENT` from another tool is read as a tray), `IfcCableSegment`, `IfcElectricDistributionBoard`, `IfcOutlet`, `IfcSwitchingDevice` and `IfcLightFixture`, and read back. The project also keeps Revit's Electrical Settings: voltages (each with the band a device may read within), distribution systems (phases, wires and the voltages each supplies) and wire types (material, insulation, temperature and an ampacity for each section, always in mm²), through `voltage`, `distribution_system` and `wire_type`; it starts with 230/400 V, 127/220 V, 220/380 V and 277/480 V, and copper wires of the NBR 5410 tables (PVC 70 °C, XLPE or EPR 90 °C) and of the NEC (THHN, THW; AWG sizes kept in mm²), whose ampacities are the contributor's and unchecked. Manage > Electrical Settings edits all three in one dialog, applied as one undo step. |

22 | Reinforcement | `rebar` makes reinforcing bars: a round bar of a diameter (3 to 100 mm) and a steel grade (CA-50 unless told) bent along points in mm, in the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces, which it goes with; `closed` makes a hoop, and `count` with `step` a layer of bars or hoops along a beam. A schedule of rebar lists grade, diameter, length, count and weight (steel at 7850 kg/m³) and, grouped, is a bar schedule. IFC writes and reads each as an `IfcReinforcingBar`, aggregated to its host. The 3D view draws them as tubes (inside their host, so hide it to see them), a section draws the bars it cuts as dots over the poché, and a plan draws each bar of its level as a thin line (solid under the cut plane, dashed over it and under the view range's top, a bar that stands as a dot, bars lying on one another drawn once), hidden with the category. `reinforce` arms a beam, a column, a footing or a floor (round columns and footings, and sloped floors, too) by rules: the engineer gives the cover (or the host's `Cobrimento` parameter) and how many bars, how thick and how far apart (a beam's bars below and above, stirrups with closer ends and hooks, skin bars and anchors; a column's bars on each face, stirrups and ties; a footing's two layers of mesh with their ends turned up; a floor's meshes below and above, stopping short of its outline and openings), and it lays them out inside the cover, checks they fit with room between them and says what to change; a beam's bars and a column's end in hooks if told, some of a beam's bottom bars bend up at each end to the top at an angle (`bent`) and a column's bars step in toward its axis near the top (`jog`); each bar is on a layer, and reinforcing again replaces what it made and leaves bars drawn by hand. `hosts` arms a list alike, all or none (up to 1000 hosts and 20000 bars), and `reinforcement_preset` keeps a named set of the parameters for a kind of host in the project, which `reinforce` takes with `preset` and lets what is given replace. The numbers are the engineer's; `check` "NBR 6118" (with the aggressiveness class and `fck`) adds notes, never a refusal, where the bars made fall short of its usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars), typed from public handbooks and not from the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. On the desktop, the Structure tab's Reinforce (RF) opens a dialog for the elements selected (any number, of one kind), with the fields of their kind, saying a refusal inside itself, keeping what was typed for the next of its kind, saving the fields as a preset to choose for another and deleting one, and with Remove Bars for the bars it made. Not yet: bends other than a hook, a bent-up bar and a column's jog, round beams, bars beyond a section's cut seen through the concrete. |

34 | Schedules | Schedule views of rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, pipes, conduits, cable trays, wires, down conductors, earthing conductors, cables, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, as Revit's Schedule/Quantities makes them: the fields chosen and ordered from the category's own (Area, Width, Count…), the project parameters for it and, for components, their families' parameters; calculated fields, formulas over the row's other fields as a family's are (`Area * 120`, `Perimeter * Finish Height / 1e6`); filters (equals, greater than, contains, begins with, has a value…) that every row holds to, comparing values as the schedule shows them; sorting by fields in turn, ascending or descending (the phase fields in the project's order of phases, not by name), and grouped, a row for each set of their values, its count and totals summed; totals under the rows. Every project has a Room, Door, Window, Wall, Floor and Level Schedule, each the project's own once changed; CSV; on sheets, totals and all |

38 | Families | BIMCraft's own parametric components, never Autodesk's `.rfa`: a family has parameters (lengths, numbers, angles, yes or no, materials; each type's, or each component's), types that set them, and forms, each a profile drawn in its own axes and swept across them, every size a number or a formula as Revit's are (`Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`), each form of a material, there while a yes/no parameter or a formula says. A new project comes with ten of them (tables, chairs, beds, sofas, desks, wardrobes, base cabinets, WCs, washbasins, bathtubs), named and worded in its language; more load from .json files. A component places a family's type at a point, turned and mirrored, its instance parameters its own; plans show it from above, the parts under a higher one hidden (a table's legs under its top), and sections and elevations beyond their line, never cut, as Revit shows furniture; the 3D view shades each form in its material's colour, textured as its material is. A form may be turned about an axis in its plane (a pipe, a bowl, a shade: `axis`, and `from` and `to` in degrees, up to a full turn), and a `void` form cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through (a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, a sash round its pane), exactly: a solid cut by a solid, in any shape. The Family Editor in the desktop edits a family's parameters, types, forms and symbols as text, shows it on a preview you can turn, and makes it the project's, saves it to a `.json` file, or keeps it, with the materials it's made of, in the Favorites |

results.content:
point_cloud [] :: {path | cloud, name?, level?, at?: [x, y], offset?, angle?, units?, spacing?, origin?} brings in a laser scan (`path`: PTS, XYZ, PLY, LAS or E57 (each of its scans placed by its pose), or a list of the files of one scan's stations, brought in as one; `units` of its coordinates mm, cm, m (the default), in or ft; one point kept in each cube `spacing` mm wide) or places one the project holds again (`cloud`, its name), as an element: its middle on `at` (the origin) and its foot on the level, or with `origin: file` where its file's coordinates put it; `offset` raises its middle over the level, `angle` turns it. Returns its id, the scan's name, the points kept and read, and where its middle was in the file

floor [] :: {boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline

ceiling [] :: {point: [x,y] | boundary: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?} a ceiling, its underside `offset` mm (2600) above the level, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart): in the room around `point`, out to its walls' faces and round the walls standing inside it, or along `boundary`. Reflected ceiling plans show it

shaft [] :: {boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`

edit_shape [] :: {id, points?: [{at: [x,y], z, id?}, …], lines?: [{a: [x,y], b: [x,y], id?}, …], absolute?} gives a floor's top, or a flat roof's by footprint (its underside following), its shape anew, all at once: points `z` mm above (negative, below) where its top would be without them (with `absolute`, at that elevation), and split lines it folds along, between which it's flat triangles, merged where neighbours lie in one plane: falls to drains, ridges, valleys. Its outline's and openings' corners stay at 0 unless a point is there; a line's end that is no point and no corner becomes a point at the height the top has there. Sent back with its `id`, a point or a line keeps it. A shaped floor has no slope arrow, a shaped roof no `slope`. Without `points` or `lines`, gives the shape: its points and lines with their ids, its corners at their heights, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest (`top`, mm above zero)

add_point [] :: {id, at: [x,y], z?, absolute?, offset?} a point on a floor's or flat roof's top: `offset` mm over the top as it is there now (Revit's Along Surface), or `z` mm above where it would be without its shape (with `absolute`, at that elevation); with neither, at the height the top has there now. Within a millimetre of a point it has, sets that one's height

add_split_line [] :: {id, a: [x,y], b: [x,y]} a line a floor's or flat roof's top folds along; an end that is no point of its shape and no corner of its outline or an opening becomes a point, at the height the top has there now

reset_shape [] :: {id} takes a floor's or roof's points and split lines all off: it's flat at its offset again

falls [] :: {id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes (`faces`) and its top's lowest and highest. Refused, saying why and where: a corner a drain can reach only over the outline or a ridge, or a plane that can't fall as asked to a drain

mass ['MS'] :: {boundary: [[x,y],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?, top?: [[x,y],…], lean?: [dx,dy], name?} a mass, Revit's conceptual volume: the footprint extruded from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`. With `top`, an outline of as many points as the footprint (twin for twin, running the same way round), it is lofted straight from the footprint to it; `lean` makes one by moving the footprint sideways by [dx, dy] for its top, a sloped mass. Drawn dashed in plans and sections (the outline at the height they cut it, between the two when lofted), a see-through solid in 3D; its own category, `mass`, which views may hide. Its areas and volumes, per level too, are those of the cross sections between its outlines, exactly. Make floors from it with `mass_floors`, walls, a floor and a roof from its faces with `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face`

mass_floors ['MF'] :: {mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level

wall_by_face ['WB'] :: {mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

floor_by_face ['FB'] :: {mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on

roof_by_face ['RB'] :: {mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on

update_by_face ['UF'] :: {mass?, ids?} rebuilds what `wall_by_face`, `floor_by_face` and `roof_by_face` made from the mass as it is now (Revit's Update to Face): the walls on its edges, as tall as it is, a floor and a roof on its top face. The ones of `mass`, or the `ids` given, or every one in the project; what was done to them since (their type, a roof's slope) stays. A face that is gone (a footprint with fewer corners) refuses the lot and says which; a deleted mass's are ordinary elements. Revit has no default shortcut for it: UF is BIMCraft's. The reply has `updated` and `unchanged`

show_mass ['MH'] :: {view?, show?} hides the masses in a view if it shows them, shows them if it hides them (or as `show`, a yes or no, says): the `mass` category of `graphics {hide|show}`, in one step. The reply has `shown` and `hidden`, the categories the view hides. Revit's Show Mass has no default shortcut; MH is BIMCraft's

roof [] :: {level?, boundary?: [[x,y],…], courtyards?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], slope?, slopes?: [degrees, …], overhang?, gables?: [edge, …], gable?, offset?, extrusion?, openings?: [[[x,y],…],…], join?, type?} a roof on `level` (by default the one above the lowest), its base `offset` mm above it. Over `boundary` or else the walls of the level below, `overhang` mm (500) past their faces, round any `courtyards` (holes in it, inside it and apart, with eaves of their own; over the walls, by default each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it): flat at `slope` 0, else every edge sloping up at `slope` degrees (30), hips, valleys and ridges where the slopes meet, but the edges in `gables` (edge i runs from point i to the next, the courtyards' edges numbered on after the boundary's) left upright, gable ends; `gable` leaves a rectangle's short ends upright. `slopes`: a slope in degrees (up to 75) for each edge, numbered as `gables` are, 0 for an edge that takes `slope`; none, every edge does; the eaves stay level and an edge in `gables` stays upright whatever its slope. A `sketch` line may carry a `slope` for the edges along it. Or with `extrusion` {line: [[x,y],[x,y]], profile: [[along, up],…], from?, to}: its underside's profile in the upright plane through `line`, along it from its start and up from the base, swept square to it from `from` (0) to `to` mm to its left. `openings` are holes through it in plan; with `join`, a roof it runs into, it ends where it meets that one's top

dormer [] :: {host, at: [x, y], width?, height?, slope?, window?, type?} a dormer on roof `host`, its front wall across the slope through `at`: walls of `type` `width` mm (1600) apart, standing on the roof and `height` mm (1200) tall at the front, under a gable roof of its own sloping `slope` degrees (30) that runs back into the host; the host open under it, and with `window` (a window type) a window in its front. Replies with its roof, walls and window

spot_slope [] :: {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot slope in a level's plan (the lowest by default): how steeply the top of the floor or roof at `at` (or `host`) falls there, %, an arrow pointing downhill; it follows the top. The reply gives `slope` and `toward`, the way down in plan (null on the level)

split ['SL'] :: {id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`

join_polyline ['PJ'] :: {ids: [id, …]} joins detail lines of one view, lines, arcs and polylines that meet end to end, into one polyline in the first's line style (closed when they come round); the first keeps its id, the rest are deleted, and a dimension that measured one of the rest loses that reference (and is deleted, left with fewer than two): the reply's `notes` say which

load_points [] :: {rooms?: [{name, area, perimeter, kind?: bath|kitchen|service|dry|veranda|other, points?}], alternative?} the lighting and the general-use outlets (TUG) of a dwelling's rooms as NBR 5410:2004 item 9.5.2 asks. The rooms are `rooms` (`area` in m², `perimeter` in millimetres, `points` the outlets the room has, the least it needs when absent) or, without it, the rooms of the model, measured inside the walls' finish. A room's kind is known by its name (Portuguese or English: banheiro, cozinha, copa, área de serviço, lavanderia, sala, dormitório, varanda…) unless `kind` gives it; a name that says none is `other`. Lighting: 1 ceiling point of 100 VA up to 6 m² and 60 VA more for each whole 4 m² above. Outlets: a bathroom 1; kitchen, pantry, service area, laundry one for each 3.5 m of perimeter; room, bedroom one for each 5 m; veranda 1; the others 1 up to 6 m² and one for each 5 m above. Power: in a bathroom, kitchen, pantry, service area or laundry 600 VA for each of the first 3 points and 100 VA for the others; elsewhere 100 VA a point; on the points a room has. Where those rooms have more than 6 points together `alternative: true` takes 600 VA for the first 2 of each (`alternative_possible` says when). A kitchen or pantry also needs 2 outlets over the sink's counter (`counter_outlets`). Not applied: the exceptions to the lighting point and to a veranda's outlet, the placement of the outlets and the TUE (`not_covered`). It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it. It changes nothing

import math
cr = lambda p, q: p[0]*q[1] - p[1]*q[0]
sub = lambda p, q: (p[0]-q[0], p[1]-q[1])
add = lambda p, q: (p[0]+q[0], p[1]+q[1])
sc = lambda p, k: (p[0]*k, p[1]*k)
dot = lambda p, q: p[0]*q[0] + p[1]*q[1]
def unit_h(v):
    l = math.hypot(v[0], v[1]); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
def unit_s(v):
    l = math.sqrt(v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1]); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l)
def unit_m(v):
    l = math.sqrt(v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1]); k = 1.0 / l; return (v[0]*k, v[1]*k)
cs, ce = (3000.0, 7000.0), (0.0, 0.0)
os_, oe = (0.0, 0.0), (10000.0, 0.0)
want = (6.496390726949487e-14, 0.0)
res = {}
for un_name, un in (('h', unit_h), ('s', unit_s), ('m', unit_m)):
    d = sub(ce, cs); e = sub(oe, os_)
    u = un(d); ue = un(e)
    L = math.hypot(d[0], d[1]); L2 = math.sqrt(d[0]*d[0]+d[1]*d[1])
    res['u*s cross e ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, cr(sub(os_, cs), e) / cr(u, e)))
    res['u*s cross ue ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, cr(sub(os_, cs), ue) / cr(u, ue)))
    n = (-ue[1], ue[0])
    res['u*s normal ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, dot(sub(os_, cs), n) / dot(u, n)))
    res['u*L ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, L))
    res['u*L2 ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, L2))
    # t along d then
    t = cr(sub(os_, cs), e) / cr(d, e)
    res['u*(t*L) ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(u, t * L))
    # from the location line offset: centre = start + n*0
    nn = (-u[1], u[0])
    res['offset0 ' + un_name] = add(add(cs, sc(nn, 0.0)), sc(d, 1.0))
    # line as point+unit, meet with other's point+unit
    den = cr(u, ue)
    s = cr(sub(os_, cs), ue) / den
    res['pu meet ' + un_name] = (cs[0] + u[0]*s, cs[1] + u[1]*s)
    # the end recomputed as start + u*len then meet
    e_end = add(cs, sc(u, L))
    t2 = cr(sub(os_, cs), e) / cr(sub(e_end, cs), e)
    res['recomp end ' + un_name] = add(cs, sc(sub(e_end, cs), t2))
for k, v in res.items():
    print('%-22s %r %r %s' % (k, v[0], v[1], '<==' if v == want else ''))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

803 /workspace/README.md

BIMCraft

Building information modeling; an open-source, clean-room take on the Autodesk Revit workflow, rebuilt in pure Rust.

Model a building the way Revit does: levels, walls, doors and windows, floors and ceilings, rooms, columns, stairs, ramps and railings, roofs and shafts that know about each other. Draw plans, sections, elevations and a 3D view from them, lay them out on sheets, and read and write IFC. Every action is a command, so agents can drive it as well as you can.
By IPedrax.



The sample house (cargo run --release -p bimcraft -- --sample): Revit's layout in BIMCraft's own icons and colours, with dimensions, door and window tags, a spot elevation, a note, a section and the four elevation marks, all built from BIMCraft commands.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/46488109-fdc4-4ce5-a6bd-92b3b95af16c

BIMCraft in 34 seconds (AI-generated voiceover; download the mp4, 8.4 MB): the sample house built from 58 lines of text, its plans, sections, sheets and 3D view, a wall moved with its doors and room areas following, IFC in and out, and an agent building a house over MCP.

Screenshots · Why BIMCraft · What works today · Quick start · The desktop app · Agents, MCP and the CLI · Commands · Architecture · Roadmap · Downloads · License and credits

## Screenshots
3D view: from the south-east, as Revit's default 3D view looks. Orbit, pan and zoom; click to select; the axis triad in the corner turns it to look from the top, bottom, front, back, left or right. Section: the cut in poché, the roof along its slope, what lies beyond in hidden line, levels and grids.
Sheets: views placed at a scale under a title block, printed to PDF a page each. Dark mode: the window and the views go dark; sheets stay white paper.
Snaps and the ruler: guides at angles from east and from the line before, so a 60° corner comes out exact. Wall grips: drag an end, with the same snaps and guides from the other end.
Schedules: the fields chosen, project parameters and calculated ones among them, totalled. Schedule Properties: fields, filters, sorting and grouping, as Revit's tabs have them.
Graphics overrides: what a view hides and how it draws the rest, by category, filter and element. Visibility/Graphics: categories, filters and elements, projection and cut each with their own line and fill.
Phases: what stood before in halftone, what comes down dashed red, what is new as the category draws it. Phasing: phases in order, and phase filters that say how a view shows each status.
Textures: a material's texture at its real size on the faces it lies on: brick in courses, boards, glass. Paint: a material laid over one face, as Revit's Paint does; Remove Paint takes it off.
Family Editor: parameters, types, forms (extrusions, revolves, voids) and a door's or window's plan symbols, with a preview. Materials: a texture from a pattern or a picture of yours, its tile size, and a favorite kept for every project.
Structure: beams, structural columns, isolated and wall footings and structural floors; Revit's Structure tab on one new element, the run (design). Section: a beam is cut across its section, a round run (a pipe, a steel tube) in a ring.
Beam tool: two clicks, or a chain of them, each step a beam; sketched before the click. Beam properties: heights at both ends, justification, and the system it belongs to.
Pipe tool: two clicks, or a chain; centred on its height by default, falling or rising with a second height. Pipe type: its diameter (or width and depth, if it isn't round) and its material.
Section: a pipe is cut in poché along the line, across it in a ring.
Device tool: the Type Selector lists only the families of its kind; Space turns what you place. Cable tray type: a width by a depth, or round, in a material.
Plumbing: the starter fixtures, a pipe falling to a drain and a riser, in 3D with the walls hidden. Electrical: a tray, a board, luminaires and devices at their mounting heights.
Lightning Protection (SPDA): NBR 5419's vocabulary on the same runs and fixtures; Revit has no such tab. SPDA in 3D: terminals, down conductors and the earthing ring and rods.
Data tab: outlets, a rack, a patch panel and cabling, in NBR 14565's words. Data in 3D: a tray, cables dropping to their outlets, a rack.
## Performance sample Start an original 20-storey, 9,521-element tower with `bimcraft --highrise`, or generate a native file with `bimcraft-cli run --highrise --save highrise.bimcraft`. The script is [`samples/highrise.txt`](samples/highrise.txt). See the [performance baseline](docs/performance.md) for reproducible core/UI measurements and the remaining optimization work. Private local IFC fixtures and their results belong in the ignored `test_model/` folder. The 3D view can be drawn on the graphics card: File > Settings > Performance > Draw the 3D view on the graphics card, off until you turn it on. On that tower at 1920 × 1080 a changed frame took 1.3 ms on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, against 108 ms on the processor, and what is under the cursor is found in a bounding volume hierarchy instead of read from the picture. The card draws what the processor draws, with the same lighting, textures, edges, level lines and surfaces seen through (a mass, or what Visibility/Graphics makes transparent). Hidden line, wireframe, sections and sheets are still drawn on the processor, and so is everything when the card fails, when the window runs on OpenGL (the card is for Vulkan, Metal and DirectX 12) or when the computer has none; the Performance page says which. ## Why BIMCraft

## Why BIMCraft

- **The workflow you know.** Revit's ribbon, the green contextual Modify tab, the Options Bar, Properties with the Type
  Selector and Edit Type, the Project Browser, views in tabs, and Revit's shortcuts: WA, DR, WN, RM, CL, DI, TG, MV, CO,
  RO, MM, AL, TR, SL, ME, CS, SA, VV, EH, MS, WB, FB, RB, UF, MH, and KS to list them all. Click to select, Ctrl adds, Shift takes away, Tab reaches what's
  underneath.
- **A real building model.** Doors and windows live in their walls, rooms find their boundaries from the walls around
  them, walls joined at a corner stay joined when one moves, dimensions and tags follow what they measure and name, and
  every change is checked against the model's rules and can be undone.
- **Open files.** IFC2x3 and IFC4 come in from Revit and other BIM tools, and IFC4 goes back out, checked with
  IfcOpenShell. Sheets print to PDF; any view saves as PNG, plans as SVG. Revit's own `.rvt` format has no public
  specification; `bimcraft-cli` reads a `.rvt` file with a reader fenced in [docs/rvt-provenance.md](docs/rvt-provenance.md):
  `info` shows its release, levels and element counts by category, and `run` and `convert` (and the MCP server's `open`) import
  its levels, walls, floors and ceilings, doors and windows, columns, rooms and roofs (flat ones by footprint, and gables and sheds
  by extrusion) into a project, listing what was left out and why. The desktop app's File > Open takes a `.rvt` too: it is read
  while the window says so, comes in as a new unsaved project, and a "Revit import report" lists what came in and what was left out.
- **Built for agents.** Every tool, button and field is a command. Agents call any of them with JSON, inspect the model to
  check their work, and render any view to look at it, over MCP or the CLI.
- **Fast and native.** Pure Rust and egui: no Electron, no web view. Packaged for Windows, Linux and macOS; developed on
  Linux, and the macOS app isn't tried by hand yet.

"""run.py [-m] [-f file] [-k key1,key2] -- cmd1 cmd2 ...
Runs the original (or mine with -m) on a copy of file with the --cmd's given; pretty prints JSON replies.
-k: only show these keys of each element (for elements replies)
"""
import os, sys, subprocess, json, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = '/workspace/.claude/worktrees/agent-ab6ae327a17815a2f/target/release/bimcraft-cli'
a = sys.argv[1:]
exe = ORIG; f = None; keys = None; save = None
while a and a[0] != '--':
    if a[0] == '-m': exe = MINE; a = a[1:]
    elif a[0] == '-f': f = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-k': keys = a[1].split(','); a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-s': save = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    else: break
if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='wr')
args = [exe, 'run']
if f:
    shutil.copy(f, d)
    args.append(os.path.basename(f))
for c in a:
    args += ['--cmd', c]
if save:
    args += ['--save', os.path.abspath(save)]
p = subprocess.run(args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=300)
for line in p.stdout.decode().split('\n'):
    if not line.strip(): continue
    try:
        v = json.loads(line)
    except Exception:
        print(line); continue
    if keys and isinstance(v, dict) and 'elements' in v:
        for e in v['elements']:
            print(json.dumps({k: e.get(k) for k in ['id'] + keys if k in e}))
    else:
        print(json.dumps(v, indent=1))
if p.stderr:
    print('STDERR:', p.stderr.decode())
print('exit', p.returncode)
shutil.rmtree(d)

import json, math, re, sys, itertools
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-agent')
from fma import fma
rows = json.load(open('/tmp/edit-agent/t36.json'))
D = 180 / math.pi
def r9(x): return math.floor(x*1e9+0.5)/1e9 if x >= 0 else -math.floor(-x*1e9+0.5)/1e9
def r3(x): return math.floor(x*1000+0.5)/1000 if x >= 0 else -math.floor(-x*1000+0.5)/1000
def L(d): return math.sqrt(fma(d[0], d[0], d[1]*d[1]))
def xf_vec(op, v):
    if op.startswith('move'): return v
    m = re.search(r'"angle": (-?\d+)', op)
    if op.startswith('rotate'):
        t = float(m.group(1)) * (math.pi/180); c, s = math.cos(t), math.sin(t)
        return (v[0]*c - v[1]*s, v[1]*c + v[0]*s)
    ax = json.loads(re.search(r'"axis": (\[\[.*\]\])', op).group(1))
    d = (ax[1][0]-ax[0][0], ax[1][1]-ax[0][1]); k = 1/L(d); d = (d[0]*k, d[1]*k)
    dv = (v[0]*d[0]+v[1]*d[1]) * 2.0
    return (d[0]*dv - v[0], d[1]*dv - v[1])
def xf_pt(op, p):
    if op.startswith('move'):
        by = json.loads(re.search(r'"by": (\[.*?\])', op).group(1)); return (p[0]+by[0], p[1]+by[1])
    if op.startswith('rotate'):
        about = json.loads(re.search(r'"about": (\[.*?\])', op).group(1))
        v = (p[0]-about[0], p[1]-about[1]); r = xf_vec(op, v)
        return (r3(about[0]+r[0]), r3(about[1]+r[1]))
    ax = json.loads(re.search(r'"axis": (\[\[.*\]\])', op).group(1))
    a = ax[0]; v = (p[0]-a[0], p[1]-a[1]); r = xf_vec(op, v)
    return (r3(a[0]+r[0]), r3(a[1]+r[1]))
score = {}
for ang, op, radii, got, centre in rows:
    t = ang * (math.pi/180)
    v = (math.cos(t), math.sin(t))
    c0 = (8000.0, 15000.0)
    cands = {}
    u = xf_vec(op, v)
    cands['r9vec'] = math.atan2(r9(u[1]), r9(u[0])) * D
    k = 1/L(u); un = (u[0]*k, u[1]*k)
    cands['r9norm'] = math.atan2(r9(un[1]), r9(un[0])) * D
    # through points: centre and centre + radius*dir
    for rad in [radii[0], 1.0, 1000.0]:
        q = (c0[0] + v[0]*abs(rad), c0[1] + v[1]*abs(rad))
        cc = xf_pt(op, c0); qq = xf_pt(op, q)
        d = (qq[0]-cc[0], qq[1]-cc[1])
        kk = 1/L(d); dn = (d[0]*kk, d[1]*kk)
        cands['pts%g' % rad] = math.atan2(r9(dn[1]), r9(dn[0])) * D
        cands['ptsraw%g' % rad] = math.atan2(d[1], d[0]) * D
    for kname, val in cands.items():
        g = got if got is not None else 0.0
        if kname not in score: score[kname] = 0
        score[kname] += (val == g or (got is None and abs(val) < 1e-12))
print(len(rows), sorted(score.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]))
