steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour; see the Schedules row), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/schedule-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/schedule-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting (shortest round-trip, `1e+16`), `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `families`, `parameters` (project parameters), `phases`, `units`, `language`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references to other elements and library entries are GUID strings; elements hold project-parameter and phase values in `params`) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`: kinds `type:wall`…, `material`, `family`, `family-type`, `family-parameter`, `parameter`, `phase`, `design-option`, …). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`, `alloc_id`.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session::execute` runs a command, checks the model, records an undo step when the model changed (labels from the catalog: `history()`); `crate::commands::changes_model` lists read-only commands (schedule isn't one: a schedule made or changed is saved as a `schedule` element).
- `src/model.rs`: levels sorted by elevation, `resolve_level`, `find`. `src/commands/params.rs`: parameter readers with the original's error wording. `src/deflate.rs`: deflate/zlib byte-identical to the original's flate2 (for .xlsx). `src/styles/` (done by another agent): units (`units` command; `src/styles/settings.rs`), language, project parameters (`src/styles/parameters.rs`), phases/design options (`src/styles/phasing.rs`) — read them for how those are stored and reuse their helpers.
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx` (the project plus a per-reading cache: `cx.cached("key", || ...)`), `r2`, lookups by GUID: `type_of`/`element_type`, `family`, `family_type`, `material_name`, `lib_name_of`, `level_elev`, `type_home`. `view.rs` — the `elements` command and `element_view(cx, id) -> Option<Value>`: an element as `elements` shows it (stored fields + `id` + derived values: a wall's `length`/`height`/`thickness`/`type` name, a room's `area_m2`/`perimeter_m`/`volume_m3`/`unbounded_height`, a door's `width`/`height`/`level`/`values`…), each category by another sub-agent's module (`walls`, `slabs`, `parts`, `notes`) — in your build those are stubs (a type name, a straight wall's length, little else). `crate::readers::parts::family_values(cx, id)` will give a door's/window's/component's family parameter values (another sub-agent; absent in your build — use the view's `values` key, which that module will fill). `file/` — the project-file loader (done).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, rooms… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet (styles commands like `units`, `parameter`, `phase`, `language` do exist). So build input projects with the ORIGINAL and test reading them: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/schedule-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`, one command per line; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters — read the `schedule` and `filter_selection` entries closely; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house with a Room Schedule on a sheet). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1`) — copy them, don't modify. Test as `run x.bimcraft --cmd 'schedule {...}' --cmd 'schedule {...}' --save y.bimcraft` (the saved file shows what a schedule element holds).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- run x.bimcraft --cmd 'schedule {"category":"doors"}'` runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs (copying the -f files in) and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and every file written (csv, xlsx, saved projects) after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: everything must match exactly.
- Ownership: edit only the files of your area. Don't edit `src/readers/common.rs`, `view.rs`, `mod.rs` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own inside your directory (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: SCHEDULE — `src/readers/schedule/` (`cmd_schedule`, `cmd_filter_selection`, `field_display`)
The whole `schedule` command, exactly as the original: every category the catalog lists (rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, pipes, ducts?, conduits, cable trays, wires, down conductors, earthing conductors, cables, components, stairs, ramps, railings, levels, rebar…) and `multicategory` (`categories`); `available` (the fields there are: the category's own, Count, project parameters for it (`parameter` command with `categories`), a component's family's parameters, Phase Created/Demolished, Design Option); `fields` (names or {name, formula, kind, heading, total}; calculated fields with formulas over the row's fields, as a family's formulas are: `+ - * / ^`, comparisons, if/and/or/not, min/max/abs/sqrt/round/roundup/rounddown/sin/cos/tan in degrees; lengths in mm, areas in m²); `filters` with every op (equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value: text in any case, numbers as the schedule shows them, an unset yes/no as no); `sort` (fields or {field, descending}; Phase Created/Demolished by the project's phase order); `grouped` (a row per set of sort values, Count and totals summed, differing fields empty); headings (the units in headings, `Area (m²)`, and the project's language: `new {"language":"pt"}` makes Portuguese headings?); totals rows; the reply's keys (`available`, `category`, `columns`, `elements` (the ids each row lists), `id` (null for a built-in schedule never changed), `name`, `rows`, `totals`…); the built-in Room/Door/Window/Wall/Floor/Level Schedules becoming the project's own once changed (saved as `schedule` elements, an undo step "Schedule"); `name`+`category` making a new one; each option replacing the last; `fields: []` going back to the category's; `path` writing `.csv` or `.xlsx` (the xlsx is a zip of XML: match the bytes — zip headers, timestamps, compression via `src/deflate.rs`; check with `cmp.py`, which compares written files byte for byte); units (`units {"length": "m"}` etc. changing how lengths show), project parameters (text, number, length, yes/no) and their values (`modify` sets them — in your build `modify` doesn't exist, so set values in the file's JSON), every error message (bad category, unknown field, bad op, bad formula, name clashes, etc.).
- Values: take each element's values from `crate::readers::view::element_view(cx, id)` (the `elements` view: a room's Area is its `area_m2`, its Perimeter `perimeter_m` × 1000?…) and from the stored element/types/families/parameters. Other sub-agents are writing those views in parallel; in your build they're stubs, so expect differences in derived values (room areas, wall heights, family values…). Don't reimplement geometry: judge your work on the schedule logic (fields, headings, formulas, filters, sort/group, totals, number formatting, csv/xlsx bytes, saved schedule elements, errors), using categories and fields whose values are stored or simple (levels, doors/windows of project types with their stored marks/types, counts, names, project parameters, phases, walls' type names and straight lengths), and list in your report each view key you rely on for each field (so I can check them once the views are in).
- `pub fn field_display(cx: &Ctx, id: u64, field: &str) -> Option<String>`: a field's value as a schedule cell shows it, for one element (tags with a `label` show it).
- `filter_selection {ids, by?, keep?}` (catalog entry): groups by Category (keys like `wall`, `door`, `detail_line`?) or by a parameter as `fields` lists them, values as schedules show them; `keep` → `ids`; errors.
Prioritise what typical scripts do (the built-in room/door/window/wall schedules, a new schedule with chosen fields, sorting, grouping, totals, filters, a calculated field, CSV) before exotic cases, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); the view keys you rely on per category/field; the public functions others can call; any edit outside `src/readers/schedule/`.

steps.message:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/inspect-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/inspect-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting, `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command; `info x.bimcraft` prints sorted + pretty.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `images`, `families`, `parameters`, `view_filters`, `view_templates`, `phases`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session` (project, path, undo steps: `history()` gives their labels). `src/commands/basic.rs`: `info(path)` = open + `crate::inspect::inspect` + `path`.
- `src/inspect.rs` — YOURS (a stub now: counts, history, language, name, levels, plus `crate::styles::inspect_entries(s)` which gives phases, phase_filters, phase_overrides, option_sets, parameters, voltages, distribution_systems, wire_types, units, project_units, room_area, standard — done by the styles agent, use it). Ready helpers by other agents: `crate::media::material::inspect_materials(pr)` and `inspect_images(pr)` give inspect's `materials` and `images`. Put any extra modules you need under `src/inspect/` (declared from `src/inspect.rs` with `mod x;`, which Rust allows).
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx`, lookups by GUID (`type_of`, `family`, `material_name`…). `view.rs` — `element_view(cx, id)`: an element as `elements` shows it, with derived values, each category by another sub-agent's module working in parallel (in your build these are stubs). For warnings about rooms, use the room's view: `enclosed`, `shares_space_with`, `area_m2` (the walls sub-agent fills them) rather than computing room geometry yourself. `file/` — the project-file loader (done).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, rooms, families… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet (styles/media commands like `units`, `parameter`, `phase`, `material`, `filter`?, `template`? may — check `src/styles`, `src/media`). So build input projects with the ORIGINAL and test reading them: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/inspect-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1` — r1 has unenclosed and redundant rooms) — copy them, don't modify. You can edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- info x.bimcraft` (or `-- run x.bimcraft --cmd inspect`) runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: everything must match exactly.
- Ownership: edit only `src/inspect.rs` and `src/inspect/`. Don't edit `src/readers/*` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: INSPECT — `src/inspect.rs` (`inspect`, and so `info x.bimcraft`)
Every key of `inspect` exactly, for every kind of project and every state of a session (`run --cmd 'inspect'` on a new project shows `path: null`; after `--save`/`open` the path; `history` the undo labels — check undo/redo): `counts` (per category), `levels`, `types` (every category's types as inspect shows them: wall/floor/roof/ceiling layers with materials by NAME, layer ids/guids, run types' materials by name, door/window types…), `families` (each family's category, `connectors` (kind, system), `parameters` (names), `types` (names sorted)… for loaded and custom families too: `family` command), `materials`, `images`, `history`, `language`, `name`, `path`, `warnings`, `view_filters`, `view_templates` (with their graphics/controls), and the entries the styles helper gives; also any key that appears only in some projects (find them: try projects with links, CAD imports, point clouds, detail groups, reinforcement presets, line styles…). Note `info` prints the same as `run x --cmd inspect` plus `path`, pretty.
Warnings are the open-ended part: find every warning the original gives and its exact wording and order: rooms not enclosed (`room 100009 (3 Room) is not enclosed: the walls around it no longer close`), redundant rooms (`room 100010 (4 Room) is in the space room 100007 has; two rooms can't share one, so it is unbounded: delete one, or part them with a room separation line`), lighting/outlet/switch families without a power connector ("a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of"), and whatever else exists (overlapping walls? doors no longer fitting? elements on deleted levels? unused things? families' formula problems? electrical circuits? design options? phases?): probe by building odd projects with the original and by editing saved files (moving a wall so a door no longer fits it, opening a room's walls, duplicating walls, etc.), and read the README for hints.
Prioritise the common keys and warnings first, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); what you need from other readers' views (keys) for warnings; any edit outside `src/inspect.rs`/`src/inspect/`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run the original and my build with the same args in fresh dirs; diff normalized outputs.
usage: cmp.py [-q] [-f file_to_copy]... -- args...
"""
import os, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile, shutil, difflib
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
MINE = os.environ.get('MINE', '/workspace/target/release/bimcraft-cli')
GUID = re.compile(r'[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}')
def norm(s):
    s = re.sub(r'"uid": \d+', '"uid": <UID>', s)
    m = {}
    def rep(mo):
        g = mo.group(0)
        if g not in m: m[g] = 'GUID-%d' % (len(m)+1)
        return m[g]
    s = GUID.sub(rep, s)
    s = re.sub(r"\.tmp[A-Za-z0-9]{6}", ".tmpXXXXXX", s)
    s = re.sub(r"'\d{4}-\d\d-\d\dT\d\d:\d\d:\d\d'", "'<TIMESTAMP>'", s)
    # IFC GlobalIds
    gm = {}
    def grep(mo):
        g = mo.group(1)
        if g not in gm: gm[g] = 'GID-%d' % (len(gm)+1)
        return "('" + gm[g] + "'"
    s = re.sub(r"\('([0-9A-Za-z_$]{22})'", grep, s)
    return s
def run(exe, args, files, stdin):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='cmp')
    for f in files: shutil.copy(f, d)
    before = set(os.listdir(d))
    p = subprocess.run([exe] + args, cwd=d, capture_output=True, input=stdin, timeout=120)
    out = {'stdout': p.stdout.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'stderr': p.stderr.decode('utf-8','replace'), 'code': p.returncode}
    fl = {}
    for root, dirs, fs in os.walk(d):
        for f in fs:
            full = os.path.join(root, f)
            rel = os.path.relpath(full, d)
            if rel in before: 
                pass
            try: fl[rel] = open(full,'rb').read()
            except Exception as e: fl[rel] = b'<unreadable>'
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    return out, fl
def main():
    a = sys.argv[1:]
    quiet = False; files = []; stdin = None
    while a and a[0] != '--':
        if a[0] == '-q': quiet = True; a = a[1:]
        elif a[0] == '-f': files.append(a[1]); a = a[2:]
        elif a[0] == '-i': stdin = open(a[1],'rb').read(); a = a[2:]
        else: break
    if a and a[0] == '--': a = a[1:]
    o, of = run(ORIG, a, files, stdin)
    m, mf = run(MINE, a, files, stdin)
    ok = True
    for k in ('code', 'stdout', 'stderr'):
        x = norm(str(o[k])); y = norm(str(m[k]))
        if x != y:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- {k} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(x.splitlines(), y.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:40]:
                print(l[:300])
    for f in sorted(set(of) | set(mf)):
        if f not in of: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in mine'); continue
        if f not in mf: ok = False; print(f'--- file {f} only in orig'); continue
        x, y = of[f], mf[f]
        try:
            xs = norm(x.decode('utf-8')); ys = norm(y.decode('utf-8'))
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            if x != y: ok = False; print(f'--- binary file {f} differs ({len(x)} vs {len(y)} bytes)')
            continue
        if xs != ys:
            ok = False
            print(f'--- file {f} differs')
            for l in list(difflib.unified_diff(xs.splitlines(), ys.splitlines(), 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1))[:60]:
                print(l[:300])
    print('SAME' if ok else 'DIFF')
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
main()

== level ['LL'] Architecture > Level
{elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

== wall ['WA'] Architecture > Wall
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

== wall_by_face ['WB'] None
{mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

== room ['RM'] Architecture > Room
{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

== room_separator [] None
{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

== column ['CL'] Architecture > Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

== structural_column ['CL'] None
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

== flip [] None
{ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

== modify [] None
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

== corner ['TR'] None
{ids: [a, b], keep?: [[x, y], [x, y]]} trims or extends two walls, or two detail lines (lines or arcs), to meet where their lines (or circles) cross; `keep` is a point on the part of each to keep

== offset ['OF'] None
{id, distance, toward: [x, y], copy?} a detail line drawn again `distance` mm beside itself on the side `toward` is, arcs round the same centres, an ellipse or a spline as a spline through points within 0.05 mm of the true offset (which Revit can't): a copy (the default), or with `copy` false moved

== trim_extend [] None
{boundary, ids: [id, …], keep: [[x, y], …]} trims or extends each detail line of `ids` (lines and arcs) to where it meets `boundary` (a detail line, a wall's location line or a grid), keeping the part of each its `keep` point is on: Revit's Trim/Extend Single Element, and Multiple Elements with several

== split ['SL'] None
{id, at: [x, y]} splits a wall or a detail line in two at `at`: a wall's doors and windows go with their part; a detail line of any shape splits where it passes nearest `at` (a spline by its control points exactly, one through points into two through points within 0.05 mm of it), and a closed one (a circle, a whole ellipse, a closed polyline) opens there instead, into one that starts and ends at `at`

== join_polyline ['PJ'] None
{ids: [id, …]} joins detail lines of one view, lines, arcs and polylines that meet end to end, into one polyline in the first's line style (closed when they come round); the first keeps its id, the rest are deleted, and a dimension that measured one of the rest loses that reference (and is deleted, left with fewer than two): the reply's `notes` say which

== room_area [] Manage > Room Area Computation
{at?: centre|finish} where the project measures its rooms' areas, perimeters and IFC spaces, as Revit's Area and Volume Computations: at the walls' centre lines (`centre`, as a project starts) or at their finish faces (`finish`, the floor inside the walls: the área útil Brazilian codes ask for). Rooms keep their points; only their measured outline changes. IFC spaces carry both areas in Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities whichever is chosen

results.content:
== door ['DR'] Door
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

== window ['WN'] Window
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

== rebar [] Rebar
{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule

== reinforce [] Reinforce
{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover short of its outline and its openings; a sloped floor's bars follow its top, the cover square to it. The bars are `rebar` elements of the host, each on a `layer`; reinforcing again replaces the ones it made and leaves any drawn by hand. `check` "NBR 6118" (with `aggressiveness` 1 to 4 for the cover, and `fck` in MPa) adds `notes` to the reply where the bars made fall short of that standard's usual limits (cover, bar sizes and spacings, stirrups, least and most steel, skin bars): they are notes, never a refusal, the numbers typed from handbooks and not the standard's text, so check one against a copy before relying on it. `preset` names a `reinforcement_preset` of the host's kind, whose parameters stand for the ones not given here. `hosts` arms each of a list alike (up to 1000, and 20000 bars in all); if one refuses, none is armed, and the refusal names it. Returns ids, count, hosts, removed, weight_kg and notes

== column ['CL'] Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

== structural_column ['CL'] Structural Column
{at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column of the structure, as `column` makes one but in its own category with its own types (`type` with category structural column): up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`. CL is `column`'s too; on the desktop's Structure tab it is this one

== footing ['FI'] Isolated Footing
{at: [x,y], type?, thickness?, offset?, angle?, level?} an isolated (pad) footing, its plan the type's (category footing), `thickness` mm thick (400) with its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it), so it hangs below

== beam ['BM'] Beam
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; `system` names the system it belongs to. It slopes up to 75°

== strip_footing ['FW'] Wall Footing
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, system?} a continuous footing under a wall for each segment of the points, its section the type's (category stripfooting), its top `offset` mm over the level (0: at it)

== pipe ['PI'] Pipe
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain falls and a riser rises; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Água fria", "Esgoto")

== duct ['DU'] Duct
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright. `system` names the system it belongs to ("Supply air", "Exhaust")

== conduit ['CN'] Conduit
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

== cable_tray ['CT'] Cable Tray
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep

== wire ['EW'] Wire
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

== down_conductor ['DC'] Down Conductor
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to

== ground_conductor ['GC'] Earthing Conductor
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)

== cabling ['CB'] Cabling
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to

== stair [] Stair
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, riser?, tread?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a stair from the middle of its first riser at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level: as many risers as keep each at most `riser` mm (180), treads `tread` deep (280), `width` wide (1000). One straight run, as long as that makes it; or with landings (each as deep as the stair is wide) after `at` risers, the next run going on as `turn` says: 0 straight on, 90 or -90 turned left or right, 180 or -180 back beside it, to its left or right. With `railings`, a railing down each side too

== ramp [] Ramp
{start: [x,y], end?: [x,y] | angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, width?, slope?, landings?: [{at, turn?}, …], railings?} a ramp from the middle of its foot at `start`, climbing toward `end` (or `angle` degrees) up to the next level, or `height` mm, `width` wide (1200), at `slope` percent (8.33, 1 in 12), as long as that makes it; with landings `at` mm up, turning as a stair's do, and with `railings`, a railing down each side. Solid down to its level

== railing [] Railing
{host: a stair or a ramp, side?: left|right, type?} | {path: [[x,y],…], level?, base_offset?, type?} a railing along the stair's or the ramp's sides (both, or the one going up it on `side`), 50 mm in from its edges and climbing with it, going where it goes; or along `path`, `base_offset` mm above the level. Its type sets how high its rail stands over what it runs along, and how far apart its balusters are

== type [] Edit Type
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

== parameter [] Project Parameters
{name, kind?: text|number|length|yesno, categories?: [wall|floor|ceiling|roof|door|window|room|column|component|stair|ramp|railing|mass, …], rename?, delete?: true} a project parameter, as Revit's Manage > Project Parameters makes one: a value of its kind each element of its categories may have of its own, set with `modify {id, params: {name: value}}` (lengths in mm, yes or no as true or false). Off a category, that category's elements lose their values of it; deleted, every element does; renamed, they follow it. `inspect` lists them

== family [] Load Family
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out

== component ['CM'] Component
{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

== flip [] Flip
{ids: [wall,…]} turns walls round about their location lines, as Revit's flip arrows do: their exterior sides go to the other side, their doors and windows stay where they are

== modify [] Modify
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

== move ['MV'] Move
{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall moves

== copy ['CO'] Copy
{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy]} copies elements, with the doors and windows of copied walls; returns the copies' ids

== rotate ['RO'] Rotate
{ids: [id,…], about: [x, y], angle, copy?} turns elements about a point by `angle` degrees, counter-clockwise; walls joined to them stay joined, and doors and windows turn with their walls

== mirror ['MM', 'DM'] Mirror
{ids: [id,…], axis: [[x, y], [x, y]], copy?} mirrors elements across the line through two points; mirrored doors and windows face the other way

== delete_type [] Delete Type
{category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type?} deletes a type of a category (`category` and `type`), a family (`family`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`), as Revit's Delete on one in the Project Browser does; refused while an element uses it (it says how many), and for the last type of a category or of a family

== rename_type [] Rename Type
{category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type, name} renames a type of a category (`category` and `type`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`) to `name`, as Rename in Type Properties does: the elements of it, and what else names it, follow, and it keeps its GUID; refused for a name another type of it has. Text types and filled region types rename with `rename` on `text_type` and `filled_region_type`

== elements [] Elements
{category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

    walls.append((x0,y0,x1,y1))

d=tempfile.mkdtemp()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Export a project file with both programs and print the normalised diff.
usage: projdiff.py FILE.bimcraft [MAXLINES]   (FILE may be a glob; the newest match is used)"""
import glob, os, sys, difflib
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/ifc-export-agent/tools')
import case
fs = sorted(glob.glob(sys.argv[1]), key=os.path.getmtime)
f = fs[-1]
mx = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 60
print('file', f)
a = case.norm(case.export(case.ORIG, f)[3]).splitlines()
b = case.norm(case.export(case.MINE, f)[3]).splitlines()
for i, l in enumerate(difflib.unified_diff(a, b, 'orig', 'mine', lineterm='', n=1)):
    if i >= mx:
        break
    print(l[:240])

results.content:
link :: {path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`

level :: {elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)

grid :: {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], name?} names follow the last grid: 1, 2… or A, B…

import_cad :: {path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given) or origin (its origin on `at`); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out

dimension :: {refs: [ref, …], at: [x, y], level?, kind?: aligned|linear|angular|radial|diameter|arc_length, orient?: horizontal|vertical} aligned (the default): the distances between parallel references, along a line through `at` (between points, along the first two; points and lines, square to the lines); linear: the same with its line horizontal or vertical as `orient` says, or without one as `at` lies: east or west of the points, vertical, else horizontal (its lines must run square to it); angular: the angle between two references that meet, on the side of `at`; radial: a round column's, curved wall's, circle's or arc's radius, toward `at`; diameter: the same across, through its centre; arc_length: how long a curved wall's centre line or face, or an arc, is along it (all of it, or with two point refs after it, between them), its line an arc through `at`. A ref is {id, face?}: a wall's centre (the default), left or right face (of its start-to-end direction), start or end; a door's or window's centre, or its jamb toward its wall's start or end; a grid's line; a straight detail line, or its start or end (radial: a circle or an arc of one). With `point: start|end`, {id, face?, point} is the point at that end of the line: a wall's centre line's end, a face's corner, a grid's, a detail line's (of any shape) or a jamb's end. Or a point [x, y] on one of those lines (for radial and diameter, on a round edge; for arc_length, on the arc), or {endpoint: [x, y]}, the end of one nearest it, within 100 mm. It follows what it measures

dimension_3d :: {refs: [ref, ref], at: [x, y, z], view?, type?} an aligned dimension in a 3D view (the default 3D view unless `view` names another, by name or id), kept by the view and drawn in it and on a sheet that holds it: how far apart its two references are, along a line through `at` moved square off them. A ref is {at: [x, y, z]}, a point of the model, or {at, edge: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]]}, a point on an edge, which it measures square to (from a point, to the edge's line; between two parallel edges, how far apart they are). `type` is a dimension type, the aligned one's unless told. On the desktop, Aligned Dimension (DI) in the 3D view runs it. Returns its id and its length

text :: {text, at: [x, y], view?, type?, angle?, leader?: [x, y], override_format?, runs?: [{from, to, bold?, italic?, underline?}, …]} a text note, its first line's top left at `at`, in a view by name or id: a level's plan (the lowest by default; `at` in plan mm), a section or an elevation (`at` along its line from its start, and up), or a sheet by number (`at` in paper mm). Lettered as its text `type` says (2.5mm unless told; `text_type` lists and makes them: its font, its size, its border), turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise; with `leader`, a line to that point. Lines break at \n. With `override_format`, each run makes characters `from` up to `to` (counted in characters, a line break one) bold, italic or underlined (true), or not (false), whatever the type says; they stay when the type changes, and `modify` with a new `text` alone keeps them on what didn't change. Font and size are the type's

dimension_constraint :: {id, equal?: bool, locked?: [segment, …]} an aligned or linear dimension's constraints, as Revit's EQ and padlocks: `equal` keeps its segments equal (what it measures to between its first and last moves to keep them so, its ends staying); `locked` lists the segments (counted from 0, west to east or south to north) kept at the lengths they have now. After any command, what a constrained dimension measures to moves with what the command moved, or the command is refused, saying which dimension can't be kept

dimension_text :: {id, segment?, prefix?, suffix?, above?, below?, replace?} a dimension's text, as Revit's Dimension Text: what goes before and after its numbers, over and under them, or in place of them. With `segment` (its numbers counted from 0, west to east or south to north, as `labels` lists them), that one's own, over the dimension's where it says something; an empty text clears it, and a segment with none left goes back to the dimension's

spot :: {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot elevation: in a level's plan (the lowest by default), the height of the top of what stands on the level at `at` (or of `host`), following it; in a section or an elevation, of its point `at`, along and up

spot_slope :: {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot slope in a level's plan (the lowest by default): how steeply the top of the floor or roof at `at` (or `host`) falls there, %, an arrow pointing downhill; it follows the top. The reply gives `slope` and `toward`, the way down in plan (null on the level)

tag :: {ids?: [id,…], label?, level?, category?, offset?: [dx, dy], leader?} tags elements with a field of theirs: a door's or window's mark, a room's name, else the type, or `label`, any field its category's schedule has (`Height`, `Area`, a project parameter); doors, windows, walls, columns, components, floors, ceilings, roofs, rooms, runs and stairs. `offset` mm from the point it names (beside the wall for a door or window, else up and right); without ids, every door and window on the level not tagged yet, or of `category`

section :: {start: [x,y], end: [x,y], depth?, name?} a section view along the line, looking to its left (drawn west to east, it looks north): it cuts the model at the line and sees `depth` mm past it, or everything

elevation :: {facing?: north|south|east|west, at?: [x,y], start?, end?, depth?, name?} an elevation view of the building's side `facing` (North shows the north side, looking south), from 3 m out, or through `at`; with `at` alone, of the side it's on; with `start` and `end`, along that line, looking to its left; with none, the four not there yet

sheet :: {number?, name?, size?: A0|A1|A2|A3|A4} a sheet of paper, landscape (A3 by default), with a title block; numbers run A101, A102…

place :: {sheet: number or id, view: a level's, section's, elevation's, schedule's or 3D view's name or id, at?: [x, y], scale?, azimuth?, elevation?} puts the view on the sheet at 1 : `scale` (by default the view's own, see `scale`, 1 : 100 when it has none of its own; a schedule keeps its size), its middle `at` mm from the paper's bottom left corner (by default right of the views there, or in the middle); a view goes on one sheet. A schedule (Room Schedule, Door Schedule…) or the 3D view ({3D}, seen from `azimuth` and `elevation` degrees) comes to be as it's first placed

crop :: {view, region?: [[x, y], [x, y]] | null} crops a level's plan to the region's south-west and north-east corners (plan mm), or a section or an elevation to its bottom left and top right (along its line from its start, and up: its line then runs between them, and the notes in it stay put); null uncrops it; without a region, it crops to what the view shows now

duplicate_view :: {view, mode?: duplicate|detailing|dependent, name?} a new plan view of a plan's level (a level's own plan, or a plan view; sections, elevations, schedules, sheets and the 3D view aren't duplicated yet): `duplicate` (the default) has the same view range, crop and graphics and no annotation of its own; `detailing` copies the dimensions, tags, notes and spot elevations in it too, as its own; `dependent` follows its parent's view range, graphics, scale and detail (change those in the parent), has a crop of its own and shows its parent's annotation as well as its own. Named `name`, else `<view> Copy 1` (`<view> Dependent 1`). Commands that take a level or a view take it by name or id, and what is drawn, dimensioned, tagged or noted there is in it

scale :: {view, scale?: 1 | … | 100000} a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, 1 : `scale`: the paper the view stands for, 1 mm of paper being `scale` mm of the model. Its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, tags, dimension ticks…) and its line weights (pens) are that paper's, so a screen shows them as the paper would at its zoom. Every view has one: 1 : 100 until it is given another, and null is refused. A view placed on a sheet takes it for the viewport's scale. Without `scale` it only says what the view has

dimension_value :: {id, value, segment?} types a length into an aligned or a linear dimension's segment (the first unless told), as a click on its number does: what the segment ends at (its second reference, as the dimension runs west to east or south to north) moves along the dimension so the segment is `value` mm; a locked segment is locked at it, and the other locks hold, or it is refused. Returns {id, moved, by}

filled_region :: {sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], view?, type?, line_style?: name | null} a filled region in a view (a plan, a section, an elevation or a sheet, in its own terms; the lowest plan by default): the loops its sketch closes into (see `sketch`: any number of outlines, a loop inside one a hole, one inside that an island), filled as type `type` (Solid Black unless told) says, its boundary in line style `line_style` (Thin Lines unless told; null, unseen: a masking region's way). It draws over the model, under the annotation; edit its sketch with edit_boundary. A model pattern starts at the region's `pattern_origin` and turns by its `pattern_angle` (see modify)

create_group :: {ids, name?} a detail group made of detail lines, filled regions and text notes of one view, as Revit's Create Group: they become type `name`'s members (Group 1, 2… unless told), and one group of it takes their place, its origin the middle of them. Place it again with detail_group; ungroup gives its members back. Returns {id, name}

detail_group :: {type, at: [x,y], angle?, mirrored?, view?} a detail group of type `type` placed in a view (the lowest plan by default): its members drawn with their origin at `at`, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, mirrored across their x axis first when `mirrored`. Move, copy, rotate and mirror take it whole

repeating_detail :: {type, start: [x,y], end: [x,y], spacing, mirrored?, view?} detail group `type` repeated along the line from `start` to `end`, every `spacing` mm from `start` (at most 2000 of them), each turned along the line, as Revit's Repeating Detail Component: brick coursing, blocking, batt ties. A view draws up to 10000 group members in all (a repeat places each member of the type again), so a type of 100 members repeats up to 100 times. Returns {id, count}

detail_line :: {view?, style?, and a curve: `points` [[x, y], …] (with `arcs`, each segment's turn in degrees counter-clockwise, and `closed`), `start` and `end` (with `arc` degrees or a `through` point), `centre` and `radius` (a circle), `centre` and `radii` [a, b] (an ellipse, with `angle` degrees and `span` [from, to] degrees for part of one), `control` [[x, y], …] (a spline by its control points, with `knots`), or `fit` [[x, y], …] (a spline through them, with `start_tangent` and `end_tangent`)} a detail line in a view, by name or id, in the view's own terms: a level's plan (the lowest by default; plan mm), a section or an elevation (along its line from its start, and up) or a sheet by number (paper mm). It draws in line style `style` (Thin Lines unless told), only in its view, and goes with it; with `insulation`, a width in mm, it draws as batt insulation along its curve, as Revit's Insulation; with `centre_mark` true, a small cross marks the centre of its arcs, circle or ellipse; with `cloud`, an arc length in mm, it draws as a revision cloud's scallops along it (outward round a loop, a scallop ending at each corner), of `revision` (any text, a label kept with the cloud and listed by `elements`; nothing else reads it); a line is insulation or a cloud, not both. An arc, a circle or an ellipse lies within 1,000 km of the origin (an arc of 359.9999999999° is a circle of radius 5.7e14 mm, and is refused), and a polyline's arcs take no more than 8,192 points to draw within 0.25 mm: 10,000 arcs of 175° are refused

units :: {length?: mm|cm|m|in|ft|ft-in} how drawings, schedules and the desktop show lengths, and read typed ones: millimetres, centimetres, metres, fractional inches, decimal feet, or feet and fractional inches (to 1/16"); areas in m², or ft² with inches and feet. The model, and every command, keep millimetres

schedule :: {name?, category?, categories?, fields?, filters?, sort?, grouped?, path?} a schedule view, as Revit's View > Schedules makes one, and its table: columns, rows, the `elements` each row lists, and totals (and a .csv file with a path, or an .xlsx workbook for a path ending .xlsx). A new one needs `name` and `category`: rooms, doors, windows, walls, floors, ceilings, roofs, columns, structural columns, footings, beams, strip footings, components, stairs, ramps, railings or levels, or `multicategory`, as Revit's Multi-Category Schedule: a row for each element of `categories` (["walls", "doors"…]; none, every built one but rooms, levels and masses), with the fields they share (Category, Family, Type, Level, Count, Width, Height, Length, Thickness, Area: a wall's length by its height, a door's width by its height; Material: its type's structure layer's, a run's type's, a family's), each empty where its category has none; `category` alone reads its own (Room Schedule, Door Schedule, Window Schedule, Wall Schedule, Floor Schedule, Level Schedule, each the project's once changed). `fields`: its columns, in order, each a field's name (`available` lists them: its category's own, Count, project parameters, a component's family's parameters) or {name, formula?, kind?: number|length|area|yesno, heading?, total?}; with a formula, a calculated field worked out from the row's other fields as a family's formulas are (lengths in mm, areas in m²; `Area * 120`); `total` sums it in a totals row. `filters`: [{field, op: equals|not-equals|greater|greater-or-equal|less|less-or-equal|contains|not-contains|begins-with|not-begins-with|ends-with|not-ends-with|has-value|has-no-value, value}, …], the elements all of them keep (text in any case, numbers as the schedule shows them, an unset yes or no as no). `sort`: [field or {field, descending?}, …], in turn (its first column unless it says; Phase Created and Phase Demolished in the project's order of phases, a phase never demolished after the last); `grouped`, a row for each set of the sort fields' values: Count and totals summed, and a field whose values differ left empty. Each one given replaces the last; `fields: []` goes back to its category's

section_box :: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again

perspective :: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands

camera :: {eye?: [x, y, z], target?: [x, y, z], lens?: mm, view?: a 3D view's name or id, name?} a 3D camera as Revit's Camera tool makes one: with `eye` (where the camera stands, mm) and `target` (what it looks at, mm) it makes a new named perspective 3D view looking from `eye` at `target` through `lens` (35 mm unless given, 10 to 600), named `name` or by number ("Camera 1", "Camera 2"…). With `view` too, it gives that 3D view the camera instead (its id stays; `{3D}` may be given one): a point left out stays as that camera has it, so `lens` alone or one point alone changes just that, and a view without a camera yet needs both. With `view` and none of `eye`, `target` or `lens` it reads the camera back: `eye`, `target`, `lens` and whether the view is in perspective (null eye/target for a view with no camera yet). The eye is never on the target, so the view always has a direction to look in

work_plane :: {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level

measure :: {from: [x, y], to: [x, y]} what a ruler laid between two points reads (mm): its `length`, its parts `dx` and `dy`, and its `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing

select_by_id :: {text} the elements a list names, each by its id, its GUID (dashes and braces or not) or its IFC GlobalId, separated by spaces, commas, semicolons or lines: `ids` found, each once in the order named, `missing` (what named none), and `plan` and `extent` ([[x, y], [x, y]] mm), the level's plan that shows them and where; it selects nothing itself, a front end does

ids_of :: {ids: [id or GUID, …]} what names each element: its `id`, its `guid`, its `ifc` GlobalId, its `category` and its `name` (or type, number, mark)

elements :: {category?, level?, limit?, offset?} elements with their `id` (six digits, what commands take) and `guid` (made once, never changed), fields and derived values (length, height, area_m2…); what an element points at (its level, host, view…) it holds by GUID. Wherever a command takes an element, its id or its GUID will do

steps.message:
I finished the EDIT area: all 19 commands are implemented and mostly match the original. The misses that remain are in the last digit of some numbers, plus refusals that depend on model rules other areas haven't written yet.

**Branch:** `worktree-agent-a76b15059404997b3`, head `5887522`, clean build with no warnings. Four sub-agents did `modify`; `corner`/`split`/`fillet`; `insert`/`link`/`reload`/`autosave`/`recover`; and `purge`/`delete_type`/`rename_type`/`match_properties`. I merged their branches and re-ran their test suites on the merged build. I wrote `move`, `copy`, `rotate`, `mirror`, `delete`, `align` and the shared code myself. All comparisons below are against the original on project files it made.

**Per command (cases identical / cases run)**

| Commands | Result | What still differs |
|---|---|---|
| `move`, `copy`, `rotate`, `mirror` | 2166/2232 on every element of the fixtures; 705/720 on random wall networks; 468/480 for `move` with `end` | 56 refused by other areas' rules. Last digit of some door offsets on slanted walls with non-round coordinates; ellipse angles; doors on curved walls (only 164/300 random curved-wall cases match). |
| `delete` | 434/436 | Both depend on ARCH's `Mass Floor` level rule. |
| `align` | 64/64 targeted, 298/304 across every category | The 6 are other areas' refusals. Locks to wall end faces use an approximation of the join outline. |
| `modify` | about 17,000 cases; every remaining difference is another area's rule | The reply for a single id is the `elements` view (READERS), so replies were compared with that view stripped. Frozen rooms use a stand-in room solver that matches 55 of 57 layouts. |
| `corner`, `split`, `fillet` | all walls and straight detail lines match | Arcs, curves and some line splits differ in the last digits. |
| `insert`, `link`, `reload`, `autosave`, `recover` | about 1000 scenarios match | `.ifc` input needs IFC-IMPORT. |
| `purge`, `delete_type`, `rename_type`, `match_properties` | all of about 1,450 cases match | Except `.ifc` input. |
| `undo`, `redo` | labels are the catalog labels | Steps recorded even when nothing changes: `modify`, `delete`, `insert`, `delete_type`, `match_properties`, `move`, `copy`, `rotate`, `mirror`, `align`, and `corner` on detail lines. |

**How the joins work (move/rotate/mirror)**
- Two walls are joined when an end is within 1 mm of the other wall's end or of its segment, and their heights overlap. They can be on different levels; walls only touching in height don't join.
- A moved wall's end goes to where its new line crosses the first such wall by id. When several moved walls share a neighbour's end, the lowest-id moved wall takes it.
- A mirrored wall keeps its old end names, which reproduces the original's "too short" refusals.

**Edits outside `src/edit` (5 lines)**
- `src/commands/mod.rs`: the `always_step` hook.
- `src/check.rs`: my "level … doesn't exist" rule runs right after the core check. The original reports a missing level before the scan checks do.
- `src/commands/basic.rs`: opening a project now loads its links and replies with `links_not_loaded`.
- `src/inspect.rs`: `elements` now shows a link's file element count (`elements`) and `loaded`.
- `src/styles/parameters.rs`: added `"Mass Face"` to `RESERVED`. Without it, any project with walls made by `wall_by_face` was refused.

**What other areas must provide**
- **ARCH:** the opening rules — a door or window fits its wall within 1 mm, two openings don't overlap by more than 1 mm, and sill + height fits the wall's height. Also: a wall longer than 1 mm, a wall's top above its base, the `Mass Floor` level rule, and the "is not a usable number" checks. Until those exist, `src/edit/standin.rs` holds stand-ins for the opening rules and "too short", with the original's wording and tolerances; remove it once ARCH's checks land. ARCH also needs the door/window/room mark-numbering rule that copies use (`transform::next_mark`) and a room solver to replace modify's frozen-room stand-in.
- **VIEWS:** the rule that a dimension measures between parallel lines (it breaks somewhere between a 0.01° and 0.1° turn), "a view goes on one sheet", unique view names, and the solver that keeps `align`'s locks after every command. A lock is stored as a dimension with `alignment: true` and segment 0 locked at length 0.
- **READERS:** full element views from `inspect::elements`; `modify`'s single-id reply is built from it.
- **IFC-IMPORT:** importing into a fresh session, for `insert` and `link` of `.ifc` files.

**Rules about the original that every area needs**
- Lengths are summed with a fused multiply-add: `x.mul_add(x, y*y).sqrt()`. Directions are normalised by multiplying with the reciprocal of that length. Dot products are not fused. The wall length printed in the opening-fit error uses `hypot`.
- Turned or mirrored points are rounded to 0.001 mm. A turned angle is measured from a point 1000 mm along the element's direction, also transformed, and rounded to 1e-9°.
- All editing commands read a library entry's GUID anywhere in their parameters as that entry's name.

    t = math.radians(arc)
    dx, dy = b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]
    c = math.hypot(dx, dy)
    r = c / 2 / math.sin(abs(t) / 2)
    mx, my = (a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2
    # distance from midpoint to centre
    h = r * math.cos(t / 2)
    # left normal
    nx, ny = -dy / c, dx / c
    s = 1 if t > 0 else -1
    cx, cy = mx + nx * h * s, my + ny * h * s
    a0 = math.atan2(a[1] - cy, a[0] - cx)
    ang = a0 + s * off / r

random.seed(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 1)
cmds = []
walls = []
y = 0
for i in range(14):
    x0 = random.uniform(-5000, 5000); y0 = random.uniform(-5000, 5000) + i * 30000
    ang = random.uniform(0, 360)
    import math
    c = random.uniform(3000, 12000)
    x1 = x0 + c * math.cos(math.radians(ang)); y1 = y0 + c * math.sin(math.radians(ang))

    walls.append((x0, y0, x1, y1, arc))

for i in range(n):
    for k in range(3):
        cmds.append('door ' + json.dumps({"wall": 100002 + i, "offset": 1000 + k * 1100 + random.randint(0, 50)}))
open('/tmp/parts-agent/arcdoors.txt', 'w').write('\n'.join(cmds) + '\n')

spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location('arcm', '/tmp/parts-agent/arc.py')
proj = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))

els = proj['elements']
byguid = {e['guid']: e for e in els.values()}
src = open('/tmp/parts-agent/arc.py').read().split('for name, f in')[0]
src = src.split('cases = [')[0] + src.split(']\n', 1)[1] if 'cases = [' in src else src
g = {}
exec(src.replace('cases = [', 'cases0 = ['), g)
fs = [k for k in g if k.startswith('m') and callable(g[k])]
score = {k: 0 for k in fs}
tot = 0
for o in outs:
    w = byguid[o['host']]
    if not w.get('arc'):
        continue
    tot += 1
    want = tuple(o['at'])
    for k in fs:
        got = g[k](w['start'], w['end'], w['arc'], o['offset'])
        if got == want:
            score[k] += 1
        elif k == 'm1':
            print('m1 miss', w['start'], w['end'], w['arc'], o['offset'], got, want)
print(tot, score)
