== highrise Synthetic Highrise []
{storeys?: 20} replace the project with an original 1–80 storey performance sample
== link Link Model ['LK']
{path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`
== point_cloud Point Cloud []
{path | cloud, name?, level?, at?: [x, y], offset?, angle?, units?, spacing?, origin?} brings in a laser scan (`path`: PTS, XYZ, PLY, LAS or E57 (each of its scans placed by its pose), or a list of the files of one scan's stations, brought in as one; `units` of its coordinates mm, cm, m (the default), in or ft; one point kept in each cube `spacing` mm wide) or places one the project holds again (`cloud`, its name), as an element: its middle on `at` (the origin) and its foot on the level, or with `origin: file` where its file's coordinates put it; `offset` raises its middle over the level, `angle` turns it. Returns its id, the scan's name, the points kept and read, and where its middle was in the file
== import_cad Import CAD []
{path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given) or origin (its origin on `at`); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out
== type Edit Type []
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)
== family Load Family []
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out
== detail_group Place Detail Group []
{type, at: [x,y], angle?, mirrored?, view?} a detail group of type `type` placed in a view (the lowest plan by default): its members drawn with their origin at `at`, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, mirrored across their x axis first when `mirrored`. Move, copy, rotate and mirror take it whole
== delete_type Delete Type []
{category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type?} deletes a type of a category (`category` and `type`), a family (`family`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`), as Revit's Delete on one in the Project Browser does; refused while an element uses it (it says how many), and for the last type of a category or of a family
== purge Purge Unused ['PU']
{kinds?: [type|family|material|picture|filter|template, …], dry_run?} takes out what nothing uses, again for what that leaves unused: types and families unless `kinds` says; a category keeps a type and a family a type; with `dry_run` it lists what would go and changes nothing
== inspect Inspect []
{} levels, element counts, types, warnings and undo history
== filter View Filter []
{name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one
== template View Template []
{name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one
== phase Phasing []
{name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides
== option Design Options []
{set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)
== circuit Size a Circuit []
{load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it
== library Library []
{kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too

wire_type [] :: {name?, material?: copper|aluminium, temperature?, insulation?, note?, sizes?: [{section, ampacity, label?}], rename?, delete?: true} a wire type of the project's electrical settings: a conductor's `material`, working `temperature` (°C) and `insulation`, and its table, `sizes`: the `section` of each row in mm² (smallest first, never less than the row before) and the `ampacity` it carries in amperes, with a `label` for how its standard names it (12 AWG). Giving `sizes` replaces the table. `note` says where the ampacities come from. Without `name`, lists them

text_type [] :: {name?, font?, size?, bold?, italic?, underline?, width_factor?, color?, border?, border_offset?, border_pen?, like?, rename?, delete?: true} a text type of the project's: its `font`, any the system has, or one BIMCraft carries (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, BIMCraft Lettering: single-stroke capitals); Arial, the default, letters on any system (where it isn't installed, Liberation Sans, Arimo, Helvetica or the like stands in, else IBM Plex Sans), and a font a file names that this system hasn't is stood in for likewise. Its capitals' height on paper (`size`, mm, 2.5 for a new one), bold, italic and underlined or not (a family's own bold and italic faces where it has them), `width_factor` (1: as the font draws it), its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), and whether a border is drawn round its notes, `border_offset` mm on paper out from their text (where a leader starts too; 1), in pen `border_pen` (0 to 16; 1). A new one starts as `like` says, or as 2.5mm Arial. A project starts with 2.5mm, 3.5mm and 5mm. `rename` renames it, its notes following; `delete` takes it away while no note is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type, the fonts this system has, and the font that letters each type here (`drawn_with`)

dimension_type [] :: {name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, …values} a dimension type of the project's, as Revit's type parameters, lengths mm on paper. Graphics: `string` continuous|baseline|ordinate (Dimension String Type; baseline lines `baseline_spacing` apart, 7), `tick` diagonal|arrow|open_arrow|dot|none, `tick_size` (2), `line_pen` and `tick_pen` (0 to 16; 4 and 7), `color` ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b]), `line_extension` past the outer witness lines (0.8), `witness` gap_to_element|fixed (Witness Line Control), `witness_length` when fixed (5), `witness_gap` off what it measures (0.6), `witness_extension` past the dimension line (0.8), `centre_mark` on radial and diameter ones. Text: `font` (as text types take; Arial), `text_size` (2.5), `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor` (1), `text_offset` off the line (1), `background` opaque|transparent, `read` up_then_left|up_then_right (Read Convention), `units` (mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in; null for the project's) and `decimals` (0 to 6; null as the units show), `radius_symbol` (R), `diameter_symbol` (Ø), `equality_text` (EQ). A new one starts as `like` says, else as the default. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial` (aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in it) and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial` (radial and diameter ones). `rename` renames it, its dimensions following; `delete` takes it away while no dimension is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

type [] :: {category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)

paint ['PT'] :: {id | ids, face?, material} paints a face of the elements with a material of the library, as Revit's Paint does: its colour and texture show in the 3D view over what their types are made of. `face`: a wall's `exterior` or `interior`, a floor's, roof's or ceiling's `top` or `bottom`, and `all` for a column, a component, a door, a window, a stair, a ramp or a railing; without it, every face the elements have. `material` null takes the paint off

modify [] :: {id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it

filled_region_type [] :: {name?, foreground?: pattern | null, foreground_color?, background?: pattern | null, background_color?, masking?, rename?, delete?: true} a filled region type of the project's: its foreground pattern over its background one, each in its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), over the paper when `masking` (it hides what's under it). A new one starts with none. A project starts with Solid Black, Diagonal Up, Crosshatch, Sand, Brick and Masking. `rename` renames it, its regions following; `delete` takes it away while no region is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type

group_type [] :: {name?, rename?, delete?: true} a detail group type: `rename` renames it, its groups following; `delete` takes it away while none of it is placed. Without `name`, it lists each with its members and how many are placed

delete_type [] :: {category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type?} deletes a type of a category (`category` and `type`), a family (`family`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`), as Revit's Delete on one in the Project Browser does; refused while an element uses it (it says how many), and for the last type of a category or of a family

rename_type [] :: {category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type, name} renames a type of a category (`category` and `type`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`) to `name`, as Rename in Type Properties does: the elements of it, and what else names it, follow, and it keeps its GUID; refused for a name another type of it has. Text types and filled region types rename with `rename` on `text_type` and `filled_region_type`

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ids_of every library entry of a project: kind -> category mapping, names."""
import sys, subprocess, json, os
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
f = os.path.abspath(sys.argv[1])
d = json.load(open(f))
ids = [int(k) for k in d['library']]
extra = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[2:]]
p = subprocess.run([ORIG, 'run', f, '--cmd', 'ids_of ' + json.dumps({'ids': ids + extra})], capture_output=True, cwd='/tmp/notes-agent/work')
out = p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')
if p.stderr: print(p.stderr.decode())
v = json.loads(out[-1])
lib = d['library']
seen = {}
for e in v['elements']:
    le = lib.get(str(e['id']))
    if le is None:
        print('EXTRA', e); continue
    k = le['kind']
    same = (e['name'] == le['name'])
    key = (k, e['category'], same)
    if key not in seen:
        seen[key] = e
        print(k, '->', repr(e['category']), 'name same' if same else ('name %r vs lib %r' % (e['name'], le['name'])))

results.content:
== new New []
{name?, language?: en|pt|es|sv|cs|fr|nl} an empty project with Level 1 (0) and Level 2 (3000), named in its language (Nível 1, Nível 2 in Portuguese; Nivel 1, Nivel 2 in Spanish; Nivå 1, Nivå 2 in Swedish; Niveau 1, Niveau 2 in Dutch)
== open Open []
{path} a .bimcraft project
== autosave Autosave []
{path} atomically write a recovery snapshot, keeping the project path and undo history
== recover Recover Autosave []
{path, project?} open and validate a recovery snapshot; Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it
== insert Insert from File []
{path, ids?: [id, …]} elements of another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) brought into this one: those `ids` names (their ids there), else all of them, and what they point at that this project hasn't (a level they stand on is this project's of the same name, where it has one). Each keeps its id unless this project has that id, and its GUID unless this project has that GUID: then it's a copy, with a GUID of its own (the same file inserted into itself is copied whole). What they point at among themselves follows them. A name or a number taken here gets ` 2`, ` 3`…; types, families, materials and parameters this project hasn't come by name, and so do the line styles (with their line patterns), fill patterns, filled region types and detail groups a detail line, a filled region or a group uses. Returns `ids` {there: here}, `copies`, `library`, `left_out`
== reload Reload Links []
{id?} read the file of the link `id`, or of every link, again: for a project that changed on disk. Returns `reloaded` (the names) and `failed` ({name, error})
== save Save []
{path?} .bimcraft saves the project (Save As with a path); .ifc exports IFC4; .glb exports the default 3D view's scene as glTF 2.0 (metres, y up, a node for each element named by its id, GUID and category in `extras`; returns `elements` and `triangles`); .svg or .png exports the lowest level's plan; .pdf prints every sheet, a page each
== undo Undo []
{count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default)
== redo Redo []
{count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default)
== level Level ['LL']
{elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)
== material Materials []
{name, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], transparency?: 0-100, cut?, surface?, texture?: {kind?, size?: [w, h], angle?, offset?: [x, y], path?, image?} | null, rename?, delete?: true} a material of the project's library, created or changed: its colour in shaded 3D views, its `transparency` there (percent of what lies behind it that shows through, 0 opaque; the starter Glass has 70), the pattern its cut shows in plans and sections (where a layer is wide enough to hold it), and the one its surfaces show at its size in the building (a floor's top in plan, a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan). Patterns: none, solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete, insulation, or the name of one of the project's fill patterns (see `fill_pattern`), kept while the material shows it and renamed with it. Its `texture` is what its surfaces look like in the 3D view, over its colour, a tile of it `size` mm across and up, turned `angle` degrees and moved `offset` mm: a pattern drawn in code, `kind` brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof, fabric, metal or insulation (at its natural size unless `size` says); or `image`, a picture: the PNG or JPEG file at `path`, taken into the project (up to 1024 px a side, 24 pictures), or one the project holds (`image`, its id from `inspect`); null takes the texture away. `rename` renames it, the layers using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no layer uses it. `inspect` lists the library and the pictures
== component Component ['CM']
{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)
== modify Modify []
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it
== graphics Visibility/Graphics []

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Free walls of random lengths, heights and thicknesses, each with a window and a door: their
quantities round where formulas differ. Writes x_qto_fuzzS."""
import json, random, sys
for seed in sys.argv[1:]:
    random.seed(int(seed))
    cmds = []
    for k in range(10):
        t = round(random.uniform(90, 400), 1)
        cmds.append('type ' + json.dumps({"category": "wall", "name": "T%d" % k, "layers": [{"function": "structure", "material": "Concrete", "thickness": t}]}))
    nid = 100002
    ids = []
    for k in range(80):
        L = round(random.uniform(3000, 9000), random.choice([0, 1, 2, 3]))
        H = round(random.uniform(2400, 4000), random.choice([0, 1, 2]))
        y = 3000.0 * k
        cmds.append('wall ' + json.dumps({"points": [[0, y], [L, y]], "type": "T%d" % (k % 10), "top_level": None, "height": H}))
        ids.append((nid, L))
        nid += 1
    for wid, L in ids:
        cmds.append('window ' + json.dumps({"wall": wid, "offset": round(L * 0.3, 1), "sill": round(random.uniform(300, 1200), 1)}))
        cmds.append('door ' + json.dumps({"wall": wid, "offset": round(L * 0.75, 1)}))
    open('/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases/x_qto_fuzz%s.txt' % seed, 'w').write('\n'.join(cmds) + '\n')
print('ok')

results.content:
undo | {count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default)

redo | {count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default)

wall | {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them

door | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door

window | {at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)

floor | {boundary?: [[x,y],…], openings?: [[[x,y],…],…] | sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, type?, offset?, slope?, arrow?: [[x,y],[x,y]], structural?} a slab (a structural one with `structural`, as Revit's Floor: Structural), its top at the level, or `offset` mm above it, open through `openings` (holes inside it, apart); no boundary = the outline of the level's walls along their centre lines, open over each loop of them standing free inside, joined to none of the outer ones and with no room in it (a courtyard). Sloped: its top rises `slope` degrees (negative, falls) along the slope arrow, from its tail, where it's at the offset, toward its head. Its top's model pattern starts at `pattern_origin` and turns by `pattern_angle` (see modify). An outline, and each opening, is simple: no edge across another or along it, none ending part way along one, no spike or keyhole slit (`ceiling`, `roof` and `shaft` too, and `modify`, `move` and `edit_boundary` of any of them: they are refused, saying which edges); a file that has one still opens, and works until a command changes its outline

room | {point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen

column | {at: [x,y], type?, angle?, level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a column, its width along `angle` degrees; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall, or up to `top_level`

component | {family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)

delete | {ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted

option | {set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)

# Levels, walls, roofs, floors, ceilings, shafts, stairs

Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.

Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the

and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time

the 3D view, sections and the element's details take them. In IFC a shaped slab is one closed `IfcFacetedBrep`
(`Model::shape_solid`: its top's planes, the same planes under them, plumb sides round its outline and openings, each
corner written once), and a sloped or shaped slab gives `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`, its plan through its depth plumb;
every floor's details give `volume_m3`, what's left of it in plan (shafts too) through that depth. A shaped floor is its type's thickness plumb, so its planes meet
underneath too, and has no slope arrow (`Model::check`, `shape_ok`, refuses one, and points outside the outline or in an
opening, points within a millimetre of each other, a split line's end that is no point and no corner, and lines that
cross). A wall attached to one follows `Model::shape_triangles`, its top over the whole outline as if its openings were
closed, as a slope arrow's plane runs on over them. Plans draw each plane's edges as thin as the outline. `edit_shape`
gives the shape anew or says what it is, `add_point`, `add_split_line` and `reset_shape` change it a piece at a time (an
end of a line that is no point becomes one, at the height the top has there), `edit_boundary` keeps what stays inside the
new outline and its openings, cuts a split line where it leaves them, and gives each new end and each new corner a point at
the height the top had there, so a hole cut through a shaped top leaves it as it was round the hole; it names what it
`dropped`, `cut` and `added`. Moves and mirrors take the shape along, and snaps find its points. A flat roof by
footprint (`slope` 0, no extrusion, joining none) takes a shape too (`Roof::shape`, `Roof::unshapeable` says why another
can't): the commands, checks and both views' tools see its top as a floor's (`Model::shapeable`, `Model::roof_as_floor`:
its footprint, its courtyards and openings as openings, at its top), and `roof_faces` lays each plane's underside its
thickness below, plumb (`roof_rise`), so its slabs, IFC, sections and the walls attached under it follow its falls; plans
draw its creases thin. Under its type's variable layer a shaped roof's underside stays level at its base
(`Model::roof_under`, `roof_prisms`), as a floor's does: its layers in 3D and sections share `Variable::bounds` through
`Model::variable_under`, walls attached under it stop at that underside, IFC writes it as one closed faceted Brep
(`Model::roof_solid`), and `Model::check` refuses a point that leaves the layer thinner than nothing. `falls` (`falls.rs`) gives a floor or a flat roof its shape from its drains and the least fall:
catchments nearest each drain, ridges between them at the top's height, valleys from each drain to its catchment's corners,
each drain as deep as the fall takes its farthest corner; round an opening the valleys turn at its corners, which lie on
the drain's cone, and ridges drawn part the top first. A slab or flat roof whose top isn't one plane comes in from IFC
shaped (`import::shaped_top`), its variable layer marked by its `Description` or, under a level underside, guessed
(`import::guess_variable`); and a spot slope (`Spot::slope`) reads a floor's or roof's fall in a plan. A layer of a floor or roof type may be `variable` (one a type at most; never a wall's or a ceiling's): under a
shaped floor of that type, the underside stays level where the unshaped floor's was (`Model::floor_under`), the layers
above the variable one follow the top, those below it stay level, and the variable one takes up the difference
(`Variable::bounds`, which the 3D view's layers and sections share). Its pieces are then prisms from that level underside
(`Model::floor_prisms`), its volume is less where its top falls (`Model::floor_volume`, `model::volume` for IFC), a wall
attached under it stops at the level underside, and `Model::check` refuses a point that would leave the variable layer
thinner than nothing, saying by how much to raise it. Reinforcement arms a shaped floor only when a variable layer lies

saying why. In the desktop, a floor selected shows Shape Editing in its contextual tab: Slope Arrow, Modify Sub Elements (a point, a corner or an edge's two ends,
`Floor::shape_pick`, to the Options Bar's Elevation), Add Point (a
click on the top, at the Options Bar's Elevation, above the unshaped top or, with Absolute, above the level; empty, the
top's height there), Add Split Line (two clicks, snapping to points, corners and edges) and Reset Shape, each a command.
While one is on, each point's height is labelled beside it (`Model::shape_labels`); under Modify Sub Elements a point's
grip drags it in plan at its height, its split lines with it (`Shape::moved`), in one `edit_shape`. In the 3D view the
same tools work on the floor's top: each point's and corner's grip drags its height up or down, and clicks land on the top

are, and `Model::ceiling_slabs` what's left. A shaft cuts each floor,
ceiling and roof its span reaches into over its outline, all the way through (`Model::less_shafts`). A stair or a ramp

called `category`, the tag every element carries.

Sketches (`sketch.rs`) are how an outline is drawn, the one solver everything with an outline and holes uses: floors,
ceilings, roofs by footprint, shafts and filled regions now, topography next. A sketch is `SketchLine`s, straight or
arcs (a point `through`), in any order, either way round; `sketch::solve` cuts arcs into chords no more than 5° round,
welds ends within `TOL`, then names every problem at once with the lines it's about, what to fix first first
(`Problem::rank`: a line too short or out of range; two lines crossing, or one ending part way along another; two along
each other; three or more at a point; an end no other meets; a loop with no area), and otherwise walks the loops and nests
them by how many others each is inside: even, an outline (counter-clockwise), odd, a hole (clockwise) of the innermost loop
round it, so an island in a hole is an outline again. `solve_one` wants one outline (a floor's, a roof's). The element
keeps the sketch it was drawn or last edited by (`sketch` on floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; empty when it was made
over the walls or read from a file): each line is a part with an id and a GUID of its own (`HasPart`, listed in
`parts_now` by the element's GUID), going with the element when it moves and new on a copy; part ids are not given
again once a line is gone, for as long as the project is open (the library remembers the lowest it has held; a file holds the
ids in use, so one a line had before it was deleted and the file saved may be given again after the file is reopened). Commands take `sketch` (lines `[[x,y],[x,y]]`, arcs `[[x,y],[x,y],[x,y]]`, or
`{start, end, through?, id?}`) in place of `boundary` and its holes; `edit_boundary` without one gives the lines to edit
(the kept sketch while it still draws the outline, `sketch::draws`, else the outline's edges as new lines) and with one
redraws it, a line sent back with its `id` keeping it (keeping a roof's gables on edges that stay); the `sketch` command
solves without making anything. Messages name a line by its id, or its place in the list while it has none. A boundary
given as points is cleaned (a repeated point dropped, and one within a millimetre of the last), and every outline a command
makes or changes, whichever command (`floor`, `modify`, `edit_boundary`, `move`…), is judged as the sketch of its edges
(`Model::check_edits`, asked by the engine after each command but Insert from File): a floor's, ceiling's or roof's boundary,
an opening or a courtyard, a shaft's boundary, that crosses itself or lies along itself, has an edge ending part way along
another, or a spike or keyhole slit, is refused, saying which edges and where, and what to do: redraw it with `edit_boundary`; give
`boundary` or `sketch` (with the walls that touch at a corner named only when it was taken from walls), or simple `openings` or
`courtyards` for one of those rings, for one a command was making;
redraw the mass whose outline it is, for one made by face or by `mass_floors` (a mass itself may still have a bow tie outline,
a spike or a corner touching an edge, so the message says the outline isn't simple, not that it crosses itself);
and, for a roof's opening, which `edit_boundary` does not edit, give `modify` a simple `openings`, and from `dormer` change the
dormer's width, height or position. That is a change from the base, which let
`modify` and the commands that weren't given points set such an outline. `Model::check` doesn't judge the whole project by
it: a file, an IFC import or a Revit import with a keyhole outline still opens, and what leaves its outline alone (`modify`
of its offset, `delete`, `edit_boundary` with a sketch that is simple) still works, and so does what moves, copies, turns or mirrors
it, which makes it no worse (a copy is judged against the elements the command was given, so a new floor drawn with a bow tie
the file also holds is refused); what changes its shape is asked to redraw it first. One line that crosses itself (a closed polyline round a bow tie, a spline with a loop) is found as two lines
crossing are, and a sketch is refused at once past 200,000 straight pieces (a circle is up to 8,193 of them), or when its
pieces lie so close together that telling which cross would take six million steps.

The desktop's sketch mode (`crates/ui-egui/src/sketch.rs`) holds the lines until Finish Edit Mode, which solves them
first and says what's wrong for whoever drew it (`sketch::friendly`: what to fix, kind by kind, where, in the project's
units, and the lines by id) with those lines in the error colour; solved, it runs the command. Draw has every shape of
the Draw panel (`draw.rs`; lines, rectangles, polygons, circles, the arcs, Fillet Arc on two sketch lines, splines, ellipses,
polylines, Pick Lines: see [views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)) and Pick Walls (a line along each wall's location
line, an arc along an arc wall); a sketch line is any curve, so a circle or an ellipse is a loop of its own. Modify picks
sketch lines (a click, a window box from the left, a crossing box from the right), a picked line's handles (its corners, a
spline's points, a circle's centre) are grips that take every one joined there with them, and Delete removes them; Ctrl+Z takes back a line; the plan's snaps take the
sketch's own ends, middles, crossings and curves as well as visible view-specific detail (`snap::in_sketch`). Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft each start a new one (Boundary

import json
cmds = []
nid = 100002
ids = []

print(len(ids))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""zipdump.py file.xlsx : parse the zip's local headers, central directory and end record field by field."""
import sys, struct, zlib
b = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
i = 0
while i < len(b):
    sig = b[i:i+4]
    if sig == b'PK\x03\x04':
        (ver, flag, meth, mtime, mdate, crc, csz, usz, nlen, xlen) = struct.unpack('<HHHHHIIIHH', b[i+4:i+30])
        name = b[i+30:i+30+nlen]
        print('LOCAL @%d ver=%d flag=%#x meth=%d time=%#x date=%#x crc=%#x csz=%d usz=%d name=%r xlen=%d' % (i, ver, flag, meth, mtime, mdate, crc, csz, usz, name, xlen))
        data = b[i+30+nlen+xlen:i+30+nlen+xlen+csz]
        print('   first bytes', data[:16].hex())
        try:
            raw = zlib.decompress(data, -15)
            print('   inflated ok', len(raw))
        except Exception as e:
            print('   inflate err', e)
        i = i + 30 + nlen + xlen + csz
        if flag & 8:
            print('   data descriptor', b[i:i+16].hex())
            i += 16 if b[i:i+4] == b'PK\x07\x08' else 12
    elif sig == b'PK\x01\x02':
        (vmade, vneed, flag, meth, mtime, mdate, crc, csz, usz, nlen, xlen, clen, disk, iattr, eattr, off) = struct.unpack('<HHHHHHIIIHHHHHII', b[i+4:i+46])
        name = b[i+46:i+46+nlen]
        print('CENTRAL @%d made=%#x need=%d flag=%#x meth=%d time=%#x date=%#x crc=%#x csz=%d usz=%d name=%r xlen=%d clen=%d disk=%d iattr=%d eattr=%#x off=%d' % (i, vmade, vneed, flag, meth, mtime, mdate, crc, csz, usz, name, xlen, clen, disk, iattr, eattr, off))
        i = i + 46 + nlen + xlen + clen
    elif sig == b'PK\x05\x06':
        print('END @%d' % i, struct.unpack('<HHHHIIH', b[i+4:i+22]), b[i+22:].hex())
        break
    else:
        print('?? @%d %r' % (i, b[i:i+8]))
        break

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Viewport size experiments: run setup cmds (a list of lists) then sheet+place Level 1 and print viewport size.
usage: vp.py 'cmd1' 'cmd2' ... ; with -v VIEW to place another view; -s SCALE"""
import sys, subprocess, json
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
a = sys.argv[1:]
view = 'Level 1'
scale = None
cmds = []
while a:
    if a[0] == '-v': view = a[1]; a = a[2:]
    elif a[0] == '-s': scale = float(a[1]); a = a[2:]
    else: cmds.append(a[0]); a = a[1:]
pl = {'sheet': 'A101', 'view': view}
if scale: pl['scale'] = scale
cmds += ['sheet {}', 'place ' + json.dumps(pl), 'elements {"category":"viewport"}']
args = [ORIG, 'run']
for c in cmds: args += ['--cmd', c]
p = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, cwd='/tmp/notes-agent/work')
out = p.stdout.decode().strip().split('\n')
if p.stderr: print('ERR', p.stderr.decode().strip())
try:
    v = json.loads(out[-1])
    for e in v['elements']:
        print('size', e['size'], 'at', e['at'], 'scale', e['scale'])
except Exception as ex:
    print(out[-3:])

"""craft.py base.bimcraft 'python statements on d (the doc) and E (elements dict by int id)' [command]
Writes a crafted copy, opens it with the original (and mine with -b), runs a trivial command, prints the result."""
import json, sys, subprocess, tempfile, os, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'

E = {int(k): v for k, v in d['elements'].items()}

exec(code)

"""Floors, rooms and openings whose quantities fall on halves of the last written digit:
x_qto_half3."""
import json
cmds = []
k = 0
for t in [125, 175, 225]:
    cmds.append('type ' + json.dumps({"category": "floor", "name": "F%d" % t, "layers": [{"function": "structure", "material": "Concrete", "thickness": t}]}))
dims = [(2000.5, 2999), (3000.5, 2501), (4400.5, 2753), (5200.5, 3001), (6100.5, 2611)]
for t in [125, 175, 225]:
    for (W, D) in dims:
        x0 = 10000.0 * (k % 6)
        y0 = 10000.0 * (k // 6)
        k += 1
        b = [[x0, y0], [x0 + W, y0], [x0 + W, y0 + D], [x0, y0 + D]]
        hole = [[x0 + 500, y0 + 500], [x0 + 1200.5, y0 + 500], [x0 + 1200.5, y0 + 1501], [x0 + 500, y0 + 1501]]
        cmds.append('floor ' + json.dumps({"boundary": b, "type": "F%d" % t, "openings": [hole]}))
# rooms in walled boxes of such sizes
for (W, D) in dims:
    x0 = 10000.0 * (k % 6)
    y0 = 10000.0 * (k // 6)
    k += 1
    cmds.append('wall ' + json.dumps({"points": [[x0, y0], [x0 + W, y0], [x0 + W, y0 + D], [x0, y0 + D]], "closed": True}))
    cmds.append('room ' + json.dumps({"point": [x0 + W / 2, y0 + D / 2]}))
open('/tmp/ifc-export-agent/cases/x_qto_half3.txt', 'w').write('\n'.join(cmds) + '\n')
print(k)

"""Which corner of a closing pair the original keeps: the IFC's first triangle and its points."""
import sys, os, re, json, subprocess, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'


def first(profile):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='dd', dir='/tmp/family-agent')
    fam = {"name": "Q", "types": {"T": {}}, "forms": [{"profile": profile, "to": 10}]}
    subprocess.run([ORIG, 'run', '--cmd', 'family ' + json.dumps(fam), '--cmd', 'component {"family":"Q","at":[0,0]}', '--save', 'x.ifc'], cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    text = open(os.path.join(d, 'x.ifc')).read()
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    pts = re.findall(r"\(([-\d.E]+),([-\d.E]+),([-\d.E]+)\)", re.search(r"IFCCARTESIANPOINTLIST3D\((\(.*?\))\);", text).group(1))
    top = sorted(set((float(x), float(y)) for x, y, z in pts))
    return [(float(x), float(y)) for x, y, z in pts[:3]], top


for prof in [
    [[0.0002, 0.0001], [1, 0], [100, 0], [100, 50], [0, 50], [0, 0]],
    [[0, 0], [100, 0], [100, 50], [0, 50], [0.0002, 0.0001]],
    [[0, 0], [100, 0], [100, 50], [0, 50], [0, 0]],
    [[0, 0], [0, 50], [100, 50], [100, 0], [0, 0]],
    [[0, 0], [0, 50], [100, 50], [100, 0], [0.0002, 0.0001]],

    [[0, 0], [0, 50], [100, 50], [100, 0.0003], [100, 0]],
]:

== detail [] None
{view, detail?: coarse | medium | fine} how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts: coarse, one poché and openings as their gaps; medium, compound layers with the lines between them and an opening's leaf, swing and glass; fine (the default), the layers' patterns and a floor's surface pattern too. Without `detail` it only says what the view has

== inspect [] None
{} levels, element counts, types, warnings and undo history

== render [] None
{family?, type?, mode?: 3d|plan|elevation, wall_thickness?, view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, a sheet's number, or {3D}, ceiling?, width?, height?, path?, azimuth?, elevation?, eye_elevation?} a family on its own with `family` — its `type` (the first by default) standing in a model of its own, in a wall `wall_thickness` mm thick (200) if it's a door's or a window's, nothing of this project's touched or left behind: `3d` (as seen from the south-east), `plan` (what its symbols draw) or `elevation` (front-on, as seen from the north), a PNG as `pngBase64` or at `path`. Without it: a level's floor plan (with `ceiling`, its reflected ceiling plan, looking up from 2300 mm), a section, an elevation, a sheet (at 5 px a paper mm), or the 3D view seen from `azimuth` degrees round from east (counter-clockwise) and `elevation` degrees up (by default from the south-east, 30° up), fitted; in perspective (see `perspective`) through its lens, and with `eye_elevation` from an eye that high (mm) looking at the same point, as a PNG (pngBase64), or written to a path: .png, .svg for a plan, .pdf for a sheet. A plan, section, elevation or sheet that could not draw something as asked (a fill pattern too dense for the view, more ink behind a region than is kept above it) says so in the reply's `notes`

== graphics [] None
{view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the phase the view shows (the project's last unless it says) and `phase_filter` how it shows each status of what's in it (see `phase`); `options` chooses the design option it shows of a set (the set's primary unless it says; see `option`); `layers` the layers of each CAD drawing it hides, by the drawing's name (null shows them all again)

== section_box [] None
{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again

== measure ['ME'] None
{from: [x, y], to: [x, y]} what a ruler laid between two points reads (mm): its `length`, its parts `dx` and `dy`, and its `angle` in degrees from east, counter-clockwise; it changes nothing

USAGE:
  bimcraft-cli run [FILE] [--sample | --highrise] [--cmd 'ID {json}']… [--script FILE]… [--save PATH]…

"""Profile corner merging: the number of corners kept (from the triangle count) and the first
triangle (top cap) the original writes. python3 dedupe4.py"""
import sys, os, re, json, subprocess, tempfile, shutil
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'


def probe(profile):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='dd', dir='/tmp/family-agent')
    fam = {"name": "Q", "types": {"T": {}}, "forms": [{"profile": profile, "to": 10}]}
    subprocess.run([ORIG, 'run', '--cmd', 'family ' + json.dumps(fam), '--cmd', 'component {"family":"Q","at":[0,0]}', '--save', 'x.ifc'], cwd=d, capture_output=True)
    text = open(os.path.join(d, 'x.ifc')).read()
    shutil.rmtree(d)
    pts = re.findall(r"\(([-\d.E]+),([-\d.E]+),([-\d.E]+)\)", re.search(r"IFCCARTESIANPOINTLIST3D\((\(.*?\))\);", text).group(1))
    tris = re.findall(r"\((\d+),(\d+),(\d+)\)", re.search(r"IFCTRIANGULATEDFACESET\(#\d+,\$,\.T\.,(\(.*?\)),\$\);", text).group(1))
    n = (len(tris) + 4) // 4
    t0 = [tuple(float(c) for c in pts[int(i) - 1][:2]) for i in tris[0]]
    return n, t0


if __name__ == '__main__':
    for prof in json.loads(sys.argv[1]):
        print(prof, '->', probe(prof))

`power-unbalanced` connector's `load_va` may be a list, one load for each pole, and a single number is shared out evenly.
`Family::check` refuses a family of two `power` connectors, a kind and system that don't go together, poles, voltage, power factor
or load out of range for any type, and a load on a switch. A connector is a part (`HasPart`: an id and a GUID, kept by place
while the family is edited), and a family without any reads and places as it always did. A component's `element_json` carries
`connectors` worked out for its type (`Family::connector_values`: `load_va` in all, `load_va_by_phase`), which a circuit will sum;
there are no circuits, panels or fitting-to-pipe joins yet, and the connector holds no position. `Model::warnings` (shown by
`inspect`; `Model::check` stays an error only) says which lighting, outlet or switch family in use holds no connector, so its devices
count as zero load. IFC writes each device with a connector `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` (`NumberOfPoles`, and for a power
connector `PowerFactor` and `RatedVoltage`) and `BIMCraft_Connector` (`System`, `Classification`, `LoadVA`, `LoadVAPhase1`…); IFC
import doesn't read them back.
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it
and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time
of many rooms; moved, rotated or mirrored, its boundary goes with it, and only a bounded room can be frozen. Walls and columns (and structural columns) bound
rooms while their Room Bounding is on (`Wall::room_bounding`, `Column::room_bounding`, on unless set; `Model::room_bounding`,
`bounding_columns`, `room_lines`): a column's outline either way rooms are measured, a free one an island. A wall with it off
still bounds floors and roofs picked by their walls. Walls and columns bound a level's rooms where its
Computation Height (`Level::computation_height`, 1200 mm unless set) cuts them; room separation lines bound them whatever
it is. Two rooms can't share a space (`Model::room_bound`, `Unbound`): the one placed first (the lower id) keeps it, the
other is unbounded, and `room` and `inspect` warn. A room can be placed where nothing encloses it: unbounded, it covers a
`UNBOUNDED_ROOM` square round its point (`Model::room_outline`), as Revit's. A plan labels it NOT ENCLOSED, or REDUNDANT where another
room has its space. Its reference, a cross from the point it was placed at out along the diagonals to its boundary
(`geom::ray_hit`), drawn as the room's own lines (a click on it picks the room), is the subcategory `roomreference` under
Rooms, off unless shown (`graphics {show: ["roomreference"]}`), beside `roomseparator`, the separation lines.
Subcategories are general (`graphics::SUBCATEGORIES`: a key, its category, a name, whether it is off unless shown):
a view holds them as categories, with `Override::shown` for the ones off unless shown, `Graphics::hides` answers for
them (a category hidden hides its subcategories), and Visibility/Graphics folds them under their category. In a 3D
view rooms are off until shown (`graphics::OFF_IN_3D`, `Graphics::shows_in_3d`; `graphics {view: "{3D}", show: [rooms]}`,
button runs it); a family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing and an edited family is
never overwritten (`loaded` and `kept` in the reply). Each family has one type, `Standard`, no forms, and the symbols of
`crates/core/data/arei-symbols.json`, in the family `symbols` schema (mm, y up, the origin at the symbol's own origin): a
switch is in category `switch`, a socket in `outlet`, a data socket in `dataoutlet`, a light point or luminaire in `lighting`
and everything else (appliances, consumers, sources, domotics, protection) in `generic`, so the Device and Lighting Fixture
tools list their own kinds and the others are placed with the Component tool. They have no connectors, loads or 3D forms: they
are plan symbols only for now, and a family without a connector raises no warning in `inspect`.

| Command | Params | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `edit_shape` | `{id, points?: [{at, z, id?}], lines?: [{a, b, id?}], absolute?}` | Replaces the shape all at once, as `edit_boundary` does a sketch: what is sent back with an `id` keeps it. Without `points` or `lines`, it replies with the shape as it is: the points, including the corners with their heights; the split lines; the generated creases; and the pieces with their planes. That reply is what agents need to reason about falls. |
| `add_point` | `{id, at, z?, absolute?}` | One point; `z` defaults to the top's height there now (0 relative). |
| `add_split_line` | `{id, a, b}` | One line; loose ends become points at the current height. |
| `reset_shape` | `{id}` | Removes the shape. |
| `type` (floor, roof) | layers take `variable: true` | At most one per type; not on walls or ceilings. |
| `modify` (floor) | unchanged | Rejects `slope` or `arrow` on a shaped floor, with the reason (see Validation). |
| `falls` (phase 5) | `{id, drains: [[x, y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x, y], [x, y]], …]}` | Better than the established tools: sets point heights so water runs to the drains at no less than `fall` %, adding split lines along the valleys. Agents and architects describe a terrace this way, not point by point. |

Every reply lists the pieces' count and the lowest and highest point of the top. `inspect` on a floor already reports
`top: [lo, hi]` (`commands.rs:2122`); it must take the shape's points into account, not only the outline's.

New rules, each with an error that says what to fix:

- A point outside the outline, or inside an opening: "point 100231 at (12500, 3400) is outside floor 100190: move it inside, or delete it".
- A split line that crosses another, crosses an opening, or leaves the outline (reuse `sketch::solve`'s problem kinds and wording).
- A split line end that is neither a point nor an outline corner.
- Two points within 1 mm of each other.
